title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:

title: The Longest Transaction in Your Low-Code Platform Is the One Nobody Designed
description:
The first message was three words long: "Saving is frozen."

It came from a production planner at a components manufacturer, forwarded by her IT lead with no commentary. She had opened a work order, changed one quantity, and pressed save. The button had been spinning for eleven minutes. She tried it three times, then stopped, because the second attempt made her nervous.

By the time we got on a call, two things were true. Her save had not failed — it was still running. And nobody else in the plant could edit that work order, or the four records downstream of it. The system was not down. It was busy in a way that looked exactly like being down.

The cause took an afternoon to find and four seconds to explain. The work order's automation recalculated a bill of materials, looping over every component line and calling a partner API for current pricing. Nine hundred lines, roughly three seconds per call. Forty-five minutes of work, wrapped in a single database transaction, holding locks the whole time, because of a boundary nobody had ever drawn.

The transaction is bigger than the drawing

In our platform, the transaction boundary is not something the builder chooses.

An automation is one transaction. All of it. The documentation is unambiguous — a complete automation runs inside a single transaction, and if anything throws, or the flow is stopped, the whole thing rolls back. It goes further: the before-create event, the creation, and the after-create event of a single step are also one transaction, so aborting anywhere in that chain discards the creation itself. The listener model matches. Listeners — the rules that fire on record creation, on data change, on user action — execute in the same transaction as the thing that triggered them. A listener that throws rolls back the form submission that woke it up.

None of that is wrong. Atomicity is not a bug. But look at what it means in a visual builder. The person who drew that recalculation was drawing logic — sequence, branches, API responses. They were not drawing a transaction, and nothing on the canvas told them they were. The transaction is inferred from the shape of a graph they built for an entirely different reason.

The graph is precise. The transaction is a side effect.

The number nobody computes

Our own documentation contains the clearest illustration of this failure I have read, and it is offered as friendly advice.

The example is two data tables, two thousand records each, and a nested loop with an HTTP request at the innermost level. Average request time: three seconds. The documentation does the arithmetic honestly — two thousand times two thousand times three seconds is more than thirty hours — then says what you would expect, that a flow like this running frequently is a disaster for the system, and recommends estimating execution time before you build.

That paragraph is correct and I am glad it exists. It is also a confession. A thirty-hour transaction is not something the platform prevented. It is something the platform documented. The canvas renders a nested loop as a modest little box, the same size as a single API call. There is no meter, no warning, no estimate, no ceiling. We outsourced the work of noticing to the person with the least information about what it costs.

There is a transaction timeout in the API — thirty seconds, if you set it — but you can only set it from script. Which brings us to the real problem.

Everything that governs a transaction lives where the builder cannot see

Our script API for transactions is more complete than I remembered. Seven propagation modes, including nested and requires-new. Isolation levels from read-uncommitted up to serializable. A timeout. A read-only flag. Transaction synchronizations — hooks that fire before commit, after commit, after completion — exactly the mechanism you would use to send a notification after the data is safe rather than inside the lock.

There is even a name for the transaction, and the documentation explains its purpose: a name helps developers identify and track transactions in logs and monitoring tools.

Count how many transactions in a real customer application have names. Approximately none. Not because the feature is missing, but because there is no moment in the visual workflow where a transaction becomes a thing a person is asked to think about. It is a constructor you must know exists before you can name it, in a document you only read after something has already gone wrong.

The one hint that reliably reaches builders is a tip telling them to paste three lines of script if they want a step to open a new transaction — a curious way to teach someone that they were inside one all along.

The scheduler has one lane, and it deletes the future

Transactions do not only come from user actions. They come from scheduled work, and the scheduling model has the same shape of problem.

Scheduled tasks fire at one-minute precision, and at any given moment exactly one is running. Consider a job configured every five minutes that takes six to finish. The run scheduled for minute five does not queue and does not wait. It is cancelled. A slow job does not merely finish late; it quietly accumulates runs that never happened. And after an outage, the misfire policy offers two choices: execute everything that was missed, or throw all of it away. Neither answers the question, which is whether a job that runs long should be allowed to run long, run chunked, or run at all.

The first time I watched a nightly reconciliation silently lose two cycles because one cycle was slow, I stopped thinking of schedules as triggers and started thinking of them as a single-lane road with no shoulders.

Termination is a person, and it is a destructive act

The runtime page does try. It lists what is executing right now — scripts, scheduled jobs, automations, API calls — and lets you terminate one by hand. The documentation names the reasons you would need to. Long-running tasks. Slow execution. Infinite loops. Database deadlocks.

Read that list again as a design document. Those are the system's own admitted failure modes, and the remedy for all four is a human noticing and clicking a button. Now consider what the button does. It does not pause and it does not checkpoint. It rolls back — which can mean discarding forty-five minutes of calculation, plus every record a colleague created inside a listener that shared the transaction, plus the save the user believed had succeeded.

A platform whose only answer to "this is taking too long" is "have someone destroy it" has not finished designing the feature.

Abort is the only word we gave you for no

Because listeners share the trigger's transaction, the way you implement a business rule at the data layer is to abort. Rule violated, flow stopped, everything rolls back. There is no vocabulary for reject this field but keep the record, no partial acceptance. The state machine has two states: it all happened, or none of it did. Builders who need a third state invent it outside the platform, and the validation they were asked to implement quietly becomes a reliability hazard instead of a guardrail.

And when a script reaches across to an external ERP over a raw JDBC connection, holds it in manual-commit mode, writes to both systems, and commits once — there is no coordinator. Two databases, one commit call, no two-phase protocol. The transaction that spans two systems is the most optimistic object in the building.

The uncomfortable conclusion

Every other finite resource here has a visible number. Storage is gigabytes. Tables have row counts. Usage points are metered and show up on an invoice. Customers can see the ceiling and argue about where it should be.

Transaction duration has no number at all, because on the canvas a transaction is not a thing that exists. It is a consequence of a diagram. So the most expensive decision in the system — how long we hold a lock on your data, and therefore how many other people are standing behind you — is a decision nobody is ever asked to make.

We moved application development up the stack, into a canvas a process analyst can read. Transactions stayed down in milliseconds and isolation levels and lock waits. We never built the bridge.

Which is why "why is saving frozen?" took an afternoon to answer out of pieces that were all in the documentation. The platform knew.

The most expensive thing in a low-code platform is not a feature you chose not to build. It is a duration you never knew you were choosing.

title: AWS Agent Registry now supports custom metadata for registry records
description:
AWS Agent Registry is the centralized, governed catalog for agents, MCP servers, agent skills, gateways, and custom resources within your organization. As organizations scale to hundreds of such resources, a name and description alone are insufficient for effective governance and discovery. Custom metadata lets you extend every registry record with your organization's own structured fields, so both people and automated systems can find and govern resources consistently.

With custom metadata, publishers can record fields like team ownership, data classification, or review status directly on each registry record. You define a schema once per registry with common attributes, then extend it with type-specific fields — such as a model family for agent records. Each field supports free text, a URL, a Boolean, or a choice from a list of allowed values, and the registry validates required fields and values on every record creation or update. You can then filter search results on any custom metadata field from the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, the AWS SDKs, or the registry's MCP endpoint.

Custom metadata is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland).

To learn more, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation. For detailed setup guidance, see Define a custom metadata schema and Set custom metadata values on a record.

title: tuning tokio thread pool to cut latency spikes in high‑throughput services
description:
in a recent microservice that ingests 200k requests /s, we saw occasional latency outliers up to 200 ms while the 99th‑percentile stayed under 5 ms. the spike source turned out to be the tokio runtime's default thread‑pool configuration, which silently oversubscribes the CPU and induces cache line contention.

The Bottleneck

tokio builds a work‑stealing scheduler on top of a fixed number of worker threads. by default it uses the number of logical cores, which on a hyper‑threaded 8‑core box means 16 workers. each worker pulls tasks from a shared deque; when many short tasks compete, the deque's head pointer is updated concurrently, causing false sharing on the cache line that holds the queue metadata. the result is a series of cache‑miss stalls that amplify latency under load.

A Minimal Fix

pinning the runtime to a core‑count that matches physical cores and padding the deque structures eliminates the false sharing. the code below shows a tuned builder that also raises the stack size to avoid guard‑page faults when deep recursion occurs.

use tokio::runtime::{Builder, Runtime};

let rt: Runtime = Builder::new_multi_thread()
    .worker_threads(8)               // match physical cores, not logical
    .max_blocking_threads(32)        // bounded blocking pool
    .thread_stack_size(2 * 1024 * 1024) // 2 MiB stacks for heavy recursion
    .enable_all()
    .build()
    .expect("failed to build runtime");

The runtime now creates exactly eight workers; each worker’s local queue resides in its own cache line because the scheduler pads the queue header to a full 64‑byte line. this reduces inter‑worker cache traffic and brings the 99th‑percentile back to sub‑5 ms even under sustained peak load.

Trade‑offs & Edge Cases

  • More workers → higher parallelism but also more context switches and larger total stack memory (8 workers × 2 MiB ≈ 16 MiB). on memory‑constrained containers this can push the RSS close to limits and trigger OOM.
  • Increasing max_blocking_threads helps when legacy blocking I/O is unavoidable, yet each extra thread adds a kernel scheduler overhead that can negate the latency gains.
  • Thread affinity: on Linux you can bind each worker to a distinct physical core via taskset or numactl. without it, the OS may migrate workers across cores, re‑introducing cache line bounce.
  • Hyper‑threading: keeping workers equal to physical cores avoids the “two‑threads‑per‑core” contention, but if your workload is I/O bound you might benefit from the extra logical threads; profiling is the only way to decide.

When It Still Fails

if latency spikes persist, look for hidden blocking calls inside async tasks (e.g., std::fs::read_to_string). such calls fall back to the blocking pool, which can starve the worker pool if max_blocking_threads is too low. also verify that the executor’s yield_now is used in long loops to give other workers a chance to steal work.

how do you balance thread‑pool size, stack allocation, and cache‑line padding in your high‑throughput async services? share the configuration that gave you the most stable latency curve.

title: Writing tests in python?
description:
from colorama import init, Fore
from duration import *

def print_pass(the_data, i):
print(f'{Fore.GREEN}Test {i} with {the_data} passed')

def print_fail(the_data, i):
print(f'''{Fore.RED}*** Test {i} with {the_data} failed.''')

def print_tests():
_test_default = Duration(60)
_test_minutes = Duration(10, "m")
_test_hours = Duration(2, "h")
_test_sec = Duration(120, "s")

print('''

Test #1 - simple declarations
-----------------------------''')
test_objects = (
_test_default,
_test_minutes,
_test_hours,
_test_sec
)

test_print_out = (
    "60.00 s",
    "600.00 s",
    "7200.00 s",
    "120.00 s"
)

test_repr_out = (
    "Duration(60.00, 's')",
    "Duration(10.00, 'm')",
    "Duration(2.00, 'h')",
    "Duration(120.00, 's')"
)

for i, test_obj in enumerate(test_objects):
    try:
        assert str(test_obj) == test_print_out[i], f'Expected {test_print_out[i]} received {str(test_obj)}'
        print_pass(f'print of {test_obj}', i+1)
        assert repr(test_obj) == test_repr_out[i], f'Expected {test_repr_out[i]} received {repr(test_obj)}'
        print_pass(f'repr of {repr(test_obj)}', i+1)

    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, i+1)
        continue

def add_tests():
print('''

Test #2 - Addition
------------------''')
_test_default = Duration(60)
_test_minutes = Duration(5, "m")
_test_hours = Duration(1, "h")
_test_list = [Duration(10), Duration(2, 'm'), Duration(1, 'h')]
_test_inc = Duration(60)

test_objects = (
    _test_default + _test_minutes,
    _test_default + 30,
    sum(_test_list),
    15 + _test_minutes
)

test_add_out = (
    "Duration(360.00, 's')",
    "Duration(90.00, 's')",
    "Duration(3730.00, 's')",
    "Duration(5.25, 'm')"
)

for i, test_obj in enumerate(test_objects):
    try:
        assert repr(test_obj) == test_add_out[i], f'Expected {test_add_out[i]} received {repr(test_obj)}'
        print_pass(f'print of {repr(test_obj)}', i+1)

    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, i+1)
        continue

_test_inc += 30
try:
    assert repr(_test_inc) == "Duration(90.00, 's')", f'Expected Duration(90.00, s) received {repr(_test_inc)}'
    print_pass(f'Incremental test of {repr(_test_inc)}', 1)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, 1)

def sub_tests():
print('''

Test #3 - Test all subtraction cases
------------------------------------''')
_test_default = Duration(120)
_test_minutes = Duration(1, "m")
_test_dec = Duration(100)

test_objects = (
    _test_default - _test_minutes,
    _test_default - 30
)

test_sub_out = (
    "Duration(60.00, 's')",
    "Duration(90.00, 's')"
)

try:
    reverse_sub = 200 - Duration(60, "s")
    assert repr(reverse_sub) == "Duration(140.00, 's')", \
        f"Expected Duration(140.00, 's') received {repr(reverse_sub)}"
    print_pass(f'reverse subtraction: {repr(reverse_sub)}', 6)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, 6)

for i, test_obj in enumerate(test_objects):
    try:
        assert repr(test_obj) == test_sub_out[i], f'Expected {test_sub_out[i]} received {repr(test_obj)}'
        print_pass(f'print of {repr(test_obj)}', i+1)

    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, i+1)
        continue

_test_dec -= 40
try:
    assert repr(_test_dec) == "Duration(60.00, 's')", f'Expected Duration(60.00, s) received {repr(_test_dec)}'
    print_pass(f'Decremental test of {repr(_test_dec)}', 1)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, 1)

def comp_tests():
print('''

Test #4 - Test comparisons between Duration objects
--------------------------''')

_test_comp1 = Duration(60)
_test_comp2 = Duration(1, "m")
_test_comp7 = Duration(100)
_test_comp8 = Duration(101)

count = 1
try:
    assert _test_comp1 == _test_comp2, f'Equality tested failed for {repr(_test_comp1)} and {repr(_test_comp2)}'
    print_pass(f'comparison: {repr(_test_comp1)} = {repr(_test_comp2)} ', count)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, count)

count += 1
try:
    assert not (_test_comp7 > _test_comp8), f'Greater than test failed for {repr(_test_comp7)} and {repr(_test_comp8)}'
    print_pass(f'comparison: {repr(_test_comp7)} not > {repr(_test_comp8)} ', count)
    assert _test_comp7 < _test_comp8, f'Less than test failed for {repr(_test_comp7)} and {repr(_test_comp8)}'
    print_pass(f'comparison: {repr(_test_comp7)} < {repr(_test_comp8)} ', count)
except AssertionError as test_data:
    print_fail(test_data, count)

def exception_tests():
print('''

Test #5 - Test Exceptions
-------------------------''')
count = 1
try:
Duration("abc")
print_fail(f'Value error not thrown when value is string', count)
except ValueError as msg:
try:
assert str(msg) == "Value must be a number", f'Value error does not have correct message. Received {msg}'
print_pass(f'Value error thrown with message: {msg} as expected', count)
except AssertionError as test_data:
print_fail(test_data, count)
count += 1

try:
    Duration(-10)
    print_fail(f'Less than zero exception not thrown when value is negative', count)
except DurationLessThanZeroException as msg:
    try:
        assert str(msg) == "Duration cannot be negative", f'Exception does not have correct message. Received {msg}'
        print_pass(f'Negative-value error thrown with message: {msg} as expected', count)
    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, count)

count += 1
try:
    Duration(10, "abc")
    print_fail(f'Incorrect unit exception not thrown', count)
except TimeUnitNotDefinedException as msg:
    try:
        assert str(msg) == "Unit cannot be used", f'Exception does not have correct message. Received {msg}'
        print_pass(f'Unit error thrown with message: {msg} as expected', count)
    except AssertionError as test_data:
        print_fail(test_data, count)

if name == "main":
init(autoreset=True)
print_tests()
add_tests()
sub_tests()
comp_tests()
exception_tests()

title: Why client SDK generation belongs in the open
description: Google has partnered with Speakeasy to open-source their OpenAPI code generation suite under the AGPLv3 license, a strategic move prompted by the sudden shutdown of Google's previous proprietary SDK provider. The newly open-sourced suite equips developers with deterministic, multi-language SDK generators that natively support strict typing and SSE streaming, alongside tools for compiling agent-native CLIs and documentation MCP servers. Engineering teams can now safely integrate this robust tooling directly into their CI pipelines to automatically generate reliable client libraries for their own APIs, all while retaining complete licensing control over the output code.

title: Gemini 3.8 text-to-speech models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS from Google are now available on AI Gateway.

Both models generate speech from text in more than 100 languages and support long-form narration, control over delivery, and two-speaker dialogue.

  • google/gemini-3.8-flash-tts is optimized for expressive voice generation and custom character design, with controls for acting cues, pacing, accents, and conversational reactions.

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.12

Feature

Cold transfers auto-resume

Feature

For more information, see Get network diagnostic information.

Feature

Agent desktop: Open from the CCaaS portal

For more information, see Open the agent desktop.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where SmartAction statuses were incorrectly marked as "failed" when a call ended before a photo or video upload completed.

  • Fixed an issue where loading the outbound numbers list timed out or caused significant delays for organizations with large teams and custom roles.

  • Fixed an issue where estimated wait times of less than one minute were incorrectly rounded down to zero, preventing the system from accurately triggering over-capacity actions.

  • Fixed an issue where sudden spikes in call volume bypassed a team's capacity protections and reduced the team's agent availability to below configured minimums.

  • Fixed an issue where nested object values in custom data were incorrectly displayed as [object Object] in the agent desktop session data feed.

  • Fixed an agent desktop issue where the navigation bar in the Previous Interactions page of the call adapter was overlapped by summary text and didn't stay fixed while scrolling.

  • Fixed an issue where answered voice calls triggered a second, unrequested callback after the end-user hung up.

  • Fixed an issue where intermittent IMAP connection rejections caused email fetch workers to enter an extended backoff loop, resulting in several hours of mailbox downtime.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound voice call recordings weren't exported to external storage when a virtual agent escalation was deflected to voicemail due to over-capacity.

  • Fixed an issue where manual wrap-up sessions were incorrectly attributed to the most recent call in the Agent Activity Timeline and in raw data exports, even when the wrap-up was unrelated to that call.

  • Fixed an issue where the "agent leg" of a call connection stalled in a connecting state for the full timeout duration before failing silently and moving the agent to an available status.

  • Fixed an issue where custom form responses weren't exported to external storage for instances without an external CRM integration.

  • Fixed an issue where a queue name saved in the SLA thresholds for queues dialog didn't persist after saving.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice calls triggered a session error during wrap-up.

  • Fixed an issue during high-capacity redirections where voicemails weren't saved.

  • Fixed an issue where completed call transfers generated duplicate queue duration records, leading to inflated reporting for queue volume and SLA metrics.

  • Fixed an agent desktop issue where the sentiment banner in the call adapter didn't immediately appear at the start of a call.

  • Fixed an issue where saving the Upload audio recording for Language Selection option of the Languages dialog didn't persist and switched to Text-to-speech.

  • Fixed an issue where inefficient database queries caused high CPU utilization and performance degradation across all communication channels.

  • Fixed an issue where transient connection errors during Twilio ICE token fetching caused agent call setup to fail or take longer to connect.

  • Fixed an issue where temporary connection drops during chat webhook delivery caused unnecessary delays.

  • Fixed an issue where work time and wait time durations overlapped in reporting metrics.

  • Fixed an issue where the agent adapter call history incorrectly displayed English queue names for French-Canadian calls.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were assigned calls from secondary queues even when their primary queue fell below the minimum availability threshold.

  • Fixed an issue where canceled virtual-agent-to-human escalations incorrectly reported negative queue durations and inaccurate SLA metrics in chat session data and reports.

  • Fixed an issue where creating or updating queues failed and returned a timeout error.

  • Fixed an agent desktop issue where an outbound call canceled by an agent while connecting was recorded as an unknown failure instead of an agent cancellation.

  • Fixed an issue where clicking the rewind and forward buttons on the voicemail page of the call adapter restarted the voicemail from the beginning.

  • Fixed an agent desktop issue where the chat adapter displayed a loading progress indicator instead of the chat transcript when a chat session was assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where a disposition prompt didn't appear in the call adapter after a disconnected call, even when mandatory disposition was configured.

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist real-time transcription didn't start on Vonage BYOC calls.

  • Fixed an issue where changes made outside of browser-originated HTTP requests (such as from API clients or background jobs) failed to generate audit log records.

  • Fixed an issue where over-capacity phone deflection didn't activate for direct agent calls, resulting in an error message or callers waiting indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where transient network connection failures during call and chat DAP lookups caused inbound calls to route to default queues or prevented chat sessions from starting.

  • Fixed a web SDK issue where static, non-interactive text within the chat widget incorrectly received keyboard focus, disrupting the navigation flow for keyboard and screen reader users.

  • Fixed an issue where temporary asset errors during deployments were cached by the CDN, leading to web SDK initialization failures.

  • Fixed an agent desktop issue where incomplete configuration settings prevented call control buttons from updating or rendering properly.

  • Fixed an issue where the audio for an over-capacity deflection played in the source queue's language instead of the destination queue's language following a cross-language transfer.

  • Fixed an issue where waiting chats weren't immediately offered to available agents who became eligible for a queue through a team membership update or direct queue assignment.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

Agent Substrate on GKE is now available for evaluation and non-production use. Production support is offered on an allowlist basis under a limited GA program.

Agent Substrate runs agentic workloads at scale on GKE clusters. To reduce resource usage, Agent Substrate suspends idle agents and takes a snapshot of the agent's active memory (RAM) and local files. When a suspended agent is triggered, the system restores the agent's state onto an available sandbox with sub-second latency.

Agent Substrate improves on the capabilities of Agent Sandbox by bypassing the bottlenecks of the standard Kubernetes control plane to run significantly more concurrent agents per machine.

For more information, see About GKE Substrate.

Effective January 25, 2027, write permissions will be removed from the chronicle.readonly OAuth scope, restricting it strictly to read operations. You can continue using chronicle.readonly for read operations. Make sure you update any workflows performing write operations to use the chronicle OAuth scope.

  • Element key uniqueness validation option: You can configure the validate_element_key_uniqueness option in the property graph OPTIONS clause to control whether Spanner Graph validates element key uniqueness at schema creation time.

title: Freelancing from Pakistan as a Web Developer in 2026: The No-Fluff Playbook
description:
Pakistani freelancers pulled in a record $1.76 billion in foreign exchange
during FY26, up 78% from the year before, with IT freelancers contributing
$1.16 billion of it. Nearly three million Pakistanis now freelance, making
the country the world's fourth-largest freelance market. This post is the
no-fluff version of how a web developer actually gets into that number:
which platform to pick, what the fees really cost, how the 0.25% tax works,
how to get paid, and what to do in your first 90 days.

The short answer

Start freelancing as a web developer from Pakistan in 2026 by picking one
niche (Next.js builds, e-commerce, or AI integrations), building two or three
portfolio projects that look like paid work, opening on Fiverr (free to start,
20% commission) or Upwork (variable 0-15% fee, ~10% typical, plus $0.15
Connects per bid), registering with PSEB to qualify for the 0.25% final tax
rate on IT export income, and receiving payments through Payoneer or Wise.
Expect your first client in 30-90 days of daily effort.

Why 2026 is genuinely a good year to start

Most "start freelancing" guides lean on vibes. The State Bank of Pakistan
numbers do not need any:

  • $1.76B freelance earnings in FY26 (State Bank of Pakistan data, reported by Dawn, The News, TechJuice, July 2026)
  • 78% year-on-year growth (Up from $984 million in FY25 - SBP figures)
  • ~3M freelancers in Pakistan (Industry estimates (PAFLA) - fourth-largest freelance workforce in the world)

The breakdown matters more than the headline. IT freelancers generated $1.16
billion (up 49%), while non-IT freelance earnings tripled to $592 million -
writing, design, marketing, and virtual assistance. Two readings of that: the
demand for technical work keeps compounding, and clients are buying wider
skill bundles than before. A web developer who can also ship the landing
page, wire up the analytics, and write the launch copy sells a bigger ticket
than one who ships code alone.

Where these numbers come from
Freelance remittance figures are from State Bank of Pakistan data released
in July 2026 and reported by Dawn, The News, Pakistan Today, TechJuice,
and ProPakistani. The 0.25% tax extension comes from coverage of the
Finance Act 2026 by Business Recorder, TechX, and PhoneWorld. Platform fee
figures are 2026 published rates; confirm the current number on each
platform's official fee page before you quote it to yourself, because these
change without notice.

Pick your platform: the 2026 fee reality

Your platform choice is a tax on your income, so do the math before you fall
in love with anyone's marketing. Here is what each major platform actually
costs a Pakistani web developer in 2026:

Platform Freelancer fee Bidding cost Best for
Fiverr Flat 20% on every order None (gig-based) Zero-capital starts, packaged services
Upwork Variable 0-15% per contract (most report ~10%) $0.15 per Connect, ~2-16 Connects per proposal Custom projects, long-term clients
Freelancer.com 10% (or $5 minimum) Free bids on plan tiers Contest-style and budget work
Toptal 0% to the freelancer Screening, not bidding Senior devs who can pass the vetting

Two practical conclusions. First, Fiverr's 20% is the highest headline rate
in the table, but it costs you nothing before you earn, which makes it the
only rational first platform when you are bootstrapping from zero. A $100
order nets you $80 from day one with no ad spend. Second, Upwork's effective
rate is lower than Fiverr's for most freelancers, but the Connects system
means you spend $3-5 per proposal with no guarantee of a reply. If you burn
through 50 Connects a week at $0.15 each with weak proposals, Upwork is a
hole you pour money into.

The right sequence for most Pakistani beginners: Fiverr first for the first
client and first reviews, Upwork second once you can afford to bid on ten
jobs a week, and direct clients third once you have a portfolio worth
showing off-platform. Never build your entire income on one platform - an
account flag, a fee change, or an algorithm shift can take 100% of your
revenue overnight.

The six things you need before your first client

Nothing on this list costs more than a few evenings. Every item you skip
becomes a delay later, so treat it as a checklist, not advice.

One niche, not five

"Web developer" is not a niche, it is a commodity listing. Pick one: Next.js
marketing sites, Shopify/WooCommerce builds, SaaS MVPs, or AI integrations
(chatbots, RAG, MCP tools). Your niche decides your gig titles, your
portfolio, and which jobs you bid on. Everything below compounds from this
choice.

Three portfolio projects that look like paid work

Build three projects in your niche as if a client paid for each one: real
brief, real deadlines, live deployment link, GitHub repo, and a short
case-study writeup explaining the problem and your decisions. Clients do not
read code on a first pass, they look at the live thing and the writeup.
Three strong projects beat ten tutorial clones every time.

One platform profile done properly

Profile photo (real face, decent light), headline with your niche and one
outcome ("Next.js sites that load in under 2s"), a description written for
buyers not recruiters, and your portfolio projects linked. On Fiverr, build
2-3 gigs with tiered packages (Basic/Standard/Premium). On Upwork, pick 10-15
skills that match your niche exactly. Generic profiles get generic results.

One payment rail, verified with a small withdrawal

Set up Payoneer or Wise (Elevate Pay is worth comparing as a
Pakistani-built option) before you need it, and run one small test
withdrawal to your local bank. Discovering your payout path is broken the
day a $500 client payment lands is a special kind of panic you only need
once. PayPal is still not functional in Pakistan, so do not plan around it.

PSEB registration on your 90-day list

Registration with the Pakistan Software Export Board is what qualifies your
IT and IT-enabled service export income for the 0.25% final tax rate under
Section 154A, instead of normal income-tax treatment. It is a government
portal process, not a lawyer's job. Do it once your income is real and
before filing season, not after.

A written proposal template, not a begging letter

Your template: one line naming the client's actual problem, two lines on
how you would solve it, one line of proof (a link), and the price. Custom
beats clever every time. Send 3-5 tailored proposals a day on Upwork or
answer every Fiverr inquiry within the hour. Volume of quality attempts is
the whole game at the start.

What web developers actually charge

Rate anxiety kills more freelancing careers than competition does. The
numbers below are indicative ranges seen across platforms for Pakistani
developers in 2026 - not guarantees, and your niche, reviews, and how well
you sell all move you up or down the band:

Service Starter range With reviews + niche
Landing page / marketing site $100-300 $500-1,500
Full website (Next.js / WordPress) $300-800 $1,000-3,000
E-commerce build $500-1,200 $1,500-5,000
SaaS MVP $1,000-2,500 $3,000-10,000+
Hourly dev work $15-30/hr $40-80/hr
AI integration / chatbot build $400-1,000 $1,500-4,000

Price for take-home, not for the platform
These are gross figures. Run every quote through your platform's cut before
you accept it: a $1,000 Fiverr order is $800 in your account, and a $1,000
Upwork contract at a 10% fee is $900 minus whatever Connects you spent
winning it. The section below works the math on a real example so you stop
doing it in your head mid-proposal.

The money math: what a $1,000 project leaves you

Concrete example, because fee percentages stay abstract until you lose real
money to them. You win a $1,000 fixed-price website build:

  • On Fiverr: 20% commission = $200 to the platform, $800 to you. No bidding cost, 14-day clearance hold before withdrawal.
  • On Upwork: ~10% service fee = ~$100 to the platform, ~$900 to you, minus Connects. Say you spent 12 Connects ($1.80) across two rounds of bidding to win it: you keep ~$898, minus withdrawal fees depending on your method.

Then the tax layer: if you are PSEB-registered and the income qualifies as
IT export proceeds under Section 154A, the 0.25% final tax on $900 is $2.25,
and that is the whole tax bill on that income. Without PSEB registration,
the same income can fall under normal tax treatment - a difference of
hundreds of dollars on a $1,000 project. This is why the paperwork section is
not bureaucratic decoration.

The lesson is not "Upwork always wins." It is that Fiverr's simplicity costs
about $100 per $1,000 project versus Upwork's cheaper-but-pay-to-bid model,
and that the tax setup dwarfs both. A freelancer who fixes their tax
registration earns more from a Fiverr order than one who ignores it earns on
Upwork.

The tax setup nobody explains properly

Pakistani freelancers get two pieces of tax news in 2026, one good and one
demanding attention. The good: the Finance Act 2026 extended the 0.25% final
tax rate on IT and IT-enabled service export income for PSEB-registered
exporters through June 30, 2029. It is a final tax - once it is deducted
from your export proceeds, you owe nothing more on that income.

The part that needs attention is qualification. The 0.25% rate applies to
export proceeds from computer software, IT, or IT-enabled services where the
exporter is registered with and certified by PSEB, received through proper
banking channels. Receiving money from a foreign client does not
automatically make every service PSEB-qualified, and non-filers face higher
withholding on top. Keep client invoices, bank records, and your PSEB
registration in one folder. Filing season runs on its own calendar - the
September 30 deadline catches first-timers every year.

Register with PSEB, get paid through banking channels, file your return.
Everything else about freelancer tax in Pakistan is detail around that sentence.

-- The one-sentence version

Getting paid: pick one rail and verify it

Three rails matter for Pakistan in 2026. Payoneer is the default most
platforms integrate with natively. Wise usually wins on exchange rates for
direct client transfers. Elevate Pay is the Pakistani-built option designed
for cheaper direct transfers and keeps your dollars in a foreign-currency
account with local withdrawals. Each has different fee structures and payout
speeds, and the cheapest rail for a $50 gig is not always the cheapest for a
$5,000 contract - that comparison deserves its own post, and it is coming.

For now, the rules: one primary rail plus one backup, a test withdrawal
before you need it, and never your entire balance sitting on a platform.
Withdraw on a schedule, keep payment screenshots with your invoices, and
remember every withdrawal is also your tax documentation.

Your first 90 days, week by week

Days 1-14: build the machine

Pick your niche, finish one portfolio project end-to-end with a live URL and
a writeup, set up your payment rail, and complete your platform profile.
No proposals yet. A half-built profile sending proposals is how beginners
burn their first 100 Connects for nothing.

Days 15-45: ship and propose daily

Finish portfolio projects two and three. Start sending 3-5 tailored
proposals a day on Upwork, or launch your Fiverr gigs and share them where
your buyers are (LinkedIn, relevant communities - not spam, answers). Target
small jobs first: clients hire beginners for $100-300 test projects, not
$5,000 builds.

Days 46-90: convert, deliver, repeat

Your goal is 3-5 completed jobs with 5-star reviews, not one big win. Over-
deliver on the first ones - fast communication, clean handoff, a short Loom
walkthrough. Each review multiplies your next proposal's reply rate. Start
your PSEB registration the week your second client pays.

The fluff version:

  • "Just create an Upwork profile and wait for clients!"
  • "Charge $5/hour to get started!"
  • "Taxes? Worry about that when you're rich."
  • One generic profile, copied proposals, rage-quitting at week six.

The version that works:

  • Niche down, build three projects that look like paid work.
  • Price at the starter band of your niche, raise every 5 reviews.
  • PSEB registration + banking channels + invoices from the second client.
  • Daily proposals, weekly shipping, 90 days of patience.

FAQ

How much can a Pakistani web developer earn from freelancing?
Ranges vary by niche, but Pakistani web developers on international platforms
commonly report $15-40/hour starting out and $50-150/hour with specialization
and reviews. In FY26, Pakistani freelancers earned a record $1.76 billion,
with IT freelancers contributing $1.16 billion, so the demand side is real -
your earnings depend on niche, positioning, and how consistently you ship.

Is Upwork or Fiverr better for beginners in Pakistan in 2026?
Fiverr costs nothing to start: no bidding fees, you build gig listings and
clients come to you, but you pay a flat 20% commission on every order. Upwork
charges a variable 0-15% fee per contract (most report around 10%) plus $0.15
Connects to bid, so it costs money before you earn. Start with Fiverr if you
have zero capital, add Upwork once you can afford to bid strategically.

Do I need PSEB registration to freelance legally from Pakistan?
You can start freelancing without it, but registering with the Pakistan
Software Export Board is what unlocks the 0.25% final tax rate on IT and
IT-enabled service export income under Section 154A. Without registration,
the reduced rate does not apply to you, so the tax difference is large enough
that registration should be on your 90-day list.

What is the freelancer tax rate in Pakistan in 2026?
For PSEB-registered IT and IT-enabled service exporters, the rate is 0.25%
final tax on eligible export proceeds received through banking channels,
extended by the Finance Act 2026 through June 30, 2029. Other export income
under Section 154A is taxed at 1%. The 0.25% rate is final - you owe nothing
more on that income.

How do Pakistani freelancers receive money from foreign clients?
The common rails are Payoneer, Wise, and Elevate Pay, with bank withdrawals
into local accounts. PayPal still does not work properly in Pakistan, so do
not plan around it. Pick one rail, verify it with a small withdrawal before a
big one, and keep client payments and personal spending separated for clean
tax records.

How long does it take to get your first freelancing client?
With daily effort - 3-5 quality proposals a day on Upwork or a few well-built
Fiverr gigs - most beginners land a first small project in 30-90 days. The
first client is the slowest because you have no reviews; after five completed
jobs with ratings, reply rates climb sharply. There is no shortcut here that
does not involve sending proposals and shipping work.

Tool What it does Link

Upwork Proposal-based marketplace for custom projects https://www.upwork.com
Payoneer Receive international payments, local bank withdrawal https://www.payoneer.com
Wise Multi-currency transfers, usually best exchange rates https://www.wise.com

title: Android 10's clipboard restriction and serverless phone-to-PC sync: building Clipboard+
description:
I'm a solo developer making small utility apps for Android and Windows. The one with the most users is Clipboard+, a clipboard history manager. Two problems shaped almost every design decision in it: Android 10's clipboard restriction and syncing between phone and PC without running a server. Here's how I handled both.

1. Since Android 10, background apps can't read the clipboard

From Android 10 (API 29), only the app that currently has input focus (or the default keyboard) can read the clipboard. The classic clipboard-manager design, a background service that saves every copy, simply stops working. There are workarounds through accessibility services or log permissions, but given Play policy and user trust I didn't want to go there.

So I changed the promise instead of fighting the platform:

  • No "auto-save" claim. I removed that wording from the store listing too.
  • Save every time the app legitimately gets focus: when the app opens, when you tap the floating panel, and when you use the home-screen widget. The floating panel is an overlay window that is normally FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE; on tap it briefly clears that flag to take focus, reads the clipboard, then gives focus back.
  • For saving without switching apps, there's an entry in the text selection menu (ACTION_PROCESS_TEXT). Select text anywhere, pick "Clipboard+", and it lands in the history.

You lose "everything you copy just piles up", but "the moment you open the panel to paste, the last thing you copied is saved too" covers most real use.

2. No sync server

Clipboards are full of passwords, addresses, account numbers and one-time codes. I didn't want any of that passing through my server, and as a one-person studio I didn't want to run one forever either.

So the storage is the user's own Google Drive:

  • The Android and Windows apps each connect to the user's Drive and sync through the hidden, app-only appDataFolder. It doesn't show up in the Drive UI, and the app can't see the user's other files. Sync uses the drive.appdata scope; backup files use drive.file, which only covers files the app created.
  • On Android I skipped the old Drive Android API: AuthorizationClient just gets an access token, and the app calls Drive REST v3 directly. Fewer dependencies, and the same API shape as the Windows side.
  • No server means no hosting cost, and I can honestly tell users "your data only lives in your own Drive".

3. Don't hold data hostage when people switch phones

Backup and restore started as paid features. Keeping someone's data locked when they change phones felt wrong, so backup file export/import and Drive restore are now free. Pro is ad removal, live phone-PC sync, unlimited image clips and the larger panel/widget.

Feedback welcome

  • Cases where something doesn't get saved (which app, which Android version)
  • Whether the "your own Drive, no server" setup feels trustworthy, or whether the permission screen makes it feel the opposite

I read every comment.

  • Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.codedac.clipboard
  • Windows (Microsoft Store): https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9N9SRKQV1R6D
  • More: https://codedac.com/apps/clipboard.html

description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

BigQuery

Feature

Feature

The gemini-embedding-2 model works well for embedding long strings, including multilingual and unstructured data. It supports a mix of text, images, audio, video, and PDF files. You can use this model in the AI.EMBED, AI.SIMILARITY, and AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING functions. This model is generally available.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

This feature is in Preview.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: Z3 machine types that have 8 to 44 vCPUs can use Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes to synchronously replicate data across two zones.

For more information, see About Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability.

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (260900) is available.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.12.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Hidden file scanning: Added the --include-hidden flag to cm find (or include_hidden under scan in config.yaml) to include hidden directories and files, such as .github/ and .config/, in vulnerability scans.
  • Larger file support: Raised the default file discovery size limit (max_file_size_kb) from 500 KB to 2 MiB so cm find no longer skips large source files. Existing configurations that use the previous 500 KB default are upgraded automatically, and --deep and --diff scans can now read beyond the inline preview of files larger than 64 KB.
  • Report output for every scan mode: cm find --output now writes the scan report for standard, --deep, --parallel, and --diff scans.
  • Scoped fixes: cm fix now prevents the agent from modifying CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configurations, build definitions, and repository configuration files that are outside the scope of the vulnerability being fixed.
  • Accurate session token usage: cm now reports the total token usage across all turns of a session, instead of only the final turn, so token counts in cm stats and session exports match billed usage.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed duplicate findings in cm report and cm stats, and stopped merging distinct vulnerability types reported on the same line.
    • Fixed database is locked errors during cm find --deep scans with multiple workers.
    • Reduced false positives by requiring a concrete, viable exploit before reporting a finding with high confidence.
    • Included sessions from cm find --deep and cm find --diff workers in cm stats.
    • Fixed cm verify resolving relative finding and exploit artifact paths against the current working directory instead of the project root.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Deprecated

Starting on July 1, 2026, Identity Service for GKE is deprecated in GKE version 1.36 and earlier. This feature is also unavailable in organizations that were created on or after July 1, 2025. GKE version 1.37 and later don't support Identity Service for GKE. Before you upgrade clusters to 1.37 and later, disable this feature and migrate to Workforce Identity Federation.

For more information, see Identity Service for GKE deprecation.

Feature

GKE support for using the c4-standard-* machine types (up to 192 vCPUs) as Confidential GKE Nodes with Intel TDX is generally available. For more information, see the following pages:

  • To use this feature with GKE , see Encrypt workload data in-use with Confidential GKE Nodes.
  • To learn more about the feature from Compute Engine, see Confidential VM overview.
  • To see supported configurations, including machine support, see Supported configurations and its "Machine types, CPUs, and zones" section.

Google SecOps

Feature

[Spotlight Feature] Terraform and client libraries for multiple features using Chronicle API

Terraform providers and Google Cloud client libraries are now available for several Google SecOps features using Chronicle API including Feeds, Parsers, Rules, Findings Refinements, Retrohunts, Dashboards, Data Tables, Watchlists, Custom Lists, Environments, Environment Groups, Data Export, SOAR Domains, and SOAR Networks. For more information, see Terraform reference.

Terraform providers enable programmatic provisioning and management of Google SecOps resources as code, while Client Libraries enable developers to build custom integrations and automate Google SecOps workflows in their preferred programming languages. For more information, see Client libraries.

Guest Environment

Feature

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following features:

  • The managed workload identity certificate refresher is now a locally bundled extension. For more information, see Managed workload identities overview.
  • The guest telemetry extension is updated to version 1.1 and polls every 15 minutes instead of every 24 hours. However, it will only send data to the API every 24 hours, unless it detects a change in the system since the previous poll. The extension supports the following capabilities:
    • Running a command as the user associated with a discovered process.
    • Configuring regular expressions to match against the version command output.

Fixed

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following fixes:

  • The NetworkManager setup now no longer reloads the primary NIC when it applies changes to the network configuration of secondary NICs, unless necessary.
  • If the core plugin successfully rolls back any configurations, then it force-reloads the configurations to make sure that the instance re-obtains DHCP leases for secondary NICs.
  • The core plugin now respects the address-manager configuration flag and the corresponding metadata attribute.
  • The extensions manager now ignores install and remove requests from ACS for the core plugin and locally bundled extensions.
  • The extensions manager no longer logs that there are no local plugins to install when it's installing local plugins.
  • The metadata script runner now respects the sysprep_specialize configuration flag.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Data products in Knowledge Catalog now support Looker (Google Cloud core) assets. You can package, govern, and share Looker (Google Cloud core) dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, Explores, and LookML projects, models, and views in a data product using Google Group mirroring and IAM access controls. This feature is generally available.

For more information, see About data products and Create data products.

Managed Service for Apache Spark

Change

Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark): Users may now specify short template names when creating a serverless session.

Network Intelligence Center

Feature

Flow Analyzer displays packet drops, allowing you to analyze packet loss in your traffic flows. For more information, see Display flows in packet drop mode.

Network Service Tiers

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier in Preview. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Virtual Private Cloud

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.
