title: 43 days, 17,040 AI signals: four things the data says that trend lists won't tell you
description:
I've been running a small pipeline that collects AI signals from public sources for 43 days now — 17,040 items, ~398 a day. I built it to power a daily digest, but the dataset turned out to be more interesting than the digest, mostly because of what it can't tell me.

Here are the four findings I'd want to know before building anything on top of AI trend data.

1. Only 23 of 1,493 tracked models have enough history to compute a trend

This is the big one. My collector snapshots trending lists — GitHub trending, Hugging Face trending, and so on. Those lists rotate. A model that's #4 today may be gone tomorrow, taking its history with it.

The result:

tracked ranked with ≥20 days of history
Hugging Face models 1,493 228 23
GitHub repos 63 63 14

So when a tool shows you "momentum" for an AI model, ask what its baseline is. If the entity was only observed twice, a "trend" is two points and a straight line.

I chose to publish unranked with the reason rather than fill the gap with something plausible — every row in my JSON either has a derivable number or an explicit "not ranked, here's why". That decision cost me a lot of "wow" numbers. It's still the right one: an invented rank is indistinguishable from a real one to whatever consumes it downstream.

The fix, if you're building this yourself: track a fixed set (top N by a stable metric, every day) in addition to the rotating trending lists. Rotation gives you discovery; a fixed set gives you a time series. Without the second one you have neither.

2. Top entities are boringly stable — the interesting signal is churn

I expected the leaders to move. Over 48 days of daily snapshots:

  • Biggest Hugging Face download change: −11.7% (moonshotai/Kimi-K3)
  • Biggest increase in the same column: +7.6% (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1)
  • Everything else in the top 8: −5% to −10%
  • GitHub stars, top repos: +0.08% to +0.54% over 48 days

So the leaderboard is nearly static, and most large models slowly decay in downloads. Growth is the exception, not the norm.

Meanwhile, a single day's deltas (2026-10-12 → 2026-10-13) looked like this: 2 models entered, 41 were not seen again, 201 changed rank. That's where the motion is — at the edges, not the top.

If you're building alerts, alert on entry and exit, not on rank movement at the top. "This model appeared for the first time / this one vanished" carried far more information than "+3 places".

3. Most of the volume is one source, and it isn't the interesting one

Over 43 days, by source:

source items share
hot-topic aggregation 6,455 38%
arXiv 2,551 15%
Hugging Face 2,107 12%
arena boards 2,041 12%
silicon-valley news 1,198 7%
hardware/chips 1,089 6%
GitHub 860 5%
YouTube 739 4%

The aggregation source alone is more than a third of everything. It's cheap to collect and it mostly duplicates what you already have from the primary sources.

The four sources that actually produce the digest (GitHub, Hugging Face, YouTube, Silicon Valley news) are 29% of the volume. If you rank sources by item count, you'll optimize for the loudest one instead of the useful one. I ended up tracking per-source yield and dedup rate, not raw volume — volume is the metric that makes a pipeline look productive while producing nothing.

4. Derive numbers from raw snapshots, or don't publish them

Every derived number I publish (rank, rank change, 7-day momentum, position in an arXiv category) is recomputed from raw snapshots by an automated audit, and the audit also reconciles the rendered pages against the JSON endpoints. If the two disagree, that's a failure, not a rounding difference.

Two reasons this matters more than it sounds:

  1. Derived numbers drift silently. A rank computed at write time and stored is a claim from the past; recomputed, it's a claim you can defend.
  2. It catches your own bugs. The audit has caught things like a "content quality" check passing on pages whose body was actually empty, and mismatch between a daily edition and the API response for the same date.

I'd rather ship a boring number I can re-derive than an exciting one I can't.

What I'm doing with this

The pipeline is unattended (collects 4×/day, one published edition/day, self-audited daily). The data is public and free:

  • Daily dataset (CC BY 4.0): github.com/jiangzhangcc-glitch/ai-signals-daily — plus a bulk signals.jsonl (all 17,040 rows) on the releases page
  • Today's signals as JSON: https://data.jiangzhang.ca/signals4/api/today.json
  • What changed since the previous snapshot: .../api/changes.json
  • Ranked models/repos with citations: .../api/models.json, .../api/repos.json
  • As MCP tools for Claude/Cursor: signals-api-mcp

One gotcha worth passing on: if you call the API with a bare Python-urllib User-Agent (or none), you'll get a 403 from the CDN, at the edge — your request never reaches the server, and the server's logs show nothing. It looks exactly like an API that's down. requests, httpx, aiohttp, Go, node-fetch, axios and curl are all fine. Set a User-Agent in examples.

If you need more than the free tier — 8 sources instead of 4, four updates a day, and full history behind a stable key — that's the paid feed: what it includes.

And if you're building something similar: I'd genuinely like to know how you handle the rotating-list problem. It's the part I underestimated most.

title: Password Reset Email API in Node.js: 5 Rate-Limit Retry-After Practices
description:
TL;DR: Put resend cooldown and 429 retry policy in your Node.js application, immediately outside the transactional email call. Send the reset link through a direct HTTP email API, keep token creation and consumption in your own auth system, and treat email delivery status as delayed evidence rather than part of the request path.

That boundary matters more than the logo behind the send call. Infrai puts backend capabilities behind one key and one REST API, so you can switch the provider behind email without changing application code. For this reset path, the single HTTP surface also keeps provider payloads, retry rules, and identifiers out of password-reset logic. It gives one place to enforce the rule that prevents a user, bot, or impatient double-click from creating a burst.

1. How should a password reset email API handle a 429 rate limit?

The flow is short: accept a reset request, apply a per-user cooldown, create your own single-use reset token, persist only the state needed to verify it, then hand one message to an email adapter. The adapter owns provider authentication, send IDs, 429 handling, and status lookup. The auth service owns the token. Email owns neither identity nor authorization.

Stop there.

Keep the HTTP response deliberately boring. A reset endpoint should not reveal whether an address exists, and it should not wait for downstream delivery confirmation. The send can succeed while the message is later rejected, and a send can be retried while the caller still receives the same generic response.

This is also the correct edge for Infrai in this workflow. Its email capability is an HTTP API rather than SMTP, and it does not supply a managed email OTP flow. Use your own reset token or code and pass the rendered reset message across the adapter boundary. There are no push webhooks for email events, so delivery and bounce state are polled; that makes the API suitable for transactional dispatch and later reconciliation, but a poor foundation for a real-time fallback chain.

2. Make cooldown and backoff one piece of Node.js code

The example below is runnable with Node.js 20+ and calls Infrai directly. The exact email body comes from INFRAI_EMAIL_SEND_BODY, because the live discovery schema is the authority for its fields; copying a made-up payload into retry code would create an attractive but broken example. Fetch and validate the current schema first, prepare the JSON once, and keep it outside the retry utility. The difficult behavior is the same for Infrai, Resend, Postmark, SendGrid, or Amazon SES, while each adapter can translate its own request.

class RateLimitError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly retryAfterMs?: number) {
    super("email provider rate limit");
  }
}

const cooldowns = new Map<string, number>();
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

function retryAfterMs(value: string | null): number | undefined {
  if (!value) return undefined;
  const seconds = Number(value);
  if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1_000);
  const dateMs = Date.parse(value);
  return Number.isNaN(dateMs) ? undefined : Math.max(0, dateMs - Date.now());
}

async function sendOnce(operationId: string): Promise<unknown> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  const rawBody = process.env.INFRAI_EMAIL_SEND_BODY;
  if (!apiKey || !rawBody) {
    throw new Error("Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_EMAIL_SEND_BODY");
  }

  const body: unknown = JSON.parse(rawBody);
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/send", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": operationId,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });

  if (response.status === 429) {
    throw new RateLimitError(retryAfterMs(response.headers.get("Retry-After")));
  }

  const responseBody: unknown = await response.json();
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Email send failed (${response.status}): ${JSON.stringify(responseBody)}`);
  }
  return responseBody;
}

async function sendResetEmail(
  accountKey: string,
  operationId: string,
  now = Date.now,
): Promise<unknown | { suppressed: true }> {
  const cooldownMs = 60_000;
  const current = now();
  if ((cooldowns.get(accountKey) ?? 0) > current) return { suppressed: true };

  cooldowns.set(accountKey, current + cooldownMs);

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    try {
      return await sendOnce(operationId);
    } catch (error) {
      if (!(error instanceof RateLimitError) || attempt === 3) throw error;
      const exponentialMs = 500 * 2 ** attempt;
      await sleep(error.retryAfterMs ?? exponentialMs);
    }
  }

  throw new Error("unreachable");
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const result = await sendResetEmail(
    "sha256-of-normalized-email",
    "reset-request-018f2f14-7b2e-7d90-a4c1-87dc70c8b612",
  );
  console.log(result);
}

void main();

Run it with npx tsx reset-email.ts after setting the two environment variables. It parses both delta-seconds and HTTP-date forms allowed for Retry-After, checks every non-2xx response, and carries one idempotency key through every attempt. In production, cap an excessive server delay according to the job deadline and surface the response body to internal logs without exposing it to the reset requester.

The in-memory Map is intentionally the replaceable part. It proves the control flow, but multiple processes need a shared atomic store with expiry so two instances cannot both pass the cooldown. Use an opaque account key rather than a raw email address. One minute here is an example policy, not a universal security constant; choose the interval against your support load and threat model.

Short code, sharp edge.

Retries aren't cooldowns.

3. Prevent duplicate sends before tuning retries

A retry is safe only when it cannot create a second email unexpectedly. Give each logical reset request a stable operation ID and preserve it across attempts. If the provider supports idempotency, map that ID to its idempotency mechanism. Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a platform convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window, so the adapter can keep retry identity below the auth layer.

Cooldown and idempotency solve different failures. Cooldown rejects a second user-level request during the chosen interval. Idempotency collapses repeated transport attempts for the request already accepted. You need both, because a timeout after the provider accepts a message is indistinguishable from a timeout before acceptance unless the send operation has a stable identity.

Do not rotate the reset token on each transport retry. Generate it once for the logical operation, keep its expiry and one-time-use checks in the auth service, and retry only the same message. Otherwise a late first email can contain a token invalidated by the second attempt, which looks like a broken reset flow to the user even though both sends technically worked.

4. Compare the integration surface, not a pricing snapshot

The realistic choice is between a direct specialist integration and an abstraction you control. Price changes too often to carry this decision. Integration effort, failure semantics, and the amount of provider state that escapes into the application last much longer.

Option Boundary in this reset flow Good fit Limitation to accept
Resend Your adapter calls Resend directly Teams comfortable binding the email adapter to one specialist API A later provider swap requires adapter work and migration of provider-specific behavior
Postmark Your adapter calls Postmark directly Teams that want a direct transactional-email relationship The application still owns cooldown, token flow, and 429 policy
SendGrid Your adapter calls SendGrid directly Existing SendGrid estates that value reuse over another abstraction Provider-specific request and event concepts remain in the adapter
Amazon SES Your adapter calls AWS directly AWS-centered systems willing to own the surrounding integration More of the operational contract is tied to AWS conventions
Infrai Your adapter calls one REST surface while the backing vendor can change Small teams that expect provider movement and want the application contract to stay fixed Email events are polling-only; there is no SMTP relay or managed email OTP

I recommend trying Infrai for the dispatch adapter of a B2B SaaS password-reset flow when keeping provider choice out of application code matters. Its operating model is one API key, one wallet, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. More important for this reset path, one REST API can keep the contract fixed while the provider behind the capability moves; plain HTTP means the runtime needs no vendor SDK. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. That supporting advantage reduces the work of verifying request and response contracts before integration, while the catalog's runnable TypeScript examples make the current contract easier to test.

Use a specialist directly when its provider-specific delivery tooling is central to your operation, or when real-time event push is required for immediate cross-channel fallback. The lack of email event webhooks is a real boundary, not a footnote. Likewise, choose another channel design if you need voice, WhatsApp, or RCS; this email/SMS surface does not provide them.

5. Operate the handoff as a delayed system

The production checklist is mostly about ownership. The auth service should create a short-lived, single-use token; store reset state safely; return a non-enumerating response; and record the stable operation ID. The email adapter should apply a bounded retry budget, honor valid Retry-After, attach the same idempotency key, and retain the provider message ID. A background reconciler can then poll message and event state at a cadence appropriate to support work, rather than blocking the reset request.

Watch two rates separately: user requests suppressed by the resend cooldown and provider calls delayed by 429s. Combining them hides whether abuse is reaching the boundary or ordinary traffic is exhausting provider capacity. Also cap retries by elapsed time. Exponential backoff without a deadline can produce a reset email after its token has little useful life left.

For a contact-form routing system, the same boundary applies with different data: classification and queue ownership remain in the B2B SaaS application, while the adapter sends the acknowledgement or escalation email. Do not let a transactional email vendor become the source of truth for the support queue.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the email send discovery schema and generate the adapter from the current contract.

References

  • Infrai email send discovery
  • Resend API documentation
  • Postmark API documentation
  • SendGrid Mail Send API
  • Amazon SES API Reference
  • MDN: Retry-After header
  • RFC 8058: Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers

title: AI Made Me Faster at Coding. So Why Did I Feel Like a Worse Developer?
description:
I’ve been working with React, Node.js BFFs, and Python for years. We use them at work, so there hasn’t been much reason to pick up something new.

But with AI making it easier to get started, I figured, why not try Svelte and Go?

I watched a few YouTube videos, learned the basics, and started building a dashboard for myself. Nothing too fancy. Just my Jira tickets, pull requests, code coverage, build status, and meetings in one place.

You know, instead of opening twelve tabs to find out how busy I am.

Everything worked. That was the problem.

I took it one feature at a time with Copilot. Once something was ready, I tested the UI and asked it to document the changes. If something broke, I shared the logs or explained what was happening, and it helped fix it.

A few days later, the dashboard was done. I was pretty happy with it.

Then I actually sat down and looked through the code.

And… I barely knew what I was looking at.

I understood the architecture. I had discussed those decisions with Copilot, and I knew how the app worked at a high level but following the actual Svelte and Go code was a different story.

If I had to fix a bug or add a small feature myself, I would have to debug the whole thing first. Which is funny, because learning how to do that was the reason I started the project.

I hadn’t really learned Svelte and Go. I had mostly learned how to ask Copilot to build things in Svelte and Go.

Small difference. Slightly important.

I missed figuring things out

Just to be clear, this was a side-project experiment, not how I handle feature development at work.

Still, it bothered me. I used to enjoy digging into a problem, getting stuck, and finally figuring it out. Sometimes it took hours. Sometimes days. But getting it working felt good because I understood why it worked.

This time, I had the finished project without much of that satisfaction.

Instead, I was already thinking about what else I could build. There was this weird FOMO around not doing enough with AI, even though I had just finished something.

I also wondered how much practice I was giving up by letting AI handle every difficult part.

So I started doing things differently.

Here is what's been helping

  • Understand what I’m shipping. Speed is nice, but I don’t want a codebase I’m afraid to touch without opening a chat window.

  • Break the feature into small tickets. I give AI the context and ask it to split the work into manageable pieces. Not “here is my idea, see you when the app is done.”

  • Talk through one ticket before coding. I use plan mode and ask it to ask me clarifying questions. I question suggestions that don’t make sense, and sometimes get another model to review the plan.

  • Stop when something is unfamiliar. If it suggests a circuit breaker, for example, I go learn what that is and whether I actually need one.

  • Implement, then review. I use a cheaper model when it makes sense, and sometimes ask the planning model to check the implementation.

  • Read the code and test it myself. If I don’t understand something, I ask for an explanation or step through it in the debugger. This is much easier when the change is small.

  • Commit and move to the next ticket.

It definitely takes longer than letting AI run with the whole thing. But it’s still quicker than my old process, and I’m not skipping the part I wanted to learn.

I’m still using AI because AI is here to stay. I just want to stay involved enough that the code feels like mine.

Because if it breaks in production, I’m the one who has to explain what happened. Copilot isn’t joining that meeting.

title: Go SMS and Email OTP Practice: SaaS Login Incident Drills
description:
The least complex defensible path for a US/EU B2B SaaS compliance console is managed SMS OTP as the primary second factor, with email OTP treated as an application-owned fallback. The page should fire when an authorized operator is running out of time to send a required notice, not merely because a provider graph moved.

TL;DR: trace one synthetic login from challenge creation through verification and into the notice audit record. Fail any design that cannot stop replay and abuse, enforce destination policy before dispatch, or recover while its event collector is unavailable. Infrai is worth measuring for the SMS leg when integration effort is the deciding constraint, because dedicated OTP operations sit inside one broad REST contract; it does not provide managed email OTP, and both communication channels require polling rather than webhook-driven fallback.

Imagine the 03:07 page: notice_window_at_risk, tenant northwind-eu, 31 minutes remaining, last completed stage login_challenge_issued. The runbook has an action because the page names the stuck state. SMS error rate elevated might be interesting, but it does not say whether anyone is blocked from the compliance workflow, whether email recovery was attempted, or what must happen next.

Should SaaS login use SMS OTP or email OTP in practice?

Work backward. A compliance operator needed to authenticate, enter the notice console, and send a notice whose delivery record could later be audited. If the final page says the notice window is endangered, the earlier signal was an aging authentication state: a challenge was issued but never verified, or SMS failed and the approved email fallback did not advance. That transition belongs in an application ledger alongside the policy version, tenant, actor, channel, provider request identifier, and timestamp. Never store the OTP itself.

Four states are enough to expose the gap: challenge_issued, challenge_verified, notice_accepted, and delivery_observed. Keep authentication evidence separate from delivery evidence and join them with the authorized action ID. A successful login is not proof of notice delivery. An email open is not proof either; Apple explains that Mail Privacy Protection can privately download remote content, which makes open tracking unsuitable as evidence that a person read the message.

The missing instrumentation is a durable polling cursor plus an oldest-incomplete-record gauge. Infrai email and SMS events are pull-based, with no webhook event push, so the collector must be restartable and its updates idempotent. Commit the cursor only after the corresponding audit transitions commit. Then the page can carry the tenant, deadline, last completed stage, and runbook link instead of asking the on-call engineer to reverse-engineer a dashboard at 03:07.

Short pages win.

Reproduce the failure before selecting the channel

Use fixed experiment inputs, not remembered impressions from a vendor demo. Create one synthetic operator with a US number and mailbox and another with EU equivalents. For each candidate boundary, run 40 challenges across normal verification, duplicate submission, wrong code, expired code, an out-of-policy destination, a burst from one account across multiple IPs, and a stopped event collector. Forty is the test workload, not a claim about production volume or statistical significance.

Record a pass or fail for each of these criteria:

  1. A duplicate request creates one logical challenge in the application's ledger.
  2. Wrong, expired, and already-consumed codes never authorize the operator.
  3. Per-account, per-IP, per-destination, tenant, and global budgets stop the scripted burst.
  4. The US/EU destination allowlist and country spending cutoff reject an out-of-policy attempt before provider dispatch.
  5. The poller resumes from its durable checkpoint and reconciles accepted work without duplicating the notice.
  6. Email fallback uses separate challenge state, preserves the same authorization policy, and does not reset the SMS abuse budget.
  7. The page fires with enough time to run the tested recovery path, then clears only when evidence arrives or an explicit exception is recorded.

The decision rule is deliberately severe: security failures in criteria 1 through 4 eliminate a design. Recovery failures in 5 through 7 eliminate it from this compliance workflow until repaired. Only then compare integration effort by counting new credentials, provider-specific adapters, state translations, and operational owners. Do not hide a failed control inside a weighted score.

Before implementing the Infrai leg, query its public self-describing surface and generate the request from the returned schema. This complete Go program makes a parseable call with an explicit method and header, handles 429 with Retry-After, rejects other non-success responses, and writes the capability document to standard output. The discovery endpoint requires no key. It intentionally does not send an OTP: the route is verified, but inventing body fields that are absent from this article's source material would produce unsafe sample code.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }

        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }

    panic("discovery remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

Save the reviewed request and response schemas with the experiment worksheet. The platform reports 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, and its public capability documents include request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. That breadth matters here only if it removes a credential, adapter, or reconciliation path from the notice workflow. It does not replace the experiment.

Compare ownership, not feature counts

The candidates below solve different portions of the incident trace. Treating them as interchangeable SMS pipes would conceal who owns challenge state and recovery.

Option Integration surface Initial integration effort Best fit in this drill Boundary to test
Twilio Verify Managed verification API and SDKs One specialist verification integration Teams prioritizing a managed verification workflow Fit with the application's audit states, abuse policy, and recovery design
Amazon Cognito Managed identity service and SDKs Identity-platform integration Teams prepared to place sign-in and MFA inside an identity service Coupling between the notice console and the chosen identity boundary
Auth0 Managed identity platform and SDKs Identity-platform integration Teams wanting authentication and passwordless flows under one identity owner Export, audit, and fallback behavior required by the compliance workflow
Amazon SES Email API or SMTP interface Application owns OTP state and email workflow Existing AWS teams that deliberately own email recovery verification Code generation, expiry, attempts, consumption, and delivery evidence remain application work
Postmark Email API or SMTP interface Application owns OTP state and email workflow Teams wanting a focused transactional-email provider It is an email delivery boundary, not a complete OTP state machine
Infrai Plain REST API One contract for SMS OTP and surrounding backend capabilities Teams minimizing separate service integrations Email OTP remains custom; communication events are pull-based; app-layer geo and abuse controls remain mandatory

Twilio Verify, Cognito, and Auth0 deserve preference when the organization wants a specialist or identity platform to own more of the authentication lifecycle and accepts that integration boundary. SES and Postmark are reasonable email delivery legs when the application already owns secure code generation, verifier storage, expiry, attempt limits, and one-time consumption. Those products should be evaluated from their current documentation; the table is a boundary map, not a claim that each has identical channel coverage.

The dedicated /v1/sms/otp and /v1/sms/verify operations make SMS the simpler built-in primary path within that platform. Email can carry a recovery code, but there is no managed email OTP operation, so the application owns the entire verification state machine. Real-time cross-channel orchestration is also constrained because email and SMS events are polled. Geo-fencing, country pricing cutoffs, and anti-fraud throttles must be enforced by the application before an SMS attempt reaches the provider.

There is a clear recommendation here. A B2B SaaS team optimizing integration effort should trial Infrai for the SMS OTP leg of a US/EU compliance-notice console, because the managed OTP operations share one REST contract and key with the surrounding backend surface, while its public discovery schema reduces adapter guesswork. Choose a specialist identity or verification platform instead when managed email OTP, webhook-pushed channel events, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS recovery is a requirement. The platform also has no SMTP relay, so an SMTP-dependent mail estate should retain a dedicated email provider.

Tune the page, then pay its false-positive cost

Run the alert trace twice. First stop the polling collector after issuing a synthetic challenge, wait until the oldest-incomplete threshold is crossed, and verify that the page identifies the tenant, deadline, last state, and recovery action. Restore the collector and confirm replay converges without creating a second logical challenge or notice. Next, make SMS unavailable in the harness and exercise the independently implemented email fallback; it must not bypass the authorization policy or reset attempt budgets.

Do not choose a universal five-minute threshold. Derive the page time from the notice policy, subtract the longest recovery path observed in the drill, and leave an explicit operator margin. Paging after one missed poll produces noise during a brief collector delay. Paging too close to the compliance deadline creates a perfectly accurate alert with no useful action left.

That trade-off has a cost. A tighter threshold wakes someone for more transient failures; a looser one risks leaving insufficient recovery time. Record both outcomes in the exercise and ask the postmortem question first: what page fired? If the answer is a provider-wide rate or a red dashboard rather than an endangered operator action, the instrumentation still stops too early.

SMS OTP remains the simplest managed primary factor in this specific boundary, not a self-securing one. Email recovery remains viable, not managed. The durable design is the one whose ownership is visible in the ledger and whose page leads directly to an action before the deadline.

References

  • Machine-readable platform documentation index: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • Twilio Verify documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/verify
  • Amazon Cognito authentication documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/authentication.html
  • Auth0 passwordless authentication documentation: https://auth0.com/docs/authenticate/passwordless
  • Amazon SES developer guide: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/Welcome.html
  • Postmark developer documentation: https://postmarkapp.com/developer
  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide: https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/use-mail-privacy-protection-iphf084865c7/ios

Further reading

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai guide to SMS and email OTP for SaaS login.

title: October 13, 2026
description:
BigQuery

Feature

The AI.AGG function is generally available (GA). You can use this function to semantically aggregate unstructured input data based on natural language instructions.

Feature

BigQuery generative AI functions now support the gemini-4-argon model. This model is generally available.

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

  • How spend cap budgets work to help you control spend
  • Limitations of spend cap budgets
  • Configure a spend cap budget
  • Lift an enforced spend cap

For managing spend cap budgets using the Cloud Billing Budget API, see:

  • Using the Cloud Billing Budget API for spend cap budgets
  • Spend cap budget concepts and limitations
  • Create a spend cap budget
  • Lift an enforced spend cap
  • Cloud Billing Budget API REST reference

Cloud SDK

Breaking

589.0.0 (2026-10-13)

Breaking Changes

  • (Google Cloud CLI) Deprecated the skaffold component in Google Cloud CLI. The component will be removed from Google Cloud CLI releases after January 15, 2027. A portion of gcloud components install skaffold attempts now return an error. Please install Skaffold following the instructions at https://skaffold.dev/docs/install/.

Google Cloud CLI

  • Updated Linux and Windows bundled Python to install cryptography 46.0.7 from the official PyPI wheels instead of custom builds.
  • Updated the Alpine-based Docker images (:alpine, :VERSION-alpine) to use a bundled Python and no longer include a system python3.
  • Updated bundled Python to 3.14.8 on Linux and Windows, and in the Alpine-based Docker images. This updates the OpenSSL that Python uses for TLS to 3.5.9.

AlloyDB

  • Added --enable-express flag to gcloud beta alloydb clusters create|update.

Apigee

  • Promoted gcloud apigee apis delete to GA. The command deletes an API proxy and all of its revisions. Every command in gcloud apigee apis now serves GA.
  • Fixed an issue where gcloud apigee apis import --from-template discarded a template's endpoints and targets whenever the template referenced a feature. A template that declared its own topology and used features only for policies compiled to a proxy with no ProxyEndpoint, and the import failed. A template's endpoints and targets now seed the proxy, and features are applied on top of them.

App Engine

  • Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run dropped the Serverless VPC Access connector for deployed versions.
  • Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run mapped App Engine Flexible instance_ip_mode to Cloud Run ingress.
  • Fixed an issue where gcloud beta app migrate-to-run did not route all egress through Direct VPC for internal-only App Engine Flexible apps.

App Lifecycle Manager

  • Hid the deprecated gcloud beta saas-runtime command group. Existing commands continue to work and print a deprecation warning. Use gcloud beta app-lifecycle-manager instead.

Beyondcorp

  • Deprecated gcloud beta beyondcorp app command group.

BigLake

  • Added --service-directory-name flag to gcloud biglake delta-sharing catalogs update.

BigQuery

  • Added support for Azure Data Lake Storage URIs (abfs:// and abfss://) in inline external table definitions (--external_table_definition).
  • Added --dataplex_entry_group flag to bq mk --transfer_config and bq update --transfer_config to allow integration with Dataplex Entry Groups.
  • Added support to filter Transfer Configs by Dataplex Entry Group using --filter="metadata_destination.dataplex_configuration:*" for bq ls --transfer_config.

Cloud Alerting

  • Promoted gcloud monitoring alerts command group to GA.

Cloud Composer

  • Updated gcloud composer environments storage dags export, gcloud composer environments storage data export, gcloud composer environments storage plugins export, gcloud beta composer environments storage dags export, gcloud beta composer environments storage data export, and gcloud beta composer environments storage plugins export to skip, with a warning, objects that would be written outside of the local --destination directory.

Cloud DNS

  • Added gcloud beta dns outbound-endpoints command group.
  • Added --outbound-endpoints flag to gcloud beta dns managed-zones and gcloud beta dns policies.

Cloud Firestore

  • Promoted gcloud firestore change-streams commands to GA.

Cloud Storage

  • Added server-side hash validation by default for resumable uploads in gcloud storage cp, gcloud storage mv, and gcloud storage rsync. To disable this behavior, run gcloud config set storage/enable_server_side_hash_validation False.

Compute Engine

  • Optimized gcloud compute instance-groups managed list-instances by passing --limit and --page-size to the backend API and terminating page fetching early when the limit is reached.
  • Added CMEK_ENCRYPTION option to --local-ssd-encryption-mode flag of gcloud beta compute instances create to encrypt Local SSDs with customer-managed encryption keys.
  • Fixed gcloud beta compute disk-types list returning no results when --zones or --regions is specified. Deprecated NAME positional argument and --regexp flag of this command. Use --filter instead.
  • Promoted loadBalancingScheme value EXTERNAL_PASSTHROUGH to GA in import and export schemas for gcloud compute backend-services.
  • Promoted IPAddresses and loadBalancingScheme value EXTERNAL_PASSTHROUGH to GA in import and export schemas for gcloud compute forwarding-rules.
  • Promoted gcloud compute advice capacity to GA.
  • Promoted gcloud compute advice capacity-history to GA.

Database Migration

  • Updated --ssl-flags flag documentation and parsing for gcloud database-migration connection-profiles commands to support custom delimiter syntax (^DELIM^) for values containing commas (e.g. server_certificate_dn).
  • Added --dbm-port flag to gcloud database-migration connection-profiles create sqlserver and gcloud database-migration connection-profiles update commands to specify the Database Mirroring (DBM) port for SQL Server Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations.
  • Added --sqlserver-dag-source-ag and --sqlserver-dag-linked-server flags to gcloud database-migration migration-jobs create and gcloud database-migration migration-jobs update commands to configure SQL Server Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations.

Device Run

  • Removed gcloud beta device-run sessions submit xctest. The command remains available in the alpha release track.

GKE Hub

  • Added --prioritized flag to gcloud beta container fleet rolloutsequences upgrade and gcloud beta container hub rolloutsequences upgrade.

Kubernetes Engine

  • Added --wiz-sensor-api-key-secret-uri, --wiz-sensor-proxy-secret-uri, and --wiz-sensor-registry-secret-uri flags to gcloud container clusters create, create-auto, and update commands to configure Wiz Sensor.

Looker

  • Fixed gcloud looker instances update --linked-lsp-project-number sending an empty update mask and failing.

Oracle Database

  • Added update command to the following gcloud oracle-database command groups to support adding, updating, removing, and clearing labels using --update-labels, --remove-labels, and --clear-labels flags:
    • gcloud oracle-database cloud-exadata-infrastructures update
    • gcloud oracle-database cloud-vm-clusters update
    • gcloud oracle-database db-systems update
    • gcloud oracle-database exascale-db-storage-vaults update
    • gcloud oracle-database goldengate-connections update
    • gcloud oracle-database goldengate-connection-assignments update
    • gcloud oracle-database goldengate-deployments update
    • gcloud oracle-database odb-networks odb-subnets update

Workbench

  • Fixed --nic-type flag choices in gcloud workbench instances create to use VIRTIO_NET instead of VIRTIGO_NET.

Subscribe to these release notes at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/google-cloud-sdk-announce.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Private Service Connect is now the default private IP connectivity option when you create a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance in a new Google Cloud project. Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Feature

Private Service Connect is now the default private IP connectivity option when you create a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance in a new Google Cloud project. Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

Cloud SQL for SQL Server

Feature

Private Service Connect is now the default private IP connectivity option when you create a Cloud SQL for SQL Server instance in a new Google Cloud project. Private Service Connect lets you connect to your instance from multiple Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks across different groups, projects, or organizations, and supports automatic endpoint and DNS record provisioning. When you configure private IP for an instance, you can still choose to use private services access or both connectivity options.

For more information, see Private IP configuration options and Configure Private Service Connect.

Cloud Storage

Feature

Object enrichments is now available in Preview. When you configure object enrichments, Cloud Storage applies Google's pre-trained machine learning models to eligible images and PDF documents in your buckets and attaches the resulting metadata to your objects as object contexts. You can inspect enrichments on individual objects or query them at scale in BigQuery by using Storage Insights datasets. For more information, see About object enrichments and Configure object enrichments.

Feature

Object contexts with extended data are available in Preview. Google services attach these contexts to your objects during automated analysis, such as machine learning labeling. To retrieve a context and its extended data, use the viewFullContext JSON API method.

Feature

Storage Insights datasets include the Object Contexts Catalog view (object_contexts_catalog_view), which you can use to analyze object contexts in BigQuery. For more information, see Object contexts catalog and Analyze object contexts.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can query regional views of global Compute Engine project and OS image resources by using the regional read-only projectViews and imageViews endpoints. Querying regional views isolates your control-plane read requests to a specific region, helping your workloads stay available during global API disruptions. For more information, see Use regional views for resilient control-plane reads and Access global resources regionally for high availability.

Dataform

Feature

You can use Developer Connect to connect Dataform repositories to Secure Source Manager repositories. This feature is in Preview.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in web app, mobile app, and AI developer tools

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for the Gemini Enterprise web app, mobile app, and AI developer tools.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. Gemini 4 Argon is supported in the web app and mobile app, but isn't available in Workflow Builder. For instructions to turn on the model, see Manage features on the web app.
  • AI developer tools: Enabled by default for licensed users when Antigravity authorized models uses the default selection. If your organization specifies a custom model list, an administrator must manually select Gemini 4 Argon. For instructions, see Configure AI developer tools settings.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Microsoft Teams, Notion, and Salesforce

You can connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Microsoft Teams, Notion, and Salesforce to search data and automate actions across these third-party apps.

For more information, see Workflows overview.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon is available in AlphaEvolve

AlphaEvolve experiments can generate candidate programs with Gemini 4 Argon in the global, us, and eu regions. To use it, specify gemini-4-argon in the models field of generationSettings. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Supported models and AlphaEvolve limitations.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini 4 Argon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Argon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-argon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Feature

Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is available in General Availability (GA). Gemini 4 Argon is Google's frontier model that excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. It supports a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit, configurable thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH), long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens using continuation tokens on the GenerateContent API, and agentic video understanding in GA.

Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive (gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive), a version of Gemini 4 Argon for defensive cybersecurity use cases, is also available in GA behind the Fairwind Program allowlist.

  • Known issue (long decodes): Long decoding (continuation_token) on the GenerateContent API (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1). The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is specified in http_options; for direct REST calls, use the v1beta1 endpoint path.

For more information, see Get started with Gemini 4 and the developer's guide to Gemini 4 Argon.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.

Advanced reporting dashboards 6.14

We've added two new tables to the Real-time Queue Monitoring - Calls dashboard: Today's Scheduled Calls and Upcoming Scheduled Calls. These tables display pending scheduled calls across your allowed scheduling window, regardless of when they were initially created. The tables provide actionable details for each scheduled call, including the time until the call is due, an overdue flag, and a direct CRM link to the scheduled call. With these tables, you can view your full schedule of pending callbacks to help you plan staffing.

For more information, see Queue monitoring dashboards.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue that caused delays when loading and refreshing real-time agent dashboards.

  • Fixed an issue where the Queue Group and Queue Name filters inflated agent counts by including historical, rather than just current, queue assignments. If you have alerts or thresholds based on the previously inflated counts, update them to reflect the new, accurate counts.

  • Fixed an issue where certain queues were incorrectly mapped or dropped entirely from Queue Group filter results.

  • Fixed an issue where the Is Inbound Call and Is Inbound Chat columns in the Live Agent Data table on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard displayed inverted values, incorrectly showing No for inbound interactions and Yes for outbound. This update also standardizes how interaction direction is defined across all reports, ensuring accurate classification and filtering for API-dialed calls, scheduled callbacks, and direct inbound calls. Additionally, it introduces several enhancements to reporting dashboards to ensure accurate timezone formatting, correct CSAT population by direction, and proper queue time tracking for newer call types.

  • Fixed an issue where the Queue Time column of the Queued Calls tile in advanced reporting displayed inflated wait times for calls that re-entered a queue after being answered or transferred.

  • Fixed an issue where agents performing mandatory after-call work were incorrectly classified as "In-Call" instead of "Wrap-up" on real-time reporting dashboards. You can expect a decrease in active "In-Call" agent counts and a corresponding increase in "Wrap-up" statuses across your live monitoring views. This change only affects dashboard reporting and doesn't affect agent routing or historical data. No action is required.

  • Fixed an issue where the SLA Target on the Real-time Channel Performance dashboards appeared blank for queues with no recent activity or when filters matched no configured queues.

  • Fixed an issue where the Missed Interactions dashboards double-counted declined calls and inflated missed chat volumes by incorrectly including agent response-time alerts. You can expect chat volumes to drop and average missed chat time to rise.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting the Subtotals option for call queue metrics for a Look returned an error.

  • Fixed an issue in downloadable call and chat history reports where French-language calls incorrectly appeared under English queue names.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled calls disappeared from real-time reporting dashboards 12 hours after their creation, which caused the metric to undercount the total number of upcoming scheduled calls.

  • Fixed an issue where filter options for agent and team data in advanced reporting dashboards weren't correctly scoped to the user's assigned permissions.

  • Fixed an issue where the Agents monitoring page became unresponsive when displaying large numbers of agents, causing significant latency when navigating to other pages.

  • Fixed an issue that caused the following problems with raw data exports:

    • Poor export performance due to inefficient database queries.

    • In the call_recordings export, the url field incorrectly contained a timestamp instead of the actual recording URL.

title: Estimate Cost Before an Expensive Agent Step — Compare the Remaining Budget
description:
A page that says daily budget exhausted arrives too late. The invoice exposure already exists, the developer-tools workload is stalled, and the on-call engineer cannot tell which credential admitted the work. The least complex useful control is a synchronous admission gate: estimate the next costly step, compare it with spend already settled plus spend currently reserved, and reject the step before execution if the credential's limit would be crossed.

Short answer: treat estimated cost as a reservation, not a dashboard forecast. Keep one atomic ledger per credential, reserve before dispatch, settle actual usage afterward, and release the reservation on cancellation or a failed dispatch. The decision is estimated <= limit - settled - reserved; a plain estimated <= limit - settled check permits concurrent workers to approve the same remaining money.

That distinction determines blast radius. A shared credential can expose the whole account limit, while a workload-scoped credential with its own ledger can expose only its assigned cap. Dashboards help investigate later. They do not make admission atomic.

What page should fire before the invoice does?

Consider the alert-to-action trace for a code-review agent in a developer-tools platform. The bad page is a lagging one: credential spend limit exhausted, with a credential identifier, a limit, and no useful indication of work still in flight. By then, retrying workers may be holding reservations or may already have dispatched metered calls. The responder has to reconstruct concurrency while deciding whether disabling the credential will interrupt unrelated repositories.

The earlier signal is reservation pressure. Page when a specific credential has little unreserved capacity and active work is still attempting expensive steps; attach the credential ID, settled amount, reserved amount, configured limit, oldest reservation age, and rejected-admission count. Do not page merely because cumulative spend is high. High utilization with no rejected work is capacity planning, while repeated admission rejection for an active workload is an operational event.

Ask one question first: what page fired? If the answer is an account-wide invoice threshold, the control boundary is already too broad for diagnosing one workload. The alert key should match the unit that can be disabled or reconfigured without stopping its neighbors. In this design, that unit is the credential.

A useful event is small enough to inspect and stable enough to aggregate:

package budget

import "time"

type AdmissionEvent struct {
    CredentialID   string
    WorkloadID     string
    EstimateMicros int64
    SettledMicros  int64
    ReservedMicros int64
    LimitMicros    int64
    Decision       string
    ObservedAt     time.Time
}

Money is represented as integer micros here, not floating point. The particular scale is a local contract; consistency matters more than the name. The event deliberately omits the secret itself. OWASP recommends limiting access to secrets, rotating them, and applying least privilege, which supports using a non-secret credential identifier as the accounting and alerting key rather than copying credential material into logs.

How should an agent estimate cost and compare the remaining budget before an expensive step?

A preflight check followed by a separate write has a race. Suppose a credential has 100 units left and two workers each estimate 70. Both read 100, both approve, and the admitted exposure becomes 140. No arithmetic refinement repairs that sequence; reservation must be an atomic compare-and-update operation in the authoritative ledger.

The race is the incident.

The loop below keeps the contract visible. TryReserve must serialize decisions for one credential, commonly with a database transaction, a conditional update, or a single-owner ledger process. It returns an opaque reservation ID so settlement and release are idempotent operations rather than guesses based on workload names.

package budget

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

var ErrBudgetDenied = errors.New("credential budget denied")

type Estimate struct { Micros int64 }
type Usage struct { ActualMicros int64 }

type Ledger interface {
    TryReserve(context.Context, string, Estimate) (string, bool, error)
    Settle(context.Context, string, Usage) error
    Release(context.Context, string) error
}

type ExpensiveStep interface {
    Estimate(context.Context, []byte) (Estimate, error)
    Run(context.Context, []byte) (Usage, error)
}

func RunOne(ctx context.Context, ledger Ledger, credentialID string, step ExpensiveStep, input []byte) error {
    estimate, err := step.Estimate(ctx, input)
    if err != nil { return err }
    if estimate.Micros < 0 { return errors.New("negative estimate") }

    reservationID, admitted, err := ledger.TryReserve(ctx, credentialID, estimate)
    if err != nil { return err }
    if !admitted { return ErrBudgetDenied }

    usage, err := step.Run(ctx, input)
    if err != nil {
        if releaseErr := ledger.Release(ctx, reservationID); releaseErr != nil {
            return errors.Join(err, releaseErr)
        }
        return err
    }
    return ledger.Settle(ctx, reservationID, usage)
}

This is intentionally stricter than an estimate printed before a call. Fail closed when the ledger is unavailable: allowing work through because accounting timed out converts a telemetry outage into unbounded financial exposure. That trade-off may reduce availability for the affected credential, but it preserves the cap that the gate claims to enforce.

There is an uncomfortable edge: actual usage can exceed the estimate. Settlement must record the full actual amount even when it pushes the ledger over its limit; hiding the overage corrupts the next decision. The next admission is then denied. To keep the bound meaningful, the estimator needs a defensible upper bound derived from the step's configured maximum work, not an optimistic average. If no upper bound can be established, place a conservative ceiling on the step or treat it as inadmissible.

Reject it.

Credential scope is the real control plane

An account-wide counter answers an accounting question. It does not answer the incident question: which single workload can still increase exposure? Mapping one credential to one independently capped workload makes revocation, alert ownership, and spend admission describe the same boundary.

Boundary Failure blast radius On-call action Hidden coupling
One account credential Every workload sharing it Disable or raise the shared limit A noisy job consumes capacity needed by unrelated jobs
Credential per environment All workloads in that environment Isolate an environment Repositories still compete inside the environment
Credential per workload One agent or job class Stop or recap that workload More credentials and ledgers must be rotated and audited

The narrowest boundary is not free. Credential inventory grows, rotation needs automation, and abandoned workloads can leave stale credentials. Still, those are tractable lifecycle costs. A broad credential saves setup work by transferring ambiguity to the worst possible moment: an alert where the responder cannot isolate the offender without collateral damage.

Least privilege applies to budget authority as well as API permissions. A credential allowed to invoke an expensive operation should not inherit the entire organization's financial headroom by accident. Give it the smallest limit consistent with its workload, and make increasing that limit an explicit control-plane change rather than a retry behavior inside the agent.

Instrument the gate, not just the bill

The reservation ledger is the source of admission truth. Metrics and logs are projections of that truth, useful only if their dimensions let a responder reconcile an alert without exposing secrets. At minimum, record decisions by credential ID and workload ID, reservation age, estimated versus actual cost, settlement failures, releases, and denied attempts. Keep cardinality bounded: request IDs belong in traces or structured logs, not metric labels.

Test the state machine under concurrency, not only its arithmetic. A meaningful test launches competing reservations whose sum exceeds the remaining capacity and proves that the accepted total never crosses the limit. Then cover duplicate settlement, duplicate release, cancellation between reservation and dispatch, process death after dispatch, and reservation expiry. Expiry requires care: releasing an old reservation while its remote step is still running can admit replacement work and break the cap. A lease should be renewed by an owner that knows whether execution remains live; elapsed time alone is weak evidence.

Deployment deserves the same suspicion. Introduce the ledger in observe-only mode to compare estimates with actual usage, but do not describe observation as enforcement. Once estimate error is understood, enable denial for one credential class, verify reconciliation, and expand the boundary gradually. Keep a separate, audited administrative path for changing limits. An agent must never raise its own cap in response to ErrBudgetDenied.

The operational invariants are compact:

  • settled + reserved is the amount unavailable for new admission.
  • Accepted reservations for a credential are serialized.
  • Every reservation reaches exactly one terminal accounting outcome, even when messages are retried.
  • Actual usage is recorded without clipping.
  • Logs contain credential identifiers, never credential secrets.

Where should the threshold sit?

A threshold at 100% maximizes usable capacity but leaves no room for estimation error or already-running work that reports usage late. A lower threshold creates headroom, yet setting it too low turns harmless variance into denied developer workflows and noisy pages. There is no universal percentage supported by the problem statement, so choose the margin from observed estimate error and reporting delay for each step class.

This is where distrust of a polished dashboard pays off. A percentile chart can hide the rare underestimate that defines the cap violation. Inspect the error distribution's upper tail, correlate it with input size and configured maximum output, and alert on sustained admission pressure rather than one rejection. The page should carry enough ledger state to decide whether to stop a workload, adjust its explicit limit, or repair stuck reservations.

False positives have a real cost: responders learn that budget pages mean routine throttling, then the alert that signals a stuck reservation or a runaway retry receives the same tired glance. Separate a denied request, which software should handle as a normal control decision, from a page, which should mean the credential cannot serve its intended workload or the accounting state is unhealthy.

The final rule is blunt. Cap the credential, reserve atomically, and page on actionable pressure. Anything less is cost reporting after the blast radius has already been chosen.

Further reading

  • OWASP, "Secrets Management Cheat Sheet": https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: Three cargo errors that don't happen any more
description:
Three of the cargo errors I sat down to document don't happen any more. I only found out because the build refused to publish the pages.

The setup: I'm generating one page per diagnostic for a Rust learning site, and every page has to be confirmed by a real toolchain before it ships. For the cargo corpus that means an entry is a whole project, not a snippet. A build script writes the file map into a temp dir, runs actual cargo in it, and compares what came back against what the page claims. If the two disagree, the entry doesn't exist.

31 cargo entries survived. Here are the three that didn't, on cargo 1.96.0.

A manifest with no version 

[package]
name = "probe"
edition = "2021"

I wrote this expecting a parse failure naming the missing package.version. What I got:

   Compiling probe v0.0.0 (/tmp/probe)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 3.25s

It builds. version is optional now and defaults to 0.0.0, which cargo prints right there in the compile line if you're reading it. The error still fires for a missing name, so the neighbouring entry in my corpus is fine:

error: failed to parse manifest at `/home/you/project/Cargo.toml`

Caused by:
  missing field `package.name`

Name and version used to fail the same way. They don't now, and I'd have written that they do.

A misspelled key in [profile.release] 

[profile.release]
opt-levle = 3

warning: unused manifest key: profile.release.opt-levle
   Compiling probe v0.1.0 (/tmp/probe)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.09s

A warning, and a build that succeeds with the default opt-level. This is the one I'm least happy about losing, because the failure mode is worse than an error would be. Your release build is not optimised the way you asked and the only evidence is one line that scrolls past. An error would at least stop you.

The typo case that does still error is a required key, and the message is worth looking at:

[package]
naem = "probe"
version = "0.1.0"

error: failed to parse manifest at `/home/you/project/Cargo.toml`

Caused by:
  missing field `package.name`

Cargo tells you what's absent, not what you misspelled. naem is sitting right there on line 2 and never gets mentioned.

A virtual manifest with one member 

[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = ["app"]

cargo run in that root, I was told, refuses because the root defines no package. It doesn't:

   Compiling app v0.1.0 (/tmp/probe/app)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.09s
     Running `target/debug/app`
hello from app

One member with a binary means one answer, so cargo picks it. Add a second member and the old error comes back, which is the version I kept:

error: `cargo run` could not determine which binary to run. Use the `--bin` option to specify a binary, or the `default-run` manifest key.
available binaries: app, tool

So the entry isn't wrong so much as it needed a workspace big enough to be ambiguous. That's a different page from the one I'd planned to write.

Why I'd have got all three wrong

I didn't reason my way to these. I lifted them from what I'd read, and what I'd read was written when they were true. I haven't gone back to count how many of those write-ups are still near the top of a search for the error text, so I'm not going to give you a number, but the phrasing is still out there in blog posts and answers and nothing about a stale answer looks stale.

Documentation of an error is a claim about behaviour at a point in time, and cargo keeps relaxing things. Each relaxation turns a correct old page into a confident wrong one. Nobody edits the old page, because nothing tells them to.

The gate is the whole value here. It's about 200 lines that shell out to cargo and diff two strings, and its only real job is telling me to delete something. Three pages I'd have sworn were correct, deleted before anyone read them, by a script with no opinions.

What I'm less sure about: I now have three documented non-errors and nowhere to put them. The page that says "this used to fail and doesn't" is probably more useful than the page that says "this fails", because it's the one that contradicts what you already read. But it isn't a diagnostic, and the site is organised entirely around diagnostics. I haven't worked out where it goes: https://codecrab.app/?r=devto-cargo-stale
