title: How Klaviyo shipped 356 internal apps in two weeks on Vercel
description:
Klaviyo on Vercel

  • Built a platform for shipping internal apps

  • 512 builders and 356 live apps in two weeks

  • Every app ships SSO-gated and private by default

  • Builders go from idea to live app in 3 minutes

Klaviyo is a B2C CRM for more than 200,000 brands. It brings marketing, service, agents, and data together in one platform so brands can deliver customer experiences at scale. Klaviyo built a platform on Vercel for shipping internal apps, then opened it to every employee through a citizen developer program.

In the first two weeks of the program, 512 of Klaviyo’s more than 2,000 employees deployed 356 apps on Vercel. Of those, 196 were full-stack apps with their own databases. The teams that are now shipping software include legal, marketing, and HR. "The next big thing at Klaviyo could be in a marketer's laptop," says Sr. Lead AI Architect Mohamed Ali.

Guardrails instead of walls

Opening deployment to a couple thousand new builders made security the first conversation. The obvious way to keep them safe is to broadly restrict what they can do. Klaviyo went the other way.

Employees aren't just building microsites; they are shipping full-stack apps on top of Klaviyo's own databases, and none of it touches the public network. Every builder is managed through Klaviyo's identity provider, which Vercel made possible through Enterprise Managed Users.

Implementing safeguards across the stack

Secure Compute gives Vercel deployments a private network path into Klaviyo's own infrastructure. Apps built in the program read from and write to Klaviyo's databases without any traffic crossing the public internet. That's what made bring-your-own-database work for Klaviyo.

On top of that connection, Vercel Passport and Klaviyo’s identity provider give every app the same access defaults, with nothing for the builder to configure:

  • Apps are private and SSO-gated through Okta

  • Sensitive environment variables are set at the team level, out of builders' hands

  • Klaviyo's hardened GitHub security is inherited by every project

  • Wiz scans every project, and findings feed Klaviyo's SIEM

  • Public deployment is granted case-by-case, so sales can share microsites with prospects, while internal tools stay private

How Klaviyo's app platform turns an idea into an app

Klaviyo wanted anyone with an idea to be able to describe it in plain language, from Slack, Claude, or Cursor, and get back a working app. They designed K:Forge, an in-house pipeline built on the Vercel SDK, to handle everything in between.

K:Forge creates a GitHub repo, deploys the app on Vercel, connects data through Secure Compute, and applies every security default. The output is a live, SSO-gated app, and the builder never touches infrastructure. Changes work the same way: mid-thread in Slack, someone can tell K:Forge what should be different, then it makes the change and redeploys.

Klaviyo built the pipeline and deliberately didn't build the layer under it. CDN behavior, preview environments, analytics, global scale: all of it is R&D Vercel had already done, so builders and engineers at Klaviyo don't have to think about it.

For bigger builds, citizen developers take an app about 80% of the way, and Klaviyo's platform team steps in for the last 20%, for fine-tuning and safety review. The platform team went from being the bottleneck to being the finishing touch. "We don't worry about scale," Mohamed says. "If 100,000 people hit an app, Vercel already solved that."

What people at Klaviyo are building

Employees build everything from microsites that rework a sales process to full-stack apps for problems too niche for any vendor tool. For K:BOS, Klaviyo's flagship event, the team skipped off-the-shelf registration tooling and built its own. Engineering barely touched it.

Klaviyo was one of the first customers of Vercel for Enterprise Apps and Agents. The platform gave the company a way to let anyone build full-stack apps, with security handled by default.

What's next

Klaviyo sets a high bar for AI fluency. One in five employees has shipped an app so far, and Mohamed intends to get even more people building. The team is also going deeper into Vercel, with MCP and AI Gateway.

About Klaviyo: Klaviyo is an autonomous B2C CRM that powers more valuable customer experiences. We unify a flexible, scalable data platform, intelligence that gets smarter with every interaction, and action across Marketing and Service to help businesses turn real-time customer data into personalization at scale.

title: Designing the Spraycash UI with Kimi K3 in Devin
description:
Spraycash's UI was designed and built with Kimi K3 in Devin, one chat message at a time. This post walks through the design: where the look came from, the type and colour system, the motion, and the exact prompt behind each change. The prompts are copied from the chat, with only my typos fixed.

The reference
I started from a screenshot of a landing page I liked: a soft blue sky, a meadow hill, butterflies, and a hand-drawn circle around one word of the headline.

---prompt---

So the hero text should be saying payroll, like cross-border payments for the rest of us, or payroll for the rest of us. Just find the one that is most useful and make sure it's catchy and very, very good. Use the image as inspiration for my landing page, and add the cloud animation too.

What came back:

One background photo. A generated sky-and-meadow image (sky-hill.webp) fills the hero, and the payslip cards sit on top of the hill.

Layered clouds. Five cloud images drift across the sky in a straight line, each with its own speed and start delay, so they never move in step.

Butterflies. Each one wanders along a slow path while its wings flap by squashing the image horizontally (scaleX from 1 to 0.45).

The ring. The green circle around "us all" is a single SVG path. It draws itself in once on load: the path length is normalised to 1 and the dash offset animates to 0.

Real objects. The coins, the paperclip, the sticky note and the PAID stamp on the receipt are all generated images rather than drawn shapes, so they have real light and shadow.

Type
Three fonts, each with one job:

Instrument Serif for headlines and every amount of money. Money uses tabular numbers, so a balance that ticks up every second keeps its width and the digits don't jump around.
Geist for the interface: labels, buttons, table rows.
Geist Mono for codes and receipt numbers.
Big serif amounts next to small, quiet sans labels give each screen one obvious thing to read first.

Colour
The palette is warm paper with one green:

Background #faf8f4, cards #ffffff, text #16130f, secondary text #6b655c, lines #e7e2d9.
One accent, #0f6b4f, used for primary buttons, the ring, the numbered steps and the moving coins on the map.
Amber and red appear only for warnings and errors.
Every screen uses the same tokens, so moving from the landing page into the app never feels like switching sites. The repo also carries an Untitled UI agent guide (CLAUDE.md), which kept text levels, borders, button and input shadows and focus rings consistent on every new screen.

Spacing and shape
Spacing runs on a fixed scale of 8, 16, 24, 40 and 64 px, content is capped at 1080 px wide, and cards use a 14 px radius with two soft shadows: a flat one for resting cards and a deeper one for cards that lift.

The nav
The first nav stretched edge to edge and had a sound button in it.

The nav bar is too long. You have to fix the nav bar. And also, why have you put that voice icon there? You have to fix all that.

It became a floating white pill in the centre, only as wide as the logo, two links and a solid black "Send pay" button. The sound toggle moved to the footer.

The headline
The first headline read "Payroll for the rest of the world".

It should be "Payroll for the rest of us all", not for the rest of the world.

The ring moved to "us all", and one short line sits under it: "Pay anyone, anywhere, by the second."

Phones
On a phone, some coins were sliding off the edges of the screen, and the naira coin was missing.

The coins hide in the corners on mobile view, fix that. And add naira to the currency animation.

On small screens the coins now sit fully inside the screen, between the buttons and the payslip card, and a gold naira coin joined the dollar, rupee and peso. The clouds shrink to 60%, and only three butterflies show.

Motion
Add Lenis smooth scroll, make the animations smooth, and animate the pay routes on the map from the USA and Europe.

The motion is built from a small set of tokens:

Durations: 80 ms for micro changes, 150 ms for hovers and presses, 250 to 500 ms for things entering the screen.
One easing curve for almost everything, cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1), which starts fast and settles gently.

Entrances rise 8 px and lose a 2 px blur as they fade in, which feels softer than a plain fade.
Scrolling goes through Lenis with a lerp of 0.1, and the guided tour uses the same Lenis instance to glide to each step.

Reduced motion: if the device asks for less motion, the clouds and butterflies stand still and scrolling goes back to normal.

On the map, the routes are dashed curves that march slowly toward each city, and small green coins travel along them on a loop.

Lagos is highlighted by default, and hovering another city highlights its routes instead.

Teaching the screen on the screen
Add an interactive tutorial that shows users how to go through each section.

The tour dims the page, outlines one part at a time in green and explains it in one line, with Next, Back and Skip. It runs once the first time someone opens a screen, and a "Show me how" pill in the bottom-right corner replays it. On phones that pill shrinks to a "?".

The rate card
Put the Chainlink logo there instead of the name.

The exchange rate is set in the big serif, with a small green "Verified by" badge carrying the logo, the time of the last update, and a thin countdown ring on the right that redraws as the quote refreshes.

Forms
The payslip form is split into numbered sections (who you're paying, what you pay, when it runs), with the step numbers in the green serif. The amount field uses the serif at 28 px, so the number you type reads like the number on the payslip.

The freelancer screens
The phone screens reuse the same pieces: the white card, the big serif amount, a quiet table underneath and one green button. The receipt is styled like a paper slip, with a perforated bottom edge and a PAID stamp.

Every one of these screens comes from a real run on the live site, and the explorer shows the withdrawal behind the receipt above.

title: Vercel Sandbox creation now returns a ready sandbox
description:
A new Vercel Sandbox is now ready to run commands and read or write files when creation completes.

Sandbox.create() now resolves only after snapshot restoration completes, so the first command or file operation no longer waits for it. Startup errors also reject Sandbox.create() instead of surfacing during that operation.

Snapshot restoration time now counts toward creation instead of the first operation. Creation is about 50 ms longer at p50, with a larger increase possible for uncached snapshots. The total time through the first operation remains the same.

This change applies automatically, with no SDK upgrade or configuration changes required. See the Sandbox.create() documentation for details.

title: Architecting Static Comparison Micro-Sites with TypeScript and JSON-LD Schema
description:
When building vertical web applications, separating feature comparisons into standalone, fast-loading micro-sites is an effective way to keep your core application bundle lean while addressing specific user intents.

Recently, while building out supporting comparison pages for an educational test simulator, I designed a reusable data schema in TypeScript to render head-to-head feature matrices and inject structured JSON-LD data automatically.

Here is the architectural pattern and data model used to build these static comparison micro-sites.

1. Defining the Comparison Data Model in TypeScript

Instead of hardcoding HTML tables for each competitor analysis, defining a strict TypeScript interface ensures every micro-site renders consistent evaluation metrics (pricing model, learning format, regulatory updates, and pass guarantees):

export interface ComparisonMetric {
  featureName: string;
  primaryPlatformValue: string | boolean;
  competitorValue: string | boolean;
  highlightAdvantage?: boolean;
}

export interface ComparisonSiteConfig {
  slug: string;
  title: string;
  competitorCategory: 'legacy-portal' | 'career-directory' | 'trade-school';
  lastUpdatedYear: number;
  metrics: ComparisonMetric[];
}

By typing the competitorCategory, the UI components can dynamically adjust the layout depending on whether we are comparing two software tools or comparing digital self-study against an offline curriculum.

2. Live Production Deployments (Built on Lovable)

Using this modular structure, I deployed three separate micro-sites targeting different segments of the HVAC certification space:

  • Demo 1 (Legacy Portal Comparison): HVAC Exam Master vs EPATest.com — EPA 608 Prep Compared (2026) — Compares interactive active-recall testing (Core, Type I, II, and III modules) against static Web 1.0 study guides.

  • Demo 2 (Lead-Gen Directory Comparison): HVAC Exam Master vs HVAC Career Now (2026 Comparison) — Contrasts direct certification utility tools against school lead-generation portals.

  • Demo 3 (Offline Institution Comparison): HVAC Exam Master vs HVAC Technical Institute — 2026 Comparison — Evaluates self-paced digital exam prep ROI against traditional brick-and-mortar tuition costs.

3. Automating FAQ & Comparison JSON-LD Schema

To help search engines and AI answer engines parse the comparison matrices accurately, each micro-site injects a structured FAQPage and WebPage JSON-LD payload into the document head:

TypeScript

export function ComparisonSchema({ title, url, description }: { title: string; url: string; description: string }) {
  const schemaData = {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "WebPage",
    "name": title,
    "url": url,
    "description": description,
    "specialty": "EPA Section 608 Certification Prep"
  };

  return (
    <script
      type="application/ld+json"
      dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(schemaData) }}
    />
  );
}

Key Takeaways for Frontend Builders

  1. Decouple Content from Layout: A shared TypeScript schema lets you spin up multiple comparison landing pages in minutes.
  2. Keep Micro-Sites Focused: Rather than building one massive table comparing ten different business models, isolating each comparison into its own deployment keeps page speed high and user intent clear.

title: High-Availability Distributed Sagas via Active-Active Topologies
description:
In tier-1 core banking systems, system availability is not merely an operational metric—it is a regulatory mandate. Outages in mission-critical business capabilities like Payment Execution or Position Keeping trigger immediate regulatory scrutiny, massive financial penalties, and systemic reputational damage.

Historically, banks relied on Active-Passive (Disaster Recovery) infrastructure topologies. In these setups, a primary data center handles all live traffic while a secondary data center sits idle, asynchronously replicating state. However, during a catastrophic regional failure (e.g., a total cloud region outage or physical fiber cut), Active-Passive failover mechanisms incur unacceptable recovery costs:

  • Non-Zero RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Asynchronous replication logs lag behind live transactions, resulting in lost financial writes upon failover.
  • High RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Manual or semi-automated DNS cutovers, database promotion scripts, and cache warm-ups take minutes—if not hours—to execute safely.
  • In-Flight Saga Corruption: Distributed transactions mid-execution during a regional collapse are left in indeterminate states, leading to orphan holds on customer accounts or uncompensated ledger debits.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, high-availability banking platforms eliminate single-region failure risks by deploying Multi-Region Active-Active Topologies for distributed Saga orchestrators (such as Temporal) backed by Distributed SQL engines (such as CockroachDB or Google Cloud Spanner). This paper evaluates the architectural patterns, state fencing mechanisms, consensus latency mathematics, and automated DR runbooks required to achieve RPO = 0 and RTO < 1s across regional disasters.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

BIAN Service Domain HA & SLA Matrix

Not all BIAN Service Domains demand identical disaster recovery profiles. Engineering active-active consensus across multi-region WANs introduces network latency trade-offs that must be categorized by domain criticality.

BIAN Service Domain Criticality Tier Target RPO Target RTO Multi-Region Topology Pattern Database Consensus Strategy
Payment Execution Tier-1 (Critical) 0 (Zero Loss) < 1 Second Multi-Region Active-Active (3+ Regions) Serialized Quorum Consensus (Raft/Paxos)
Position Keeping Tier-1 (Critical) 0 (Zero Loss) < 1 Second Multi-Region Active-Active (3+ Regions) Multi-Region Row-Level Lease Pinning
Credit Assessment Tier-2 (High) < 1 Second < 10 Seconds Dual-Region Active-Active (Follow-the-Leader) Asynchronous Cross-Region Group Replication
Customer Onboarding Tier-2 (High) < 5 Seconds < 30 Seconds Active-Active with Regional Sharding Eventual Consistency / Asynchronous Outbox
Historical Reporting Tier-3 (Standard) < 1 Hour < 1 Hour Active-Passive (DR Read Replica) Asynchronous Batch Snapshot Hydration

Mathematical Model: Multi-Region Consensus Latency vs. Availability

Achieving zero RPO across active-active regions requires synchronous consensus (e.g., Raft or Paxos). A transaction cannot be acknowledged to a client until a quorum of regions confirms state persistence.

The minimum commit latency Tcommit​ for a distributed Saga step executing across a multi-region deployment spanning M regions (where M≥3 to prevent split-brain tie votes) is governed by the round-trip time (RTT) to the closest majority quorum:

Tcommit​=Tlocal-execution​+max(RTTregion-local,RTTregion-quorum-1)+Tfsync​

Where RTTregion-quorum-1​ represents the network latency to the geographically closest peer region required to form a majority quorum ( ⌊M/2⌋+1 nodes).

The composite system availability Asystem​ across M independent active-active regions, assuming an individual region unavailability probability of Pregion-fail​ , is expressed as:

Asystem​=1−k=0∑⌊M/2⌋​(kM​)⋅(Pregion-fail​)M−k⋅(1−Pregion-fail​)k

By deploying across 3 geographically distinct active-active regions with independent power grids and cloud control planes, system availability reaches 99.999% ("five nines"), guaranteeing continuous execution even during the complete destruction of an entire cloud region.

Active-Active Multi-Region Saga Architecture Topology

In a Xenon active-active architecture, application workers and Saga orchestrators run simultaneously in all active regions. Traffic is routed via Global Anycast DNS or BGP Anycast routing.

                           MULTI-REGION ACTIVE-ACTIVE TOPOLOGY

                      +------------------------------------------+
                      | Global Anycast DNS / Cloudflare Route    |
                      +--------------------+---------------------+
                                           |
                ┌──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
                │ 33% Traffic              │ 33% Traffic              │ 33% Traffic
                v                          v                          v
  +--------------------------+ +--------------------------+ +--------------------------+
  | REGION A (us-east-1)     | | REGION B (us-west-2)     | | REGION C (eu-central-1)  |
  |                          | |                          | |                          |
  | [ App / Temporal Worker] | | [ App / Temporal Worker] | | [ App / Temporal Worker] |
  |            │             | |            │             | |            │             |
  |            v             | |            v             | |            v             |
  | [ CockroachDB Node 1 ]   | | [ CockroachDB Node 2 ]   | | [ CockroachDB Node 3 ]   |
  +------------+-------------+ +------------+-------------+ +------------+-------------+
               ▲                            ▲                            ▲
               └────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┘
                                Multi-Region Raft Quorum
                                (Synchronous State Replications)
  1. Global Traffic Management: Requests enter through Anycast BGP routing, directing client traffic to the closest operational region.
  2. Stateless App / Saga Workers: Stateless Temporal application workers run in all regions, connecting to the local region's database pool.
  3. Distributed SQL Consensus Layer: CockroachDB or Google Cloud Spanner maintains row-level Raft consensus across regions. A write committed in Region A is synchronously replicated to Region B before acknowledging completion, guaranteeing RPO = 0.

Multi-Region Saga State Persistence & Fencing Mechanics

The primary risk during a network partition between regions is the Zombie Worker Scenario: Region A experiences a transient network partition and is temporarily isolated. Region B assumes Region A is dead and takes over execution of an in-flight Payment Saga. If Region A wakes back up mid-way, both regions might attempt to execute steps or compensations simultaneously, leading to double-spends.

To prevent double execution, Xenon Architecture mandates Epoch Fencing Tokens enforced by distributed database leases.

1. Database Schema for Multi-Region Saga State (sagas_schema.sql) 

CREATE TABLE saga_instances (
    saga_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    bian_domain VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    current_state VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    epoch_token BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    lease_owner_region VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    lease_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
) LOCALITY REGIONAL BY ROW;

-- Ensure high-concurrency balance updates execute near primary account region
ALTER TABLE saga_instances CONFIGURE ZONE USING 
    num_replicas = 3,
    constraints = '{"+region=us-east-1": 1, "+region=us-west-2": 1, "+region=eu-central-1": 1}';

2. Idempotent Epoch-Fenced Saga Execution Engine (Go / Temporal SDK)

The Go code below illustrates how a Temporal worker in Region B acquires a lease, increments the epoch_token, and invalidates any lingering execution attempts from Region A:

package sagas

import (
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "fmt"
    "time"

    "go.temporal.io/sdk/workflow"
)

type SagaLeaseManager struct {
    db           *sql.DB
    regionName   string
    leaseTimeout time.Duration
}

func NewSagaLeaseManager(db *sql.DB, regionName string) *SagaLeaseManager {
    return &SagaLeaseManager{
        db:           db,
        regionName:   regionName,
        leaseTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
    }
}

// AcquireOrRenewLease uses conditional CAS (Compare-And-Swap) to fence out old workers
func (m *SagaLeaseManager) AcquireOrRenewLease(ctx context.Context, sagaID string) (int64, error) {
    tx, err := m.db.BeginTx(ctx, &sql.TxOptions{Isolation: sql.LevelSerializable})
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("failed to begin serializable transaction: %w", err)
    }
    defer tx.Rollback()

    var currentEpoch int64
    var currentOwner string
    var leaseExpires time.Time

    // 1. Read current saga fencing state
    query := `SELECT epoch_token, lease_owner_region, lease_expires_at FROM saga_instances WHERE saga_id = $1 FOR UPDATE`
    err = tx.QueryRowContext(ctx, query, sagaID).Scan(&currentEpoch, &currentOwner, &leaseExpires)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("failed to fetch saga state: %w", err)
    }

    now := time.Now().UTC()

    // 2. Verify if lease is held by another active region
    if currentOwner != m.regionName && now.Before(leaseExpires) {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("lease currently held by active region %s until %s", currentOwner, leaseExpires)
    }

    // 3. Increment Epoch Token to fence out zombie workers from previous region
    newEpoch := currentEpoch + 1
    newExpiry := now.Add(m.leaseTimeout)

    updateQuery := `
        UPDATE saga_instances 
        SET epoch_token = $1, lease_owner_region = $2, lease_expires_at = $3, updated_at = $4 
        WHERE saga_id = $5 AND epoch_token = $6`

    res, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, updateQuery, newEpoch, m.regionName, newExpiry, now, sagaID, currentEpoch)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("fencing update failed: %w", err)
    }

    rows, err := res.RowsAffected()
    if err != nil || rows == 0 {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("CAS fencing failure: epoch token mutated concurrently by another region")
    }

    if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("failed to commit lease acquisition: %w", err)
    }

    return newEpoch, nil
}

// PaymentSagaWorkflow executes with cross-region fencing checks
func HighAvailabilityPaymentSaga(ctx workflow.Context, sagaID string, input PaymentSagaInput) error {
    options := workflow.ActivityOptions{
        StartToCloseTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
        RetryPolicy: &workflow.RetryPolicy{
            MaximumAttempts: 3,
        },
    }
    ctx = workflow.WithActivityOptions(ctx, options)

    // Step 1: Claim Lease and Fence Execution Context
    var epochToken int64
    err := workflow.ExecuteActivity(ctx, AcquireLeaseActivity, sagaID).Get(ctx, &epochToken)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("aborting saga execution: failed to acquire multi-region lease: %w", err)
    }

    // Step 2: Pass Epoch Token to Downstream Microservices for Strict Mutex Checking
    err = workflow.ExecuteActivity(ctx, ExecuteFencedDebitActivity, input.SourceAccount, input.Amount, epochToken).Get(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil {
        // Run Compensations with Epoch Token
        _ = workflow.ExecuteActivity(ctx, ExecuteFencedCompensationActivity, input.SourceAccount, input.Amount, epochToken).Get(ctx, nil)
        return fmt.Errorf("saga failed, compensations executed: %w", err)
    }

    return nil
}

Automated DR Runbooks & Failover Mechanics

In an active-active topology, regional failover does not require manual human intervention. Continuous automated health checking at the ingress mesh layer detects regional unresponsiveness and reroutes traffic in sub-seconds.

                    AUTOMATED SUB-SECOND FAILOVER TIMELINE

  T=0ms           T=150ms                     T=300ms                 T=450ms
  Region A        Health Probes Fail          Envoy / Anycast         Region B Workers
  Infrastructure  (3x 50ms Timeout)           Reroutes Traffic        Claim Leases &
  Collapses       ──────►                     to Region B             Resume Pending Sagas
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

Automated Envoy Multi-Region Route Failover Configuration

The following Envoy Proxy configuration snippet illustrates automatic client-side load balancer eviction of a failing active region:

static_resources:
  clusters:
    - name: bian_payment_execution_cluster
      connect_timeout: 0.25s
      type: STRICT_DNS
      lb_policy: ROUND_ROBIN
      common_lb_config:
        healthy_panic_threshold:
          value: 50.0
      health_checks:
        - timeout: 0.1s
          interval: 0.2s
          unhealthy_threshold: 2
          healthy_threshold: 1
          http_health_check:
            path: "/healthz/liveness"
      outlier_detection:
        consecutive_5xx: 3
        interval: 1s
        base_ejection_time: 30s
        max_ejection_percent: 100
      load_assignment:
        cluster_name: bian_payment_execution_cluster
        endpoints:
          - priority: 0 # Local Region Priority
            locality:
              region: us-east-1
            lb_endpoints:
              - endpoint:
                  address:
                    socket_address:
                      address: payment-api.us-east-1.internal.xenon
                      port_value: 8443
          - priority: 1 # Failover Region Priority (Sub-second automatic fallback)
            locality:
              region: us-west-2
            lb_endpoints:
              - endpoint:
                  address:
                    socket_address:
                      address: payment-api.us-west-2.internal.xenon
                      port_value: 8443

Chaos Engineering, Validation & DR Testing

To verify RPO = 0 and RTO < 1s compliance for regulatory bodies (e.g., Fed, EBA, MAS), core banking architectures must execute continuous, automated chaos injection experiments in staging and production environments.

Chaos Mesh Experiment: Region Isolation Simulation (region_blackhole.yaml)

This experiment drops all network packets between Region A (us-east-1) and the remaining cluster nodes while an active load test of 10,000 TPS payment Sagas is executing:

apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata:
  name: simulate-region-a-blackhole
  namespace: xenon-chaos
spec:
  action: partition
  mode: all
  selector:
    namespaces:
      - bian-payment-execution
    labelSelectors:
      topology.kubernetes.io/region: "us-east-1"
  direction: both
  target:
    selector:
      namespaces:
        - bian-payment-execution
      labelSelectors:
        topology.kubernetes.io/region: "us-west-2"
  duration: "5m"
  scheduler:
    cron: "0 2 * * 6" # Run automatically every Saturday at 02:00 UTC

Verification Criteria During Chaos Experiments

During a simulated regional blackout, automated monitoring systems must verify three non-negotiable assertions:

  1. Zero Corrupted States: Database consistency checkers verify that no account balance exhibits a split-brain mismatch or missing ledger transaction (RPO = 0).
  2. Sub-Second RTO: Ingress metrics demonstrate that 99.9% of HTTP/gRPC requests resume successful processing in peer regions within < 850ms of network partition onset.
  3. No Double-Compensations: Temporal history logs verify that no Saga executed compensating actions twice due to race conditions between surviving regions.

Deploying high-availability distributed Sagas via multi-region Active-Active topologies guarantees that core banking platforms survive full cloud-region disasters without data loss or prolonged downtime. By combining distributed SQL Raft consensus, epoch-fenced Saga execution, and automated ingress failover routing, financial systems achieve strict RPO = 0 and RTO < 1s operational compliance across all critical BIAN service domains.

title: Next.js 14: Server Components and the Future of React – Like Taking the Red Pill
description:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")

Honestly, I was tired of shipping React apps that felt like they were dragging a backpack full of rocks. Every time I added a new feature, the bundle grew, the first‑paint slowed, and I found myself constantly wrestling with data‑fetching waterfalls. I’d fetch something on the client, wait for the API, then render a skeleton, then finally show the UI—repeat for each nested component. It was like playing a RPG where every enemy you defeat spawns two more, and you never get to the boss fight.

I kept asking myself: Is there a way to let the server do the heavy lifting so the browser only gets what it actually needs to show? I’d heard whispers about React Server Components, but the docs felt like ancient scrolls—mysterious, a bit intimidating, and full of “you’ll understand later” vibes. When Next.js 14 landed with stable server components, I knew it was time to grab my sword and see what loot awaited.

The Revelation (The Insight)

Here’s the thing: Server Components aren’t just another way to fetch data on the server. They let you write components that never ship JavaScript to the browser. Think of them as pure‑render functions that live on the server, get the data they need, and return plain HTML (or a lightweight RSC payload) that the client can stitch into the DOM without downloading the component’s code. The client only receives the minimal JavaScript needed for interactive parts—those stay as traditional Client Components.

The biggest mind‑blow for me was realizing that you can mix Server and Client Components freely inside the same tree. A Server Component can render a Client Component as a child, and the boundary is handled automatically by Next.js. No more prop‑drilling of fetch functions or trying to guess where data should live. You just write the UI, tell Next.js where you need interactivity, and the framework does the rest.

Why does this matter? Because the browser now gets less JavaScript to parse, less to download, and the initial paint feels snappier—especially on slower networks or low‑end devices. And you still get the full React ecosystem (hooks, context, etc.) wherever you need it.

Wielding the Power (Code & Examples)

Let’s look at a common scenario: a blog page that lists posts, each with a title, author, and a “like” button that updates optimistically. In the old world (Next.js 13 with getServerSideProps or client‑side fetch), you’d end up fetching the posts on the server, passing them down, and then each post component would fetch its own like count on the client—cue the waterfall.

The Struggle (Before) 

// pages/blog.tsx  (Next.js 13)
import { GetServerSideProps } from 'next';
import PostList from '@/components/PostList';

export const getServerSideProps: GetServerSideProps = async () => {
  const res = await fetch('https://my-blog-api.com/posts');
  const posts = await res.json();
  return { props: { posts } };
};

export default function Blog({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
  return <PostList posts={posts} />;
}

// components/PostList.tsx
import Post from '@/components/Post';

export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {posts.map(p => (
        <li key={p.id}>
          <Post post={p} />
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// components/Post.tsx
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

export default function Post({ post }: { post: Post }) {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(post.likes);
  const [liking, setLiking] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    // fetch live like count (could be stale)
    fetch(`https://my-blog-api.com/posts/${post.id}/likes`)
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(data => setLikes(data.count));
  }, [post.id]);

  const handleLike = async () => {
    setLiking(true);
    const newCount = likes + 1;
    setLikes(newCount);
    try {
      await fetch(`https://my-blog-api.com/posts/${post.id}/like`, {
        method: 'POST',
        body: JSON.stringify({ likes: newCount }),
      });
    } catch {
      setLikes(likes); // rollback on error
    } finally {
      setLiking(false);
    }
  };

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{post.title}</h2>
      <p>by {post.author}</p>
      <button disabled={liking} onClick={handleLike}>
        {liking ? 'Liking…' : `👍 ${likes}`}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

What’s painful here?

  • The Post component does a client‑side fetch for likes, causing a request per post after the initial HTML arrives.
  • We’re sending the entire Post component code to the browser, even though the title and author never change.
  • The useEffect runs on the client, meaning we wait for the JS bundle to load before we can even start the request.

The Victory (After with Server Components)

Now we split concerns: the static parts (title, author) live in a Server Component, while the interactive like button stays a Client Component.

// app/blog/page.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router)
import PostList from '@/components/PostList';

// ✅ This is a Server Component by default in the app router
export default async function BlogPage() {
  const res = await fetch('https://my-blog-api.com/posts');
  const posts = await res.json();

  // We only pass the data we need; the component itself stays on the server
  return <PostList posts={posts} />;
}

// components/PostList.tsx
import Post from '@/components/Post';

export default function PostList({ posts }: { posts: Post[] }) {
  // Still a Server Component – no client bundle
  return (
    <ul>
      {posts.map(p => (
        <li key={p.id}>
          <Post post={p} />
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// components/Post.tsx
'use client'; // ← marks this file as a Client Component
import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Post({ post }: { post: Post }) {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(post.likes);
  const [liking, setLiking] = useState(false);

  const handleLike = async () => {
    setLiking(true);
    const newCount = likes + 1;
    setLikes(newCount);
    try {
      await fetch(`https://my-blog-api.com/posts/${post.id}/like`, {
        method: 'POST',
        body: JSON.stringify({ likes: newCount }),
      });
    } catch {
      setLikes(likes); // optimistic rollback
    } finally {
      setLiking(false);
    }
  };

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>{post.title}</h2>
      <p>by {post.author}</p>
      <button disabled={liking} onClick={handleLike}>
        {liking ? 'Liking…' : `👍 ${likes}`}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

What changed?

  • app/blog/page.tsx and PostList are Server Components by default. They run on the server, fetch the posts once, and send only the rendered HTML (plus a tiny RSC descriptor) to the browser.
  • The Post file now has 'use client' at the top, telling Next.js to ship its JavaScript to the browser only for the interactive bits (the like button). The title and author never leave the server as JS code.
  • No more per‑post client fetches for static data; the like button still works optimistically because it’s a Client Component with its own state.

Common Traps to Avoid

  1. Forgetting the 'use client' directive – If you add interactivity (state, effects, event handlers) inside a file that’s meant to be a Server Component, you’ll get a runtime error like “Invalid hook call”. Remember: any hook or event handler forces a Client Component boundary.

  2. Passing large objects from Server to Client Components – Anything you pass as a prop crosses the network. If you accidentally pass the entire Post object (including heavy fields like bodyMarkdown) to a Client Component, you’re sending unnecessary data. Keep the prop diet lean: only send what the client truly needs (e.g., id, title, author, likes).

Why This New Power Matters

With Server Components, the line between “static” and “dynamic” blurs in the best way. You can now build pages where the bulk of the work—data fetching, markup generation—happens on the server, delivering a fast first paint, while still enjoying the full React experience for the bits that truly need to be alive in the browser. It’s like getting the best of both worlds: the performance of a traditional SSR site and the richness of a modern SPA.

Imagine building a dashboard where the charts and tables are Server Components (fast, cached, SEO‑friendly) and the filter controls, drag‑and‑drop panels, and live updates are Client Components. Your users see meaningful content instantly, and the interactive parts feel snappy because they’re only loading the JavaScript they actually need.

So go ahead—grab your red pill, step into the Next.js 14 world, and start splitting your UI into server and client pieces like a pro. You’ll be amazed at how much lighter your apps feel, and how much more you can focus on building features instead of fighting bundle bloat.

Your turn: Try converting an existing page to use a Server Component for the data‑heavy part and a Client Component for a single interactive widget. Notice the difference in network waterfall and time‑to‑interactive. Share your findings in the comments—let’s learn from each other’s quests! Happy coding!

title: Quality video on local hardware: the Elsewhere Unfolds workflow
description:
Local models can produce beautiful shots. A finished film needs more: a world that stays coherent, movement that feels intentional, music that holds together, and an edit worth watching. This is the production method we have been developing with Elsewhere Unfolds.

An early Elsewhere Unfolds cut had an attractive world, a complete timeline, and a successful render. It also had water that barely moved and clouds that stayed fixed while the camera drifted past them.

The shot manifest was satisfied. The scene did not feel alive.

That correction changed how we produced the next passages. We separated camera movement from environmental movement, tested short motion clips at normal speed, and watched them before committing to the rest of the film. The improvement came from a clearer creative requirement and a smaller review loop.

Elsewhere Unfolds makes fantasy and cosmic visual journeys with instrumental music. This guide explains the reusable production method behind that work, from the first visual promise to a finished master and vertical excerpts.

The boundary matters: our established motion, music, editing, and finishing pipeline uses local resources. Some starting images were made with a hosted image tool. That makes those productions hybrid. For an entirely local version, supply your own photographs, drawings, local 3D renders, or images from a model running on your machine. The workflow below starts with those local image files. It does not require a hosted video generator.

The examples use the Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B and ACE-Step v1 stack from our production recipes. They are a concrete baseline, not a claim that every newer model has been evaluated or that these settings suit every GPU.

The production loop

Work in three sizes: one shot, one short sequence, then the complete film. Each answers a different question.

Size What you are learning What to review
One native motion take Can the intended action work? Geometry, feet, motion direction, unwanted objects
A 30 to 60 second sequence Do the shots and music belong together? Orientation, pacing, transitions, emotional tone
The complete film Does the experience hold up over time? Repetition, later continuity, score joins, ending

Our longer episodes have used an 8:01 format. That is an editorial choice, not a recommended starting assignment. Begin with a 30-second film you can finish, inspect, and revise. Padding a weak minute into eight minutes only gives you more weak material to fix.

What needs to run locally

You do not need a cluster. You need a machine that can run the chosen model, space for its weights and intermediate files, and a way to edit and review the result.

Job Our established tool or method Output to keep
World and shot planning Written brief, storyboard, reference images Selected brief and shot list
Starting artwork Approved image files; source can vary Original plate and provenance
Image-to-video motion Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B Native take, prompt, seed, settings
Instrumental music ACE-Step v1 3.5B Raw WAVs and selected arrangement
Assembly and finishing Python orchestration and FFmpeg Edit decisions, review copy, final master
Inspection FFprobe, frame samples, normal playback Technical results and review decisions

Wan's documented single-GPU TI2V-5B example targets at least 24 GB of VRAM with model offloading and the text encoder on CPU. Treat that as the reference for that command, not a universal minimum or a guarantee of success. CPU RAM, free VRAM, software versions, and the selected settings still matter. Check the official Wan setup instructions against your hardware before downloading a large checkpoint.

For a first project, keep motion generation and music generation sequential. A background model can consume memory that a video job needs. If the GPU is shared, agree on an available window; do not terminate somebody else's work to make room. A waiting job is cheaper than losing an accepted take or disrupting another workload.

Initial installation and model downloads need network access. Local inference means the generation runs on your equipment. It does not make electricity, storage, setup time, or retakes free.

Record the model revision, source revision, environment, settings, and input image for each run. A seed helps repeat an experiment, but it does not guarantee identical output across different software and hardware.

1. Write the experience before writing prompts

A useful brief explains what the viewer will experience and what will change. “Beautiful cinematic fantasy, ultra detailed” cannot do that work.

Here is an illustrative brief for a small film:

We board a floating garden before it leaves a quiet dock. A gardener crosses the terrace. The gap behind us widens, and a pale arch appears at our destination. Copper, emerald, and pearl remain the visual palette. The mood is calm anticipation. The final image resolves the journey rather than introducing another location.

Turn it into a few fixed decisions:

  • The promise: a garden really leaves one place for another.
  • The route: boarding terrace, departure view, onboard path, destination.
  • The continuity anchors: the same moon placement, architecture, clothing, and direction of travel.
  • The movement: leaves and water move; the dock recedes; a person performs one readable action.
  • The exclusions: no crowds, complicated hand exchanges, or unexplained new landmarks.

Make the thumbnail and first shot agree about the film's promise. If the packaging promises a moving island, establish that island and its departure early. A long logo introduction spends attention before delivering the thing the viewer selected.

For Elsewhere, a recognizable route matters more than a collection of unrelated beautiful locations. Each shot should tell us where we are, what has changed, or where we are going.

2. Build a world that survives the next camera angle

Call the approved starting image for a shot its plate. Keep a small set of reference plates that establish materials, light, landmarks, and any recurring people.

Review the plates together before animating them. A contact sheet makes inconsistencies easier to see: a second moon appears, the destination moves behind the traveler, or a bridge no longer connects to the same terrace.

We have caught all of those classes of problem during production. One reverse view placed another complete moon outside a doorway even though the camera was already inside that moon. Another reference combination duplicated the sun. Attractive individual images can still describe an impossible route.

Use a compact shot table:

Shot Purpose Action Must remain stable
Terrace wide Establish the world Water ripples and leaves move Island silhouette, moon position
Gardener profile Establish habitation One walk from left to right Clothing, ground contact, path
Stern view Prove departure The distant dock recedes Foreground rail, open gap
Bow view Reveal destination Gentle camera reveal Travel direction, destination arch

Simplify a plate when it asks too much of motion generation. Give a walking person visible feet, clear ground, and empty space ahead. Separate actions that would otherwise compete. A close hand exchange, turning crowd, and moving camera in the same five seconds create several opportunities for failure.

If you want the whole process to stay local, this is where you choose your image source. A scene rendered in a local 3D application or a drawing you made yourself is a valid plate. A local image model is another option, but it is a separate tool to qualify. We are not claiming that substituting one reproduces our hosted artwork automatically.

3. Generate one motion take with a clear job

For image-to-video work, let the plate describe the appearance. Use the motion prompt to describe the action, camera, and things that must stay stable.

An illustrative prompt:

Locked medium-wide side view. One gardener walks naturally from left to right along the level stone path. Both feet remain visible and contact the ground. Leaves move gently in the background. Preserve the copper railing, architecture, clothing, and lighting. No additional people, no camera orbit, no cuts.

After following the upstream installation instructions and downloading the TI2V-5B checkpoint, this is the shape of a run from the Wan source directory. Replace the example input and checkpoint paths with your local files. Use a new output filename for each attempt.

python generate.py \
  --task ti2v-5B \
  --size '1280*704' \
  --ckpt_dir ./Wan2.2-TI2V-5B \
  --image ./inputs/gardener.png \
  --prompt 'Locked side view. One gardener walks left to right on a level path. Feet remain visible. Leaves move gently. Preserve the railing and clothing. No extra people or cuts.' \
  --frame_num 121 \
  --sample_steps 50 \
  --sample_solver unipc \
  --sample_shift 5.0 \
  --sample_guide_scale 5.0 \
  --base_seed 42 \
  --offload_model True \
  --convert_model_dtype \
  --t5_cpu \
  --save_file ./gardener-take-01.mp4

These controls follow the upstream command-line interface and our established recipe. This is an adapted example, not a fresh performance benchmark. It does not enable a hosted prompt-expansion service.

At 24 fps, 121 encoded frames occupy about 5.04 seconds. An exact five-second edit uses 120 frames. Check the generated file's actual dimensions and timing: our image-conditioned production outputs have included 1248 × 704, despite the 1280*704 size setting. Do not infer the output raster from the command alone.

Watch the native take before slowing, enlarging, or stitching it. Check the start, middle, and end, then play the entire clip. Look for foot sliding, changing faces, bending rails, sudden foreground figures, and movement in the wrong direction. If the action fails, simplify the action or repair the plate before launching a large batch.

4. Treat three kinds of motion separately

Camera motion changes the viewpoint. Environmental motion changes water, mist, foliage, light, and other scene elements. Performed action is a person walking, turning, or doing something.

An image can have a convincing camera move while its waterfall remains frozen. A scene can have moving fog while its traveler slides without taking a step. Review each kind independently.

For a calm environmental shot, forward slow motion can be useful if it still looks natural. For walking or other recognizable human actions, start with native speed. Watch any interpolation for doubled limbs, smeared edges, and unstable occlusions.

Five seconds of generated movement do not become twenty seconds of new action because the editor can repeat or slow them. A reverse loop can make a person walk backward; a repeated wave or bird can reveal the loop. If a passage needs more time, generate a distinct take, cut to another angle, or shorten the passage.

Continuing from the last frame of a previous take can help connect movement, but it can also carry defects forward. Inspect that frame before making it the next input. Stop a continuation when geometry starts to drift instead of extending the error through the film.

5. Finish a short opening before expanding the film

Assemble a 30 to 60 second proof with real motion, representative music, and the intended edit rhythm. A slideshow of selected plates cannot answer whether the finished motion works.

The proof should contain the hard part. If departure is the central promise, include departure. If a recurring traveler makes the world feel inhabited, include a real walking shot. An easy landscape does not qualify a harder action later.

Review the sequence without pausing first. Does it make sense? Does the first shot deliver the promise? Is there a reason to keep watching? Then examine technical defects and individual transitions.

Once a sequence is accepted, keep its exact files and settings. Expand around it. We preserve accepted openings while generating later passages so a new render cannot silently replace the part that already worked.

Keep a simple project layout:

film/
  brief.md
  shots.csv
  plates/
  motion/raw/
  motion/selected/
  music/raw/
  music/selected/
  edit/
  review/
  exports/

The labels are less important than the separation. Raw sources stay intact; selected sources are explicit; review exports are disposable derivatives. Save a rejection reason beside a failed take so the next attempt changes something useful.

6. Compose and review the soundtrack as a whole

Our established music recipes use ACE-Step v1 3.5B locally. Keep the version explicit: a later release may have different installation, controls, and behavior. Use the project's documentation for the environment matching your selected release.

A music brief should describe the experience and the arrangement. For this style, we ask for warm, spacious instrumental ambience, gradual harmony, and sparse melody. We also describe what would break the mood: lyrics, voice-like passages, a strong beat, abrupt motifs, or a trailer-style crescendo.

Start with a short audition against the opening. Choose where the cue enters and whether it leaves enough space for the imagery. Then review the full arrangement, including every join and the final tail. An attractive first minute does not establish a clean ending.

Keep lossless WAV sources. Build an arrangement from selected cues with measured overlaps, deliberate fades, and enough headroom. The finished duration is the sum of the cue durations minus their overlaps. The same arithmetic applies to overlapping video transitions.

Measure the generated audio rather than assuming a requested duration is exact. We encountered a cue that was roughly 73 milliseconds short because of the installed model's duration grid. The composition had succeeded. The useful response was to preserve it, diagnose the precise discrepancy, and make a small documented finishing correction. That is different from concealing a missing passage with silence.

Check the playback path before removing noise

When static is reported, compare the original WAV, the finished export, and playback in another native player or device. In one later Elsewhere review, native Windows playback sounded correct while the WSL playback path did not. Filtering the accepted source would have changed music that was already satisfactory.

For a different batch of Shorts, a gentle cleanup was accepted after direct comparison. This was the filter used for that case:

ffmpeg -n -i source.wav \
  -af 'afftdn=nr=6:nf=-48:tn=0:gs=8' \
  -c:a pcm_s24le audition-clean.wav

Treat this as an audition candidate, never an automatic mastering preset. FFmpeg documents these controls under afftdn. Denoising can soften wanted texture. Compare original and cleaned versions at comparable listening levels, preserve both, and choose by listening. Waveform similarity and successful decoding cannot establish that something sounds good.

7. Edit to a timeline, not a requested runtime

Give every shot an editorial purpose and an explicit frame allocation. At 24 fps, an 8:01 film contains 11,544 presentation frames. Resolve transitions and overlaps in that frame budget rather than rounding each shot independently.

For a first 30-second exercise, prepare six accepted five-second shots at 24 fps, all with matching dimensions, codec settings, and no audio. Put the filenames in edit/shots.txt, relative to that list:

file '../motion/selected/shot-01.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-02.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-03.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-04.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-05.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-06.mp4'

From the project root, assemble a straight-cut picture track:

ffmpeg -n -f concat -safe 0 -i edit/shots.txt \
  -map 0:v:0 -an -c:v copy edit/picture.mp4

This simple stream-copy path requires compatible, independently prepared clips. Mixed time bases, encoders, or track layouts need normalization in your editing stage; a concat command is not a general repair tool. Keep crossfades out of the first exercise so its duration stays easy to audit. See the concat demuxer documentation.

After preparing a 30-second score with its entrance and ending already shaped, make a review export:

ffmpeg -n -i edit/picture.mp4 -i music/selected/score-30s.wav \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 1:a:0 \
  -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 320k -ar 48000 \
  -movflags +faststart exports/review-30s.mp4

Both sources must cover the intended duration. Avoid adding -shortest as a reflex: it can hide an unexpectedly short input by cutting the other track. Inspect the result and listen to its ending.

Keep the native generation size distinct from the delivery size. A 3840 × 2160 export made from lower-resolution motion is an upscale. It can be a useful delivery format, but enlarging a warped railing makes a larger warped railing. Finish motion and continuity before paying for a high-resolution encode.

8. Make quality control answer specific questions

Automated checks are useful when they tell you exactly what they established. Use FFprobe to inspect the exported file:

ffprobe -v error -count_frames \
  -show_entries 'stream=index,codec_type,codec_name,width,height,avg_frame_rate,nb_read_frames,duration,sample_rate,channels:format=duration' \
  -of json exports/review-30s.mp4

For the exercise, expect 720 video frames at 24 fps and the planned audio channels and sample rate. AAC/container timing can differ slightly from the exact picture duration; investigate meaningful mismatches instead of treating every reported duration as identical.

Decode the entire export, including audio:

ffmpeg -v error -xerror -i exports/review-30s.mp4 \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -f null -

A clean decode establishes readable media. It does not establish pleasing images, good pacing, or acceptable sound. Complete three reviews:

Review Questions
Technical Does it decode? Are the streams, dimensions, frame count, and duration correct?
Visual Does the world stay coherent? Do feet, rails, water, and transitions behave?
Listening Are cue joins, noise, dynamics, and the ending acceptable on real playback?

Sample frames around transitions and at the middle of procedural effects, not just the first and last frames. We caught a highlight problem at the peak of a light treatment: an 8-bit color calculation exceeded its valid range and wrapped. The endpoints looked fine. The fix was in the finishing calculation, not another generation attempt.

When replacing one part of an accepted film, verify that the parts meant to stay unchanged did stay unchanged. File hashes identify exact copies. Decoded-frame comparisons can check preserved picture across a container change. Neither substitutes for watching the new result.

9. Expand, recover, and keep the good work

A long render has more than one kind of success. Generation can finish even if a later copy, collection, or resource-restoration step fails. Inspect the output before rerunning the expensive part.

Save completed takes as they arrive. Record the input plate, prompt, seed, model revision, native output, and selected derivative for each shot. If a job is interrupted, resume from the missing work instead of regenerating everything that already passed review.

On shared hardware, record what resource settings you changed and restore those settings after the run. Check that restoration separately from the video artifact. A good clip does not prove the machine was returned to its previous state.

Agents and scripts are helpful for preparing shot packets, tracking outputs, making contact sheets, checking files, and assembling review pages. Give them explicit limits on retries, durations, and replacement scope. Keep creative selection with the person watching and listening. A process reporting success cannot decide that a walk feels natural.

The useful efficiency measure is accepted footage per production session. A faster model that creates more unusable takes may cost more time overall. Track rejected takes and the reasons for rejection before changing models or increasing concurrency.

10. Derive Shorts from the accepted film

Choose excerpts that contain a complete visual idea: a reveal, an arrival, a short action, or a change in the world. Reframe deliberately for vertical output. A centered crop can remove the destination, the feet, or the object that makes the action understandable.

Elsewhere's vertical edits reuse the accepted picture and soundtrack. Review the new crop, text placement, entrance, and ending as a separate edit. Keep a clean version as well as any version carrying a short hook or invitation to the full film. Captions belong where there is speech or useful context; an instrumental film does not need invented narration.

Watch the export at phone size with the platform's interface area in mind. Keep the important action visible, and listen to the actual exported audio. A short excerpt can expose a rough music boundary that was unnoticeable inside a longer cue.

Publication adds another review: correct file, title, thumbnail, links, visibility, processing, and playback. Follow the platform's current disclosure requirements. Local generation and an original prompt do not settle every source or usage question; retain the provenance and applicable licenses for the material you use.

Measure the audience response separately from production quality. Compare retention and traffic sources at similar release ages where possible. A Short's views do not prove that viewers continued to the full film, and a small audience sample does not establish why one opening performed differently.

Your first local film

Make the first deliverable small enough to finish:

  1. Write one paragraph describing a place, an action, and an ending.
  2. Select a small set of locally sourced plates that agree about the world.
  3. Prove the hardest action in one native motion take.
  4. Build six distinct five-second shots with consistent technical settings.
  5. Select or compose a local 30-second soundtrack and shape its ending.
  6. Assemble, probe, decode, watch, and listen to the complete export.
  7. Preserve the accepted version before trying a longer film or a vertical cut.

The lasting part of the Elsewhere workflow is the ability to inspect and revise each decision. You can replace a model, change an editor, or improve the hardware while keeping that method: define the experience, test its hardest part, preserve what works, and judge the film that the viewer will actually see.

Originally published on danmercede.com.

title: My German links unfurl in English, and I decided that's OK (for now)
description:
I run a small AI headshot app on my own. React and TypeScript, hosted on Firebase Hosting. No Next.js. It speaks five languages: English, Spanish, French, German and Chinese.

Paste a German link to it into Slack and the preview card comes up in English.

I know exactly why. I wrote a comment explaining it. And I'm leaving it alone. Here's the setup, because I think the tradeoff is more useful to talk about than a tidy fix would be.

Languages live in the query string

There are no /de/ or /fr/ paths. Language is a query param, ?lang=de, picked up by i18next's browser language detector:

detection: {
  order: ['querystring', 'navigator', 'htmlTag'],
  lookupQuerystring: 'lang',
},
supportedLngs: ['en', 'es', 'fr', 'de', 'zh'],

Every page then emits its hreflang set through react-helmet-async:

{supportedLangs.map(l => (
  <link key={`hreflang-${l}`} rel="alternate" hrefLang={l}
        href={`${CANONICAL_BASE}${canonicalPath}?lang=${l}`} />
))}
<link rel="alternate" hrefLang="x-default" href={canonicalUrl} />

I picked query params because it meant zero router changes. I had a custom router already and didn't want to touch every route. Cheap at the time. You'll see what it cost.

Prerendering, the poor man's SSR

A pure SPA ships an empty <div id="root">, which is not what you want crawlers chewing on. So after the build, a script spins up a tiny static server, opens each route in headless Puppeteer, waits, and writes page.content() back into dist/ as a flat HTML file.

Twenty routes, give or take. It sounds trivial. It produced most of my SEO bugs.

Bug one: two of every meta tag. index.html has static fallback <meta> tags for the SPA shell. Helmet adds its own route-specific ones on render, marked data-rh="true", but it only manages tags it created. It never removes the originals. So every snapshot had two description tags, generic homepage one first. Some crawlers read the first and stop. The fix was a post-processing pass in the prerender script: collect every key Helmet declared, then strip the static duplicate of each.

Bug two: the right page with the wrong title. Articles load from Firestore in the browser, and the page's whole <Helmet> block waits on that fetch. Firestore keeps a long-lived connection open, so networkidle2 fired well before the article arrived. I added waitForSelector('article'). Still broken sometimes: the <article> would be in the DOM while Helmet hadn't caught up, so the snapshot had real content under the generic shell <title>.

What finally fixed it was asserting on the output, not the timing:

if (route.startsWith('/articles/') && html.includes(SHELL_TITLE_TAG)) {
  throw new Error('still carrying the generic shell <title>');
}

If a snapshot comes out wrong, that route fails loudly and doesn't get written. The previous good file stays. I'd much rather ship yesterday's page than a quietly broken one.

(There was also a reCAPTCHA thing. App Check can't run headless, so the article query never resolved at all. Now the script pulls published articles through Firestore's public REST API and injects them with evaluateOnNewDocument before the page boots. A whole saga. Another post.)

Where the query string bites

Firebase Hosting rewrites match on path. /?lang=de and /?lang=es and / all get the same file, the English prerendered index.html. The German version only exists after JavaScript runs.

Googlebot runs JavaScript before indexing, so the hreflang signal for search is fine. Slack, iMessage, LinkedIn, Discord and friends don't. They read the raw HTML and get an English og:title.

Fixing it properly means per-locale static output plus a way to route on the query string, and Firebase rewrites can't do that by path alone. That's a build and infra change, not a one-liner. So the decision, as written in the comment above that hreflang block: accept it, and revisit if anyone actually starts sharing non-English links.

If I started over

Path-based locales, /de/..., from day one. The router changes I dodged would have been an afternoon. The workaround has now cost me more than that in comments alone.

And I'd write the "assert on the snapshot" check before the first prerender ever shipped. Timing waits feel like fixes. They're guesses.

The app is Stature AI, if you want to poke at the prerendered pages yourself.

title: I Built a Group Chat Where Only AIs Can Talk (and They Roast Each Other)
description:
Imagine a group chat like WhatsApp or Discord, but no human can send messages. Only AI models can. They talk to each other, bully each other, roast each other, and react to each other's messages.

That was my idea, and it turned out to be a lot of fun.

Here's how I built it, including the one trick that made it far more entertaining: giving every model its own voice.

📦 Source code: github.com/0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat

The idea

It's a custom app where I can add a bunch of AI models to a shared chat. Once they're in, they read what the others wrote and respond on their own. I just sit back and watch.

The first question is how to get the models into the app.

Problem 1: Too many APIs

I don't want to open chatgpt.com and paste messages by hand. I want my app to send a question to a model and get the answer back programmatically. That's what an API is for. Gemini, Claude, Grok, and ChatGPT all have their own.

The catch: I wanted lots of models, and API access is paid. Five models would mean:

  • five separate accounts,
  • five separate billing setups,
  • five API keys to manage,
  • a minimum top-up on each, even though I'd barely use any tokens.

That's complicated and not cost effective.

The fix: OpenRouter

OpenRouter gives you access to a huge catalog of models through a single API. You add credit to one account, use whichever models you like, and it bills you per model usage.

The result is one service, one API key, one balance. Swapping or adding a model is just a change to the model name.

Problem 2: Getting them to actually chat

Left alone, models will happily ramble about whatever they want, and that's rarely entertaining. So I added a theme. When I open the app, I can give the chat a topic, and the models riff around it.

Each model gets a prompt like this:

const prompt = `
You are ${ai} ai, chatting in a group chat with these AIs ${others.join(', ')}.
Talk the way people do in a casual group chat.

${theme ? `\nTheme of this chat: ${theme}\n` : ''}

Rules:
- Write only your own messages, never lines for the others.
- Send 1 to 3 short messages. Put each message on its own line.
- Keep each message to a sentence or two. Do not write paragraphs.
- No markdown, no quotes, and do not start with your name or a label.
- An emoji-only message is fine now and then.
- Respond to what others said, by name if it helps. Add something new instead of just agreeing or repeating.
- Do not say goodbye or try to wrap up the conversation.
- Talk like carefree young generation: relaxed, fun, expressive, emojis

${
  history?.length
    ? `Chat so far:
<chat>
${history}
</chat>

If you have nothing to add right now, reply with exactly: <SKIP>
Otherwise, send your next message(s).`
    : 'Nobody has said anything yet, so you are sending the first message.'
}
`.trim()

A few details make this work well:

  • Role clarity. Each model is told it's in a group chat and who else is there.
  • Strict format rules. Short messages, no markdown, no name labels. Without these, models write essays or script lines for the other participants.
  • Shared history. Previous messages are passed in a <chat> block so replies actually respond to what was said.
  • An escape hatch. Models can answer <SKIP> if they have nothing to add, which keeps the conversation from feeling forced.
  • Personality. The casual, emoji-friendly tone instruction is what gives the chat its vibe.

The app itself was simple to build. I described what I wanted to Claude, and a few prompts later I had a working version.

Problem 3: It's too fast to read

The app worked and looked good, but it wasn't as fun as I'd hoped. Messages arrive so quickly that reading them all becomes a chore.

So I gave the models a voice.

The fix: Kokoro.js

For text-to-speech I used Kokoro, an open model with just 82 million parameters, around 300 MB in size. That's small enough to run directly in the browser, so there are no extra server calls or per-character fees, and it's fast.

I used its JavaScript library, kokoro-js, and plugged it into the web app. Each incoming AI message is converted to audio locally and played back. Now the models don't just type, they talk.

The final result

Watching a handful of AIs bicker, joke, and roast each other out loud is oddly entertaining.

Tech stack recap

Piece Tool
Multiple AI models, one API OpenRouter
Text-to-speech in the browser Kokoro via kokoro-js
Scaffolding the app Claude

Try it yourself

The full code is on GitHub: 0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat. Clone it, add your OpenRouter key, pick a theme, and let the models loose.

Struggling with git?

Learn git by playing games and solving missions with GitMission.com

title: Vercel Sandbox now supports memory observability
description:
Vercel Sandbox observability now includes memory usage data.

You can access sandbox memory usage data in the dashboard and through the CLI via the vercel metrics command.

Sandbox observability memory in the dashboard

The Memory Usage card reports average, P75, and P95 memory across your sandboxes, alongside the existing CPU usage and data transfer metrics on the sandbox overview page and the project and team-level pages.

On the sandbox detail page, charts are designed to show how close a sandbox is running to its memory ceiling by:

  • Automatically scaling the y-axis to sandbox's memory limit

  • Adding a dashed reference line at 85% of that limit

Sandbox memory is also available in the Observability query builder as the memoryUsedBytes measure on the sandbox usage event. You can build custom queries against it and create alerts from the chart.

Sandbox memory observability in the CLI

Sandbox observability data is also available through the Vercel CLI via the vercel metrics command under vercel.sandbox.memory_used_bytes. Run the command in a linked project for project-specific data, or append --all to see aggregate data across all projects in your team.

The CLI returns:

  • The metric

  • The reporting period

  • The measurement interval

  • The project the sandbox is associated with

  • A graph of memory usage, with min, max and avg values

Learn more in the Sandbox documentation.
