title: Test document extraction before an agent acts on it
description:
An agent can follow its instructions perfectly and still pay the wrong amount, because the parser misread a table in the invoice. The agent never sees the PDF, only the extraction. If that step is wrong, everything downstream is confidently wrong too.

Jerry Liu, co-founder and CEO of LlamaIndex, made this point in a June 2026 episode. A parser that represents a table wrong, or hallucinates at a meaningful rate, puts a workflow below the accuracy bar you can operate with, and the downstream agent workflow gets disrupted. His bar for the use cases he sees:

And so a lot of these require really high accuracy, 95% plus, especially in more sensitive use cases, with human-in-the-loop review on some of the extracted data.

Jerry Liu, co-founder and CEO of LlamaIndex, on Chain of Thought ep 61

He was describing what those customers need, so set your own bar per field from what a wrong value costs you. The practical move is to treat extraction as a pipeline stage with its own tests, measured on the fields your agent consumes.

Label a small set of real documents

Pick the document types you plan to support and hand-label a few dozen real examples of each. Include the ugly layouts along with the clean ones. Hold some back and don't look at them while you tune prompts or rules.

Label fields, not documents. For an invoice, the amount due and the due date may need a much higher bar than a free-text note, and a single overall score hides that. Decide the missing-value rules up front: a field that isn't in the document has an expected value of None, while a field the extractor fails to return counts as wrong.

Compare values in a canonical form. Normalize dates and currency, but be careful: stripping punctuation from an ID can turn two different IDs into the same string.

Illustrative sketch, not a production library or anyone's actual implementation. extract_fields(doc) is a hypothetical function that returns a dict.

from collections import defaultdict


def evaluate(cases, extract_fields):
    scores = defaultdict(lambda: {"correct": 0, "tested": 0, "misses": []})
    for case in cases:
        predicted = extract_fields(case["document"])
        for field, expected in case["gold"].items():
            s = scores[(case["doc_type"], field)]
            s["tested"] += 1
            if field in predicted and predicted[field] == expected:
                s["correct"] += 1
            else:
                s["misses"].append((case["id"], predicted.get(field)))
    return {
        key: {**s, "accuracy": s["correct"] / s["tested"]}
        for key, s in scores.items()
    }

Report accuracy per document type and field, with the tested count next to it. A perfect score on eight invoices says very little. Keep the misses, too. Seeing which cell got confused for which gives you something concrete to fix, and rerunning the held-out set after each change shows you what regressed.

Turn the scores into a review gate

An offline score tells you how the extractor does on labelled documents. It can't tell you whether a new document's values are right, because production documents arrive without labels. So use the eval to decide what may run unattended, then check each incoming document against that.

Condition What happens
Document type has no eval coverage Hold the whole document for review
Field's measured accuracy is below its bar Review that field for that document type
Required field missing or fails a format check Block the actions that depend on it
Values break a business rule (line items don't sum to the total) Show the values and the source region to a reviewer

Scope the hold to what depends on the bad value, so one disputed total doesn't freeze unrelated work. Show reviewers the extracted value next to the source passage or image region. Store the correction and feed adjudicated examples back into the labelled set, keeping a separate held-out set. Sample some auto-accepted documents too, since errors that pass every rule are the ones you won't otherwise see.

Store extracted facts with their review status

Extraction output often ends up as memory, and a wrong value saved for later can outlive the run that produced it. Liu's take on memory is deliberately simple. He described it as a form of persistent context and pointed to files as a starting point:

And so this concept of having memory just be a pool of files on your file system is kind of nice to think about because it's pretty easy to represent and store.

Jerry Liu, co-founder and CEO of LlamaIndex, on Chain of Thought ep 61

He was clear that he hasn't spent a ton of time building more complicated memory systems, so treat it as a place to start. For an extraction pipeline, it suggests a simple rule: keep candidates and accepted facts in separate places. Each record carries its source reference, its review status, and the extractor version that produced it. An agent can write candidates but can't promote them to accepted. When a reviewer corrects a value, mark the old one superseded instead of overwriting it, so you can trace where it came from.

Takeaway

Before an agent acts on extracted data:

  • Label real documents per type and define comparison rules per field.
  • Report per-field accuracy with sample counts and keep the misses.
  • Route uncovered document types and weak fields to a human.
  • Store extracted facts with their source, status and extractor version.

The full conversation, with the transcript, is on Chain of Thought.

Drafted with AI assistance from the episode transcripts, then edited by me.

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.13

Fixed

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata and data feed files were missing from external storage for chats that ended before the first message from the end-user.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly marked agents as still being on a call after it ended, which either prevented them from changing their status to Available or silently blocked them from receiving new calls.

  • Fixed an issue where processing delays for ended calls caused timeout errors.

  • Fixed an issue where a sudden spike in calls bypassed capacity limits, causing agent availability to drop below required minimums.

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Activity Timeline report incorrectly attributed manual agent logins and logouts to System instead of the appropriate agents.

  • Fixed an issue where calls with a missed offer became permanently stuck in the queue, preventing them from being routed to other available agents. This occurred with queues configured with multicast fallback disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where manual or cascade outbound calls that were canceled before connecting were missing from team-filtered Call History reports.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented over-capacity deflection from triggering when an agent warm-transferred an outbound call to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where calls weren't correctly routed to the top-ranked agent when using agent priority overrides.

  • Fixed an issue where escalated voice calls were incorrectly reported as both answered and abandoned.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were missing from the All Call History and Voice Inbound History reports if the caller hung up before leaving a voicemail.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce click-to-dial outbound calls were incorrectly associated with the most recent open case instead of the case from which the call was initiated.

  • Fixed an issue where email accounts remained disconnected indefinitely after a temporary authentication failure.

  • Fixed an issue in Agent Assist where long periods of silence during calls caused connection timeouts, triggering false-positive error alerts.

  • Fixed an issue where the arrow-down-icon and arrow-up-icon arrows on the Agents > Filter Settings page were rendered at an incorrect scale.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls incorrectly created duplicate Salesforce accounts instead of linking to existing accounts.

  • Fixed an issue where the outbound call queue list displayed stale information, potentially causing calls to be placed in a queue that didn't match the agent's selected language.

  • Fixed an issue where the menus for transferring calls and forwarding calls to voicemail appeared in English instead of the agent's selected language.

  • Fixed an issue where the wrap-up disposition panel froze after a network reconnection even though the submission had completed successfully.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound, click-to-dial calls initiated in Salesforce incorrectly linked to and reassigned ownership of other cases associated with the same phone number.

  • Fixed an issue where the agent adapter went blank and prevented new calls from reaching the agent if an end-user hung up immediately after the agent received the call notification.

  • Fixed an issue where calls that failed to connect got stuck in a silent 'connecting' state in the call adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce CRM connections dropped for organizations enforcing OAuth Refresh Token Rotation.

  • Fixed an issue where part of an agent's audio was dropped from recordings when a virtual task assistant ran in the middle of a call.

  • Fixed a web SDK issue where menus in the pre-chat and chat screens didn't comply with WAI-ARIA keyboard navigation standards.

  • Fixed a web SDK issue where screen readers couldn't identify the purpose of the Text size options for the chat screen.

We made the following dashboard improvements:

    • Total Consumer Talk Time. Total time since the call first connected to a virtual agent or a human agent.

    • Total Hold Time. Total time the call has spent on hold so far, including a hold currently in progress.

  • Real-time Chats - Chats Connected dashboard. Added the following column to the Connected Chats table:

The Real-time Calls - Calls Queued dashboard has a new Projecting column in the Call Queued table. Indicates whether the routing engine (deltacast) is currently projecting this queued call to an available agent.

  • Fixed an issue where the Productive Agents column in the tables of the Queue Group Performance - All dashboard didn't display values appropriate to the queue group settings.

    • All Interactions – Calls and All Interactions – Chats. The IVR Interactions (calls only) and Virtual Agent Interactions tables correctly reflect the filter setting.

  • Fixed an issue with the Queue Performance - Calls dashboard when short abandons were present in the specified date range. The Avg Queue Time column in the Queue Summary table incorrectly displayed the raw sum of queue durations instead of a true average.

  • Fixed an issue where team filters didn't apply correctly when generating the Individual Call History Report and the Individual Chat History Report. This resulted in the inclusion of data from unmanaged queues.

  • Fixed an issue where French Canadian translations for several dashboard metrics and labels were incorrect, incomplete, or missing.

  • Fixed the following issues with the Real-time Calls - Calls Queued dashboard:

title: We installed 12,915 MCP servers and started each one. 41% never answered.
description:
MCP registries list tens of thousands of servers. Most of what is written about their safety comes from reading them: the tool descriptions, the README, the code. We wanted the other half. What happens when you actually install one and start it, the way a client does? Does it answer? What does it ask for? What does it touch while it starts?

So HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, now installs the npm and PyPI servers it finds, starts each one in a sandbox and writes down what happened. The registries it follows list 47,586 npm and PyPI packages; it runs up to 8,000 per crawl. This post is the state on 13 October 2026, after 12,915 of them.

How we ran them

  • The latest version, installed fresh. npm with --ignore-scripts (install scripts then run on their own, traced); PyPI wheels only, nothing built from source.
  • gVisor (runsc), an unprivileged user, a read-only root, 512 MB and one CPU. 360 s to install, 150 s to start and answer.
  • No route out. Every DNS name resolves to our traps, which record what reaches them and forward nothing.
  • Decoys. ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.npmrc, ~/.netrc, shell history and a few more in HOME, a decoy .env in the working directory.
  • The observer speaks MCP: initialize, tools/list, then up to 15 tools called once each with canary arguments. gVisor writes its own syscall trace, outside the sandbox, so a package cannot hide what it opened, started or dialled.
  • What it asks for, as placeholders. A server that exits with MYTOOL_API_KEY is not set or a usage text naming serve is started again with MYTOOL_API_KEY=histor-envkey-<run> or serve. The names only ever come from the package's own error text or its registry entry. The values are ours and work nowhere.

59% answered

7,656 of 12,915 answered initialize and tools/list: 64% on npm, 52% on PyPI. Between them they listed 182,157 tool definitions, a median of 10 per server (one listed 3,631).

1,239 of those started only with something they asked for: 1,039 with a placeholder key, 177 with a start argument, 23 with both. A client config would have given them that, so we count them as working. But look at the 1,039 again. A key that works nowhere was enough for every one of them to tell us its tools. None needed a real key to do that; they just refused to start without one.

Why 5,259 never answered

We read what each package printed as it exited, last run first.

  • Almost half, 2,476, are broken as published. 874 crash with an error of their own. 636 will not install: no wheel for some dependency, conflicting pins, the wrong platform. 490 hang, stay silent or speak something that is not MCP. 292 were written for MCP SDK 1.x (next section). 184 miss one of their own files, ship TypeScript that Node will not load from node_modules, or import a dependency they never declared.
  • 793 ask for a key or a setting and stop, even with a placeholder. The usual reason: they check the key's format at startup (must start with sk_) or call their API before answering anything, and our trap is not their API.
  • 924 print a usage text. Some want a start argument we pass next time (serve, mcp, --stdio). Many are command-line tools that mention MCP somewhere. With the 666 that declare no command at all, or exit 0 having done something else, up to one package in eight listed as an MCP server is not a stdio MCP server when installed the way its listing says.
  • 164 start an HTTP server instead of answering on stdin. Their next run gets --transport=stdio.
  • 236 need something the machine does not have: another program (git, Java, Bun, a desktop app), the internet at startup, or another operating system.

MCP SDK 2.0 broke 292 PyPI servers

mcp 2.0.0 (28 July 2026) renamed FastMCP and changed the low-level server's decorators. A PyPI server that depends on mcp with no upper bound installs 2.x today and dies on import: cannot import name 'FastMCP', or 'Server' object has no attribute 'list_tools'. We started 269 of them again with pip held to mcp<2, and 207 (77%) answered. Anyone who installs them today gets the crash, not the server.

What they did in the sandbox

11,891 runs carry a gVisor trace.

  • 2,239 npm packages ran install scripts, about 30% of the npm packages we ran. 580 of them tried to reach the network while installing, mostly to fetch a prebuilt binary (prebuild-install, node-gyp's headers, esbuild). Here that fails. On your machine it runs with your credentials in reach.
  • 1,484 reached for the network at startup, before any tool was called. The names they asked for most: pypi.org (613), github.com (478), nodejs.org (245), registry.npmjs.org (243). Mostly version checks and downloads.
  • 295 opened a decoy credential file (not counting .env). Before anyone panics: Python's requests reads ~/.netrc before every HTTP request (141), npm and npx read ~/.npmrc (103), boto3's credential chain reads ~/.aws (39). Each of the other 17 (~/.kube, ~/.docker, ~/.ssh, shell history, gh's config) was opened by a server whose job is Kubernetes, Docker, SSH or "ops context". Opening a credential file is evidence, not a verdict. What matters is whether it fits the server's purpose and where the bytes go next.
  • 73 runs sent the placeholder key over the network. Most went to an identity provider (Microsoft's login 17 times, Google OAuth 7) or to the vendor's own API. Each package's page shows where.
  • Decoy content left three packages, each time when a tool forwarded the canary arguments we called it with to its own API, which is what tools do. A fourth record said a package had mailed decoy data to an extra recipient at startup. That one was ours; see the last item below.

Testing the tester

A sandbox that reports wrong things is worse than none, so here is what we got wrong on the way.

  • 880 servers looked silent. They had printed their help to stdout, and we kept only stderr. Now we keep both and the exit code; 179 are really silent.
  • About 400 "install failed" because they require Python 3.13 or 3.14 and our image had 3.12. pip then says from versions: none, which reads like a missing package. The sandbox now picks the image from Requires-Python.
  • 1,917 Python servers were flagged as "reached out at startup". asyncio's event loop writes a byte to its own socketpair; our trace reader saw a send with no destination and listed it as network. gVisor does not print the file descriptors socketpair returns, so the rule is now: a send that names no destination, on a socket that socket() did not make and no connect() reached, after a socketpair, stays in the process. All of them have since been traced again, including servers that fail to start, whose pages kept the old reading until we noticed they were never re-read.
  • 126 "persistence" writes were relative paths the old reader could not resolve, such as node-gyp's buildcheck.gypi. gVisor prints the directory next to each openat; we were not reading it.
  • One missed case, found by our red team (MOMUS). After we moved to Debian images, one of its 72 behaviour cases went unseen under load: glibc's resolver gave up on a late DNS answer, the package never connected, and the run still said "complete". The resolver now waits longer, and a DNS query our logger never saw makes the run incomplete, never clean. Every change to the observer now has to pass those 72 cases again, or HISTOR's release gate stays red.
  • A real package was shown mailing decoy data to an extra recipient. It had not. The traps know a run only by its container's address, and Docker hands a freed address to the next container. Our window opened before docker run, so it took in the last request of a red-team fixture that had held the address a moment earlier. The recipient carried the fixture's run tag, which is how we caught it. Evidence is now matched only from the container's own start to its removal, and by when a connection opened; every record holding another run's canary is being traced again.

If you publish an MCP server

  • List your tools without a key. Ask for it when a tool is called. Do not check its format at startup.
  • Default to stdio, or name the flag that turns it on in your error text.
  • Pin mcp<2 or move to 2.x.
  • Ship one command. If your package also has a CLI, put mcp in the server's name.
  • Keep stdout for JSON-RPC. Logs, banners and help go to stderr.
  • Set Requires-Python honestly and publish wheels.
  • Do not download binaries at install or startup. Ship them as per-platform optional dependencies.

Check what you run

Every package's record is public on histor.modelmarket.dev: its tools, what it asked for, what it touched, which image it ran in. WARDEN reads the same log. npx -y @aimarket/warden@0.14.0 scan --histor asks HISTOR, for every server in your Claude, Cursor or VS Code config, whether you get the tool set everyone else gets, and shows what its package did in the sandbox.

We build HISTOR and WARDEN. The numbers are a snapshot of 13 October 2026; the crawl continues, so the site will have moved on. No package is named here. The method and the observer's code are in alexar76/histor (docs/architecture.md, sandbox/histor_observe.py).

title: Reproducing Olmo 3 7B Pre-training in MaxText: case study of large scale training on TPUs

title: Architectural Breakdown: What's Your Favorite Car, and Why? (Mine Is the Lamborghini Urus, and Yes,
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+What%27s+Your+Favorite+Car%2C+and++round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# When a 500-Request Burst Hits at 2 AM, Your Architecture Either Drives or Dies

Let us be honest. Nobody wakes up proud of their checkout service. Not until it burns down at 02:17 on a Tuesday during a flash sale and you are reading your own error logs like a crime scene report.

The alert that night was brutal: **checkout-service: 500, DB connection pool exhausted**. A junior dev had glued everything into one file with a global pool. Another team shipped the same weekend with a plug-in mesh. Only one survived.

I have been building production systems since before microservices was a LinkedIn buzzword. The code below is from real builds I have shipped. [Full-stack reference codebase here](https://www.shipmvp.tech) if you want to see the patterns in context.

---

## 1. What Went Wrong: The Junior's Single-File Trap


js
// checkout.js - 300 lines of "just get it done"
const { Pool } = require('pg')
const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL })
const express = require('express')
const app = express()
app.use(express.json())

app.post('/checkout', async (req, res) => {
const client = await pool.connect()
try {
await client.query('BEGIN')
const { items, userId } = req.body
if (!items?.length) throw new Error('Empty cart')
// Sequential loop: each SKU blocks the event loop
for (const i of items) {
await client.query(
'UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - $1 WHERE sku = $2 AND qty >= $1',
[i.qty, i.sku]
)
}
const orderRes = await client.query(
'INSERT INTO orders(user_id, status) VALUES($1, $2) RETURNING id',
[userId, 'pending']
)
const orderId = orderRes.rows[0].id
for (const i of items) {
await client.query(
'INSERT INTO order_items(order_id, sku, qty) VALUES($1, $2, $3)',
[orderId, i.sku, i.qty]
)
}
await client.query('COMMIT')
res.json({ orderId })
} catch (e) {
await client.query('ROLLBACK')
console.error(e)
res.status(500).send('checkout failed')
} finally {
client.release()
}
})

app.listen(3000)


This is not just bad code. It is a bomb with three fuses:

1. **Global pool defaults to size 10.** Five hundred parallel requests queue behind ten connections. Pool exhausts. Gateway times out. PagerDuty screams.
2. **Sequential `for...await` loops.** Each inventory update blocks the event loop. One request walks its SKU list while the entire service sits idle.
3. **Zero separation of concerns.** Validation, inventory, ordering, and transaction handling all live together. One typo and the whole thing detonates.

---

## 2. The Senior Approach: Plug-in Mesh Architecture

The fix treats each responsibility as a swappable module. The orchestrator stays thin. The plugins do the work.

### Directory layout


plaintext
src/
├─ adapters/db/pgPool.js
├─ domain/checkout/
│ ├─ validator.js
│ ├─ inventoryService.js
│ ├─ orderService.js
│ └─ useCase.js
└─ index.js


### Pool Sized for 8 GB RAM, Not Guesswork


js
// src/adapters/db/pgPool.js
const { Pool } = require('pg')

// 1 PG connection ≈ 50 MB heap. On 8 GB, leave headroom for Node runtime.
const availBytes = process.memoryUsage().heapTotal
const poolSize = Math.max(2, Math.floor(availBytes / 1024 / 1024 / 50))

const pool = new Pool({
connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
max: Math.min(poolSize, 20),
idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,
connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000
})

module.exports = pool


Stop hardcoding pool sizes. Your heap tells you what it can handle.

### Parallel Inventory Reservations


js
// src/domain/checkout/inventoryService.js
module.exports = class InventoryService {
constructor(pool) { this.pool = pool }

async reserve(items, client) {
// Promise.all fires all SKU updates concurrently within the same transaction
const queries = items.map(i =>
client.query(
'UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - $1 WHERE sku = $2 AND qty >= $1',
[i.qty, i.sku]
)
)
// Fails fast: one out-of-stock SKU rolls back everything
await Promise.all(queries)
}
}


### The Orchestrator


js
// src/domain/checkout/useCase.js
module.exports = class CheckoutUseCase {
constructor({ validator, inventoryService, orderService, pool }) {
this.validator = validator
this.inventoryService = inventoryService
this.orderService = orderService
this.pool = pool
}

async execute(payload) {
this.validator(payload)
const client = await this.pool.connect()
try {
await client.query('BEGIN')
await this.inventoryService.reserve(payload.items, client)
const orderId = await this.orderService.create(
payload.userId, payload.items, client
)
await client.query('COMMIT')
return orderId
} catch (err) {
await client.query('ROLLBACK')
throw err
} finally {
client.release()
}
}
}


Clean. Testable. Swap any plugin without touching the others.

---

## 3. Failure Modes Under Burst Load

| Scenario | Junior Code | Senior Code |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| 500 parallel checkouts | Pool exhausts, 500 errors | Parallel `Promise.all` cuts latency; pool auto-sizes to 16 |
| One SKU out of stock | Transaction hangs in sequential loop | Fails fast; ROLLBACK fires immediately |
| GC pressure on 8 GB box | No heap awareness; pool grows unbounded | Pool capped at 20; idle connections released after 30s |
| Partial failure mid-transaction | Rollback may silently fail | Explicit `try/catch/finally` guarantees ROLLBACK |

The race condition wins here. `Promise.all` within a single transaction eliminates the TOCTOU gap. The database enforces atomicity: all reservations succeed or all roll back. No gray areas.

---

## 4. Observability: Because Console Logs Are for Hobbyists


js
// After successful checkout:
console.log(JSON.stringify({
event: 'checkout_success',
orderId,
latencyMs: Date.now() - start,
items: payload.items.length,
traceId: req.headers['x-trace-id']
}))


Prometheus counters. Latency histograms. A circuit breaker on the inventory service. When the pool hits 90 percent utilization, return `503 Service Unavailable` instead of queuing until the server buckles.

Graceful degradation beats heroic collapse every time.

---

## 5. The Question That Keeps You Up at Night

**If you size your connection pool purely by heap memory, how do you account for load balancers, sidecars, and logging agents eating the same 8 GB?** The answer separates services that survive Black Friday from services that become cautionary tales on your ops team's Slack channel.

My Lamborghini Urus is not the fastest supercar. It is not the most refined. But it handles situations no other car in its class touches: gravel, rain, steep mountain passes, and city traffic. Same philosophy here. Your architecture does not need to be the prettiest. It needs to handle whatever the road throws at it.

The code above ships. [See the full reference](https://www.shipmvp.tech) if you want production-hardened patterns, not just theory.

---

**Open Loop:** When your connection pool is sized dynamically from heap memory, which other hidden consumers of that same memory footprint should factor into your capacity calculation: the Node.js V8 engine itself, OS-level buffer caches, or the overhead of your process manager's forked workers? And how do you measure those without guessing?

title: How We Built and Scaled a Modern Web App Workspace for Creators & Devs
description:
Modern web development moves fast, but the gap between building an idea and putting it into production is still frustratingly wide. Creators and developers often get stuck juggling fragmented tooling—from setting up responsive frontend layouts and backend databases to managing cloud hosting, automated deployments, and custom domains.

That is why we created Heydigi.

What is Heydigi?

Heydigi is built as an all-in-one software workspace and studio platform. The goal is simple: empower builders to turn ideas, prompts, and architectures into production-ready web applications without getting bogged down by infrastructure headaches.

Core Focus Areas

  • Prompt-to-Product Workflows: Bridging visual tools and AI workflows into clean, maintainable web projects.
  • Reliable Cloud Infrastructure: Streamlining hosting, container configurations, and database integrations (like Supabase and modern cloud providers) out of the box.
  • Fast Prototyping for Agencies & Founders: Letting teams validate MVPs and deploy client solutions in hours instead of weeks.

Looking Ahead

We are continuously refining how creators and developers ship web software. Whether you are building internal tools, client portals, or SaaS products, you can explore the platform and see what we are building at heydigi.dev.

We would love to hear feedback from the DEV community: What is your biggest friction point when deploying modern web apps today?

title: Prisma 8 Postgres connection pools: replace connection_limit with pg.Pool
description:
A new application replica can quietly multiply its database connections.

With Prisma ORM 8, the old connection-pool URL limit is no longer the setting to rely on. You must know which pool you are configuring, how many copies can run, and what happens when all its connections are busy.

What changed in Prisma ORM 8

Prisma’s 12 October issue roundup describes the fix for a long-standing PostgreSQL connection-slot error. Its entry for issue #7120 says Prisma 8 no longer uses the engine pool or the connection_limit URL parameter. The runtime uses node-postgres pg.Pool; you can tune the pool through the documented options or construct and size a pool yourself. The roundup says the listed behavior was checked against 8.0.0-rc.16, released on 7 October, and labels Prisma 8 a release candidate.

That last detail matters. Treat the change as an RC feature until Prisma declares general availability. Verify the package versions and current reference docs in the exact project you are upgrading; the example below illustrates the documented shape, not a promise that the API will remain unchanged.

The practical consequence is simple: connection capacity is now a driver-level budget you need to make explicit. A URL parameter that used to look like a universal cap is not a substitute for sizing the pool that your app processes actually create.

Separate pool size from pool timeouts

Pool size and timeout answer different questions.

The size limit is how many database connections one pool may hold at once. With a custom pg.Pool, that is the driver's max setting. A connection timeout limits how long a request waits to obtain or open a connection. An idle timeout controls how long an unused connection stays open.

Prisma’s poolOptions are for timeout settings on a pool Prisma creates from a URL. They do not set the custom pool’s max. If your concern is “how many PostgreSQL slots can these app processes consume?”, set max on the pg.Pool you pass into Prisma, then budget every running process.

Create one bounded pool per process

For a Node service using the Prisma 8 PostgreSQL runtime, a custom pool makes the cap visible in application code:

import postgres from '@prisma/orm-postgres/runtime';
import { Pool } from 'pg';
import type { Contract } from './contract.d';
import contractJson from './contract.json' with { type: 'json' };

const max = Number(process.env.PG_POOL_MAX ?? '5');
if (!Number.isInteger(max) || max < 1) {
  throw new Error('PG_POOL_MAX must be a positive integer');
}

const pool = new Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  max,
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,
  idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
});

const db = postgres<Contract>({
  contractJson,
  pg: pool,
});

// On graceful shutdown:
await db.close();
await pool.end();

The value 5 is only an example. Choose a cap from the database budget, not from the snippet. The pool is created once at module or process scope and shared by requests. Do not construct a new pool inside a route handler: one pool per request defeats the limit because every request brings another set of possible connections.

Passing your own pool also means your code owns its lifecycle. Close the Prisma client and then end the pool during graceful shutdown. Do not close it after each request. In serverless environments, keep the pool at module scope so warm invocations can reuse it, and account for the fact that each live instance can own a separate pool.

If you do not need to choose a custom maximum, you can let Prisma create the pool from the URL and use poolOptions for timeout behavior:

const db = postgres<Contract>({
  contractJson,
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  poolOptions: {
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000,
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
  },
});

This controls waiting and idle lifetime; it does not make connection_limit=5 work again. If you need a deliberately bounded maximum, use a custom pool and set its max.

Budget across replicas before deployment

A safe per-process value depends on how many processes can exist at the same time. Write down the database’s connection ceiling, reserve room for migrations, monitoring, administration and other services, then divide the remaining application budget across the maximum number of replicas.

For example, suppose the database can spare 24 connections for this service after those reservations. If autoscaling can start six processes, a per-process maximum of four uses the entire app budget: 6 × 4 = 24. That leaves no burst room, so a lower setting or a separate pooler may be safer. This is arithmetic for an example, not a recommended universal limit. Count workers, scheduled jobs and deployment overlap too; a rolling deploy may briefly run old and new replicas together.

Do not calculate from the number of database clients in one process and stop there. The database sees the sum across all live processes. A pool cap of ten can be harmless for one long-lived process and excessive when dozens of short-lived instances each create their own pool.

Keep transactions and slow work from pinning the pool

A bounded pool can still feel exhausted if each request holds a connection for too long. Keep database work inside a short query or transaction. Do not check out a connection, call a slow external service, then hold the same connection while waiting for that service. Finish the database operation and release its connection before doing unrelated network work.

Give acquisition a finite timeout so overload produces a visible failure instead of an unbounded queue of requests. Log pool-wait timeouts separately from SQL errors; they point to different fixes. A timeout is not extra capacity, though. Increasing it can make callers wait longer without creating another PostgreSQL slot.

For a broader checklist covering Postgres pool budgets, poolers and saturation canaries, see the production connection-pooling guide. This article focuses on the Prisma 8-specific change: where the cap now lives and how to keep the sum of pools inside the database budget.

Test the limit you intend to run

Before moving production traffic, verify the exact Prisma RC and driver versions in staging. Confirm the old URL parameter is not being treated as your cap, confirm the custom pool’s max is applied, and exercise more concurrent requests than the pool can serve. The test should show that active database connections stay within the combined process budget and that excess work waits only up to the configured timeout.

Then test the deployment shape, not just one local process. Start the maximum expected number of replicas, include background workers, and observe the database connection count while they run. Repeat with rollout overlap if the platform can run old and new versions at once. If the observed total exceeds the budget, lower each pool maximum, cap concurrency, or add an appropriate pooler before launch.

Also check the paths that use a database connection outside normal requests: migrations, admin tools and long-running jobs may need a separate connection strategy. Keep those connections in the reserved portion of the database budget instead of silently letting them compete with request traffic.

What the OTF kit does and does not provide

The SaaS Dashboard kit is an optional editable Postgres app and UI starting point. Its data layer uses Drizzle; it does not include Prisma ORM 8 or this pool configuration. You would add and validate the Prisma integration yourself. Check current pricing before choosing a kit.

The durable takeaway is not a magic pool number. In Prisma ORM 8, choose the pool you intend to own, put the maximum on that pool, and multiply it by the largest number of processes your deployment can run. Test that total against the database’s available slots before the first production spike.

Sources

  • Prisma ORM 8: We closed 330 of your most-requested issues (published 12 October 2026; entry #7120; behavior checked by Prisma against 8.0.0-rc.16).

Conceptual migration illustration: supply a separate pool rather than relying on the old engine-managed pool.

Conceptual illustration: set the maximum on the custom pg.Pool; use poolOptions for timeouts.

The SaaS Dashboard is an optional editable UI starting point; it does not include this Prisma integration.

title: Config precedence in Python: why your resolver shouldn't know what "CLI" means
description:
Most config systems I've written have the same shape. A function that looks at the environment, looks at the command line, looks at a YAML file, and decides which one wins. Something like this:

def load_config():
    if cli_args.timeout:
        return cli_args.timeout
    if os.getenv("TIMEOUT"):
        return os.getenv("TIMEOUT")
    return yaml_config.get("timeout", 30000)

Multiply that by every setting and you get a function that's 200 lines long, impossible to test in isolation, and impossible to change precedence on without editing every branch.

The version I've been working on separates two things the if/else version fuses together. What order sources apply in. And how they merge. Once those are separate, precedence stops being code and starts being structure.

The resolver doesn't know what "CLI" means. Here's the merge function in full:

def resolve_config(sources: Iterable[SourceSpec]) -> dict:
    merged_config = {}

    for spec in sources:
        try:
            config = spec.source.get_config()
        except Exception as error:
            if spec.failure_policy == FailurePolicy.REQUIRED:
                raise
            logger.warning(
                "Optional configuration source %s failed: %s",
                spec.source.__class__.__name__,
                error,
            )
            continue

        merged_config = {**merged_config, **config}

    return merged_config

Read that and notice what it doesn't do. It doesn't check whether a source is a CLI source, an env source, or a YAML source. It doesn't sort anything. It doesn't decide that one kind of source should win over another kind. It takes a list of sources, merges them left to right, and returns the result.

The last source in the list wins. That's the entire precedence rule.

That's not a limitation. It's the design. The moment the resolver knows what "CLI" means, it can start making decisions it shouldn't. It can start reordering. It can start special-casing. And once it does that, you can't test precedence without also testing the resolver's opinions, and you can't change precedence without reading the resolver's code.

Precedence is a list. That list comes from a builder:

def build_standard_pipeline(file_path: str, env: Environment, cli_args=None) -> list[SourceSpec]:
    yaml_source = YAMLSource(file_path, env)
    env_source = EnvSource()
    cli_source = CLISource(args=cli_args)
    return [
        SourceSpec(source=yaml_source, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=env_source, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.OPTIONAL),
        SourceSpec(source=cli_source, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.OPTIONAL),
    ]

YAML first. Env second. CLI last. Since the resolver merges left-to-right and later sources override earlier ones, CLI wins over env wins over YAML. That's the whole precedence system, and it's expressed as three lines of a list.

If you want to change precedence, say you decide env should beat CLI, you change the order of that list. Nothing else changes. No if branches to hunt down. No settings that read precedence from a config file. Just the order of the list.

The tests are where the pattern earns its keep, because they lock in behaviors, not implementation details.

First test. Later source wins.

def test_1_later_source_wins():
    source_a = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "chromium"})
    source_b = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "firefox"})
    source_c = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "webkit"})

    specs = [
        SourceSpec(source=source_a, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=source_b, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=source_c, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED)
    ]

    result = resolve_config(specs)
    assert result["browser"] == "webkit"

That's the base contract. Merge is left-to-right, last write wins. It's obvious in isolation and it's the thing every other behavior depends on.

Second test. Reordering changes result.

def test_2_reordering_changes_result():
    source_a = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "chromium"})
    source_b = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "firefox"})
    source_c = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "webkit"})

    specs = [
        SourceSpec(source=source_c, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=source_a, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=source_b, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED)
    ]

    result = resolve_config(specs)
    assert result["browser"] == "firefox"

This one looks trivial and isn't. It proves the resolver has no hidden opinion about which source should win. If someone ever helpfully adds logic to the resolver that reorders sources, say putting CLI sources last regardless of where they appear, this test fails. That's the category of mistake it prevents. Someone trying to make precedence smarter inside the merge.

Third test. The resolver doesn't sort.

def test_3_resolver_does_not_sort():
    # Simulate a logically reversed order: CLI-like -> YAML-like -> ENV-like
    # The resolver should NOT know these names mean anything.
    cli_like = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "webkit"})
    yaml_like = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "chromium"})
    env_like = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "firefox"})

    specs = [
        SourceSpec(source=cli_like, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=yaml_like, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=env_like, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED)
    ]

    result = resolve_config(specs)
    assert result["browser"] == "firefox"

This is the one I'd defend hardest. It uses three sources named after the standard precedence chain, CLI, YAML, ENV, but passes them in a deliberately wrong order. The resolver's job is to merge them in the order given, not to fix it.

If you ever find yourself wanting to add precedence knowledge to the resolver, this test is the one that will stop you. That's the point. Tests aren't just assertions about current behavior. They're arguments against future versions of yourself who will have worse ideas.

There's a subtle thing in the resolver that's easy to miss.

try:
    config = spec.source.get_config()
except Exception as error:
    if spec.failure_policy == FailurePolicy.REQUIRED:
        raise
    logger.warning(...)
    continue

Each source carries its own failure policy. YAML is required. If the file is missing or malformed, the pipeline fails. Env and CLI are optional. If they fail to load, the pipeline continues with what it has.

This is deliberately a separate concern from precedence. A source can be last in precedence, highest priority, and optional, failing silently. A source can be first in precedence, lowest priority, and required. The two axes are independent.

def test_5_failure_policy_remains_independent(caplog):
    valid_yaml = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "chromium", "timeout": 30000})
    failing_env = FailingSource()
    valid_cli = FakeConfigSource({"browser": "webkit"})

    specs = [
        SourceSpec(source=valid_yaml, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED),
        SourceSpec(source=failing_env, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.OPTIONAL),
        SourceSpec(source=valid_cli, failure_policy=FailurePolicy.REQUIRED)
    ]

    with caplog.at_level("WARNING"):
        result = resolve_config(specs)

    assert result["browser"] == "webkit"
    assert result["timeout"] == 30000
    assert "Optional configuration source" in caplog.text

Env fails. The pipeline continues. CLI still overrides YAML. Timeout from YAML still applies because nothing else set it. Precedence and failure handling do their jobs without interacting.

Fusing these two concerns is the most common mistake I see in config systems. It looks natural. If the CLI arg is missing, fall back to env, which falls back to YAML. But it collapses two orthogonal decisions into one tangled function. Keeping them separate makes each one testable in isolation and changeable without touching the other.

One more test, because it's the one that guards the whole design:

def test_7_resolver_remains_unchanged():
    sig = inspect.signature(resolve_config)
    params = list(sig.parameters.values())
    assert len(params) == 1
    assert params[0].name == "sources"

This asserts that resolve_config takes exactly one parameter. Nothing else. No pipeline name, no environment, no flags. Just the list of sources.

It sounds pedantic, and it is, deliberately. Six months from now, someone (probably me) will want to pass an Environment into the resolver so it can adjust precedence based on the environment. This test makes that change fail loudly, which forces a conversation about whether the resolver should know anything about environments. The answer is almost always no. But without the test, the answer quietly becomes yes, one small change at a time.

What this pattern buys you.

Precedence is a list. Changing it means reordering a list, not editing logic.

The resolver does one thing. It merges dictionaries left to right. That's it. It's 20 lines and it doesn't know what a CLI is.

Failure handling is orthogonal. Each source declares whether it's required or optional. The resolver respects that declaration without conflating it with priority.

Tests lock behaviors, not implementations. Each test asserts something category-level about what the system should never do, not just what it currently does.

None of this is novel. It's the same pattern behind a dozen config libraries. But the version where precedence is structure, rather than a decision buried in a conditional, is the version I've found easiest to live with. Because the day you need to change precedence is the day you least want to be reading the resolver's code.

title: Realtime Event Observability API Boundaries Explained for Go (Live Auction Dashboards)
description:
Short answer: use a realtime API for transport, but make presence, subscription state, authentication, and auction events separate observable signals; clients need stable event identifiers so they can reconcile after reconnecting instead of guessing what they missed.

For a live auction dashboard, presence accuracy is the deciding constraint. A green socket indicator doesn't prove that a bidder is authenticated, subscribed to the right auction, or caught up to the current bid. I would treat those as different states, attach an SLO to each one, and choose an API boundary only after the client and server responsibilities are written down. Infrai is a credible option for the publish boundary when a team expects to add other backend capabilities later: its 295 routes across 20 modules share one REST surface, so the integration does not require another SDK and credential set for every new module. The catch is that this breadth is less important when realtime is the product's dominant technical problem; in that case, evaluate a specialist first.

How should realtime event observability define API boundaries for a live auction dashboard?

Start with four signals, not one catch-all “connected” metric. Authentication answers whether the session may act. Subscription state answers whether the client asked for and received the intended auction channel. Presence answers whether the system currently considers the participant present. Business-event progress answers whether the client has applied the latest known auction event. Mixing these together makes a dashboard look healthy while it is stale — precisely the failure an operator needs the screen to expose.

The boundary should also say who owns recovery. The server returns stable identifiers and publishes events with enough application-level identity for a client to detect duplicates or gaps. The client persists its last applied identifier, reconnects, and reconciles before declaring itself current. Expiry and partial failure are normal states, not exceptional branches hidden behind a generic red badge.

Keep it explicit.

For capacity planning, model reconnects as bursts. If 10,000 viewers lose connectivity at once, the steady-state event rate tells you very little about the resulting authentication, subscription, presence, and replay pressure. The useful SLO is therefore not merely “socket connected”; it is a bound on time from reconnect to reconciled auction state, measured alongside the share of clients whose presence and event cursor agree. The exact target depends on auction rules and traffic shape. I'm not sure a universal number would be defensible without peak concurrency, event rate, and acceptable staleness; those three inputs should resolve it.

Choose the boundary before the vendor

The buy-versus-build decision is mostly an ownership decision. A managed transport can remove infrastructure work, but it cannot decide whether a late bid is valid, define the authoritative auction sequence, or choose what the dashboard shows during reconciliation. Those remain application responsibilities.

Option Setup and credential question What to verify for this dashboard Better fit when
Build and operate the transport Can the platform team own deployment, scaling, and on-call response? Presence semantics, reconnect bursts, replay, and operator visibility Realtime behavior is core intellectual property and lock-in is unacceptable
Pusher How many SDKs and credentials enter the application and CI system? Presence accuracy and reconciliation behavior under the auction's traffic shape A specialist evaluation proves a closer fit than a broad backend surface
Ably How quickly can a Go service produce the first useful event and expose recovery state? Stable identifiers, subscription observability, and reconnect semantics Specialist realtime depth dominates integration consolidation
PubNub Which client and server responsibilities are imposed by the chosen integration? Authentication, presence, and business-event signals can be inspected separately The specialist's contract matches the required presence model
Infrai Can plain HTTP and one key reduce integration and credential sprawl? The publish boundary and presence query meet the application's explicit contract The team values a consistent surface across multiple backend modules

This table is an evaluation runbook, not a benchmark result. Pusher, Ably, and PubNub deserve workload-specific tests before selection; no latency, uptime, or presence-accuracy measurements are asserted here. Stick with a specialist when its realtime model wins those tests or when deep realtime controls matter more than reducing SDK surface. Self-host when the team can afford the on-call load and needs direct control over recovery semantics. Infrai should be tried by platform teams that need a small publish integration now and expect adjacent backend work later, because its broad module set remains accessible through the same plain REST contract. A second practical benefit is discovery: the public discovery surface returns request schema, response schema, billing details, and runnable examples, which shortens the path from a route name to a reviewable integration without committing the codebase to another vendor SDK.

Implement reconciliation as application logic

Do not guess a publish payload from a route name. The small Go program below asks Infrai's public discovery surface for the current metadata, locates the verified realtime publish capability, then retrieves its full request and response schema. It is a read-only first integration: a reviewer can inspect the actual contract before anyone writes transport-specific auction code. The API key is still read from the environment and sent with Bearer authentication, so the HTTP client can be reused when the integration moves from public discovery to an authenticated capability.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type Discovery struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

type Capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if when, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(when); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func get(client *http.Client, endpoint, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: status=%d body=%s", endpoint, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: retry limit reached after rate limiting", endpoint)
}

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}

    body, err := get(client, baseURL+"/discovery", key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var manifest Discovery
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode discovery: %w", err)
    }

    var publish Capability
    for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
        if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && capability.Path == "/v1/realtime/publish" {
            publish = capability
            break
        }
    }
    if publish.ID == "" || !publish.Available {
        return fmt.Errorf("realtime publish capability is not available in discovery")
    }

    detailBody, err := get(client, baseURL+"/discovery/"+url.PathEscape(publish.ID), key)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var detail Capability
    if err := json.Unmarshal(detailBody, &detail); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode capability: %w", err)
    }

    fmt.Printf("%s %s\nrequest schema: %s\n", detail.Method, detail.Path, detail.Params)
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The discovery response exposes capability IDs, methods, paths, availability, and vendor readiness; the single-capability response adds the full request JSON Schema and response schema. Generate the eventual request from that path field and schema, rather than from descriptive prose. After publishing is wired, the application should stop its “current” indicator on an event gap, fetch authoritative state through its own recovery boundary, and replace the cursor only after reconciliation succeeds. Authentication, subscription health, presence, and business-event progress still need separate signals.

The same discipline applies to a live poll during a gaming session. A vote event, participant presence, and permission to vote are related, but they aren't interchangeable. A reconnecting player should not be counted twice merely because the presence view and the applied event cursor recover at different speeds.

Verify the failure modes, not the happy path

The first useful test is a forced disconnect between two consecutive auction events. Record the last stable identifier on the client, reconnect, and verify that the dashboard stays in a reconciling state until its authoritative auction state and event cursor agree. Repeat with an expired credential, a lost subscription, a duplicate event, and an event sequence gap. Each result should land in a distinct metric or structured log field; one aggregate connection error discards the evidence needed during an incident.

Then test the herd. Ramp concurrent reconnects toward the expected peak rather than extrapolating from a single client, and watch the full path: credential issuance, subscription restoration, presence convergence, recovery reads, and business-event application. Capacity should be reserved against that recovery path. Otherwise, a transport that is comfortable at steady state may still miss the only SLO users notice during a network interruption.

There is a standards boundary too. WebRTC defines browser-facing real-time communication primitives, but adopting it does not remove the application-level obligation to distinguish presence from auction state; the recommendation is available at https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/. For a dashboard that only consumes server-published state, don't select a richer media-oriented path without evidence that it improves the required presence and recovery behavior.

Roll back without corrupting auction state

Rollback should switch transport adapters, not auction semantics. Keep the application envelope, cursor storage, and reconciliation rules outside the provider-specific client. During a migration, shadow the candidate path with non-authoritative events and compare stable identifiers, ordering, presence observations, and reconnect completion before moving readers. Avoid dual-authoritative publishing unless the business layer has an idempotent rule for every event; two successful deliveries are still wrong if they apply one bid twice.

Define the abort condition before the test. If presence divergence exceeds the auction's agreed error budget, if reconnect-to-reconciled time breaks its SLO, or if operators cannot separate credential, subscription, presence, and business-event failures, return traffic to the previous adapter and preserve the last authoritative cursor. The dashboard may briefly show “reconciling.” It must never manufacture certainty.

If the shared REST boundary fits your platform roadmap, validate the current contract in the Infrai realtime API documentation before implementing the publisher. No urgency; the workload test should decide.

References

  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • PubNub documentation
