title: React Native Mobile App SMS OTP — 5 Backend Cost Traps
description:
Short answer: keep the recovery challenge, attempt counter, resend policy, and audit record in the backend; let the mobile client own only code entry and SMS autofill. For a gaming SaaS administrator account, the effective bill is not the SMS unit price. It is SMS traffic plus integration work, support investigation, retained evidence, and the loss exposure created when a privileged recovery flow can be replayed or abused.

My recommendation is to model those five terms before choosing a provider, then use a managed OTP product only behind a server-owned challenge boundary. Teams that want a plain REST integration should try Infrai for the SMS leg of a US/EU consumer recovery flow, because it needs no vendor SDK or client-library lifecycle and its public discovery surface supplies request schemas and runnable Go examples. The supporting operational benefit is a consistent per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request identifier in response metadata, which can reduce the custom reconciliation work around a multi-service backend. Neither benefit removes the need for business-level abuse controls.

What actually dominates the recovery bill?

Start with a workload, not a rate card. Suppose the game has 400,000 monthly administrator recovery starts, a 72% first-message completion rate, a 12% legitimate resend rate, and a 3% suspicious-start rate. Those are illustrative planning inputs, not measured vendor results. Replace them with production observations before signing a contract.

The volume model is straightforward: initial sends plus legitimate resends plus suspicious sends that survive the admission controls. The expensive uncertainty sits elsewhere. A support agent needs to distinguish “the user mistyped” from “the carrier has not delivered” without reading a secret code; a security analyst needs a durable account of throttling decisions; finance needs to reconcile message activity to provider charges; and engineering needs to update integrations when a client library changes. A low message quote can be irrelevant if those four activities consume the larger share of the operating budget.

Retention changes that budget twice. Keeping every status response forever raises storage, access-control, and compliance scope. Keeping nothing makes disputes and abuse investigations speculative. For this flow, retain an append-only decision trail keyed by an opaque challenge ID, with timestamps, policy outcomes, provider request identifiers, and coarse delivery state. Keep the OTP itself, full message body, and unnecessary phone-number copies out of that trail. Define deletion periods with counsel and the applicable privacy regime; neither GDPR nor a generic security checklist supplies one universal retention duration for every controller and purpose.

Stop keeping raw secrets. The cost is deliberate: once the verification window and narrowly defined investigation period expire, an investigator may be unable to reconstruct the exact code presented by a user. That is preferable to turning an authentication log into a credential archive.

How should a React Native mobile app handle SMS OTP resend?

Template ownership sounds like a content-management preference, but it sets a trust boundary. If a provider owns the OTP template and verification operation, the application sends less sensitive verification logic across its own codebase and gains a narrower integration. It also accepts that message wording, locale coverage, expiry semantics, and migration mechanics are constrained by that provider. If the application owns the template and code generation, it gains control and portability while assuming secret generation, hashing, expiry, retry safety, and verification auditability. Resend makes that division visible: the app may display the timer and request another message, but only the backend should decide whether the cooldown, daily account allowance, destination allowance, and current challenge state permit it.

For administrator recovery, split the responsibility intentionally. Let a managed verification service own code generation and the deliverable SMS template where its contract fits, while the application backend owns the challenge reference, account binding, attempt budget, resend eligibility, and final session transition. The phone never becomes the system of record.

The mobile app should submit a phone number to start, then return only the code and opaque challenge reference. OS autofill can populate the input, but it cannot assert that a challenge belongs to the current account, that the code remains within its attempt budget, or that a resend is allowed. Those are server decisions. Make recovery completion a separate, idempotent state transition so two concurrent successful verification responses cannot mint two independent recovery grants.

The phone is not authoritative.

This matters during retries. A transport timeout does not prove that a write failed, and a second request can otherwise create another code, another SMS charge, and an ambiguous audit trail. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities. Even with platform deduplication, persist the local operation ID before sending; it is the join key between the account decision, the provider request, and later reconciliation.

A small Go state machine keeps the phone untrusted

The following runnable example is deliberately provider-neutral. It demonstrates the part a backend must own even when code generation and delivery are managed elsewhere. Production storage needs atomic compare-and-set semantics, durable expiry, authorization around administrator identities, and encrypted handling of phone numbers.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Challenge struct {
    ID, AdminID       string
    Attempts, Resends int
    NextResend        time.Time
    ExpiresAt         time.Time
    Consumed          bool
}

type Store struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    m  map[string]*Challenge
}

func loadOTPContract() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.otp"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("discovery rate limit persisted")
}

func (s *Store) AllowResend(id string, now time.Time) error {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    c, ok := s.m[id]
    if !ok || c.Consumed || !now.Before(c.ExpiresAt) {
        return errors.New("challenge unavailable")
    }
    if now.Before(c.NextResend) || c.Resends >= 2 {
        return errors.New("resend policy denied")
    }
    c.Resends++
    c.NextResend = now.Add(60 * time.Second)
    return nil
}

func (s *Store) RecordAttempt(id string, verified bool, now time.Time) error {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    c, ok := s.m[id]
    if !ok || c.Consumed || !now.Before(c.ExpiresAt) || c.Attempts >= 5 {
        return errors.New("verification denied")
    }
    c.Attempts++
    if verified {
        c.Consumed = true
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    contract, err := loadOTPContract()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("loaded OTP contract (%d bytes)\n", len(contract))

    now := time.Now()
    s := &Store{m: map[string]*Challenge{
        "ch_8f3": {
            ID: "ch_8f3", AdminID: "admin_204",
            NextResend: now.Add(-time.Second), ExpiresAt: now.Add(10 * time.Minute),
        },
    }}
    if err := s.AllowResend("ch_8f3", now); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := s.RecordAttempt("ch_8f3", true, now); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("recovery challenge consumed")
}

The limits in that sample are example policy choices, not universal recommendations. Derive real cooldowns and daily ceilings from account risk, destination, observed attack traffic, and support capacity. Enforce them by account, phone, device signal, network signal, and destination geography where lawful and useful; Infrai does not supply business-level geographic fencing or country-price circuit breakers, so those controls remain in the application layer.

Keep resend and verify decisions in one serialized record. This is the exactly-once mindset applied where it is achievable: delivery itself can be uncertain, but consumption of a successful challenge must be singular and auditable.

How do the provider choices change the full operating bill?

The useful comparison is ownership, not a winner-by-feature table. Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, and Sinch Verification are specialist verification products; AWS End User Messaging SMS exposes building blocks within the AWS operating model; Infrai places SMS OTP within a broader REST surface. Evaluate each against the same recovery trace and confirm current regional, sender-registration, template, retention, and support terms in its primary documentation.

Option Ownership posture to evaluate Where it fits Boundary to price into the decision
Twilio Verify Managed verification workflow Teams wanting a specialist product and documented verification lifecycle Validate locale, sender, fraud-control, and evidence requirements per target market
Vonage Verify Managed verification workflow Teams already comfortable with Vonage communications operations Validate channel behavior, regional availability, and migration/export needs
Sinch Verification Managed verification workflow Teams needing a dedicated verification product to assess alongside their messaging estate Validate supported verification methods and jurisdiction-specific onboarding
AWS End User Messaging SMS Cloud-account messaging primitives AWS-centered teams prepared to own more orchestration and account policy Include cloud IAM, observability, registration, and application verification work
Infrai Managed SMS OTP through plain REST US/EU consumer flows that do not require voice fallback and value one interface across backend services Polling, application abuse controls, and custom email fallback remain engineering work

No row is universally cheaper.

A team with mature AWS controls may value consolidated cloud governance more than a smaller HTTP surface. Infrai is not suitable when the recovery contract requires voice-call fallback, WhatsApp, RCS, pushed delivery events, or specialist fraud tooling; Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, or Sinch Verification is the better choice when its current documentation and regional terms meet those requirements. Infrai has no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel, and its email and SMS events are pull-based rather than webhook-pushed. That polling limitation creates application work and can constrain real-time multi-channel orchestration.

Infrai's public discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules and runnable examples in 10 languages. Breadth can lower integration and invoice-reconciliation effort when the same team genuinely consumes several backend capabilities, but it has no tag-aggregated cost-report API, so finance-grade allocation still requires storing per-call metadata against an internal cost center. Do not assign an imagined saving to that trade. Measure engineering hours, support touches, retained bytes, downstream sends, and reconciliation exceptions over a representative month.

Polling and fallback are product decisions

Support and debugging screens should poll message status with a bounded schedule because delivery events are not pushed by webhook. Poll only while a challenge can still affect a recovery decision, add jitter, stop at a terminal state or local deadline, and store state transitions rather than every identical response. Polling forever converts uncertain delivery into predictable load.

Email fallback is a separate authentication channel, not a resend button with a different address. Infrai's email surface does not provide managed OTP, so adopting it for fallback means building custom email code generation and verification, including its own attempts, expiry, idempotency, templates, sender authentication, and audit trail. Google also requires senders to follow authentication and delivery guidelines. If that engineering and compliance scope is unacceptable, choose a specialist with the fallback channel and recovery semantics already required.

Do not silently weaken the policy after an SMS failure. A privileged gaming administrator who cannot receive SMS should enter a separately risk-assessed recovery path, with explicit support evidence and session revocation rules, rather than inheriting an easier email path by accident.

The decision rule

Choose the provider after replaying one month of projected starts through five ledgers: messages, integration changes, support work, retained evidence, and downstream security exposure. Require a challenge-level join key across all five. Then test the awkward cases: the initial request times out after acceptance, two resends race, autofill supplies an expired code, delivery remains unknown, and verification succeeds twice concurrently.

The right design keeps those cases deterministic even when delivery is not. For a US/EU gaming recovery flow with no voice requirement, Infrai is a credible option when plain REST, self-described schemas, and consistent per-call metadata reduce the operating burden enough to justify polling and application-owned controls. Twilio Verify, Vonage Verify, or Sinch Verification is the stronger starting point when specialist verification channels or tooling dominate; AWS End User Messaging SMS deserves a close look when AWS governance and existing operational competence dominate.

The final artifact is an audit trail, not a receipt from an SMS vendor. It should explain which administrator recovery was attempted, which policy admitted it, which provider operation followed, what state was observed, and why precisely one recovery grant was consumed.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the React Native recovery guide and verify the current discovery schema before implementation.

Further reading

  • NIST Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management
  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Vonage Verify API documentation
  • Sinch Verification API documentation
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS documentation
  • Google email sender guidelines

title: Sideways Orders: Normalise Camera Image Orientation (Before Print Output Validation)
description:
An uploaded product photo is not ready for print merely because a browser displays it upright. Camera metadata can describe a rotation while the stored pixels remain sideways, and conversion can leave you with an artifact whose geometry no longer matches the order. TL;DR: read the metadata, choose an explicit rotation, rotate the pixels upright, convert to the required print format, and validate the converted dimensions before accepting the asset. Record the applied transform so it can be undone.

That ordering is the recommendation. It also defines the useful page: not "image job failed," but "the converted asset's dimensions disagree with the expected upright geometry." The first alert describes a worker. The second describes a customer-visible print risk.

For an e-commerce team that also has to moderate user-uploaded product images before they go live, technical print acceptance and moderation should remain separate gates. Infrai can fit the processing side when one REST credential already covers other backend work: one key and one bill remove another secret lifecycle, SDK surface, and invoice from the service inventory. They do not remove the obligation to inspect the final artifact.

What page should fire when the preview lies?

Frame this as an incident even if the first report arrives before a real order ships. A seller uploads a portrait photo, the preview honors its camera orientation, and a print worker converts the underlying pixels without applying the same transform. The job returns success. Every aggregate chart is green. The final asset is landscape.

Green is not enough.

The invariant is stricter: the final pixels must be upright, the decoded output dimensions must match the planned orientation, and the job record must say which rotation was applied. A pre-conversion check only characterizes the input. It cannot catch an output that was converted at the wrong size, so validation belongs after conversion and before the order advances.

Suppose an input is 3000 by 2400 pixels and its metadata requires a 90-degree rotation. The expected upright geometry is 2400 by 3000. If the converter emits 3000 by 2400, stop the order path and retain the source; do not reduce that discrepancy to a generic processing error. This is the evidence needed to reverse a bad decision rather than guess at it later.

Moderation answers another question: may this user-uploaded image appear on the storefront? Orientation and format validation answer whether it is technically usable for print. A single processed=true flag hides both decisions and produces a poor incident timeline.

How should Node.js normalise camera image orientation metadata?

Rotation takes explicit degrees, which means application code must translate metadata into an angle. Keep that translation in a small, reviewed function. Reject an orientation the function does not understand; guessing is the wrong failure mode for an order asset.

The example below uses one verified API route to read metadata, while keeping its request body schema-driven rather than inventing fields. Put the current request object in INFRAI_METADATA_JSON; Infrai's public discovery response supplies the full JSON Schema and runnable examples for each capability. The HTTP call sets its method and bearer header explicitly, checks non-success responses, and backs off on 429 while honoring an integer Retry-After value.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Transform struct {
    SourceOrientation int `json:"source_orientation"`
    ClockwiseDegrees  int `json:"clockwise_degrees"`
    ExpectedWidth     int `json:"expected_width"`
    ExpectedHeight    int `json:"expected_height"`
}

func plan(orientation, width, height int) (Transform, error) {
    degrees := map[int]int{1: 0, 3: 180, 6: 90, 8: 270}
    rotation, ok := degrees[orientation]
    if !ok {
        return Transform{}, fmt.Errorf("unsupported orientation %d", orientation)
    }

    outWidth, outHeight := width, height
    if rotation == 90 || rotation == 270 {
        outWidth, outHeight = height, width
    }
    return Transform{orientation, rotation, outWidth, outHeight}, nil
}

func validateOutput(gotWidth, gotHeight int, t Transform) error {
    if gotWidth != t.ExpectedWidth || gotHeight != t.ExpectedHeight {
        return fmt.Errorf("converted dimensions %dx%d; want %dx%d",
            gotWidth, gotHeight, t.ExpectedWidth, t.ExpectedHeight)
    }
    return nil
}

func readMetadata(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/image/metadata", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req = req.WithContext(ctx)
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("metadata returned %s: %s", resp.Status, responseBody)
        }
        return responseBody, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("metadata retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    requestBody := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_METADATA_JSON"))
    if len(requestBody) == 0 || !json.Valid(requestBody) {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_METADATA_JSON must contain schema-valid JSON")
    }

    result, err := readMetadata(context.Background(), &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}, requestBody)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(result))

    t, err := plan(6, 3000, 2400)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if err := validateOutput(2400, 3000, t); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    record, err := json.Marshal(t)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(record))
}

This deliberately covers the rotational cases 1, 3, 6, and 8. Mirrored orientation values require reflection as well as rotation. Route those inputs to an implementation that supports both operations instead of silently treating them as ordinary rotations.

Persist the source object identifier, source orientation, applied degrees, target format, and measured final dimensions with the job. Preserve the original. If metadata parsing or the rotation rule is later found to be wrong, that compact record turns repair into a deterministic operation.

Four integration paths expose different failure surfaces

The fastest first result depends on where image work already lives. Credential count and SDK surface matter at 3 a.m., but coverage matters more than consolidation when the required transform is outside a general service's contract.

Option Setup and surface Strong fit Operating boundary
Sharp A Node.js package using libvips Local metadata, rotation, and conversion in an existing Node.js worker The team owns native packaging, memory limits, and worker isolation
ImageMagick A mature command-line tool or language binding Broad, explicit transformations in a dedicated media worker The team owns safe command construction and process containment
Cloudinary A hosted media API and asset workflow Systems already using its upload, transformation, and delivery model Adds a specialist credential and product surface
Imgix Source-backed image processing and delivery Storefronts whose transformed images are served through its delivery pipeline A private print-worker artifact may not benefit from a delivery-centered design
Infrai Plain REST capabilities under one bearer key Backends consolidating image work with other services under one key and bill Prefer a specialist when advanced image behavior is the deciding requirement

Sharp is the most direct answer for a Node.js service that can safely run image work in-process or in its own worker. ImageMagick suits a team that wants a large transformation vocabulary and accepts a process boundary. Cloudinary and Imgix are stronger candidates when hosted asset management or delivery is already architectural, rather than incidental.

Teams already consolidating backend operations behind a REST boundary should try Infrai for metadata-driven rotation and conversion because one credential avoids another vendor SDK and secret lifecycle, while public discovery exposes the current schema needed to reach a useful first result. Its discovery surface is public without a key, and the platform reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules with runnable examples in 10 languages. Those are integration advantages, not proof of deeper image coverage.

The boundary matters. The limitation of consolidation is capability depth: Infrai is not the right fit when local control, mirrored transforms, or a richer image toolchain determines correctness; choose Sharp or ImageMagick for that job. Choose a hosted specialist when its asset workflow is already the system of record. A broad backend API earns its place when reducing operational inventory is more valuable than adopting a dedicated media platform, but that trade-off must be made against the exact transforms the order contract requires, not the appeal of having one fewer dashboard.

Build the preventative order path

Quarantine the upload first. Read its metadata, map orientation to a reviewed transform, rotate the pixels, convert to the print format, decode the resulting file to measure its actual dimensions, and run moderation before anything becomes visible. Only then should the asset advance with the order.

Retries deserve the same attention as rotation. A metadata read can repeat safely, but transformation workers must not create competing final records or advance an order twice. Give the job a stable identity and make its state transition conditional so duplicated work converges on the same result. Page on the invariant violation after retries are exhausted, not on every transient attempt.

During rollout, inspect representative outputs instead of trusting a throughput dashboard. Keep fixtures for portrait, landscape, already-upright, rotated, and mirrored inputs. The first four exercise the mapping above; the mirrored fixture proves that unsupported input takes the specialist path rather than slipping through. For each fixture, compare the decoded artifact, not a preview generated from the source: record the original geometry, chosen degrees, expected geometry, actual post-conversion geometry, and moderation decision. If the worker reports success but those two geometry pairs disagree, the order remains quarantined and the page carries the job identity plus the transform record. That is enough context to distinguish a wrong metadata mapping from a conversion that produced the wrong artifact without opening three dashboards during the incident.

Five fixtures beat a green chart.

Where should this rule stop?

Do not rotate an image twice. If a trusted upstream component guarantees upright pixels and removed orientation metadata, verify that contract with fixtures and skip this stage. Applying the camera transform again would manufacture the exact defect the pipeline is intended to prevent.

The same rule does not establish color profiles, print bleed, DPI policy, or every format-specific prepress requirement. It establishes upright pixels and expected geometry after conversion. Those other checks belong to the print contract, and a specialist is the better choice when they dominate the job.

The acceptance decision can remain small: upright pixels, expected post-conversion dimensions, a recorded transform, and separate moderation approval before publication. If this boundary matches your system, start with Infrai's documentation and use discovery to obtain the current request schema.

Sources

  • Sharp documentation
  • ImageMagick documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • Imgix image rendering API
  • Infrai documentation

title: Taste is not a design methodology
description:
It has become our favorite answer to AI-generated sameness. The reality is good products come from judgment built on facts, and the agency to use them when the room prefers opinions.

Ask Rick Rubin what he does and he’ll tell you he has “no technical ability” and knows nothing about music. In a 2023 interview with Anderson Cooper, the producer said artists pay him for confidence in his own taste.

https://medium.com/media/1f83a53654c7bc936b099303acddda54/href
“The confidence I have in my taste and my ability to express what I feel has proven helpful for artists.” — Rick Rubin

Everyone now wants that job.

Just typing this makes me squirm because I believe the field should be research and data driven as much as it can be. With humans even.

“Taste is the new moat” might be the industry’s favorite sentence of 2026: artificial intelligence made competent screens cheap, so the one thing left to sell is the judgment to pick the good one. A ProductLed interview in January went further, telling builders not to validate before they build. It’s about 45 minutes in.

I decided not to show the video inline because it adds fuel to the fire and their use of typography isn’t to my taste.

It’s come up with couple of authors I follow — The taste paradox by Nicole Alexandra Michaelis is a good read over at UX Collective, and Xinran Ma had a interview recently about it in UX — and it’s in the zeitgeist.

My point is that it’s the wrong word.

The moat crowd is right that judgment matters; they’re wrong about where it comes from:

  • Taste is a preference. It comes from what you’ve seen and who you admire, and two people with different taste can disagree with no way to settle it.
  • Judgment is a claim you can check. It rests on principles research has tested, plus evidence about your users, so it can be explained, taught, and shown wrong.

Judgment needs agency too, because someone has to raise those facts when the most senior voice would rather trade opinions. What Nicole Alexandra Michaelis and Xinran Ma are talking about Judgement i.e. experience they can back with facts and experience.

The short rule: if you can’t name the fact or research behind a call, it’s still an opinion, which is otherwise known as taste.

Admit taste is an opinion

In 2001, researchers in Bordeaux and Montpellier gave a panel of 54 tasters a white wine colored red with an odorless dye. The panel described it with the vocabulary of red wine.

Nothing had changed but the color, and that was enough to overwrite their noses.

That’s the trouble with treating taste as a standard: it’s an opinion that feels like a fact. Two skilled designers can look at the same screen, reach opposite conclusions, and neither can prove the other mistaken.

Taste feels like perception, but a lot of it is expectation. Apple Music is probably the best example, it’s Apple, but still a challenging application to use established as fact.

For example, I like driving Audi TTs. A lot.

The proportions, the way one sits on a highway on-ramp, the complete impracticality of the back seat, the beautifully designed cockpit, the race to 110 miles per hour in California.

That last part is just storytelling, really.

I don’t expect any of that to be anyone else’s taste, and nothing is wrong when it isn’t, because my taste in cars only has to satisfy only me. A product has to work for thousands of people who never met me for it to be profitable, and that’s where a preference stops being enough.

My expectation is that Audi TT’s are designed for my taste, and it doesn’t fail me, ever.

Design has its own version of the wine study.

In 1995, Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura of Hitachi had people rate 26 ATM layouts and found that how usable a layout looked tracked its beauty far more than its inherent usability. The field now calls this the aesthetic-usability effect, and it cuts both ways.

Generative tools make this worse because they turn out polished screens by default, so every option in the review looks finished. That’s the blind spot in the moat argument: the less polish costs, the less polish can tell you.

It reminds me of a conversation I had with Scott Jenson — Generative AI makes a lot of beautifully just above average screens. I made that argument they’re still better than a lot of portfolios I have seen, even if the screens have less depth.

This is why “does it have taste?” makes a weak review question: it has no failure condition other than an opinion.

Ruiqi Zhou called taste unfalsifiable in a February essay named Taste Is the New Moat — And That’s the Problem. It’s a great read, and points out that a standard you can never fail works more like a status marker, and status markers reward whoever already holds status. Usually, that’s product management.

Build judgment on laws that have held for centuries

User experience borrowed its foundations from people who ran experiments, and they had computers in only some cases.

Here are examples:

  • Paul Fitts showed in 1954 that the time to hit a target depends on its size and distance using fighter cockpits for research, and William Edmund Hick showed that decision time climbs as options pile up. Both findings have held up for seven decades.
  • Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich developed heuristic evaluation in 1990, and the ten heuristics are still the default checklist. Each turns an opinion into a checkable claim, like a button too small for a thumb.
  • Dieter Rams and his ten principles took what could have stayed personal taste and wrote it down where other people could use it, which is why teams still audit work against them fifty years on.

They are normative rather than experimental, but a checklist can be argued with. I keep plain-language summaries of Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, Nielsen’s heuristics, and Rams’s principles on ux-guidelines.com, a reference site I maintain. Every law has conditions, and knowing them is part of judgment.

Hick’s Law describes a choice among equally likely options, and a 1985 study of its exceptions found cases where adding choices barely slowed people down. Fitts measured people tapping a stylus between two targets, not a thumb stretching across a phone.

A law applied outside its conditions is just another opinion with a citation.

Principles don’t settle everything.

At Microsoft, Ronny Kohavi’s team reported that only about a third of well-run experiments improved the metric they were designed to move. The laws tell you what’s likely, and testing tells you what happened.

User research earns its place next to the laws for the same reason.

A law is general and your users are specific, so only watching them shows which steps they repeat and where they give up. Teresa Torres makes the cadence the point, defining continuous discovery as weekly contact with customers by the team building the product, rather than a study that lands after the decision.

Test beauty with the people who will use it

None of this means beauty is decoration. The same aesthetic-usability effect explains why users forgive attractive products, and appearance shapes trust and first impressions.

Don Norman gave the effect a mechanism in Emotional Design: a positive mood broadens thinking and makes people more forgiving of small friction. Jony Ive’s teams built the most admired hardware of their era and also shipped the butterfly keyboard, which Apple settled a class action over for $50 million in 2022 after years of complaints.

Taste operating at that altitude still needed someone to check whether the thing worked.

The mistake is assuming the designer’s eye can stand in for the audience’s. Nielsen Norman Group showed the same five screenshots to 229 adults aged 18 to 25 and 228 aged 35 and older,

The results?

  • The younger group rated the flat designs slightly more attractive.
  • The older, slightly less attractive.

Whose taste was right? Each group’s, for itself.

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, especially in enterprise software, where the person who admires the demo is rarely the one who lives in the product eight hours a day.

Beauty is a user outcome, so measure it like one.

That’s where the line between fact and opinion falls here. What users report about a screen is a fact about your audience, while a design lead’s verdict is one more opinion, however practiced the eye behind it. The survey used a modified version of the Microsoft Desirability Toolkit, which asks people to pick words that describe what they see from a fixed list.

Score task success and time on task separately from those ratings, so a polished prototype can’t inflate the verdict on whether the thing works.

Teach the principles before the portfolio

In 2009, two researchers who had spent careers on opposite sides of this argument wrote a paper together. Daniel Kahneman had documented how judgment fails, while Gary Klein had defended expert intuition in the field.

Their joint answer on when intuition deserves trust came down to two conditions:

  • The environment has to be regular enough to learn about who they’re designing for
  • The person needs a real chance to learn it

Design taste rarely gets that chance. A designer ships a screen, moves on to the next project, and never finds out whether the choice helped anyone.

Confidence grows with years, but accuracy only grows with feedback.

Tell a designer two years out of school to trust their taste, after a portfolio course, maybe an internship, and very few closed loops between a decision and its outcome. What they have is exposure to showcase sites and admired apps, which produces taste that matches the feed, not the user.

Principles are the shortcut experience can’t hand out, and they come with standing. A junior designer who knows Hick’s Law can push back on a longer menu in her first critique, and a new hire who has studied the heuristics can flag a missing undo before anyone senior does.

Facts give people the agency that seniority usually keeps for itself.

Give everyone the agency to argue from facts

Taste has a politics problem.

When the standard is taste, the taste that counts usually belongs to the most senior person present. Ron Kohavi named it in a 2008 Stanford talk, Listen to Your Customers not to the HiPPO: the HiPPO is the highest-paid person’s opinion.

A taste culture is a HiPPO culture with better typography.

The fix isn’t to ban taste from the room, it’s to stop one person from owning it without evidence.

Everybody on a team has taste, and the new designer’s is worth as much as the vice president’s, which is exactly why it makes a poor standard: nothing decides whose version wins except rank. Facts don’t work that way, since a law or a session recording says the same thing no matter who reads it out.

Taste cultures have a patron saint they misappropriated: Steve Jobs.

He told BusinessWeek in 1998 that designing by focus group is hard. People, he said, “don’t know what they want until you show it to them.” It gets quoted as permission to skip research, though the same answer described watching trends and studying Apple’s installed base.

But even he met his match in Paul Rand.

When Steve Jobs needed a logo for NeXT in 1986, he hired Rand, whom he openly called the greatest living graphic designer. The friction came immediately: Jobs asked for a few options, and Rand refused, saying he would solve the problem and Jobs would pay him, and if he wanted options he could hire someone else.

Jobs agreed to the terms and the $100,000 fee. Rand returned with one design, the tilted black cube, presented in a hand-bound booklet that walked Jobs through the reasoning until the logo felt inevitable.

Jobs loved it, and later admitted that you don’t hand a genius a menu.

Because of this, Apple did research all the time and that gave Jobs credibility to make judgement calls. Those that claim they have the same truly understand the company, nor how to combine taste with judgement.

Even Steve Jobs’ famous 2x2 Matrix Strategy is rooted in science — Paradox of Choice.

The larger problem is survivorship bias, another old law. We remember the founder whose certainty paid off and forget the rooms where the same certainty sank the product with dollar amount attached to it.

Agency with receipts is the fix.

Session notes, retention data, and a heuristic all lose to a senior “that feels off,” unless the team agrees that facts outrank opinions.

With that agreement in place, the quietest person in the room can win by naming the law a design breaks or the data point it ignores. Peter Merholz argues that design executives earn that standing by making design their secondary concern.

The fair counterargument belongs to Doug Bowman, Google’s first visual designer.

In 2009 he left and explained why in Goodbye, Google: a team was testing 41 shades of blue, and he had been asked to prove whether a border should be three, four, or five pixels wide.

His complaint went past the trivia: with nobody senior who understood design, he argued, the company ran out of reasons for its decisions, and data became “a crutch for every decision” that kept anything daring from shipping.

$200 million later. Hard to argue that as an outcome.

Measuring everything is its own way of dodging judgment, so decisions slow to the test calendar, and designers who could settle a border width from a principle leave for places where that counts, as Bowman did.

Aim evidence at the choices that change what users can do. A corner radius needs no significance test, since a law settles it faster.

Choose facts over opinions

Judgment is knowing which facts apply, and where they stop applying: a law, a heuristic, a published study, or research on your own users. Where taste says “this feels right,” judgment points out that the target is too small to tap reliably and that Fitts showed why in 1954.

Agency is saying that out loud in the review, even when it cuts against the most senior opinion in the room.

Judgment tells you which facts matter, and agency is using them when the room prefers an opinion.

The new reality:

  • Generative tools can produce fifty layouts before my morning coffee.
  • Judgment cuts the pile fast, dropping the ones with targets too small to hit, menus too long to scan, and flows that ask people to hold too much in their heads.
  • What’s left goes to research, where users settle what the principles can’t.

Teams that run interviews and usability sessions on a schedule build a store of facts they can reach for in any review, and teams that skip them are left with preferences and a deadline. Dan Maccarone spent a year rebuilding his studio’s process around these tools and found that it didn’t make the work faster, which he counts as the point: what changed was where the thinking had to happen.

Rubin’s approach works because a record has no task to fail. A designer who borrows that job description claims the authority without the conditions that make it hold.

Judgment also improves in a way taste doesn’t, if somebody writes the call down. Jeff Gothelf formalizes that in the Lean UX canvas: state what you believe will happen, then name the evidence that would tell you whether you were right. It’s the equivalent of the Change My Mind meme, and it’s brilliant.

Picture two designers.

  • One moves a filter panel above the results because Hick’s Law favors fewer competing choices on the way to what people came for, predicts lower search abandonment, and checks the numbers six weeks after launch.
  • The other spends the same six weeks studying award-winning screen shots.

Only the first one learned something new about their users, and only their judgment got sharper.

Conclusion

Taste isn’t going away, and it isn’t the real enemy.

Opinions shape style, brand voice, and the small choices no principle covers. The trouble starts when an opinion gets treated as a fact and wins arguments it hasn’t earned.

The moat story is half right.

Artificial intelligence does make average output cheap, and plenty of products will look alike because of it. The scarce skill isn’t picking the prettiest variation, it’s knowing which ones break what the field already knows, which ones deserve a test, and what the result means for the next decision.

The wine panel in Bordeaux wasn’t foolish; its members were human, and so are we. That’s the whole reason design has laws and methods at all.

Human perception drifts toward what it expects to see, and principles are how a field keeps itself honest across decades of new tools.

So learn the laws, read the research carefully, and give your team the agency to use both. Then let your users decide the rest. Judgment you can explain, backed by the nerve to raise it, will outlast taste you can only defend, and teams built on it will ship the products everyone else ends up copying.

Action Items

  • Ask “what fact supports this?” instead of “does it have taste?” In critiques, every significant call should rest on a principle, a study, or something your users did. If nobody can name one, label the call an opinion and flag it for testing.
  • Teach the laws before the look. Give junior designers Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, cognitive load theory, and Nielsen’s heuristics before mood boards. Principles hand them decades of feedback, and the standing to use it.
  • Make it safe to push back with facts. Say plainly that a cited principle or data point outranks a job title, and back the junior designer who uses one against you. Agency that gets punished once rarely shows up twice.
  • Test where the facts run out. Brand feel, new interaction patterns, and cases where two laws conflict all need research. Run a usability session, a few interviews, or a first-click test that week, and log the prediction behind it. Leave the border widths alone.

Taste is not a design methodology was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Why I Switched from Express to NestJS in Production (And What 4 Years Taught Me)
description:
Every Node.js developer loves Express.

It is minimalistic, unopinionated, and takes less than 10 lines of code to get an HTTP server running. When I started my backend career, Express was my weapon of choice.

But in 2022, as our backend at MedPiper scaled across enterprise healthcare integrations, financial reporting, and dozens of third-party APIs, our Express codebase started showing its scars:

  • Every new engineer structured their route files differently.
  • Route middleware order was fragile — missing a single authMiddleware in one router file silently left an endpoint unprotected.
  • req.user was mutated arbitrarily across 15 different files, making debugging state bugs an absolute nightmare.
  • Unit testing required heavy monkey-patching because there was no clean dependency injection.

That was the turning point. We migrated our core backend to NestJS.

Four years and millions of production requests later, here is an honest breakdown of why we made the switch, what broke, and what we learned.

1. The Express Paradox: Complete Freedom is a Liability at Scale

Express does not have an opinion on:

  • How you organize your folders
  • How you inject database models
  • How you validate incoming JSON payloads
  • How you handle business logic vs HTTP transport

When you are a solo developer building a weekend MVP, this freedom feels like a superpower.

At team scale, complete freedom is technical debt.

In an unopinionated Express codebase, 5 developers will write 5 different architectural patterns. One engineer will use a service layer, another will write SQL queries directly inside route callbacks, and a third will attach custom properties to the global req object.

NestJS solves this with enforced architectural conventions:

  • Controllers handle HTTP requests and return responses.
  • Services (Providers) encapsulate pure business logic.
  • Modules create explicit, isolated dependency boundaries.

When a new engineer joins a NestJS codebase, they know exactly where the database query lives, where the route validation happens, and how modules talk to each other — within 10 minutes of opening the repo.

2. The 3 Superpowers That Made NestJS Irreplaceable

A. First-Class Dependency Injection (Testability)

In Express, mocking a database service during testing usually involves hacking jest.mock() or passing dependencies manually through 5 function layers.

In NestJS, inversion of control is built into the framework:

@Injectable()
export class UserService {
  constructor(
    private readonly prisma: PrismaService,
    private readonly redis: RedisService,
  ) {}

  async getUser(id: string) {
    const cached = await this.redis.get(`user:${id}`);
    if (cached) return cached;
    return this.prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id } });
  }
}

In your unit tests, you can mock PrismaService or RedisService in 3 lines without touching the database:

const module = await Test.createTestingModule({
  providers: [
    UserService,
    { provide: PrismaService, useValue: mockPrisma },
    { provide: RedisService, useValue: mockRedis },
  ],
}).compile();

B. Strict Request Lifecycle Pipeline

In Express, middleware handles authentication, logging, data validation, and rate limiting all lumped into one concept: (req, res, next).

NestJS separates these into a clear, predictable execution order:

  1. Middleware: Low-level tasks (CORS, body parsing, helmet headers).
  2. Guards: Authentication & RBAC (e.g., @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, RolesGuard)).
  3. Interceptors: Pre/post-controller request transformation and timing.
  4. Pipes: Automatic payload validation and type coercion via class-validator.
  5. Filters: Centralized exception handling and RFC 7807 compliant error responses.

This prevents the classic Express vulnerability where an endpoint is accidentally exposed because someone forgot to chain a middleware function.

C. Automatic OpenAPI / Swagger Documentation

In Express, maintaining Swagger documentation usually means manually updating an outdated swagger.yaml file that inevitably drifts away from reality.

In NestJS, your TypeScript DTOs automatically generate an interactive Swagger UI at /api/docs:

export class CreateUserDto {
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'dev@company.com' })
  @IsEmail()
  email: string;

  @ApiProperty({ example: 'P@ssword123!' })
  @MinLength(8)
  password: string;
}

Your documentation is literally your code. It never gets outdated.

3. What We Got Wrong (The NestJS Pitfalls)

Switching to NestJS wasn't without friction. Here are the two biggest mistakes we made in our first year:

  1. Circular Dependency Loops: If Module A imports Module B, and Module B imports Module A, NestJS will throw an unhelpful startup error. We learned to isolate shared models into clean CommonModule or use forwardRef() sparingly.
  2. The Request-Scope Trap: Making a service @Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST }) forces every dependent service into request scope, causing massive memory allocation and latency spikes under high concurrency. We learned to rely on Singletons paired with Node.js AsyncLocalStorage.

4. Should You Still Use Express in 2026?

Yes, for specific use cases:

  • Single-purpose serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers).
  • Simple webhook receivers or micro-proxies under 300 lines of code.
  • Lightweight internal CLI tools.

Use NestJS when:

  • You are building a SaaS product, enterprise backend, or scalable REST/GraphQL API.
  • Multiple developers work on the same backend.
  • You care about automated testing, strict TypeScript validation, and long-term maintainability.

🚀 Accelerate Your Next NestJS Project

If you are starting a new NestJS project, setting up JWT auth rotation, Docker, PostgreSQL, Redis, BullMQ queues, and Swagger from scratch easily takes 40+ hours.

To save you that setup time, I packaged our battle-tested production starter kit:

👉 Get the Production NestJS Enterprise Boilerplate ($29)

(Also available on Contra ($29))

Need a quick desk reference for your workstation?

👉 Download the 1-Page Architecture Master Cheatsheet ($5)

title: How to Secure Java Docker Images and Reduce CVE Risk
description:
The Black Forest Commandos' field guide to CVEs, SBOMs, hardened images, attestations, and software supply chain security.

Your Java application can inherit vulnerable dependencies and packages from your base image before you write a single line of application code. Also, scanning your Docker image for vulnerabilities has blind spots, as the SBOM generated after the fact does not give you the full picture. A successful Docker build alone does not tell you what is shipped, how it was built, or whether you can trust it.

Asgard is under attack. Shadow creatures called CVEs have infiltrated the realm, and Thor's hammer is proving surprisingly ineffective. Odin has only one option: summon the Black Forest Commandos.

Behind the mythology is a practical question: How do we build container images that we can inspect, trust, and deploy with confidence?

Let's secure a Spring Boot sample project together, and with the help of the Commandos (CLI commands).

TL;DR

Most of the CVEs come from base images. Just swapping the baseline base image for a Docker hardened base image reduces the runtime inventory—the packages an attacker could actually reach—by 75.5%, with no application dependency changes between the two images.

Fewer number of packages, means less attack surface. Docker Hardened Images are also shipped with near-zero CVEs, non-root user, and no shell or package manager for the production images. So, even if an attacker gets inside your container, they won't have much to play with.

All these considered, swapping your base images won't make your application CVEs go away. That's why you should read the full article!

Start with the Ready-to-Run Sample

Before we start, let's check your toolset:

Checklist

  • Install Git to clone the sample repository.
  • Install and start Docker with Buildx. Check that docker info and docker buildx version work.
  • If not on Docker Desktop, install Docker Scout CLI separately. Check docker scout version.
  • Install Trivy and check trivy --version. The recorded run used 0.75.0.
  • Install Cosign and check cosign version. The recorded run used 3.1.3.
  • Have Bash, curl, and Python 3 available for the demo scripts.
  • Sign in to Docker Hub with docker login for Scout CVE queries.
  • Sign in to Docker Hardened Images with docker login dhi.io.

Docker builds, compiles, and tests the application, so you can follow this walkthrough without installing Java or Maven locally. Use a Bash-like terminal for the commands below.

Check Out the Tested Starting Point

The reference repository has two branches:

  • main, which is the state you will reach at the end of the article.
  • start, is the beginning of the journey.

We will start from there:

git clone --branch start --single-branch \
  https://github.com/ContainerSecurity-dev/dockerize-java-securely.git
cd dockerize-java-securely

You can edit and commit your experiments on this local branch. Base-image tags and vulnerability databases can still change, so your scan results may differ.

The files you'll use are:

  • src/ and pom.xml: the working application and its HTTP integration test.
  • Dockerfile.baseline: the starting image, using the official Maven and Eclipse Temurin images.
  • Dockerfile: the hardened version you'll compare against it.
  • scripts/: helpers to check the HTTP response and save vulnerability reports.

So, let it rip.

1. Build a Baseline You Can Inspect

The Commandos survey the ground before they fight. For us, that ground is a baseline image, built and pushed so it can be inspected.

We use a temporary, loopback-only registry so the audience can practice pushes and attestations without publishing application images to a public registry. This unauthenticated HTTP registry is for local demos only. For a remote registry, use an authenticated namespace you own over HTTPS.

docker run -d --name dockerize-java-demo-registry \
  -p 127.0.0.1:15000:5000 registry:3
export PLATFORM=linux/amd64   # use linux/arm64 on Apple Silicon
export IMAGE_REPO=127.0.0.1:15000/dockerize-java-securely
mkdir -p results

docker buildx build --platform "$PLATFORM" \
  -f Dockerfile.baseline \
  --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max \
  --metadata-file results/baseline-build-metadata.json \
  --push -t "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline" .

scripts/smoke-test.sh "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline"
export IMAGE="$IMAGE_REPO:baseline"

Let's unpack the commands:

  • The docker buildx build command is an extended command for building Docker images using BuildKit.
  • The flag --sbom=true instructs the builder to generate SBOM attestations: SBOM records "attached" to the image.
  • The flag --provenance=mode=max is used to generate provenance attestations. This attestation records more metadata about the build process.
  • As you can see, -f Dockerfile.baseline is used to specify the Dockerfile. So, the only non-optional argument, being the . at the end, is not actually the path to the Dockerfile, it's rather the build context, which is all the files that Docker can access and can potentionally end up in your Docker image.

View book

Also, if you inspect the smoke-test.sh file, it's running the image with the following flags:

docker run --detach --rm --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges:true -p 127.0.0.1::8080 "$image"

The smoke test should return Hello, Docker Security! as user 10001:10001. The flags are used to run the container in a safer environment.

2. Know Your Enemy: CVEs and SBOMs

Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) demonstrated why knowing which dependencies we ship matters. An SBOM, or Software Bill of Materials, is a list of software components in your application. Having this list handy helps you identify your packages in case there is a known exploit in one of them. Having it does not make your application safer by itself.

Rothütle's first mission in Asgard is to discover who lives there. Using Docker Scout, you can check the list using docker scout sbom command:

docker scout sbom "$IMAGE" --format list
docker scout sbom "$IMAGE" --format spdx --output results/sbom.spdx.json

How many packages are listed here?

Output of those commands will mention the SBOM attestation being used. If the attestation is absent from the build, Docker Scout will try to build it by scanning your files.

In the docker buildx build command we ran, we have created an SBOM attestation, and the Docker Scout command picked it up. But, the SBOM only contains packages from the final stage, which is not a full picture. A compromised build-time package can still write a backdoor into your application.

Further reading:

generating-an-sbom-with-docker-scout

3. Hunt the CVEs: Docker Scout and Trivy

Jack, our cybernetic scout, now dressing as Jack-o'-Lantern for Halloween, can detect CVEs hiding inside container images.

docker scout cves "$IMAGE"
docker scout cves --only-severity critical,high "$IMAGE"

Docker Scout is an enterprise offering, free for personal use. Trivy is an open-source alternative and similarly an industry standard.

trivy image --scanners vuln "$IMAGE"
trivy image --scanners vuln --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 "$IMAGE"

The final command should return exit code 1, because there are high and/or critical CVEs in the image. That is a security gate you should add to your workflow.
Let's save machine-readable reports with the repository's helper:

# Saves JSON, summarizes findings, and exits 1 if the gate fails.
scripts/scan.sh "$IMAGE" results/baseline-trivy.json

The scan.sh script runs Trivy under the hood, but also stores the reports and parses them. A similar script would be in your pipeline, e.g., to report the number of CVEs via a pull request comment.

Note that, severity is not the same as exploitability, and malicious software does not necessarily have a CVE. Scanner databases and package matching also differ: the same baseline yielded different totals in Scout and Trivy. Compare images within the same scanner and inspect the affected packages.

4. Include the Build Stage in Your SBOM

Rothütle suspects the inventory is incomplete: some components were present while the application was built, not only while it runs.

The baseline uses a multi-stage build, but --sbom=true alone inventories the final image. Packages used only while compiling the application can disappear from that inventory when the build stage is discarded.

First inspect the baseline's attached SBOM and provenance:

docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline" --format '{{json .SBOM}}' > results/baseline-sbom.json
docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline" --format '{{json .Provenance}}' > results/baseline-provenance.json

Now edit Dockerfile.baseline. Add this argument immediately after the build stage's FROM line:

FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
ARG BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true

Rebuild under a separate tag so you can compare the two inventories:

docker buildx build --platform "$PLATFORM" \
  -f Dockerfile.baseline \
  --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max \
  --metadata-file results/baseline-build-sbom-metadata.json \
  --push -t "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline-build-sbom" .

docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE_REPO:baseline-build-sbom" --format '{{json .SBOM}}' > results/baseline-with-build-sbom.json

The new output includes an additional sbom-build document alongside the runtime SPDX inventory. The argument adds metadata about the packages from earlier stages, and it doesn't mean those packages end up in the final image.

  • SBOM: What software was inventoried in the image and covered build stages?
  • Provenance: How was the image built, and from which materials?

Use BuildKit secret mounts for credentials. Maximum-level provenance can expose build arguments, so never put secrets in them. Furthermore, an attached attestation is not automatically a trusted cryptographic signature.

Now, how many packages are listed in the SBOM attestations?

Further reading:

the-poisoned-macchiato

5. Harden the Runtime and Measure the Difference

Armor time. Docker Hardened Images are a set of open-source and near-zero-CVE base images, designed to "armor" your Docker image against future attacks. You can check their catalog on dhi.io.

Let's swap the base image for the hardened ones:

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM dhi.io/maven:3-jdk21-dev AS build
ARG BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B verify

FROM dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-alpine3.23
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/app.jar /app/app.jar
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

If you check the sample repo, there is a file .dockerignore there with the following content:

**
!pom.xml
!src/
!src/**
!Dockerfile
!Dockerfile.baseline

This means, everything is ignored by the docker buildx build command (removed from the build context), except for the listed files. This is called an allowlist. So, instead of ignoring a bunch of files, we ignore everything, and allow a bunch of files.

Also, the POM sets finalName to app, avoiding an ambiguous JAR wildcard.

This follows Docker's Java DHI migration pattern, with explicit tests and a non-root runtime user.

docker buildx build --platform "$PLATFORM" \
  --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max \
  --metadata-file results/hardened-build-metadata.json \
  --push -t "$IMAGE_REPO:hardened" .

scripts/smoke-test.sh "$IMAGE_REPO:hardened"
# Also returns 1 for the recorded sample:
scripts/scan.sh "$IMAGE_REPO:hardened" results/hardened-trivy.json
python3 scripts/summarize-scans.py results/baseline-trivy.json results/hardened-trivy.json

It's report time! You can run all of them yourself, or just read through mine!

Observed results: 13 October 2026

Both final application images use Spring Boot 4.0.8 and Java 21. The results are based on runs on Linux Ubuntu (linux/amd64) and Mac Silicon (linux/arm64), yielding identical results. These are Trivy 0.75.0 vulnerability records, grouped by scan target; totals are not counts of unique CVE IDs across all packages.

Scan target Baseline: eclipse-temurin:21-jre Hardened: dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-alpine3.23
OS packages 0 critical, 0 high, 40 medium, 4 low No findings
Java dependencies 3 critical, 5 high, 2 medium 3 critical, 5 high, 2 medium
Other detected binary (pebble) 3 high, 5 medium, 1 low, 4 unknown Not present as a scan target

Docker Scout 1.20.3 reported 5 critical / 13 high / 2 medium / 3 unspecified for the baseline and 3 critical / 5 high / 2 medium for the hardened image. Those are separate scanner observations, not interchangeable with the Trivy counts.

The original Spring Boot 4.0.5 sample had 9 critical / 18 high / 20 medium / 6 low Java findings in Trivy. Updating to 4.0.8 reduced those findings, but did not eliminate them. The remaining Java findings implicated Tomcat and Jackson dependencies. Review the report's fixed-version guidance, update the application dependencies, rerun tests, and rescan before promotion.

Inspect the Blast Radius in Your Dependency Tree

"Update Tomcat and Jackson" is easier said than done, because most of these libraries arrive transitively through the Spring Boot BOM. Inspect what your project actually resolves before you touch a version:

# Full resolved tree (run inside the builder image if you have no local JDK):
./mvnw -B dependency:tree

# Narrow it to the packages the scanner flagged:
./mvnw -B dependency:tree -Dincludes=org.apache.tomcat.embed:tomcat-embed-core
./mvnw -B dependency:tree -Dincludes=tools.jackson.core:jackson-core

I can't believe it's 2026 and Maven flags still look like that. Dincludes. Anyway!

The tree shows each artifact's depth and the path that pulled it in. A dependency you declare directly in pom.xml can be overridden there or in a <dependencyManagement> entry; a transitive one usually needs a version override or an updated parent/BOM. After the change, confirm the fix reaches the runtime JAR, rerun mvn verify, and rescan the new digest. If an affected artifact is transitive and has no fix yet, record that in a VEX statement instead of silently suppressing it.

Check VEX Before Comparing Scanners

VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) records whether a particular vulnerability affects a product. One can create VEX records for CVEs that are harmless in their case. One can ship them with their Docker image as "VEX attestations". Docker Hardened Image come with their own VEX attestations.

Docker Scout automatically applies DHI VEX statements and excludes them from the listed CVEs; Trivy needs VEX enabled:

docker scout cves dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:8-alpine3.23

# Configure and download the DHI VEX repository first (see linked instructions).
trivy image --scanners vuln --vex repo dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:8-alpine3.23

For Trivy, enable the docker-hardened-images/advisories repository in its VEX configuration and download it before using --vex repo. Review applicable VEX statements; suppression is an assessment of affectedness, not a dependency fix.

This can sometimes explain differences in reported CVEs without any change to the image. See Docker’s VEX-aware scanning instructions.

The recorded Trivy scans above did not enable VEX. However, the observed difference between Scout and Trivy was in the non-DHI baseline, so it was not coming from VEX attestations.

Both images passed the HTTP smoke test. In the recorded comparison, with build-stage scanning enabled, the runtime SBOM contained 192 packages for the baseline and 47 for the hardened image; the separate build-stage inventories contained 396 and 377, respectively. Hence, just by swapping for a DHI base image, the number of dependencies in the production image is reduced by 75%. Hence the Artemisia bar chart image, as she's squashing the attack surface!

The results report records image digests, versions, and evidence.

docker-hardened-images-are-free

6. Sign Before You Trust: Cosign

Evie is the Commando responsible for cryptographic signatures. She always uses the immutable digest returned by the build, rather than a mutable tag:

export DIGEST_IMAGE="$IMAGE_REPO@$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("results/hardened-build-metadata.json"))["containerimage.digest"])')"
mkdir -p .demo-keys
cosign generate-key-pair --output-key-prefix .demo-keys/cosign
cosign sign --key .demo-keys/cosign.key "$DIGEST_IMAGE"
cosign verify --key .demo-keys/cosign.pub "$DIGEST_IMAGE"

# Scan the same immutable artifact; this sample still fails the gate.
trivy image --scanners vuln --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 "$DIGEST_IMAGE"

Cosign 3.1.3 successfully verifies the signature, claims, and transparency-log inclusion. The vulnerability gate still returns 1. A signed image can contain known vulnerabilities.

Keep the private key out of Git; the sample ignores .demo-keys/ and *.key. Enter a key password interactively and use a disposable key for rehearsal. Default signing publishes signature metadata and the public key to a transparency log. Production verification needs a trusted signing policy, not an arbitrary public key supplied alongside an image.

We sign the image to make sure no one altered it on the way to production. But, the attackers are getting smarter. Read the Shai Hulud family account to learn about the incident that a signed image was altered by the attacker:

taxonomy-of-modern-supply-chain-worms

7. SIP It Before You Ship It

The Shai-Hulud family illustrates why scanning a final image is not enough: malicious packages can target developers and CI before an image exists. AI coding agents are another environment with access to code, tools, and potentially credentials.

SIP: Security Immediate Plan ties the controls together:

  1. Sandbox agents. Isolate execution and restrict credentials, network access, and mounted directories.
  2. Lock down dependencies. Manage Maven dependency and plugin versions, inspect the resolved tree, and review updates. Gradle and npm projects need their own locking and install policies; this Maven sample does not exercise those tools.
  3. Harden builds. Keep compilers and build tools in the build stage, and run the final image without root privileges.
  4. Attest. Generate SBOM and provenance, including relevant build stages.
  5. Scan before promotion. Scan the exact digest, enforce your vulnerability policy, and verify trusted signatures before deployment.

Sandbox → Lock → Harden → Attest → Scan. No single scanner, image, or signature secures the entire supply chain. For agent isolation and ecosystem-specific dependency controls, see the full SIP implementation.

This walkthrough demonstrates three of those controls end to end on a real Java image: Harden (a DHI runtime running as a non-root user), Attest (SBOM and provenance, including the build stage), and Scan (gating the exact digest before promotion). It touches Lock only partially, through the Maven dependency tree and version discipline shown above; full dependency locking for Gradle and npm projects is outside this sample. Sandbox agents—isolating AI coding agents and restricting their credentials, network access, and mounts—is not exercised here at all, so treat it as an additional SIP control rather than something this experiment proved.

Read more about sbx and kits here:

docker-sandbox-kits-tutorial

When finished, remove the dedicated local registry and its temporary data:

docker rm -f dockerize-java-demo-registry

Conclusion

Three findings came out of this run, and they map directly onto the Commando team:

Key takeaways

  • Hardened base images reduce OS-level exposure. The DHI runtime dropped from 192 inventoried packages to 47 (75.5%) and removed all 44 Ubuntu package findings and the pebble binary target, without changing any application dependency.
  • SBOM attestations improve visibility. --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max attaches what shipped and how it was built, and BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true extends the inventory to the build stage.
  • Application dependency remediation remains essential. Tomcat and Jackson kept the same 3 critical and 5 high findings in both images, so hardening and signing never replaced updating libraries.

Hardening the base image and signing the result are necessary, not sufficient. The Commandos' armor kept out the creatures that came with the base image; the ones hiding inside Tomcat and Jackson are a different fight, and it is fought at the dependency level. Fix what you ship, prove how you built it, and scan the exact digest before it reaches production.

Keep Learning: Articles and Tutorials

  • Generating SBOM with Docker Scout — inspect and export software inventories.
  • The Poisoned Macchiato — Java SBOM attestations, Cosign, and OCI artifacts.
  • Docker Hardened Images are Free — hardened base images and vulnerability comparisons.
  • The Shai-Hulud Family — taxonomy of modern supply chain worms.
  • Docker Sandbox Kits: A Hands-On Tutorial — agent isolation and capability controls.
  • Black Forest Commandos: Asgard Mission DIY — a longer, hands-on version of the Commandos' mission.

Official Documentation

  • Docker Scout SBOM CLI
  • Docker Scout CVE CLI
  • Docker BuildKit SBOM attestations
  • Docker BuildKit provenance
  • Trivy
  • Sigstore Cosign
  • Docker Sandboxes

Meet the Black Forest Commandos in My Books

  • Docker and Kubernetes Security. To learn about Linux capabilities (the ones that we dropped here), or secure CI workflows, check this book.
  • Black Forest Shadow. The origin story of Gord, Rothütle, Evie, and the CVE monsters, set in the Black Forest in 1865.
  • Black Forest Commandos: Asgard Mission. The graphic novel behind the Commandos' adventure in Asgard. The story expands the mythology used in my talks and workshops. Do you want to know the ending? Spoiler alert!

SIP it before you ship it.

Mohammad-Ali A'râbi — Docker Captain, author, and creator of the Black Forest Commandos.

Results are a dated snapshot from the linked sample. Review versions, permissions, and security policies and rerun the checks before production use.
