title: My crawler said 1 in 7 websites were down. They weren't, and retrying made it worse.
description:
I'm building Fresh Leads, a tool that finds local businesses and grades their websites so agencies know who to pitch. One of the strongest signals it reports is simple:

"Their website is down."

If you sell web design, that's the best cold-call opener there is. It's also the worst thing to get wrong. If a customer calls a coffee shop and says "your site is down" while the owner is looking at it working fine, the customer loses the call and I lose the customer.

So when I finally checked those verdicts properly, the result hurt.

The measurement

I took 47 sites that one crawl had recorded as unreachable and opened each one from my laptop.

6 of them loaded instantly. That's 13% wrong. A second, larger run gave the same answer: 56 of 413, or 14%. Two of the "dead" sites belonged to well-known coffee chains, and both were serving pages perfectly well.

The cause wasn't hard to guess. The crawler runs on a serverless platform, so every request comes from a datacentre IP address. Cloudflare, Shopify and similar platforms block or challenge datacentre traffic as a matter of routine. To my crawler, a site that blocks it looks the same as a site that doesn't exist.

"Did not answer us" and "is down" are not the same sentence.

I tried three fixes. The first two failed, and the way they failed taught me more than the fix that worked.

Attempt 1: just retry the failures

The original pipeline already had a "quiet re-check" stage. Any site that failed during the main crawl (24 fetches running at once) was retried later, three at a time with a longer timeout. The reasoning sounded right: a big concurrent crawl causes throttling, so a gentle second try should get a truer answer.

That stage took up 22% of every search's runtime. Nothing recorded what it actually recovered, so I added two counters, recheck_tried and recheck_recovered, and let it run on real production searches.

36 sites retried across 6 production searches
 0 recovered

Not "low". Zero.

And looking back, it could never have been anything else. A block is perfectly consistent. If an IP gets blocked, it gets blocked again eight seconds later, and it'll keep getting blocked at any concurrency and with any timeout. Retries catch slow hosts. They can't catch refusals, and refusals were nearly all I had.

I deleted the stage. Searches got 22% faster, and the results didn't change at all.

Attempt 2: wait six hours and check again

Next idea: if retrying immediately can't tell a block from a dead site, maybe time can. A dead site stays dead. A flaky one recovers.

So I wrote confirmDown(). A first failure is recorded with a timestamp but never shown to the customer. Only a second failure at least six hours later, from a fresh connection, is allowed to say "down". A success at any point clears the record.

export function confirmDown(previous: Audit | null, next: Audit, now = Date.now()): Audit {
  // It answered: whatever happened before, it isn't down.
  if (next.reachable !== false) return { ...next, firstDownAt: null, downConfirmed: false };

  const firstDownAt = previous && !previous.reachable && previous.firstDownAt
    ? previous.firstDownAt
    : new Date(now).toISOString();

  const since = now - new Date(firstDownAt).getTime();
  // A clock that has gone backwards must not confirm anything.
  const confirmed = Number.isFinite(since) && since >= SIX_HOURS;
  return { ...next, firstDownAt, downConfirmed: confirmed };
}

It's clean, testable, and it feels rigorous. Two days later I checked it against reality: of 60 sites it had confirmed down, 13 loaded instantly from a normal connection.

unconfirmed failures   14% wrong
confirmed failures     22% wrong

Confirmation made it worse.

The reason is obvious once you see it. Waiting six hours filters out transient failures, like a server that was briefly overloaded. Those were the cases that would have recovered anyway. A datacentre block isn't transient. It fails the first check and the second one too. So the filter removed the harmless cases and left a pool that was concentrated with exactly the false verdicts it was supposed to exclude.

Time can't tell a block from a dead site. I needed a different signal.

Attempt 3: read the error I was throwing away

The signal had been there the whole time. My fetch wrapper looked like this:

try {
  return await fetch(url, { signal });
} catch {
  return null; // 🪦 every reason for failure, flattened into one
}

Node's fetch tells you why a request failed, in error.cause.code. And some of those reasons are proof, while others aren't:

Error What it means Can a browser on any network load it?
ENOTFOUND DNS has no record for the domain No. It's gone.
ECONNREFUSED The host answered and nothing is listening on the port No. It's down.
timeout, ECONNRESET, aborted TLS handshake, … Something is there but won't talk to us Often, yes

The last row is exactly what being blocked from a datacentre looks like. It's indistinguishable from a slow or hostile server, so I can't call it "down".

So I kept the reason:

let lastFailure: string | null = null;

try {
  const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
  lastFailure = null;
  return res;
} catch (e) {
  // Node puts the useful part in `cause.code`: ENOTFOUND when DNS has nothing,
  // ECONNREFUSED when nothing is listening, a timeout or reset when something
  // is there but won't talk to us.
  const cause = (e as { cause?: { code?: string } })?.cause;
  lastFailure = cause?.code ?? (e as Error)?.name ?? "unknown";
  return null;
}

And I made reachable three-valued instead of a boolean:

export function failureIsFatal(code: string | null | undefined): boolean {
  return code === "ENOTFOUND" || code === "ECONNREFUSED";
}

// After both http:// and https:// have failed:
return {
  reachable: failureIsFatal(lastFailure) ? false : null,
  failure: lastFailure,
  // ...every other finding is null too: we didn't see the page
};
  • true: we fetched it.
  • false: we have proof it's down (no DNS record, or the port refused).
  • null: we couldn't reach it, and we can't say why.

confirmDown() stayed, but only for the false case. A second look is cheap, and a wrong "down" is still the most expensive thing the product can say. What it no longer does is turn an inconclusive failure into a confident one just because it happened twice.

The null that wasn't "fine"

One trap is worth calling out, because I nearly fell into it.

My scoring code treats an audited site with no problems found as a good site. If "couldn't reach it" had been stored as "audited, no problems found", every blocked site would quietly have been graded healthy. The bug would just have flipped from "falsely down" to "falsely fine".

So null means not audited. The lead shows up as "we haven't checked their website yet", and its grade can go up later once we manage to look. It never drops now because of a claim we can't back up.

I also found that a deadline test was asserting the bug. When an audit ran out of its time budget, it returned reachable: false, which reported my timeout as a fact about their website. That test now expects null.

The cache still believed the old rule

Fixing the crawler didn't fix the data it had already written. When I counted the live table, there were 2,141 businesses whose sites showed as down, and 1,501 of them had no failure code at all. They'd been decided by a rule I'd already retired. Seventy per cent of the claim rested on evidence I'd stopped trusting.

I didn't run a backfill. The verdict is now earned on read: a row has to say it failed twice and that it failed with a fatal code. A row that can't answer the second question reads as "not checked", and the next crawl settles it under the current rule.

What I took away from it

  1. Measure what your retry actually recovers. Mine cost 22% of every search and recovered nothing. Two integer counters would have told me that months earlier.
  2. Retries and waiting only fix transient failures. If the failure is consistent, as a block is, repeating the check just confirms the wrong answer with more confidence.
  3. Filtering can concentrate errors instead of removing them. If your filter removes the cases that were never the problem, what's left can be worse than what you started with.
  4. Never catch { return null } at a boundary that makes a decision. The reason for the failure was the signal.
  5. "Unknown" deserves its own value. A boolean forced me to pick between two lies. null let the code tell the truth: we didn't manage to look.

The fix ended up being a few lines. The lesson was that "we couldn't reach it" is a fact about you, not about them, and the code should never say otherwise.

Have you been burned by a check that was confidently wrong? Or a retry loop that turned out to do nothing? Tell me in the comments.

title: I built a free static analyzer for Solana programs — here's what it catches and how it's built
description:
Solana exploits keep hitting the same bug classes: missing signer checks, arbitrary cross-program invocations, unchecked account deserialization, integer overflow. These aren't exotic — they're the same patterns that have drained hundreds of millions of dollars from on-chain programs, and they're detectable with static analysis before code ever gets deployed.

So I built SolAudit: a free, MIT-licensed static analyzer for Anchor/Solana Rust programs. 0.2.0 shipped this week.

Try it in 10 seconds: npx solaudit ./your-program

What it does

Point SolAudit at a directory of .rs files and it applies 11 security rules, then gives you a report grouped by severity — no RPC calls, no wallet, no build step:

Severity Examples
CRITICAL Missing signer checks on token transfers/mints
HIGH Arbitrary CPI (caller-controlled program IDs), unchecked deserialization, type cosplay, insecure manual account closure, missing bump canonicalization
MEDIUM Integer overflow on balance math, insecure account init, missing rent-exemption checks
LOW Missing owner checks

Each finding includes the exact line and a concrete remediation hint. Exit code is 1 on any CRITICAL/HIGH finding, so it drops straight into CI as a gate.

Three ways to use it

CLI — npx solaudit ./program, or bun add -g solaudit. Outputs human-readable, --json, or --sarif.

Web app — solaudit-web.vercel.app. Paste a public GitHub repo URL or upload a single .rs file. No install.

GitHub Action — on the Marketplace. Ten lines of YAML and every push gets scanned, with findings uploaded to your repo's Security tab as code-scanning alerts:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- uses: blueeyez425-art/solaudit@main
  with:
    path: ./programs

On accuracy — honest numbers

On the committed labeled benchmark suite, the engine scores 93.8% precision, 100% recall, 96.8% F1 on rule-covered categories.

Those numbers describe that suite, not general effectiveness. One known gap remains: duplicate mutable accounts. I built a "distinctness" heuristic for it, it produced false positives on common legitimate patterns (e.g., a deposit instruction's user/vault token accounts of the same type), so I didn't ship it. A scanner that cries wolf gets uninstalled; I'd rather have a smaller rule set people trust.

Supply chain: verify the build yourself

A security tool that asks you to trust its binaries shouldn't exist. Every npm publish of SolAudit goes through GitHub Actions trusted publishing with signed Sigstore provenance — the package on npm is cryptographically bound to an exact commit and workflow run in the public repo. There's no "someone's laptop" in the loop. npm displays the provenance badge on the package page.

The dogfooding story

The repo's own CI runs SolAudit against its intentionally vulnerable example program on every push. Setting that up immediately caught a real bug — in my own Action: when a consuming repo had a local workspace package named solaudit, npx would resolve the local package instead of the pinned npm release, and the scan silently ran... nothing. The fix: install the pinned CLI into a temp dir and invoke it directly. Self-scanning found a distribution bug before any user did. That's the loop working as advertised.

What's next

  • Closing the duplicate-mutable-accounts gap with a smarter heuristic that survives the false-positive review
  • More rules from post-mortems of real exploits
  • Reentrancy-via-CPI-callback detection

Links

  • Repo: https://github.com/blueeyez425-art/solaudit (⭐ if useful)
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/solaudit
  • Action: https://github.com/marketplace/actions/solaudit-security-scanner
  • Demo: https://solaudit-web.vercel.app/

Feedback, false positives, and rule requests are all welcome as GitHub issues. SolAudit is free and will keep being built either way — development doesn't depend on tips. That said, if it saved you real time or caught a real bug, there's a tip link in the README, and it's genuinely appreciated.

Built by an independent security researcher. SolAudit is a first-pass scanner, not an audit — it doesn't replace manual review for anything holding real funds.

title: Microsoft Patches Record 1,413 Flaws, Including Exploited Windows Shell Bug
description:
Microsoft on Tuesday shattered its own Patch Tuesday record by shipping patches for a whopping 1,413 vulnerabilities, including one that it said has come under active exploitation.

These include 1,102 flaws in Windows, 134 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 36 in SharePoint Server, and 22 in SQL Server. Of these, more than 670 relate to privilege escalation, followed by over 300 remote code

description:
Anti Money Laundering AI

Announcement

New minor engine versions released for the retail line of business within the v004.005, v004.009, and v004.010 version lines (aml-retail.default.v004.005.202608-000, aml-retail.default.v004.009.202608-000, and aml-retail.default.v004.010.202608-000). These versions extend support for the major engine version and include no significant changes compared to the previous minor versions.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.16.10

On September 17, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.10.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.16.10.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
556750755 Fixed an issue where EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) dropped or truncated events following a large (>16 KB) event under load on the http-adaptor datapath.
547712217 Fixed an issue where EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) responses larger than 16 KB could be truncated or corrupted across socket reads.
519729209 Fixed a SAML XML Signature Wrapping (XSW) vulnerability in the ValidateSAMLAssertion policy.
514384893 Hardened the Script policy to block server-side request forgery (SSRF) to link-local addresses.
505645076 Fixed a security issue in the OAuthV2 policy to prevent unauthorized token injection via HTTP form parameters.
505543289 Fixed thread-safety issues in the Netty client connection pool and channel lifecycle.
503817773 Improved security in the OAuthV2 policy implicit grant redirect_uri validation.
502268966 Apigee hybrid now supports optional decoding of percent-encoded path separators (%2F and %5C) before flow selection via the request.path.decode.encoded.separators proxy property.
480770263 Fixed an issue in the SpikeArrest policy to handle edge cases that previously caused NullPointerException and 500 errors.
472526232 Improved SAML assertion validation in the ValidateSAMLAssertion policy against entity and comment injection.
470375542 Fixed a memory leak in WSFrameDecoder that could result in a spike in 503 responses with no_healthy_upstream errors.
449228485 Apigee hybrid now supports configuring custom Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable or maxUnavailable) values for Apigee hybrid components in your overrides.yaml file.
402250928 Apigee hybrid now supports routing outbound calls from AI policies, such as the Model Armor and semantic caching policies, through an HTTP forward proxy.

Feature

Kubernetes 1.36 support

Apigee hybrid v1.16.10 adds support for Kubernetes 1.36 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Google Distributed Cloud Virtual for VMware (vSphere), Google Distributed Cloud Virtual for bare metal, Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Rancher Kubernetes Engine (RKE2).

For more information, see Supported platforms.

Feature

Forward proxy support for AI policies

Apigee hybrid v1.16.10 adds forward proxy support for AI policies, such as the Model Armor and semantic caching policies. Outbound calls from these policies can now be routed through an HTTP forward proxy.

For more information, see Configure a forward proxy, Get started with the Model Armor policies, and Get started with semantic caching policies.

Feature

You can add unit tests to pipelines to validate your SQL transformation logic against mock datasets. Unit tests for pipelines are generally available (GA).

  • Workload Manager

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Change

Cloud SQL for MySQL now automatically enables point-in-time recovery (PITR) in a separate, asynchronous operation after disaster recovery (DR) switchover and replica failover operations complete. Because PITR enablement no longer blocks switchover and replica failover, these operations complete faster, helping you reduce your recovery time.

For more information, see Use advanced disaster recovery (DR).

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Change

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL now automatically enables point-in-time recovery (PITR) in a separate, asynchronous operation after disaster recovery (DR) switchover and replica failover operations complete. Because PITR enablement no longer blocks switchover and replica failover, these operations complete faster, helping you reduce your recovery time.

For more information, see Use advanced disaster recovery (DR).

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4D machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by AMD EPYC Turin processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4D instances are purpose-built for low core usage and high storage density workloads such as:

  • SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • Data analytics and data warehouses
  • Search
  • Parallel file systems for AI/ML

The Z4D machine series delivers up to 3 TB of memory and 42,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4D also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4D instances are available in predefined standardlssd and highlssd machine shapes.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataform

Feature

You can use unit tests to test Dataform actions against mock data with an expected result set. Dataform unit tests are generally available (GA).

Gemini Enterprise

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini Code Assist availability update for subscriptions

If you're getting a new Gemini Enterprise Standard or Plus subscription or renewing an existing subscription online, the subscription no longer includes access to Gemini Code Assist features. Existing subscriptions that include Gemini Code Assist features can still access the features until the end of their subscription term.

Instead of Gemini Code Assist, you can use Antigravity for IDEs with AI developer tools. For more information, see AI developer tools overview.

If you're still looking to use Gemini Code Assist with your Gemini Enterprise licenses, you can obtain a new Gemini Enterprise subscription that includes Gemini Code Assist by contacting Google Cloud sales.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Voice input for the chat box

You can speak your queries and prompts to Gemini Enterprise. Use the microphone button to record your voice, review and edit the transcribed text, and then submit the text.

This feature is generally available (GA). To make voice input available to users, a Gemini Enterprise administrator must turn on the Enable speech-to-text toggle in the Google Cloud console.

For more information, see the following:

  • Manage web app features
  • Chat with the assistant

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini Omni Flash supports stateful and streaming video generation (Preview)

Gemini Omni Flash supports stateful (store: true) and server-sent event (SSE) streaming (stream: true) video generation in the Interactions API in Preview. You can temporarily store generated videos and interaction state on the server, stream status updates and final outputs over an SSE connection, or retrieve completed asynchronous interactions using unary or streaming GET requests.

For more information, see Generate videos from text.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.34.900-gke.135 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade a cluster. Google Distributed Cloud 1.34.900-gke.135 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.900-gke.135:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between Reconciling and Running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density than the user cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue where gkectl diagnose and preflight validations failed to locate PersistentVolume datastores for user clusters deployed in a separate vSphere datacenter from the admin cluster (cpNodesInAdminDatacenter: true).
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster could get stuck because the node pool controller attempted to recreate machine resources while deletion was in progress.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.18 will roll out to Looker (original) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, September 21, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 4, 2026

Looker 26.18 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom content theme fonts were improperly applied to the Look edit mode bar. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where downloading a dashboard as a CSV or ZIP file could result in a 500 error if any dashboard elements lacked an explicit title. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where links created using the LookML link parameter could return a 500 error if no label was specified. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dashboard filter token chips didn't display an active highlighted background when a filter value was selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the Git connection test could fail to recognize Git credentials as sufficient if a branch protection rule on the Git provider restricted temporary branches. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where analytic models that referenced cross-database, schema-qualified, or dot-delimited table names failed to compile in BigQuery and Snowflake DDL generation. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom tooltips in Single Record visualizations appeared at the bottom of the Explore panel rather than directly beneath the selected row. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dashboard filter tokens and popover menus could fail to inherit fonts from custom themes. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dragging series between Y-axes on pivoted Cartesian charts could cause the Explore page to crash or prevent visualization configurations from being saved. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in Explores where you couldn't scroll within the Chart Config Editor dialog when editing JSON visualization configurations. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where scheduled PDF deliveries to Cloud Storage could produce corrupted files and unexpectedly replace spaces in filenames with underscores. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where attempting to visualize pivoted query results in SQL Runner resulted in a TypeError configuration error. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

API requests that target a LookML project whose files or directories aren't found on the instance now return a 404 Not Found error instead of a 500 Internal Server Error.

Fixed

In Conversational Analytics, the Open in Explore button and sidebar exploration links are now hidden or disabled with explanatory tooltips when you lack explore permissions for the underlying model.

Fixed

The embed preload page now supports custom theming using the theme URL query parameter.

Fixed

Donut Multiples visualizations now automatically hide overlapping value labels.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in self-service analytics where CSV and Excel uploads to BigQuery and Snowflake could fail or corrupt data when files contained multiline headers, leading numeric characters, UTF-8 BOM markers, or special characters. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where creating a shared branch based on the production branch in a bare repository project could initialize from stale remote commits, causing the Looker IDE to immediately report the branch as being behind production. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where scheduled deliveries intermittently failed with permission errors such as Cannot send all results because user permissions were incorrectly cached across scheduled jobs on worker threads. This feature now performs as expected.

NetApp Volumes

Feature

Organization Policy Service custom constraints are available for Google Cloud NetApp Volumes. You can use custom constraints to control how NetApp Volumes is used in your organization. For example, you can restrict storage pool or volume capacity, or enforce that storage pools are created only with Premium or Extreme service levels.

For more information, see Custom organization policy constraints.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

For Exadata Database Service, Oracle Database@Google Cloud is available in europe-west12 (Turin, Italy) region.

For a list of supported locations, see Supported regions and zones.

Secure Web Proxy

Feature

Secure Web Proxy supports distributed tracing by integrating with Cloud Trace. With distributed tracing, you can track the lifecycle of outbound requests from internal workloads through your Secure Web Proxy gateways to external endpoints. This integration helps you detect latency bottlenecks and troubleshoot connectivity errors.

This feature is available in Preview.

Spanner

Feature

Spanner queues are generally available (GA). Spanner queues provide transactional messaging to help you manage asynchronous work. The feature pairs this capability with the scalability and reliability of Spanner, letting you build event-driven applications. For more information, see the Spanner queues overview.

title: Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs
description: The "autofinetune" project introduces an autonomous research loop that fully automates LLM post-training workflows, including Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning via GRPO. By defining boundary conditions and evaluation metrics in a single Markdown specification, developers can deploy an AI agent to iteratively edit training scripts, launch experiments, and automatically commit verified hyperparameter optimizations to Git. Built on Google’s AI stack—including Tunix, Gemma, and Cloud TPUs—this framework eliminates manual tuning cycles, successfully demonstrating hands-off performance gains in both function calling and math reasoning models.

title: AI Gateway adds Browserbase Search and Fetch tools
description:
Browserbase Search and Fetch are now available through AI Gateway. Give your models access to current information, find relevant pages, and retrieve their contents, alongside Browserbase's existing AI SDK and Vercel Marketplace integrations.

AI Gateway lets you use Browserbase's tools across model providers with one API key. Add web search and page retrieval to any model that supports tool calling, and keep the same tools when you switch models.

These helpers are available in AI SDK 7.0.116 and later. Update with pnpm add ai@latest and set your AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY. To add search and fetch, pass the helpers in tools .

For pricing and configuration options, see the Browserbase Search and Fetch documentation.

Try the Browserbase tools in the AI Gateway model playground, or explore the model catalog.

AI Gateway provides one API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring routing, retries, and failover. You can use an AI Gateway API key or bring your own provider key.

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

title: Agents can now buy domains with the Vercel CLI
description:
Your agent can now use the Vercel CLI to buy a domain.

The agent discovers candidates with vercel domains search, checks availability and registrar pricing with vercel domains check and vercel domains price, and initiates the purchase with vercel domains buy.

The purchase decision itself stays with you by design. Run non-interactively, vercel domains buy returns a structured, machine-readable error and the suggested next commands, so the agent hands the confirmation back to you, prohibiting it from spending money without your approval.

You can confirm the price, the auto-renew choice, and the registrant contact details in an interactive terminal or the dashboard.

The CLI ships an agent-facing skill covering the discovery, pricing, and purchase workflow, so agents will follow the full sequence without being told the steps.

Read the documentation to get started.

Correction: API base path limit for Apigee hybrid organizations

The December 16, 2024 release note for enhanced per-environment proxy limits stated that the maximum number of API base paths per Apigee organization is 3000. That number is incorrect. The maximum number of API base paths per organization is 6,000 for both Apigee and Apigee hybrid.

For optimal performance, Apigee recommends using no more than 3,000 API proxy basepaths per environment or environment group. This is a recommendation, not an enforced limit.

For more information, see Limits and Enhanced per-environment proxy limits.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.10.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Impact-aware PR delta scanning: Added --diff and --staged flags to cm find to audit modified pull request hunks and 1-hop neighbor files while suppressing pre-existing vulnerabilities.
  • SARIF report export and CI gating: Added SARIF v2.1.0 export (--format sarif, --output) and severity-based CI gating (--fail-on) to cm report to integrate scan results into CI/CD pipelines and code scanning tools.
  • Adaptive hybrid deep scanning: Added --deep and --deep-workers flags to cm find to combine deterministic file pruning, parallel package-batched analysis, and post-triage verification for higher vulnerability recall and precision.
  • Custom workspace directory: Added support for the CM_HOME environment variable to override the default ~/.codemender directory for configuration, local state (state.db), backups, and artifacts.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Required build and test validation (build.command) to succeed during cm fix before marking a patch as applied and a finding as fixed.
    • Stabilized vulnerability fingerprints across multiple scans and bound cm verify directly to the target finding ID to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Restored the configured session model automatically when reconnecting to an active session with cm session resume.
    • Updated cm verify to add .exploit to .gitignore before execution so cancelled verification sessions do not leave untracked proof-of-concept scripts.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

GKE ambient networking is now available in Preview through an allowlist.

GKE ambient networking provides a simplified, sidecarless deployment model for a service mesh with Layer 4 capabilities. By moving proxy functionality to node-level components integrated into GKE Dataplane V2, ambient networking reduces resource overhead, eliminates workload restarts for proxy updates, and simplifies mesh lifecycle management.

The Preview release supports single-cluster Layer 4 mesh capabilities using the Gateway API, which includes mutual TLS (mTLS), service discovery, Layer 4 traffic management, and Layer 4 telemetry.

For more information, see Ambient networking overview and Prepare GKE ambient networking.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Knowledge Catalog support for importing dbt metadata is now generally available and includes the following updates:

  • You can import metadata from dbt Cloud job runs using the dbt Cloud interface, the dbt platform CLI, or the dbt Administrative API and webhooks.
  • You can generate and import metadata artifacts from dbt Core 2.x and dbt Fusion in addition to dbt Core 1.x.
  • You can import entry links (--include-entry-links and --skip-bigquery-link) to capture dbt lineage and semantic relationships and link materialized dbt nodes to physical BigQuery tables, and search related BigQuery entries using the lookupEntryLinks method.
  • You can configure dbt metadata import jobs and search or view imported dbt entries using the Google Cloud console, the Google Cloud CLI, or the Dataplex REST API.

For more information, see Import metadata from dbt Core.

Feature

Data products now support configuring a default IAM role in an access group. The default role, once configured, is automatically granted on all packaged and supported assets in the data product. Data product owners can override the default role for individual assets. In addition, the assets table in a data product now shows the permission state of each asset (Applied, Failed, or Unsupported).

For more information, see Create data products and Manage data products.

title: Storing Scraped Data: Why Append-Only NDJSON Beat My Database
description:
Every scraping tutorial ends at response.text. Mine used to too — and then the storage layer ate three weekends, so here is the boring half, with receipts.

I run a small daily pipeline: it pulls public Telegram channel posts every morning, cleans them, and ships a bundle. Scale is tiny — a few hundred messages a day. The rule that shaped everything: a scraped row is a fact about the past, and facts don't get edited.

The schema that survived

Each row is append-only NDJSON, one object per line:

{"url": "https://t.me/s/channel/123", "fetched_at": "2026-10-13T07:00:12+08:00", "sha256": "9f2c…", "text": "…", "channel": "channel"}

Four fields, and every one of them exists because a bug made me add it:

  • url — the locator. A buyer, my future self, or a stranger can re-fetch it.
  • fetched_at — the receipt of when the fact was true. Timestamp is a claim, not proof, and I price it accordingly.
  • sha256 — hash of the stored bytes, so a claim is checkable without trusting me.
  • text — the payload, deliberately denormalized. No joins, no foreign keys, no migration ceremony.

What append-only bought me for free

De-duplication is a hash comparison, not a merge strategy. The morning run recomputes the hash for each URL; if the hash is already in today's window, the post is skipped. No UPSERT, no conflict resolution. Content changed? New hash, new row, both rows kept. History answered the "what changed" question before I programmed it.

Migrations are copy operations. Moving from one folder layout to another was cat old/*.ndjson > new.ndjson. No schema, no dump/restore, no pgloader incident. With a few hundred rows a day, SQLite would also work fine — I chose flat files because the artifact is the product, and the artifact should not need a database engine to open.

Backups are rsync. No dump format to test, no restore drill that I keep postponing. The restore drill is "files exist, open them."

What it costs (the honest section)

  • Queries are scans. Any "find me X" is a grep over the month's files, ~40 MB. Fine at my scale, embarrassing at a gigabyte. The exit ramp is DuckDB reading the same NDJSON — one line, no re-ingestion pipeline.
  • Nothing enforces the schema. A typo in a field key lands silently in a line of JSON. My mitigation is a lint step in the cron job: every row must have the four keys; fail loud, alert, don't ship a dirty bundle.
  • Timestamps are lies you're legally required to keep. The row proves the bytes matched the hash at some point, not when. I ship this caveat with the data, priced in.

The decision rule

If your scraped rows are facts you append and never edit, start with NDJSON and a hash — you get dedup, diffs, history, and backups for the price of a text format. The moment you need updates, joins, or sub-second queries at scale, graduate — and your graduates keep working, because DuckDB and pandas read these files natively.

Storage is not the sexy half of scraping. It is the half that decides whether next month's you trusts this month's data.

— 何雨禾 (heyuhe). I run this pipeline daily and sell the bundles; the same hashes and receipts described above ship with every row.

When someone asks you to prove where your data came from — a client, an audit, a compliance box you have to tick by a deadline — the provenance is the product; the rows are just the carrier. That is exactly what ships in my bundles: the append-only files above, with provenance header, per-row sha256 and fetched_at. Grab the receipts first, pay only if they'd save you an afternoon: free Telegram OSINT sample (suggested $5) · tg-crawl Pro: the scraper wheel + daily-crawl recipes ($9). Picking a format before your pipeline bends: CSV, JSONL, or SQLite.

One question, no pitch: if my daily Telegram bundle disappeared tomorrow, would you be very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, or not bothered? Reply with one word — I use it to decide whether to keep building it.

title: October 08, 2026
description:
Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in Singapore (sg) with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus Editions and Gemini Notebook Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Overages must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure overages and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

title: Blazor ErrorBoundary
description:
Blazor is a web UI framework from Microsoft that allows developers to build interactive web applications using C#, .NET, and Razor components.

A Blazor component is a reusable part of a user interface that can contain HTML markup, C# logic, data binding, event handlers, and conditional rendering.

Let's understand this with a simple example of a product details component.

Product Details

<h5>@productName</h5>
<p>Price: ₹@price</p>


    Increase Price

@code {
private string productName = "Wireless Headphones";
private decimal price = 1500;

private void IncreasePrice()
{
    price += 100;
}

In this example:

  • HTML markup defines the structure of the product details.
  • Bootstrap classes such as card, shadow-sm, and btn btn-primary style the UI.
  • C# variables store the product name and price.
  • Data binding using @productName and @price displays variable values in the UI.
  • Event handling using @onclick calls the IncreasePrice() method when the button is clicked.

When the user clicks the button, the price increases by ₹100, and Blazor automatically updates the displayed value.

This example demonstrates how Blazor combines C# logic with HTML markup to build interactive user interfaces.

What Is Bootstrap, and Why Use It with Blazor?

Bootstrap is a CSS framework that provides predefined styling classes for layouts, forms, buttons, cards, tables, badges, and responsive designs.

For example, the product component above uses the card class to create a card-style container, shadow-sm to add a subtle shadow, and btn btn-primary to style the button.

Bootstrap handles the visual presentation, while Blazor handles the application logic and user interactions.

Important: Using Bootstrap CSS classes directly in a Razor component is different from using a dedicated Blazor Bootstrap component library. In this article, we use Bootstrap CSS classes with normal Blazor components.

What Are We Going to Build?

Now that we understand how a normal Blazor component works, let's apply the same concepts to a real-world example: a for a Gym Center and Membership Plan Management System.

The page retrieves membership plans from an ASP.NET Core Web API and displays them using Bootstrap cards.

Product Price Calculator

Price per item: ₹500

Quantity:

Total Price: ₹@(500 * quantity)

@code {
private int quantity = 1;
}

The following example demonstrates how Blazor components, Bootstrap styling, API integration, and event handling work together.

Complete Browse Membership Plans Component

and place the following code inside it. The complete component is included together below, without changing the supplied code.

@page "/gyms/{GymId:int}/plans"

@using System.Net.Http.Json

@inject HttpClient http
@inject NavigationManager navigation
@inject SweetAlertService Swal

<PageTitle>Browse Membership Plans</PageTitle>

<div class="container-fluid py-4">

    <!-- Page Heading -->
    <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-4">
        <div>
            <h3 class="fw-bold">Membership Plans</h3>
            <p class="text-muted mb-0">
                Explore membership plans available at this gym.
            </p>
            <p class="text-muted small mb-0">
                Selected Gym ID: @GymId
            </p>
        </div>

        <button class="btn btn-outline-secondary"
                @onclick="GoBack">
            Back to Gyms
        </button>
    </div>

    <!-- Search -->
    <div class="card shadow-sm mb-4">
        <div class="card-body">
            <label class="form-label">Search Membership Plan</label>

            <input class="form-control"
                   type="text"
                   placeholder="Search by plan name..."
                   @bind="PlanSearch"
                   @bind:event="oninput" />
        </div>
    </div>

    <!-- Loading -->
    @if (isLoading)
    {
        <div class="text-center py-5">
            <div class="spinner-border text-primary" role="status">
                <span class="visually-hidden">Loading...</span>
            </div>

            <p class="text-muted mt-3">
                Loading membership plans...
            </p>
        </div>
    }
    else if (hasError)
    {
        <div class="alert alert-danger">
            Unable to load membership plans.
            Please try again.

            <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger ms-2"
                    @onclick="LoadPlans">
                Retry
            </button>
        </div>
    }
    else if (FilteredPlans.Count == 0)
    {
        <div class="card shadow-sm">
            <div class="card-body text-center py-5">
                <h5 class="text-muted">
                    No membership plans found
                </h5>

                <p class="text-muted mb-0">
                    This gym has no matching membership plans.
                </p>
            </div>
        </div>
    }
    else
    {
        <!-- Plans List -->
        <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-3">
            <h5 class="mb-0">Available Plans</h5>

            <span class="badge bg-primary">
                @FilteredPlans.Count plans
            </span>
        </div>

        <div class="row g-4">

            @foreach (var plan in FilteredPlans)
            {
                <div class="col-12 col-md-6 col-xl-4" @key="plan.Id">

                    <div class="card h-100 shadow-sm">

                        <!-- Plan Header -->
                        <div class="card-header bg-white py-3">
                            <div class="d-flex justify-content-between
                                        align-items-start gap-2">

                                <h5 class="fw-bold mb-0">
                                    @plan.PlanName
                                </h5>

                                <span class="badge @(IsActive(plan.Status)
                                    ? "bg-success"
                                    : "bg-secondary")">
                                    @plan.Status
                                </span>

                            </div>
                        </div>

                        <!-- Plan Details -->
                        <div class="card-body">

                            <div class="mb-3">
                                <span class="text-muted">Price</span>

                                <h3 class="text-primary fw-bold mb-0">
                                    ₹@plan.Price.ToString("N2")
                                </h3>
                            </div>

                            <p class="mb-2">
                                <strong>Duration:</strong>
                                @plan.DurationInMonths months
                            </p>

                            <p class="mb-2">
                                <strong>Class Sessions:</strong>
                                @plan.ClassSessionsPerWeek per week
                            </p>

                            <p class="mb-3">
                                <strong>Personal Training:</strong>
                                @plan.PersonalTrainingSessions sessions
                            </p>

                            <hr />

                            <h6 class="fw-semibold mb-3">
                                Plan Benefits
                            </h6>

                            <ul class="list-unstyled mb-0">

                                <li class="mb-2">
                                    @if (plan.LockerAccess)
                                    {
                                        <span class="text-success me-2">✓</span>
                                        <span>Locker Access</span>
                                    }
                                    else
                                    {
                                        <span class="text-muted me-2">✕</span>
                                        <span class="text-muted">
                                            No Locker Access
                                        </span>
                                    }
                                </li>

                                <li class="mb-2">
                                    @if (plan.GuestAccess)
                                    {
                                        <span class="text-success me-2">✓</span>
                                        <span>Guest Access</span>
                                    }
                                    else
                                    {
                                        <span class="text-muted me-2">✕</span>
                                        <span class="text-muted">
                                            No Guest Access
                                        </span>
                                    }
                                </li>

                                <li class="mb-2">
                                    <strong>Guest Passes:</strong>
                                    @plan.GuestPasses
                                </li>

                            </ul>

                        </div>

                        <!-- Subscribe Button -->
                        <div class="card-footer bg-white border-0 pb-3">

                            @if (IsActive(plan.Status))
                            {
                                <button class="btn btn-primary w-100"
                                        @onclick="() => Subscribe(plan.Id)">
                                    Subscribe
                                </button>
                            }
                            else
                            {
                                <button class="btn btn-secondary w-100"
                                        disabled>
                                    Plan Inactive
                                </button>
                            }

                        </div>

                    </div>

                </div>
            }

        </div>
    }
</div>

@code {
    // Gym ID comes from the URL:
    // /gyms/1/plans means GymId = 1.
    [Parameter]
    public int GymId { get; set; }

    private string PlanSearch = string.Empty;

    private bool isLoading = true;
    private bool hasError = false;

    private List<MembershipPlanItem> planList = new();

    // Plans displayed after applying the local search.
    private List<MembershipPlanItem> FilteredPlans =>
        planList
            .Where(plan =>
                string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(PlanSearch) ||
                plan.PlanName.Contains(
                    PlanSearch.Trim(),
                    StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            .ToList();

    // Response model used by this page.
    public sealed class MembershipPlanItem
    {
        public int Id { get; set; }

        public string PlanName { get; set; } = string.Empty;

        public int GymId { get; set; }

        public decimal Price { get; set; }

        public int DurationInMonths { get; set; }

        public int ClassSessionsPerWeek { get; set; }

        public int PersonalTrainingSessions { get; set; }

        public bool LockerAccess { get; set; }

        public bool GuestAccess { get; set; }

        public int GuestPasses { get; set; }

        public string Status { get; set; } = string.Empty;
    }

    protected override async Task OnParametersSetAsync()
    {
        await LoadPlans();
    }

    private async Task LoadPlans()
    {
        isLoading = true;
        hasError = false;

        try
        {
            // Assumed API endpoint:
            // GET api/MembershipPlan/BrowseMembershipPlans?GymId=1
            var url =
                $"MembershipPlan/BrowseMembershipPlans?GymId={GymId}";

            var response = await http.GetAsync(url);

            if (response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
            {
                var result = await response.Content
                    .ReadFromJsonAsync<List<MembershipPlanItem>>();

                // Keep only plans belonging to the selected gym.
                // The backend should also enforce this filter.
                planList = (result ?? new List<MembershipPlanItem>())
                    .Where(plan => plan.GymId == GymId)
                    .ToList();
            }
            else
            {
                planList = new();
                hasError = true;

                await Swal.FireAsync(new SweetAlertOptions
                {
                    Title = "Unable to load plans",
                    Text = $"The server returned status {(int)response.StatusCode}.",
                    Icon = SweetAlertIcon.Error
                });
            }
        }
        catch (Exception)
        {
            planList = new();
            hasError = true;

            await Swal.FireAsync(new SweetAlertOptions
            {
                Title = "Connection Error",
                Text = "Unable to connect to the gym API.",
                Icon = SweetAlertIcon.Error
            });
        }
        finally
        {
            isLoading = false;
        }
    }

    private static bool IsActive(string status)
    {
        return string.Equals(
            status,
            "Active",
            StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    }

    private void Subscribe(int planId)
    {
        // The subscription page will receive both IDs.
        navigation.NavigateTo(
            $"/subscribe?gymId={GymId}&planId={planId}");
    }

    private void GoBack()
    {
        navigation.NavigateTo("/browse-gyms");
    }
}

Understanding the Main Concepts

1. Route parameters

The route is defined as:

@page "/gyms/{GymId:int}/plans"

The [Parameter] property receives the gym ID from the URL:

[Parameter]
public int GymId { get; set; }

For example, /gyms/3/plans supplies the value 3 to GymId.

This allows the same component to display plans for different gyms.

2. Data binding and search

The search input uses:

@bind="PlanSearch"
@bind:event="oninput"

The PlanSearch variable is updated as the user types. The FilteredPlans property uses LINQ to filter the loaded plans by name without sending a new API request for each keystroke.

3. Bootstrap cards

The component uses Bootstrap classes such as card, card-header, card-body, and card-footer to organize membership information into cards.

The responsive grid uses col-12 col-md-6 col-xl-4 to display one, two, or three columns depending on the screen width.

4. API integration

The LoadPlans() method sends a GET request to the membership-plan endpoint, deserializes the JSON response into MembershipPlanItem objects, and filters the results for the selected gym.

The backend should also enforce the gym filter. Frontend filtering alone is not a security measure.

5. Conditional rendering

The component displays different UI states depending on isLoading, hasError, and the number of filtered plans.

This provides feedback while data is loading, when an error occurs, and when no matching plans are found.

6. Event handling and navigation

The Subscribe button calls Subscribe(plan.Id), which navigates to the subscription page with the selected gym ID and plan ID.

The Back to Gyms button calls GoBack() to navigate to /browse-gyms.

Conclusion: Understanding Blazor Components Through Practical Examples

Blazor components make it possible to combine UI markup, C# logic, data binding, and event handling in a single reusable unit.

We started with a simple product details component and then applied the same concepts to a real-world membership-plans page.

Consider one final small example that demonstrates how a component can display a membership price and calculate a discounted price:

<h3>Membership Price Calculator</h3>

<p>Original Price: ₹@price</p>
<p>Discount: @discount%</p>
<p>Final Price: ₹@FinalPrice</p>

@code {
    private decimal price = 2000;
    private decimal discount = 10;

    private decimal FinalPrice =>
        price - (price * discount / 100);
}

Here, the component uses C# properties and expressions to calculate the final price and display it in the UI. When the underlying values change, Blazor can render the updated result.

The same fundamental approach is used in the Browse Membership Plans component, where data comes from an API and the UI displays prices, benefits, status badges, and subscription actions.

The key takeaway: Blazor manages the component's logic and interactivity, Bootstrap provides the styling, and services such as HttpClient connect the UI to backend data.

These concepts can be applied to many applications, including product catalogs, booking systems, hotel management, employee directories, and subscription platforms.

Thanks for reading! I hope this article helps you understand how normal Blazor components and Bootstrap work together to build practical web applications.
