title: React Server Components Guide: Architecture, Examples, and Best Practices
description:
React Server Components (RSC) introduce a different way to think about rendering React applications. Instead of sending every component's JavaScript to the browser, developers can render selected components on the server and send their results to the client, reducing the amount of JavaScript users need to download and execute.

RSC are especially useful for applications that display database records, product catalogs, dashboards, documentation, or other content that benefits from server-side data access. They also introduce important architectural decisions around component boundaries, data fetching, caching, and client-side interactivity.

In this guide, we'll explore how React Server Components work, how they differ from traditional client components, and how to build a practical example using modern React patterns. We'll also cover common mistakes and best practices that matter when building production applications.

Understanding React Server Components with a Practical Example

What Are React Server Components?

React Server Components are React components that execute on the server and can access server-side resources without exposing that implementation to the browser. Their rendered output is represented through the React Server Component payload, which the framework uses to update the UI.

Unlike traditional server-side rendering, Server Components are not simply components that render HTML on the server before hydrating in the browser. They can remain server-only components, meaning their implementation does not need to become part of the client-side JavaScript bundle.

Server Components vs. Client Components

Server Components are well suited for fetching data, accessing databases, reading files, and rendering content that does not require browser APIs. Client Components are necessary for features such as event handlers, local interactive state, effects, and browser-specific APIs.

In frameworks that support React Server Components, a component is generally a Server Component by default unless it is placed within a client boundary. Adding the "use client" directive at the top of a module marks that module and its transitive dependencies as part of the client-side component graph. It does not mean the component can never be prerendered on the server.

A Practical Product Catalog Example

Imagine building an online store that displays products from a database. A Server Component can retrieve product data directly from a server-side data source and render the catalog without requiring the browser to make a separate request for that initial data.

The following runnable JavaScript example demonstrates the core architecture using a small, framework-independent simulation. It separates server-side product retrieval from client-side interaction and uses console logs to show which responsibilities belong to each layer. It is an educational model of the architecture, not a replacement for React's actual Server Component runtime or transport protocol.

How This Maps to a Real React Application

In a framework such as Next.js App Router, the catalog page can be an asynchronous Server Component that retrieves products directly from a database or backend service. A separate component marked with "use client" can handle filtering, adding products to a cart, or responding to user input.

Keep database credentials, privileged API keys, and server-only dependencies out of client modules. Also remember that props crossing the Server Component to Client Component boundary must be serializable according to React's supported serialization rules; ordinary functions and arbitrary server resources cannot simply be passed as client props.

Important Performance Considerations

Server Components can reduce client JavaScript and simplify secure data access, but they do not automatically make every application faster. Slow database queries, excessive sequential requests, large rendered payloads, and poorly designed caching strategies can still hurt performance.

Fetch independent data concurrently when possible, use appropriate caching and revalidation policies, and keep client boundaries focused on the interactions that genuinely require them. Measure real production performance instead of assuming that moving work to the server always produces a better result.

const products = [
  { id: 1, name: "Wireless Headphones", price: 2499, stock: 12 },
  { id: 2, name: "Mechanical Keyboard", price: 3999, stock: 8 },
  { id: 3, name: "USB-C Hub", price: 1499, stock: 0 },
  { id: 4, name: "Laptop Stand", price: 999, stock: 15 }
];

// Step 1: Simulate a server-side data source.
// In production, this function could query a database or internal API.
async function getProducts() {
  console.log("[SERVER] Connecting to the product data source...");

  // Simulate asynchronous I/O without external dependencies.
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 100));

  console.log("[SERVER] Product records retrieved successfully.");
  return products.map((product) => ({ ...product }));
}

// Step 2: Implement server-side business logic.
// Keep data access and business rules outside interactive UI code.
async function getAvailableProducts() {
  console.log("[SERVER] Applying availability rules...");
  const allProducts = await getProducts();
  const availableProducts = allProducts.filter(
    (product) => product.stock > 0
  );

  console.log(
    `[SERVER] Found ${availableProducts.length} available products.`
  );

  return availableProducts;
}

// Step 3: Model a Server Component's data preparation.
// This function demonstrates the server-side responsibility only.
async function ProductCatalogServer() {
  console.log("\n[SERVER] Rendering the product catalog...");
  const catalog = await getAvailableProducts();

  // Return plain data that can be consumed by a UI layer.
  return {
    title: "Available Products",
    products: catalog.map(({ id, name, price }) => ({ id, name, price }))
  };
}

// Step 4: Model client-side interaction.
// A real React implementation would use a Client Component with state.
function ProductCatalogClient(catalog) {
  console.log("\n[CLIENT] Initializing catalog interactions...");
  let selectedProductId = null;

  function selectProduct(productId) {
    const selectedProduct = catalog.products.find(
      (product) => product.id === productId
    );

    if (!selectedProduct) {
      console.log("[CLIENT] Product not found in the catalog.");
      return null;
    }

    selectedProductId = selectedProduct.id;
    console.log(`[CLIENT] Selected: ${selectedProduct.name}`);
    return selectedProduct;
  }

  function renderCatalog() {
    console.log(`\n${catalog.title}`);
    console.log("-".repeat(40));

    catalog.products.forEach((product) => {
      console.log(`${product.name} | Rs. ${product.price}`);
    });

    console.log("-".repeat(40));
  }

  return {
    renderCatalog,
    selectProduct,
    getSelectedProductId: () => selectedProductId
  };
}

// Step 5: Run the demonstration from a server-side entry point.
// This standalone program simulates the two responsibilities in one process.
async function main() {
  console.log("=== React Server Components Architecture Demo ===");

  // Prepare data on the server before handing it to the UI layer.
  const catalogData = await ProductCatalogServer();

  console.log("\n[BOUNDARY] Passing serializable catalog data to the client.");
  const clientCatalog = ProductCatalogClient(catalogData);

  // Display the catalog and simulate a user selecting a product.
  clientCatalog.renderCatalog();
  clientCatalog.selectProduct(2);

  console.log(
    "\n[CLIENT] Selected product ID:",
    clientCatalog.getSelectedProductId()
  );

  // An unavailable product is not included in the client catalog.
  clientCatalog.selectProduct(3);

  console.log("\nDemo completed successfully.");
}

// Step 6: Handle unexpected failures without hiding the error.
main().catch((error) => {
  console.error("Demo failed:", error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Conclusion

React Server Components provide a useful foundation for building applications that keep data access and rendering on the server while delivering focused interactive experiences to the browser. Their biggest architectural advantage is the ability to separate server-only responsibilities from client-side behavior instead of treating every component as browser code.

The most effective implementations use Server Components for data-intensive UI and Client Components for focused interactions. In real applications, frameworks such as Next.js handle the React Server Component payload, routing, and rendering integration, so developers should follow the framework's conventions rather than attempting to recreate that infrastructure themselves.

Start by moving data-fetching components that do not need browser interactivity to the server, then introduce client boundaries only where state or event handling is required. Combine that approach with sensible caching, parallel data fetching, clear security boundaries, and performance measurement to build React applications that remain maintainable as they scale.

title: Choosing an Error Tracking API for Small Node.js SaaS Exception Capture
description:
Short answer: for a small B2B SaaS, retain a normalized server-side exception record at the application boundary, then send it to the least complex service that preserves searchable groups and useful detail. The lightweight option fits basic backend capture and search. Sentry is the stronger default when browser or mobile evidence matters. Datadog, Grafana, Better Stack, Rollbar, and Bugsnag belong in the wider evaluation. Healthchecks covers a different hole: scheduled jobs that never report.

Choice Best fit Boundary to plan around
Infrai Server exceptions, grouped lists, detail, and search No built-in alert routing, span-tree investigation, source-map deobfuscation, symbolication, or replay
Sentry A fuller Sentry-style frontend, mobile, and backend investigation More product surface than a basic server-only pipeline needs
Rollbar Teams evaluating a dedicated error-monitoring product Still a separate specialist integration in a broader backend stack
Bugsnag Teams evaluating a dedicated application-error product Same specialist-tool trade-off; validate the evidence workflow you require
Datadog, Grafana, or Better Stack Teams selecting a broader observability home Evaluate them as suites, not only as an exception inbox
Healthchecks Detecting scheduled work that never reported success Complements exception capture; it does not replace it

My recommendation: small SaaS teams that need searchable backend exceptions and want one consistent HTTP contract across future backend capabilities should try Infrai for the capture-to-investigation segment. The primary win is breadth behind one surface: live discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. The supporting win is mechanical but useful: public discovery exposes request and response schemas plus runnable TypeScript examples, which removes SDK selection and much of the adapter guesswork.

Infrai is the concrete lightweight option here: 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one REST API, one key, and one bill. A team doesn't have to stitch together 30 SDKs or juggle 30 credentials, while the public self-describing discovery surface keeps the capture adapter inspectable.

That recommendation has a hard edge. Choose a specialist when client-side reconstruction, automatic notifications, or distributed trace navigation is part of the incident definition. Error capture is evidence storage, not an observability system by itself.

Keep that boundary boring.

What should a small Node.js SaaS error tracking API capture?

A grouped stack trace answers "where did code throw?" It does not necessarily answer "which customer operation failed, what input class triggered it, and what happened on either side?" For B2B SaaS, the useful boundary starts inside the request or worker, before provider-specific serialization. Preserve a stable event ID, tenant-safe customer reference, release, operation, timestamp, exception name, message, stack, and any trace or span identifiers your application already owns. Keep secrets and raw personal data out.

Then the provider accepts the event, groups it, and makes the group and occurrence detail searchable. The lightweight API boundary ends before notification delivery and before a trace backend reconstructs a span tree. If an operator needs email, SMS, phone, or webhook alerts, a polling worker must query and route them. If the investigation crosses services, trace_id and span_id can correlate records only when the application supplies them; they do not create distributed tracing.

This distinction matters. A provider can retain every thrown exception and still miss the incident where a nightly invoice export never started. Add a heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks for that negative signal.

The two criteria worth benchmarking

First, benchmark reconstruction completeness with a fixed incident packet. Do not count dashboard widgets. Take one unsuccessful customer operation and ask each candidate to recover the exception, complete stack, release, customer-safe identifier, operation, occurrence time, and correlation IDs. Mark each field pass, transformed, or missing.

Seven fields.

One boring worksheet catches more than a feature grid because it tests the evidence you will actually need at 02:00. I would run the same packet through every candidate before discussing dashboards: trigger one controlled exception in an invoice export, preserve its release and tenant-safe reference, then ask an engineer who did not create it to reconstruct the operation from stored evidence. The trade-off becomes visible fast. A compact capture API wins when that packet comes back intact with one adapter; a larger product earns its footprint only when the reconstruction also needs browser state, symbolication, notifications, or trace navigation.

Second, count boundary cost. I use three numbers: application adapters, credentials, and background workers. For Infrai, basic exception capture sits on the same REST surface as many other backend modules, with one key and a self-describing contract. That can keep the adapter count down as the SaaS grows. Alert polling still counts as a worker, though. Pretending otherwise makes the comparison useless.

Sentry earns the extra surface when source maps, crash symbolication, session replay, or fuller client-side debugging are requirements. Rollbar and Bugsnag deserve the same evidence-packet trial as dedicated alternatives. Datadog, Grafana, and Better Stack are more relevant when this decision belongs inside a broader observability evaluation. Test all of them with your own stack frames and release process. This is a better buying rule than assuming every error tracker preserves identical evidence.

Put a narrow TypeScript boundary in the application

The application should own normalization. The transport adapter should own the selected provider's documented payload. Before writing that adapter, this runnable TypeScript fetches the live errors.capture request schema. Discovery is public, but the sample still shows the bearer-key pattern used by authenticated API calls. It uses an explicit method, checks errors, and backs off on 429 responses:

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/errors.capture";

async function loadCaptureContract(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/errors.capture", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const delayMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1_000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return loadCaptureContract(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery returned ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
  }

  return response.json();
}

process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(await loadCaptureContract(), null, 2)}\n`);

Generate the capture adapter from the returned path and request schema rather than copying a stale payload. The actual capture operation uses an explicit POST, status checking, and the same 429 discipline. Keep the key in process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY.

The split pays off during migration. Business code never learns a vendor envelope, while the adapter remains small enough to benchmark and replace. It also gives tests a clean assertion point: feed an Error, inspect one IncidentEvidence, and verify that sensitive request data never crossed the boundary.

When is the runner-up the better choice?

Pick Sentry when frontend or mobile reconstruction is central. The missing capabilities are decisive, not cosmetic: no source-map deobfuscation, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or session replay means a lightweight backend tracker cannot recover the same client evidence.

Pick a dedicated product such as Rollbar or Bugsnag when the organization wants a specialist error workflow and accepts another SDK, key, and vendor boundary. Run the incident packet before committing. Neither one is universally better without testing the required evidence.

Keep a tracing backend when operators need span trees across services. Keep Healthchecks or an equivalent heartbeat system when silence is itself failure. And build or buy notification routing if polling is operationally unacceptable. Those are separate decisions. Stuffing them into the phrase "error tracking" hides the architecture.

The practical decision is narrow: the shared API is workable for server-side exception capture, grouping, detail, and search when a small team values a plain contract more than specialist debugging depth. It is the wrong compression layer when the evidence lives in source maps, native crashes, replay, alerts, or traces. Small backend-focused SaaS teams should try Infrai when reducing adapter and credential sprawl matters more than those specialist workflows. If that boundary matches your system, validate the contract in the error tracking guide.

Further reading

  • OpenTelemetry logs signal concepts
  • Sentry documentation
  • Rollbar documentation
  • Bugsnag documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

title: October 09, 2026
description:
BigQuery

Feature

The BigQuery Data Engineering Agent is now available in the asia-northeast1 (Tokyo) regional endpoint and supports the gemini-3.5-flash model. For more information, see Where Gemini in BigQuery processes your data.

This feature is Generally Available (GA).

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

When you enable Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on an eligible Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026 where the integration is currently turned off, the instance now syncs schema and metadata updates to Knowledge Catalog in near real-time instead of once a day (instances created on or after April 18, 2026 have near real-time sync enabled by default).

This feature is available for instances running MySQL version 8.0 or later on the new network architecture. If Knowledge Catalog integration is already enabled on the instance with once-a-day updates, you can deactivate and re-enable the integration to switch to near real-time updates.

For more information, see Enable the integration of Knowledge Catalog on an existing Cloud SQL instance.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Feature

When you enable Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on an eligible Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance created before April 18, 2026 where the integration is currently turned off, the instance now syncs schema and metadata updates to Knowledge Catalog in near real-time instead of once a day (instances created on or after April 18, 2026 have near real-time sync enabled by default).

This feature is available for instances running PostgreSQL version 14.0 or later on the new network architecture. If Knowledge Catalog integration is already enabled on the instance with once-a-day updates, you can deactivate and re-enable the integration to switch to near real-time updates.

For more information, see Enable the integration of Knowledge Catalog on an existing Cloud SQL instance.

Datastream

Feature

Datastream now supports replicating SQL Server GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY spatial data types.

For more information, see the following:

  • Map SQL Server data types to Datastream unified types
  • Data type mappings in BigQuery

Gemini

Announcement

Sale of Gemini Code Assist subscriptions is ending. Starting October 9, 2026, new Gemini Code Assist Standard and Enterprise subscriptions can no longer be purchased. Existing subscriptions will continue to auto-renew through the rest of 2026, but auto-renewal will end in 2027. For more information, see Gemini Code Assist Standard and Enterprise subscriptions.

For alternative AI developer tools, use Antigravity, which is available through eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions and through Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

Announcement

Sale of Gemini Code Assist subscriptions is ending. Starting October 9, 2026, new Gemini Code Assist Standard and Enterprise subscriptions can no longer be purchased. Existing subscriptions will continue to auto-renew through the rest of 2026, but auto-renewal will end in 2027. For more information, see Gemini Code Assist Standard and Enterprise subscriptions.

For alternative AI developer tools, use Antigravity, which is available through eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions and through Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka

Change

The format for bootstrap addresses and broker URLs has changed for new Managed Service for Apache Kafka clusters. To learn how to get a cluster's bootstrap address, see View a Managed Service for Apache Kafka cluster.

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 5, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) instances running Looker 26.18. Feature enablement for Looker (Google Cloud core) will be announced separately.

Feature

Looker now includes built-in support for the Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) dialect. The Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) uses the bundled Apache Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver, so that you don't have to install unpackaged custom JDBC driver JAR files. See the Dremio documentation page for more information.

Feature

The AI-Assisted Quick Starts feature, called Starter questions in the new Explore experience, is now generally available.

Feature

The new Diagnose & Repair tool evaluates your LookML project repository across eight diagnostic test checks in either your personal development environment or the shared production environment. When issues are found, Looker can automatically perform repairs (such as removing stale lock files, fixing file permissions, or repairing corrupted object indexes) or rebuild damaged repositories while safeguarding uncommitted changes on a dedicated recovery branch.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now includes the Style Validator, which enforces LookML coding standards, naming conventions, and structural best practices across your LookML project. You can run the Style Validator with the default built-in ruleset or customize rule severities, file exclusions, path overrides, and custom rules by adding an lkmlstyle.yaml configuration file to your project repository.

Feature

Now available in preview, Conversational Analytics agentic workflows support scheduled agentic workflows in addition to triggered agentic workflows. You can use scheduled agentic workflows to schedule recurring deliveries of AI-generated insights summaries, data tables, visualizations, and PDF reports to email or Slack by using natural language. Recipients can select Investigate in a workflow notification to open a private, persistent conversation with the data agent.

Users and admins can manage workflows on the updated Manage Workflows user page and Manage Workflows admin page, respectively, and Looker admins can monitor scheduled workflow runs and troubleshoot errors on the new Workflow Executions admin page.

Workflows that were created in versions earlier than Looker 26.14 appear on the Legacy Workflows tab and must be recreated.

Feature

Now available in preview, Looker Data Apps are freeform canvas dashboards that are built by local AI coding agents, such as Gemini CLI, Claude Code, or Cursor, from natural-language prompts. Data Apps give you complete visual layout control (including absolute positioning, overlapping elements, and custom web components) while remaining bound to Looker's governed LookML semantic layer and user permissions.

Change

In Conversational Analytics, the default question mode is now Fast rather than Thinking. Fast mode is intended for answering quickly, and it directly maps your query to underlying LookML definitions without generating reasoning steps. You can still select Thinking mode from the question mode drop-down menu when asking complex, multi-step analytical questions about Explores or dashboards.

Change

The Modern User Interface preview feature toggle now defaults to ON.

Change

The Modern visualization theme now supports map charts (static map points and regions), word cloud charts, and donut multiples. While support for donut multiples was previously documented, it is now officially available with this release. These additions expand the range of visualization options that are available with the modern theme.

Feature

Looker now supports connections to the ClickHouse 26+ dialect. ClickHouse 26+ uses modernized JDBC drivers and introduces support for symmetric aggregates. See the ClickHouse documentation page for more information.

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor includes enhanced prompt injection and jailbreak protection for Workspace data. This capability improves detection accuracy and minimizes false positives when screening Workspace content, such as emails, documents, and files.

This capability is available on multi-region endpoints in the US (us) and EU (eu) for templates and floor setting configured with filter version v3 or later, including the Stable and Latest aliases.

Secure Web Proxy

Feature

Secure Web Proxy supports global access. You can enable this feature when creating a Secure Web Proxy instance to make sure that clients from any Google Cloud region can connect to your proxy.

With global access, you can route your outbound traffic through specific regions to meet regulatory compliance or cost requirements. You can also use this option to simplify your network administration by managing outbound traffic from a centralized location.

This feature is available in Preview.

Security Command Center

Feature

Using gcloud CLI, the securitycenter REST API, or client libraries, you can configure Pub/Sub and BigQuery continuous export to receive notifications when findings are deleted from Security Command Center due to data retention policies.

For more information, see the following:

  • Enable finding notifications for Pub/Sub
  • Stream findings to BigQuery for analysis
  • Enable real-time notifications
  • Creating and managing Notification Configs

title: The Vercel Bug Bounty Program is now publicly available
description:
In 2022, we launched a private bug bounty program through HackerOne. Over the last several years, we've worked with HackerOne's VIP program to refine our process, targets, and scope, onboarding thousands of their best researchers and hardening security across our platform.

We've translated those learnings into several public bounty programs:

  • The $1 million React2Shell hacker challenge

  • The $1 million Vercel Sandbox hacker challenge

  • Our OSS bug bounty program

Today, we are combining our private and OSS bounty programs into a single, public Vercel bug bounty program.

Why now

AI has fundamentally changed the nature of bug bounty programs, exponentially increasing the number of reports, both valid and invalid. Some companies are responding by moving to private programs.

At Vercel, we’ve found that public reports are still surfacing real, valuable findings. AI enables a much wider range of researchers to discover vulnerabilities, and we believe in evaluating reports on their own merit, so making our entire program public was the logical choice.

In preparation for the public launch, our security engineering team has streamlined our process and built tooling to filter out noise and expedite remediation. We have improved every step, from triaging reports to shipping and verifying fixes.

Our team and processes have been battle tested through our private program and several large public programs in the recent past. We are ready to open a comprehensive program to the public and have the best researchers out there responsibly explore every part of the platform.

What is covered

All products across the Vercel platform and our open-source projects are now part of our unified public program. Read the Scope page on HackerOne for full details on what is covered.

Consolidation makes sense for our processes, but we also received feedback from the research community that having multiple programs made disclosure confusing because there were multiple places to submit reports. A single program simplifies reporting across our platform and open-source projects.

New findings in our open-source projects should be reported to the main Vercel program, but if you already have submissions to the previous OSS program, you don't need to copy them over. We will still review every submission that was made through that program.

How to participate

If you’re a security researcher, visit our HackerOne program page for details, bounties, and guidelines.

To file a report, submit your findings through HackerOne with clear reproduction steps. Our security team reviews every submission and works with researchers via the disclosure process. We're committed to fast response times and transparent communication.

We appreciate the researchers who take the time to dig into our code and report issues responsibly. We would also like to thank all the researchers who have been working in our private program. You have helped build the foundation for this public program, and nothing will change for you. We look forward to your future submissions.

Learn more about security at Vercel.

Join our security team

If this kind of work excites you, we are hiring. Apply to join the Vercel security team.

title: Getting Started with the Gemini API
description:
Getting Started with the Gemini API

The Gemini API is a powerful tool for developers to integrate AI capabilities into their applications. In this tutorial, we'll walk through the basics of using the Gemini API to generate text. The API is accessible via a simple HTTP endpoint and returns JSON responses.

Prerequisites

To get started, you'll need:

  • Python 3.6 or higher
  • The requests library (install with pip install requests)

Step 1: Get Your API Key

To use the Gemini API, you need an API key. You can obtain one by signing up at the Unorouter platform (or your preferred provider). Once you have your key, you can use it in your code. The key is a string that you include in the Authorization header of your requests.

Step 2: Write the API Request

Here's a simple Python example to call the Gemini API:

import requests

api_key = "YOUR_API_KEY"
url = "https://api.unorouter.com/v1/chat/completions"

payload = {
    "model": "gemini-3.6-flash:free",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, world!"}]
}

response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"})

if response.status_code == 200:
    data = response.json()
    print(data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])
else:
    print(f"Error: {response.status_code}")

This code sends a POST request to the API endpoint with a JSON payload. The model parameter specifies which model to use (in this case, the free Gemini model). The messages array contains the user's query.

Step 3: Interpret the Response

The response will be a JSON object. The choices array contains the generated text. The first element in the array (index 0) is the response from the model. The message object within the first choice contains the actual text.

Error Handling and Best Practices

When working with the API, it's important to handle errors gracefully. Common errors include:

  • Invalid API key (401 Unauthorized)
  • Invalid request (400 Bad Request)
  • Rate limiting (429 Too Many Requests)

Always check the response status code and handle errors appropriately. Also, consider using exponential backoff for rate-limited requests.

Conclusion

The Gemini API is straightforward to use and offers a free tier for development. With just a few lines of code, you can integrate AI into your applications. Start experimenting today!

title: All About Iceberg's File Format API: simplifying the engine/format interface and Parquet's multimodal future
description:
What is the file format API?

Apache Iceberg traditionally exposed its data files through three libraries, one each for Parquet, Avro and ORC, and until this year every engine that spoke Iceberg had its own way of calling them. Spark had SparkParquetReaders, Flink had FlinkParquetReaders, the generic Java API had GenericParquetReaders, and each engine chose its own path through the format's read options, filter pushdown, split handling, encryption and metrics. The practical effect was that a feature added to one format for one engine (a new v3 type, a default value, a shredded variant column) tended to arrive for the other engines later or not at all, because the work had to be redone per engine.

The File Format API, which shipped in 1.11.0 and was announced in February, is the project's attempt to streamline all this: a single registry of "format models," each one the pairing of a file format with an engine's in-memory row type, and a single set of builders (ReadBuilder, FileWriterBuilder and its delete-file siblings) that every engine now goes through. It was also originally framed as the way to try out newer formats such as Vortex and Lance, which are fundamentally designed very differently than Parquet and meant specifically for vector work and multimodal data storage.

Note for Rust/Python users: this is a Java API. The registry lives in iceberg-core, so it reaches exactly the engines that link that jar and reuse its readers (Spark, Flink, Hive, the plain Java Record path). DuckDB, DataFusion via iceberg-rust, PyIceberg and Polars each implement the Iceberg spec with their own readers and leverage Arrow readers instead. For Trino, which is Java, it instead uses Iceberg's core for metadata and its own Parquet and ORC readers for data. DuckDB, DataFusion, Polars and PyIceberg all read into Arrow or something Arrow can hand over without copying, so the row-type axis collapses to one and a new format just needs an Arrow reader (Lance and Vortex both ship one). Java implementations have three row types and no shared memory format, which is why it needed a registry to play the role Arrow plays everywhere else.

Trino Java its own Parquet and ORC readers; Iceberg core for metadata only no
PyIceberg Python its own readers on PyArrow no
DataFusion (via iceberg-rust) Rust its own Arrow-based Parquet reader no
DuckDB C++ its own Parquet reader no
Polars Rust Arrow no

Reducing Format Model x Reader Complexity

A file format is how bytes are laid out on disk: Parquet, Avro and ORC each have their own encoding, compression, statistics and footer, and Iceberg doesn't care which one a given data file uses as long as it can read it. An engine in-memory row type, which the project calls the object model, is how one row looks in memory once it's been read, and that depends on the engine, not the file: Spark wants an InternalRow, Flink a RowData, the plain Java API an Iceberg Record. The same Parquet file can be read into any of them, and the same InternalRow can be written out as Parquet or ORC. A format model is one cell in that grid: one format, one row type.

Here is the grid as it stands at 1.12.0, with a mark wherever a format model exists:

Row type (object model) Parquet Avro ORC
Record (plain Java API) yes yes yes
InternalRow (Spark, row at a time) yes yes yes
ColumnarBatch (Spark, vectorized) read only no read only
ColumnarBatch (Arrow) read only no no
RowData (Flink) yes yes yes

Table 2. The format-by-row-type grid. Each "yes" is one registered format model.

**The API makes the engine's row type pluggable over a fixed list of file formats, such that any engine can register its own representation and read every Iceberg table through the shared builders, while a new format remains a change inside the Iceberg project; and because the formats are fixed, multimodal support is arriving as new column types defined on the Parquet side (see FILE type that was shipped in parquet-format 2.14.0, VECTOR type currently in proposal stage) and mirrored into the next table spec.

Into the weeds

Everything in the API is built on one map, which makes it the ideal place to start digging into in the codebase to gain a better understanding. If you only want to read and write files through the registry, skip ahead to "Usage." Read this section to understand why the API behaves the way it does, and come back to it when something in a later section needs the detail.

The registry key

A map here is the ordinary programming kind: a lookup table from a key to a value. In FormatModelRegistry, the key is a pair (which file format, which row type) and the value is a format model, the object that knows how to read and write that one combination. Here is the method that puts entries into the map:

// core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/formats/FormatModelRegistry.java (1.12.0)
public static synchronized void register(FormatModel<?, ?> formatModel) {
  Pair<FileFormat, Class<?>> key = Pair.of(formatModel.format(), formatModel.type());
  ...
  MODELS.put(key, formatModel);
}

The second half of the key, Class<?>, is the Java class of the row the engine wants back. For the plain Java API it is Iceberg's own Record; for Spark it is InternalRow (one row at a time) or ColumnarBatch (a block of rows); for Flink it is RowData. The Iceberg project calls this the object model.

[!note] Object model versus schema
The object model is the engine's in-memory shape for a row. It says nothing about the file and nothing about the table's schema. The schema says which columns a table has; the object model says what Java class a row of that table becomes once it is read.

The first half of the key, FileFormat, is an enum: a type whose allowed values are a fixed list written into the source code. You cannot add a value at runtime. This enum lives in iceberg-api, the module that holds Iceberg's public interfaces:

// api/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/FileFormat.java (1.12.0)
public enum FileFormat {
  PUFFIN("puffin", false),
  ORC("orc", true),
  PARQUET("parquet", true),
  AVRO("avro", true),
  METADATA("metadata.json", false);
  ...
}

Puffin and metadata appear because the enum names every kind of file Iceberg writes, not only data files. Puffin files hold statistics and deletion vectors; metadata.json is the table's root file. The three data formats are the ones in the middle: ORC, Parquet and Avro.

The two halves of the key are not the same kind of thing, and that difference organizes the rest of this post:

Half of the key Type Allowed values Who can add one
Format FileFormat enum in iceberg-api the five names above the Iceberg project, by changing the enum
Row type any Class<?> anything any engine, by calling register()

Table 3. The two halves of the registry key.

The announcement says the registry "decouples engines from specific formats and allows new formats to be added without modifying engine code." That is true as far as engine code goes. What a new format has to modify is iceberg-api, the enum itself.

What happens on a read

A scan task is Iceberg's description of one file to read, including which format it is in. From the task to the rows, a read goes like this:

  1. The engine asks the registry for a read builder, passing the task's format, its own row type, and the file.
  2. The registry looks up the (format, row type) pair.
  3. If the pair is registered, the model returns a builder. The engine sets the columns it wants, a filter, and the byte range of the file it was assigned, then calls build().
  4. If the pair is not registered, the registry throws an error that names the pair it could not find.

The dotted lines draw the open-versus-closed distinction: one input to the lookup comes from a fixed list, the other is whatever the engine says it is.

How models get registered

When the registry class is first loaded, it tries to call a register() method on four classes by name: the generic models, and the Arrow, Flink and Spark ones. If one of those classes, or something it depends on, is not on the classpath (the set of jars the program was started with), the registry logs a line and moves on. The practical consequence is that the contents of the map depend on which Iceberg jars you ship. You will see this directly in the "Usage" section. Everything the project registers at 1.12.0 is an engine's row type against a format Iceberg already had (Table 2); none of it is a new format.

Usage

It would be a terrible user experience to construct format models yourself; so instead you'll ask the registry for a builder and configure it. A builder is an object you set options on one at a time and then finish with build(). The registry exposes two of them, and together they are the whole surface an engine touches:

Call You pass You set You get back
readBuilder(format, rowType, inputFile) the file's format, your row type, the file columns to project, a filter, a byte range (split) something you can iterate over, yielding rows of your type
dataWriteBuilder(format, rowType, outputFile) the format to write, your row type, the output the schema and partition spec a writer; closing it yields a DataFile, the record Iceberg stores in its manifests, with column statistics already filled in

Table 4. The two registry calls an engine uses.

Where this code lives

If your experience of Iceberg so far is spark.sql("SELECT * FROM demo.orders") or a REST catalog behind a /v1/namespaces endpoint, the first question is where code like this even goes. It goes nowhere near either of those. There are three different places you can stand when you use Iceberg, and the File Format API only exists at the lowest one:

The program below is a plain Java main method with the Iceberg jars as dependencies. It is not a Spark job, it is not submitted to anything, and it does not need a catalog or even a table. It writes one Parquet file with Iceberg's own writer and reads it back with Iceberg's own reader, which is the single step every engine performs thousands of times per query and the only step the Format API is responsible for.

You would never run something like this in production. You run it when you want to see what the registry contains on a given classpath, or when you are writing a new format model and want the shortest possible loop between a change and a result. Here is the whole setup:

  1. Make an empty directory with two files in it: pom.xml and src/main/java/demo/Main.java.
  2. In pom.xml (Maven is Java's package manager, and this is its dependency list), declare the Iceberg modules you want on the classpath. The set is deliberately minimal: iceberg-api, iceberg-core, iceberg-data and iceberg-parquet, plus the Hadoop client jars Parquet needs and a logger. There is no iceberg-orc, and no Spark.
  3. Run mvn -q compile exec:java. Maven downloads the jars from Maven Central, compiles Main.java, and runs it on the JVM in your terminal. The output below is what it prints.

The program

I ran this against Iceberg 1.12.0 from Maven Central on Java 17, with nothing timed. The program does four things:

  1. Prints the FileFormat enum.
  2. Reaches into the registry and prints what is in the map.
  3. Writes three records through the write builder, then reads them back through the read builder.
  4. Asks for a (format, row type) pair that cannot be there. 
package demo;

import java.io.File;
import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.util.Map;
import org.apache.iceberg.DataFile;
import org.apache.iceberg.FileFormat;
import org.apache.iceberg.Files;
import org.apache.iceberg.PartitionSpec;
import org.apache.iceberg.Schema;
import org.apache.iceberg.data.GenericRecord;
import org.apache.iceberg.data.Record;
import org.apache.iceberg.encryption.EncryptionUtil;
import org.apache.iceberg.formats.FormatModelRegistry;
import org.apache.iceberg.io.CloseableIterable;
import org.apache.iceberg.io.DataWriter;
import org.apache.iceberg.types.Types;

public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

    // 1. The format half of the key: a fixed list, nothing is added at runtime.
    System.out.println("== FileFormat enum values");
    for (FileFormat f : FileFormat.values()) {
      System.out.println("  " + f + " splittable=" + f.isSplittable());
    }

    // 2. Peek inside the registry (reflection, since the map is private).
    //    Shows what the jars on the classpath registered before main() ran.
    System.out.println("== registered format models on this classpath (core + data + parquet)");
    Method models = FormatModelRegistry.class.getDeclaredMethod("models");
    models.setAccessible(true);
    Map<?, ?> m = (Map<?, ?>) models.invoke(null);
    m.keySet().stream().map(Object::toString).sorted().forEach(k -> System.out.println("  " + k));

    // An Iceberg schema. Columns are matched by the numeric field id, not by name.
    Schema schema = new Schema(
        Types.NestedField.required(1, "id", Types.LongType.get()),
        Types.NestedField.optional(2, "name", Types.StringType.get()));

    // A local file to write to; an engine would get an object store path from FileIO.
    File out = new File(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "/tmp/ffa-demo.parquet");
    out.delete();

    // 3a. Write. (PARQUET, Record.class) is the registry key; build() does the lookup
    //     and hands back the Parquet model's writer, or throws if the pair is missing.
    System.out.println("== write via FormatModelRegistry.dataWriteBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)");
    DataWriter<Record> writer =
        FormatModelRegistry.<Record, Object>dataWriteBuilder(
                FileFormat.PARQUET, Record.class,
                EncryptionUtil.plainAsEncryptedOutput(Files.localOutput(out)))
            .schema(schema)
            .spec(PartitionSpec.unpartitioned())  // required even without partitioning
            .overwrite()
            .build();

    // Record is Iceberg's generic row type; copy(name, value, ...) makes a row.
    GenericRecord rec = GenericRecord.create(schema);
    for (long i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
      writer.write(rec.copy("id", i, "name", "row-" + i));
    }
    writer.close();

    // toDataFile() returns the manifest entry an engine would commit, statistics included.
    DataFile df = writer.toDataFile();
    System.out.println("  wrote " + df.path() + " format=" + df.format() + " records=" + df.recordCount()
        + " bytes=" + df.fileSizeInBytes() + " valueCounts=" + df.valueCounts());

    // 3b. Read. Same key, other direction. An engine would also set a filter and a split.
    System.out.println("== read via FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(PARQUET, Record.class, ...)");
    try (CloseableIterable<Record> rows =
        FormatModelRegistry.<Record, Object>readBuilder(
                FileFormat.PARQUET, Record.class, Files.localInput(out))
            .project(schema)
            .build()) {
      for (Record r : rows) {
        System.out.println("  " + r);
      }
    }

    // 4. A valid format and a valid row type, but iceberg-orc is not on the
    //    classpath, so nobody registered the pair. The error names it.
    System.out.println("== ask for a model that is not registered (ORC with generic Record, no iceberg-orc on classpath)");
    try {
      FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(FileFormat.ORC, Record.class, Files.localInput(out));
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
      System.out.println("  " + e.getMessage());
    }
  }
}

Reading the output top to bottom:

  • The map holds Parquet and Avro, each paired with the generic Record and with the position-delete row type, and nothing else.
  • Avro is present without being asked for, because its model ships inside iceberg-core.
  • ORC is absent because the iceberg-orc jar is not on the classpath, and the error names the exact pair the registry could not find.
  • The write returned valueCounts: the writer filled in the DataFile statistics without the program doing anything.
  • One thing the program cannot express at all is a request for a format outside the five names. There is no FileFormat.LANCE to pass, and converting the string "lance" to a FileFormat throws "Invalid file format: lance" before the registry is ever reached.

The row-type side is open. The format side is closed.

The same call, from Spark

To connect this back to the level you already know: when you run spark.read.table("demo.orders").show() with the Iceberg connector, Spark loads the table through the catalog, plans which data files each task should scan, and then, for every file, makes exactly the call the program made by hand. Here is the Spark connector's version at 1.12.0, from BaseRowReader in the iceberg-spark module:

// Same call as the program above, with Spark's row type and all the options set.
ReadBuilder<InternalRow, ?> reader =
    FormatModelRegistry.readBuilder(format, InternalRow.class, file);
return reader
    .project(projection)          // columns the query asked for
    .idToConstant(idToConstant)   // partition values, not stored in the file
    .reuseContainers()
    .split(start, length)         // this task's byte range
    .caseSensitive(caseSensitive())
    .filter(residual)             // what is left of the WHERE clause
    .withNameMapping(nameMapping())
    .build();

The format variable is the FileFormat recorded in the manifest entry for that file, and InternalRow.class is the row type Spark registered for itself in SparkFormatModels at startup. The query you type at the top level becomes, at the bottom level, one registry lookup per file. Everything between the two is planning.

Exploring pluggability

The extension point is relatively easy to grokk and doesn't take a ton of code. This section covers what an engine supplies, what the format model owns, and what "pluggable" therefore means in practice.

Here is how the generic Parquet model is registered, with each argument labeled:

// data/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/data/GenericFormatModels.java (1.12.0)
FormatModelRegistry.register(
    ParquetFormatModel.create(
        Record.class,          // the row type
        Schema.class,          // the engine schema type
        (icebergSchema, fileSchema, engineSchema) ->              // how to write a Record
            GenericParquetWriter.create(icebergSchema, fileSchema),
        (icebergSchema, fileSchema, engineSchema, idToConstant) ->  // how to read one
            GenericParquetReaders.buildReader(icebergSchema, fileSchema, idToConstant),
        new RecordVariantShreddingAnalyzer(),                      // see below
        (Function<Schema, UnaryOperator<Record>>) ignored -> Record::copy));  // how to copy a row

The engine supplies two functions. The writer function, given a schema, builds something that writes a row's values into Parquet. The reader function builds something that reads values out of Parquet into a row; its idToConstant argument is a map from column ids to values that come from metadata rather than from the file, mostly partition columns. ParquetFormatModel wraps those two functions in the builders every caller uses, and everything else lives in the model, once, for every engine:

The engine supplies The format model owns
the row class and the engine schema type schema conversion between Iceberg's schema and the file's
a writer function (row values into the file) filter pushdown: skipping chunks of the file that cannot match
a reader function (file values into a row) splits: reading one byte range of a large file
a shredding analyzer (which variant fields to shred) encryption
a row-copy function the statistics that end up in the DataFile
the shredded write path itself

Table 6. Division of labour between an engine and a format model.

The engine never touches anything in the right-hand column.

[!note] The analyzer argument
Variant is Iceberg's type for semi-structured data such as JSON. Shredding is Parquet's technique of storing some of a variant's fields as ordinary columns so they can be filtered and read quickly. The Parquet model owns the shredded write path; each engine supplies an analyzer that says which fields to shred for its row type. There is one for Record here, and a Spark one and a Flink one in their modules. It is a small example of how the labour divides: the format owns the mechanism, the engine owns the choice.

So if you maintain an engine, or anything with its own idea of a row, this is your plugin point, and it is a good one. Register your row type against Parquet, Avro and ORC, and your engine reads any Iceberg table through the same builders Spark uses, without changing anything in the Iceberg project.

And the engines really do all go through it now, which is the part of the announcement that is simply true. Every reader in the 1.12.0 source that opens a data file (in Spark, Flink, the generic Java path, the MapReduce input format and the Arrow reader) gets its reader from the registry; none of them calls the old per-format Parquet.read, ORC.read or Avro.read directly any more. One implementation per format, shared by every engine, chosen by (format, row type).

Put that next to the dotted lines in the read diagram and "pluggable" comes into focus. What was scattered and is now unified is the engine side. What was fixed and is still fixed is the format side. That is not a flaw so much as a boundary, and the next section is about what sits on the other side of it.

Where formats come into play and the compatibility kit

This section answers two questions: how does a new file format get into Iceberg today, and what does it have to pass once it is there?

Adding a format: the Vortex example

A new format enters Iceberg the way the project's own showcase does. Vortex is a newer columnar file format, and its integration (issue 15416) has a pull request (#15915) that shows every step. The PR has been open since April, and the table shows where it lands:

Layer What a new format needs there Does the Vortex PR touch it?
iceberg-api a new FileFormat value yes, first file in the change list
a format module the format model, readers and writers yes, new iceberg-vortex module
each engine a registration of its row type against the new format yes, Spark readers and tests
the compatibility kit an entry so the whole test matrix runs against it not yet
the table spec a fifth name in the file_format sentence no

Table 7. Where a new file format has to land, and how far the Vortex PR gets.

The first file in the PR's change list is FileFormat.java, adding VORTEX to iceberg-api, the module with the strongest compatibility promises in the project; every change there is checked by a tool called Revapi and has to be acknowledged on purpose. What the PR does not touch is as telling as what it does. Iceberg's table spec is the document every implementation follows, in Java or any other language. It lists each data file in a manifest with a file_format field, and the spec at 1.12.0 defines that field as "String file format name, avro, orc, parquet, or puffin." The Vortex PR changes nothing in the spec. The Java enum is moving ahead of the spec text, which is a normal order of events in this project, but it means adding a format has two halves: the constant in iceberg-api, and the spec sentence that would need a fifth name before PyIceberg or iceberg-rust were obliged to know about it.

What a format has to pass

Behind the implementation sits the Technology Compatibility Kit (TCK). A compatibility kit is a test suite that a new component must pass to count as equivalent to the existing ones. Here, it is the set of tests a new format has to pass to be held to the same standard as Parquet. The announcement lists the TCK as in progress; the issue's author said in August that it is "more-or-less finished" apart from some v3 types and vectorized paths, which I'll take at face value and no further, since it's one comment.

The path for a format today is therefore:

  1. Get into the enum.
  2. Implement a format model.
  3. Get every engine to register its row type against it.
  4. Pass the TCK.

That is a project roadmap item, not a plugin. A closed enum is also how the DataFile metadata, the manifest field above, and every reader that switches on format stay consistent with one another, so I'd be surprised if it opened casually.

Inside the kit

Since the kit is what a format or an engine actually has to pass, it is worth looking at what it is, because it is smaller and more concrete than the name suggests.

The kit is two abstract test classes in the test folder of the iceberg-data module. Abstract means they are templates: they contain every test but leave a few blanks for an engine to fill in. ReadFormatModelTests covers reading, and BaseFormatModelTests extends it with writing. An engine joins by writing a small subclass that fills in the blanks:

  1. What its row class is.
  2. How to turn an Iceberg schema into its own kind of schema.
  3. How to turn a generic Record into one of its rows.
  4. How to compare two of its rows.
  5. How to convert a single constant value.

Spark's subclass is about a page, Flink's about the same. Everything else is inherited from the template.

What gets inherited is every test, run for every file format the kit knows about, times every data generator (a small class that produces a schema and some random rows for it). The generators cover primitives, UUID, fixed, binary, decimals, a struct, a list and a map of primitives, nanosecond timestamps and variant. The tests cover round trips in both directions (including delete files), every read builder option, default values at every nesting, statistics in each collection mode, the metadata columns, schema evolution and name mapping.

The part I find most useful is that the kit is also where the exceptions get written down. Each engine's subclass declares the Iceberg types it cannot hold, and each format declares the features it is missing. Tests for those are skipped rather than failed, so the kit doubles as the honest table of who supports what:

Cannot hold / is missing
Spark time, timestamp_ns
Flink time
Avro filter pushdown, splits, column statistics, native encryption
ORC reader-side defaults, variant, container reuse
Parquet AES stream encryption

Table 8. Exclusions declared in the compatibility kit at 1.12.0.

The nanosecond timestamp I mentioned above is a one-line entry in Spark's exclusion set, which is the clearest statement anywhere in the repository that the gap is in the engine and not in the format or the API.

The kit was not in 1.11.0. It arrived as a series of separate PRs through the year, several from contributors outside the original design group, and the last open piece is vectorized reads.

That is what sits behind the "more-or-less finished" comment, and it also tells you how a new format gets in: add an entry for it to the kit's list of formats, run the whole matrix, and write down what it cannot do in the missing-features map. That list is the contract.

Implications for native multimodal in Iceberg

Multimodal data means images, audio, video and documents, plus the embedding vectors a model produces from them. If formats are fixed, then multimodal data has to come into Iceberg through the formats it already has, and that is exactly what is happening, one level down and one project over. Two new column types are being defined in the Parquet format spec first, and then mirrored into Iceberg's table spec as part of the v4 revision. (The table spec is versioned; v3 is current, and v4 is being drafted in the open PRs below.)

Both new types are Parquet logical types. A logical type is a label on top of a physical storage type that says how to interpret the bytes: a string is bytes labeled as UTF-8, a date is an integer labeled as days since the epoch.

FILE

FILE is a column type for "bytes that live somewhere." Parquet got a FILE logical type in parquet-format PR 585, merged in July and released in 2.14.0 in September. Iceberg's FILE type proposal (Talat Uyarer, Alex Stephen, Sung Yun and Gaurav Soni; spec in PR 17918) defines the Iceberg file type by reference to it. A value is a reference with optional fields:

Field Meaning
uri where the bytes live
offset, size a byte range inside that object
content_type what the bytes are
checksum integrity check
inline the bytes themselves, for small payloads

Table 9. Sub-fields of the proposed Iceberg file type.

So a small image can sit inline inside the data file, and a large one can be a byte range inside an external object. The table carries the reference, statistics on the sub-fields, and mappings for Parquet, Avro and ORC.

Whether an engine can actually go and fetch those bytes without holding cloud credentials is a separate question, handled on the catalog side with pre-signed URLs: links that carry their own temporary permission. PR 18080 adds that to the REST catalog spec, and PR 18079 teaches the readers to use the links the catalog hands back (both by Sung Yun, both open). That is where the design is still moving.

VECTOR

VECTOR follows the same pattern, a few months behind. parquet-format PR 624 proposes a VECTOR(D) logical type, meaning a list of exactly D numbers, on top of Parquet's existing list storage. Iceberg's vector type proposal with its spec PR 18416 defines vector(E, D), a fixed-length list of D numbers of element type E, and maps it onto the three formats Iceberg has:

Iceberg v4 type Parquet Avro ORC Rules
vector(E, D) Parquet's standard nested list encoding, annotated VECTOR(D) (per parquet-format #624); element required, Parquet mapping for E array, elements non-null array, elements non-null E in int, long, float, double; exactly D non-null elements; no NaN or infinities; no type promotion to or from vector; no lower/upper bounds

Table 10. The proposed vector type and its format mappings.

What the two proposals have in common

Read those two proposals next to the registry and the shape is clear. Neither one routes embeddings or media around Parquet. Both extend Parquet to carry them, and then teach Iceberg's schema, statistics and three existing format mappings about the new type. Neither needs a new FileFormat. That was the part I didn't expect going in: the announcement talks about new formats, and the multimodal column types are being written into Parquet, the format the new formats were meant to sit beside.

The File Format API helps here, but less than you might hope, and it is worth being exact about how much. What the Parquet model shares across engines is the schema conversion, splits, filters, encryption and statistics. Turning a vector column into a Spark row field or a Flink row field is still the job of each engine's own reader and writer function, the two functions from the registration code in "Exploring pluggability." So a new type is one change in the Parquet module plus one in each engine's value readers, not one change total. (Both spec PRs are open; if either is withdrawn, or Iceberg defines the type without reference to Parquet, this section is dated.)

A useful way to hold all of this: a column type has to clear three layers before you can use it from a given engine, and the File Format API only touches the middle one. The table spec has to define it; each file format has to store it; each engine has to have somewhere to put the value. Table 11 shows four types at 1.12.0, two shipped and two proposed:

Type Table spec Parquet Avro ORC Spark Flink
timestamp_ns v3 yes yes yes no yes
geometry, geography v3 yes yes no 4.1 and later no
file v4, proposed released in parquet-format 2.14.0 mapping in the proposal mapping in the proposal no no
vector v4, proposed proposed mapping in the proposal mapping in the proposal no no

Table 11. Where four column types stand across the three layers. A "no" in the engine columns means the engine has no in-memory type to hold the value, whatever the file can store.

The nanosecond timestamp row is a keen example. The spec has it, every format stores it, and Spark's own timestamp is microseconds, so Iceberg's converter has no case for it. No change to the registry could fix that, meaning unsupported types in an engine don't suddenly become supported by this new API. Spark is in the middle of fixing it from its own side: an open proposal, SPIP: Timestamps with nanosecond precision, adds nanosecond timestamp types to Spark SQL, the types are already on Spark's main branch, and a steady stream of PRs is teaching each function about them. Once a Spark release ships them, the Iceberg side is a converter case and a one-line removal from that exclusion set, so do expect this row to change.

State of the work and future

Everything above is a reading of the Java implementation at 1.12.0 and of spec PRs that are open on the day I'm writing. It says nothing about PyIceberg or iceberg-rust, which I didn't read, and it benchmarks nothing; the run exists to show what the registry contains and what it says when a model is missing, not how fast anything is. The Vortex PR could merge in any form, and the Java enum could grow a value before the spec sentence does, as that PR already shows. If the enum is opened in some more general way, the "formats are a project change" half of this is dated. The types half stands on its own, because the FILE and vector types are defined in Parquet regardless of what the Java registry does.

Piece Status Where to look
File Format API shipped in 1.11.0; every engine in 1.12.0 reads through it announcement, proposal
Compatibility kit "more-or-less finished" per its author; vectorized reads open issue 15415
Vortex as a new format open PR, adds VORTEX to the enum PR 15915
Parquet FILE type released in parquet-format 2.14.0 PR 585
Iceberg file type (v4) open spec PR issue 17919, PR 17918
Pre-signed data access open spec and reader PRs PR 18080, PR 18079
Parquet VECTOR type open proposal PR 624
Iceberg vector type (v4) open spec PR issue 18297, PR 18416

Table 12. Status of every moving part, as of writing.

Keeping up with the Joneses: What your next step is

  • You have images or embeddings in Iceberg today. Keep the reference as a string and the embedding as a list, which the current readers handle, and plan a schema migration to file and vector when v4 is adopted rather than a storage migration to another format.
  • You want to follow the decisions. Watch the two Iceberg spec PRs, the Parquet VECTOR PR, and the two pre-signing PRs, because that is where the capability is being decided.
  • You are an engine author with your own row type. Register it. The API is for you, it works, and the run above is the whole recipe.
  • You want a new format in Iceberg. Start from the TCK issue and the Vortex PR, and budget for it as a contribution to the project, because that is what it is.

Further reading

  • Introducing the Apache Iceberg File Format API, the announcement, and the proposal issue
  • FILE type proposal and spec PR; parquet-format FILE; pre-signed data access PR 18080 and PR 18079
  • Vector type proposal and spec PR; parquet-format VECTOR
  • Vortex integration PR and the TCK issue; the kit itself is ReadFormatModelTests and BaseFormatModelTests, first merged in PR 15441
  • The run: Iceberg 1.12.0, iceberg-core + iceberg-data + iceberg-parquet, Java 17; the full program and its output are in the Usage section above

title: Getting Started with the Gemini API: A Practical Tutorial
description:
Getting Started with the Gemini API

The Gemini API lets you harness powerful language models for a variety of tasks—from generating text to analyzing data. This tutorial will walk you through setting up your environment, making your first request, and interpreting the response, all with a short, runnable Python example.

1. Prerequisites

  • Python 3.8+ installed on your machine.
  • requests library (pip install requests).
  • A Gemini API key from the Gemini console (you’ll need to create an account and enable the API).

2. Set Up the Request

Below is a minimal Python script that sends a prompt to the gemini-3.6-flash:free model and prints the generated text.

import requests
import json

API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE"
MODEL = "gemini-3.6-flash:free"
URL = f"https://api.unorouter.com/v1/chat/completions"

headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
}

payload = {
    "model": MODEL,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain in two sentences what GPT-4 is."}],
    "stream": False
}

response = requests.post(URL, headers=headers, json=payload)
data = response.json()

if response.ok:
    # Extract the assistant's reply
    assistant_reply = data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    print(assistant_reply)
else:
    print(f"Error: {data.get('error', 'Unknown error')}")

How It Works

  1. Headers – We authenticate with the API key and set the content type to JSON.
  2. Payload – The model field selects the free Gemini model. The messages array contains a single user message; you can adjust the prompt as needed.
  3. Response – On a successful request (200 OK), the generated text lives under choices[0].message.content.

3. Running the Script

Save the code to a file, e.g., gemini_demo.py, replace YOUR_API_KEY_HERE with your actual key, and run:

python gemini_demo.py

You should see a concise explanation of GPT‑4 printed to the console.

4. Tips & Best Practices

  • Rate Limits – The free tier includes a generous number of requests, but monitor your usage to avoid hitting limits.
  • Prompt Engineering – Clear, specific prompts yield more predictable results. Experiment with temperature settings if the API supports them.
  • Error Handling – Always check the response status and handle potential errors (e.g., network issues, invalid keys).

5. Next Steps

  • Explore other models (e.g., gemini-2.0-flash-exp) for different capabilities.
  • Integrate the API into larger applications using the official SDKs or REST calls.
  • Build simple tools like text summarizers, code assistants, or chatbots.

With just a few lines of code, you’ve unlocked the Gemini API’s potential. Happy coding!

title: Mastering Modern JavaScript: From ES6 to Async Patterns
description:
Introduction

JavaScript has evolved dramatically since the early days of alert('Hello World'). Today's JavaScript powers everything from tiny widgets to massive server‑side applications, thanks to ECMAScript 6 (ES6) and the ecosystem that grew around it. In this post we’ll walk through the most impactful language features introduced in the last decade, show how they simplify real‑world code, and explore async patterns that every modern developer should master.

1. Let, Const, and Block Scope

Before ES6, var was the only way to declare variables, leading to hoisting surprises.

function legacyScope() {
  var i = 0;
  for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    // i is function‑scoped, not block‑scoped
  }
  console.log(i); // 3, not 0
}

let and const fix that:

function blockScope() {
  const arr = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    arr.push(i);
  }
  // console.log(i); // ReferenceError: i is not defined
  return arr;
}
  • let – mutable, block‑scoped.
  • const – immutable binding, block‑scoped. The value can still be mutable if it’s an object.

2. Arrow Functions and Lexical this

Arrow functions give you a concise syntax and capture the surrounding this value.

// Traditional callback
setTimeout(function() {
  console.log(this); // Window (or undefined in strict mode)
}, 1000);

// Arrow version – inherits lexical this
class Timer {
  constructor() {
    this.start = Date.now();
  }
  log() {
    setTimeout(() => {
      console.log('Elapsed:', Date.now() - this.start);
    }, 1000);
  }
}
new Timer().log();

Because the arrow function does not create its own this, you avoid the common var self = this pattern.

3. Template Literals

String interpolation, multi‑line strings, and embedded expressions are now a breeze.

const user = { name: 'Ada', points: 42 };
const message = `
  Hello ${user.name}!
  You have earned ${user.points} points.
  Keep it up!
`;
console.log(message);

No more cumbersome concatenation or \n escapes.

4. Destructuring & Rest/Spread

Pull values out of arrays or objects directly in the declaration.

// Array destructuring
const [first, second, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30, 40];
// Object destructuring with renaming
const { title: postTitle, author = 'Anonymous' } = { title: 'JS Tips' };

Rest (...rest) gathers the remaining items, while spread (...obj) expands them:

const defaults = { theme: 'light', layout: 'grid' };
const userPrefs = { layout: 'list' };
const config = { ...defaults, ...userPrefs }; // { theme: 'light', layout: 'list' }

5. Modules (ESM)

Node.js and browsers now support native ES modules (import/export).

// utils.mjs
export function sum(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
export const PI = Math.PI;

// app.mjs
import { sum, PI } from './utils.mjs';
console.log(`Area of circle: ${PI * sum(3, 4)}`);

No more bundler‑only require/module.exports—you can write clean, tree‑shakable code directly.

6. Classes & Inheritance

Classes are syntactic sugar over prototypal inheritance, making OOP feel familiar.

class Shape {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  area() {
    throw new Error('area() must be implemented');
  }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
  constructor(radius) {
    super('circle');
    this.radius = radius;
  }
  area() {
    return Math.PI * this.radius ** 2;
  }
}

const c = new Circle(5);
console.log(`${c.name} area = ${c.area().toFixed(2)}`);

Static methods, getters/setters, and private fields (#value) are also part of the class spec.

7. Async/Await – Writing Asynchronous Code Like Synchronous Code

Promises turned callback hell into manageable chains, but async/await makes the flow even clearer.

async function fetchUser(id) {
  const response = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${id}`);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Network error');
  const user = await response.json();
  return user;
}

(async () => {
  try {
    const alice = await fetchUser(1);
    console.log('User:', alice);
  } catch (e) {
    console.error(e);
  }
})();

7.1 Parallel Execution with Promise.all

When tasks are independent, run them concurrently:

async function loadDashboard() {
  const [stats, recent, alerts] = await Promise.all([
    fetch('/api/stats').then(r => r.json()),
    fetch('/api/recent').then(r => r.json()),
    fetch('/api/alerts').then(r => r.json())
  ]);
  return { stats, recent, alerts };
}

7.2 Cancelable Fetches (AbortController)

Modern APIs let you abort long‑running requests:

async function fetchWithTimeout(url, ms) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), ms);
  try {
    const resp = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
    return await resp.json();
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timeout);
  }
}

8. Optional Chaining & Nullish Coalescing

Safely access deep properties without repetitive guards.

const config = { db: { host: 'localhost' } };
const port = config.db?.port ?? 5432; // 5432 if undefined or null

The ?. operator short‑circuits when a value is null/undefined, while ?? only falls back on nullish values (not 0 or '').

9. TypeScript Integration (A Quick Note)

While this post focuses on vanilla JavaScript, most production teams pair it with TypeScript for static typing. The features we covered today map one‑to‑one in TS, giving you compile‑time safety without sacrificing runtime performance.

10. Putting It All Together – A Real‑World Mini‑Project

Let’s build a tiny Todo API client using the modern features we’ve discussed.

// todoClient.mjs
export class TodoClient {
  #baseUrl;
  constructor(baseUrl) {
    this.#baseUrl = baseUrl.endsWith('/') ? baseUrl.slice(0, -1) : baseUrl;
  }

  async #request(path, options = {}) {
    const url = `${this.#baseUrl}${path}`;
    const resp = await fetch(url, { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, ...options });
    if (!resp.ok) {
      const err = await resp.text();
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${resp.status}: ${err}`);
    }
    return resp.json();
  }

  getAll() {
    return this.#request('/todos');
  }

  add(todo) {
    return this.#request('/todos', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(todo) });
  }

  delete(id) {
    return this.#request(`/todos/${id}`, { method: 'DELETE' });
  }
}

// usage.mjs
import { TodoClient } from './todoClient.mjs';

(async () => {
  const api = new TodoClient('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com');
  const todos = await api.getAll();
  console.log('First 3 todos:', todos.slice(0, 3));

  const newTodo = await api.add({ userId: 1, title: 'Learn async/await', completed: false });
  console.log('Created:', newTodo);

  await api.delete(newTodo.id);
  console.log('Deleted newly created todo');
})();

Notice:

  • Private fields (#baseUrl, #request).
  • async/await for clear flow.
  • Spread operator for request options.
  • Template literals for URL construction.
  • export/import for modularity.

Conclusion

JavaScript’s rapid evolution has turned it from a quirky browser scripting language into a robust, full‑stack powerhouse. Mastering let/const, arrow functions, destructuring, modules, and async/await equips you to write cleaner, more maintainable code today. Keep experimenting with the newest proposals (e.g., Array.prototype.at, Temporal) and remember that the language’s flexibility is both its strength and its responsibility—use the right tool for the right job.

Happy coding! 🚀
