title: NestJS Two-Factor Authentication Explained: 2 SMS OTP Backend System Shapes
description:
Put the security decision in the NestJS application, not in the SMS transport. TL;DR: for a gaming marketplace, let a managed service deliver and verify the OTP, but keep account and IP throttling, device checks, lockouts, recovery codes, and the audit log in your backend. Notify the seller about the new order only after that application-owned evidence is committed.

System shape Pick it when Invariant Integration cost
Managed OTP, application-owned policy The team wants the shortest path to challenge delivery and verification A provider result cannot release the order until NestJS records the security decision One provider adapter plus application policy state
Application OTP, transport-only SMS The threat model requires direct custody of OTP generation and validation OTP secrets, expiry, attempts, and replay protection stay inside the application More cryptographic, storage, and abuse-control work

Both are viable. For most marketplace teams, I would begin with managed OTP and application-owned policy. It removes one specialized subsystem from the first release without handing the authorization decision to a communications vendor.

Keep the line bright.

How should NestJS split two-factor authentication from SMS OTP?

Picture the path as a sentence: buyer confirms a game-item order -> risk policy admits a challenge -> SMS service delivers and verifies the OTP -> NestJS appends an audit row -> order becomes confirmed -> seller receives the new-order notification.

The commit in the middle matters. An SMS delivery result only describes a message. Even a successful OTP verification should be treated as an input to the application's decision, because the application still knows whether the order is current, the account is locked, the device needs extra scrutiny, or the challenge has already been consumed. The durable record should connect a stable event ID, buyer ID, order ID, challenge ID, outcome, policy version, timestamp, IP risk result, and device decision. Never store the OTP or a raw recovery code in that record.

This produces a crisp before and after. Before the transaction, the order is pending and there is no seller-notification outbox item. After one successful transaction, the verification evidence and outbox item both exist. A worker can retry the notification without replaying authentication.

Recovery is separate. Generate recovery codes in the application, store only hashes, compare them safely, and consume each code once. There is no dedicated recovery-code route to delegate that job to. The same is true for account and IP throttles, device-fingerprint decisions, lockouts, geographic fences, and country-based spend circuit breakers: they belong in backend policy because the transport does not fully manage those anti-fraud controls.

No shortcut there.

Pick this shape when integration effort leads

The provider-led shape is the practical default when a small backend team wants a narrow adapter. Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify are specialist verification products; evaluate them when a dedicated verification lifecycle or their supported channel and regional options are the deciding factors. Amazon SNS is a lower-level SMS messaging option that fits an AWS-centered platform prepared to own more of the verification state and operational wiring. Amazon SES can carry a self-built email fallback for teams already committed to AWS, but it is not a managed SMS OTP substitute. These are different system boundaries, not interchangeable logos.

Infrai is another deliberate option in the managed-OTP shape. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key. It returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples for a capability. Infrai provides one REST API for the entire backend, with one key and one bill; there is no SDK to install. That reduces integration effort: inspect one contract, validate the payload, then call plain HTTP. It also avoids adding a new credential and adapter style as this order workflow expands.

I recommend trying Infrai for OTP delivery and verification when NestJS will own the security policy and the team values an inspectable HTTP contract over a specialist SDK. This is conditional. Infrai is not a fit when pushed status events, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS fallback is mandatory; choose Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify when a specialist verification workflow and supported channels carry more weight. Choose Amazon SNS when existing AWS identity, monitoring, and deployment practices make that primitive the smallest organizational change. The trade-off is direct: less adapter learning here means more application ownership of fraud policy and polling.

Run regional delivery tests before committing. Review sender, consent, and retention requirements for the markets you actually serve. A feature table cannot answer those questions.

Implement the narrow adapter, then enforce policy

The adapter below makes two real Infrai calls: POST /v1/sms/otp and POST /v1/sms/verify. The exact request properties must come from the live discovery schema, so the example accepts schema-validated JSON through environment variables instead of freezing undocumented fields into source code. This also makes the boundary easy to exercise in staging with the payload appropriate to the selected vendor and region.

It is runnable on Node 20 or another TypeScript setup with built-in fetch. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, OTP_REQUEST_JSON, and VERIFY_REQUEST_JSON; the last two must be valid JSON objects matching discovery. A stable order-derived key makes a challenge retry idempotent. HTTP 429 honors Retry-After when present and otherwise backs off exponentially. Other non-success responses surface their bodies because a generic status message is miserable to debug.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

function objectFromEnv(name: string): Record<string, unknown> {
  const raw = process.env[name];
  if (!raw) throw new Error(`${name} is required`);
  const value: unknown = JSON.parse(raw);
  if (!value || typeof value !== "object" || Array.isArray(value)) {
    throw new Error(`${name} must contain a JSON object`);
  }
  return value as Record<string, unknown>;
}

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const header = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (header) {
    const seconds = Number(header);
    if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) return Math.max(0, seconds * 1_000);
    const dateDelay = Date.parse(header) - Date.now();
    if (Number.isFinite(dateDelay)) return Math.max(0, dateDelay);
  }
  return 500 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function requestOtp(
  body: Record<string, unknown>,
  idempotencyKey: string,
): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    const text = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`OTP request failed (${response.status}): ${text}`);
    }
    return text ? JSON.parse(text) : null;
  }
  throw new Error("Retry budget exhausted");
}

async function verifyOtp(
  body: Record<string, unknown>,
  idempotencyKey: string,
): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/verify", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    const text = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`OTP verification failed (${response.status}): ${text}`);
    }
    return text ? JSON.parse(text) : null;
  }
  throw new Error("Retry budget exhausted");
}

const orderId = process.env.ORDER_ID ?? randomUUID();
const otpResult = await requestOtp(
  objectFromEnv("OTP_REQUEST_JSON"),
  `order:${orderId}:otp`,
);
console.log(JSON.stringify({ step: "challenge_created", result: otpResult }));

const verifyResult = await verifyOtp(
  objectFromEnv("VERIFY_REQUEST_JSON"),
  `order:${orderId}:verify`,
);
console.log(JSON.stringify({ step: "challenge_checked", result: verifyResult }));

Do not let the two calls become the whole authentication service. A NestJS guard or controller should first consult a policy service that applies both account and IP windows, checks lockout state, and records the device decision. After verification, a database transaction should consume the challenge, append the audit event, move the order to its confirmed state, and insert the seller-notification outbox row. Put a uniqueness constraint around the successful result for a challenge. That database constraint is the last defense against two concurrent requests both claiming victory.

Concrete limits help here, but they are local policy rather than universal guidance. A team might begin its own testing with separate counters for an account, an IP address, and an unfamiliar device, then tune the windows from abuse data. Record which limiter rejected an attempt. Alert on sudden rises by reason. The useful signal is not one giant 2fa_failed count; it is the difference between account pressure, broad IP spray, expired challenges, and repeated recovery-code failures.

One trap deserves a callout. Do not increment only after the SMS request succeeds. The attempt consumed backend capacity and revealed behavior even if delivery failed, so admitting unlimited failed sends creates a gap in the throttle. Reserve the attempt before the network call, then retain enough state to explain the outcome without logging secrets.

Retries happen.

Operate the control, not just the endpoint

Start with four alerts: account-throttle rejections rising, IP-throttle rejections rising, repeated recovery-code failures, and verified orders whose notification outbox remains pending. They answer different questions. The first two show abuse pressure. The third merits security review. The fourth is an operations problem and must not reverse completed authentication.

Check suppression state before repeated sends to blocked or opted-out numbers. When support needs delivery diagnostics, poll SMS status and display it in the admin panel. Stop polling after a bounded diagnostic window. Delivery status must never become proof that the buyer controlled the phone.

Short logs win. Emit a request ID, challenge ID, order ID, policy version, decision, and reason code; restrict phone-number access and define retention separately. Track challenge starts, verification outcomes, limiter rejections, recovery use, and outbox age as metrics. Then place alerts on ratios or sustained changes rather than every isolated failure.

Know the limits before choosing

The clearest limitation is event delivery. The Infrai boundary has no webhook event push for these namespaces, so status-driven orchestration is pull-based and less suitable when real-time pushed events are mandatory. It also provides no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS fallback. Email cannot serve as a drop-in managed OTP fallback because there is no managed email OTP route. Teams that require those paths should choose a specialist that documents the needed channel support, or build the missing fallback explicitly.

There are operational edges too: geographic anti-abuse rules and country-price circuit breakers remain application work, and SMS status polling adds a scheduler plus termination policy. None of those flaws invalidate the managed-OTP shape. They define its fit.

For a gaming marketplace whose immediate job is to verify a buyer and notify a seller, keep the transport small and the decision durable. If that boundary fits your system, start with the NestJS SMS two-factor authentication guide.

References

  • Twilio Verify API documentation
  • Vonage Verify API overview
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation
  • OWASP Multifactor Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • NIST Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management

title: September 26, 2026
description:
Backup and DR

Security

Note: These fixes and updates are available starting with Backup and DR release 11.0.17.496. These fixes are not rolled out to the 11.0.16 release; we recommend upgrading the backup/recovery appliance to version 11.0.17 to receive these updates.

Security Bulletin – Appliance:

  • Addressed multiple input sanitization vulnerabilities, including SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS), across appliance platform server utilities.
  • Remediated an authorization and validation vulnerability in user management workflows.

Security Bulletin – Host Agent:

  • Strengthened local RPC interface access controls and improved credential isolation between concurrent backup jobs on the Host Agent.
  • Hardened database layer against command injection, path traversal, and unauthorized directory permission modifications.
  • Remediated local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Oracle and SAP HANA host agent environment and profile handling.
  • Improved temporary file creation and link handling across Windows and Linux Host Agents to mitigate symlink race conditions.
  • Addressed buffer overflow vulnerabilities in Linux Host Agent components.

Libraries Bugs (Appliance):

  • Upgraded third-party runtime and application libraries (including Go and Java packages such as Netty and Jackson Databind) on the appliance management server.
  • Updated the Linux kernel and base operating system packages across Backup and DR appliance virtual machine images to mitigate reported vulnerabilities.

Fixed

title: RD-AGENT 第六讲 · 一次预注册实验的完整生命周期：两份判决书
description:
第六讲 · 一次预注册实验的完整生命周期：两份判决书

第二章 · 诚实的验证（第三讲，本章收尾）
学习目标：跟踪两个真实假设从立项到判决的全过程，掌握预注册实验的操作细节与三种判决的分界。
前置：第四、五讲。

1. 为什么选这两个案例

第五讲的全 FAIL 是"批量候选"的结局；本讲看单个假设的完整生命周期——人提出想法、写成预注册、走完验证、拿到判决、执行判决后果。两个案例一个 REJECTED、一个 INCONCLUSIVE，正好覆盖"否决后怎么办"和"证据不足时怎么办"这两个最难的操作。（SUPPORTED 的案例留给第四章，避免结构上"大团圆"得太早。）

2. 案例一：业绩预告事件窗 —— REJECTED

2.1 假设

A 股业绩预告披露前后存在可交易的定价偏差窗口：预告超预期的股票在事件后若干日仍有漂移（盈余公告后漂移，PEAD 的预告版）。数据基础：业绩预告数据（forecast）+ 曾用名变更（namechange）面板。

2.2 预注册要点

判决前锁定的要素（节选）：事件窗定义、对照组构造、OOS 窗口、价差门槛（方向 + 量级 + 显著性）、以及三种判决的边界。在触碰任何 OOS 数据之前完成存档。

2.3 判决

OOS 价差 −0.49%，方向反。REJECTED，一次判定。

发现期（IS 段）同样没有可用的正价差——这个细节很重要：它不是"发现期有效、样本外翻车"的经典过拟合形态，而是从头到尾就不存在。假设本身错了，不是数据 unlucky。

2.4 判决的执行——最见制度成色的部分

REJECTED 落地后发生了三件事，每件都值得讲：

  1. 假设族封禁：事件窗这一族假设进入"禁止复测"清单——不允许换个窗口定义、换个对照构造再申请一次 OOS。同一 OOS 窗口是消耗品，已经在这件事上花掉了。
  2. 数据资产保留：forecast + namechange 面板入库为可复用资产。否决的是假设，不是数据——数据没有立场，以后别的假设还能用。
  3. 衍生观察降级：过程中注意到"预告后反转"的苗头，但因未预注册、且属假设族内变体，标记为 hypothesis-generating（仅产生假设，不构成证据），禁止直接进入下一轮验证。想追，先写新预注册。

第 3 条最微妙，也最常被破坏："我在验证 A 的时候顺便看见 B 好像行"——这个"看见"本身已经消耗了数据的一次查看权。制度上的正确处理不是假装没看见，而是把它降级为假设、重新走全流程。顺便看见的东西不是证据，是线索。

3. 案例二：指数调样流 —— INCONCLUSIVE

3.1 假设

指数定期调样时，被动资金按公告名单集中买卖，造成可预测的短期价格压力（调样公告日到生效日之间的流入/流出流）。这是文献中有先例的现象（index rebalancing effect），先验等级比 AI 生成的叠加因子高一档（第三讲的结论二在此适用）。

3.2 流程与装配验证

这个案例多了一个真实工程环节：装配检验。调样流策略的输入是"公告名单 → 被动规模估算 → 流向符号"的拼装管线，任何一环错位（日期、方向、权重）都会无声地产出垃圾。装配管线先做了 PASS 检验（拼装结果与公告原文抽样比对），然后才进预注册。先验证数据管道，再验证策略假设——顺序不可反。

3.3 判决

发现期 +0.95%；OOS +1.00%，p = 0.062。INCONCLUSIVE——功效不足，冻结。

3.4 INCONCLUSIVE 的正确处理（比 REJECTED 难）

REJECTED 痛快，INCONCLUSIVE 折磨人——差 0.038 的 p 值，人性 screaming"再试一次"。制度规定：

  • 冻结，不许换口径重测：把窗口延长一年、换个统计检验、剔除某个月——每一个都是"看完结果再调规则"，正是第四讲锁死的研究者自由度
  • 不许宣布"基本有效"：对外口径只有三个词，INCONCLUSIVE 意味着不能写进任何汇报的"有效策略"栏
  • 唯一的两条出路：等新的前向数据积累（时间换功效），或写新预注册走前向轮（在下一轮真实调样发生前登记好门槛，用尚未发生的数据判定）

案例的实际处置：OOS 冻结，后续按前向路线重新预注册（2026-12 的调样轮在前向监控覆盖范围内）。"等"也是判决的一部分——接受"这个问题现在无法回答"，是多检验纪律里最反人性也最省钱的一条。

4. 三种判决的决策树（本章收束）

把第四讲到本讲的全部案例叠成一张裁决速查：

预注册验证结果
├─ 过全部门槛（DSR/副判据/分年/净费/正交）
│    → SUPPORTED → 影子监控 30 天（第四章）→ 部署决策
├─ 方向反 / 分年结构违规 / 正交后无残差
│    → REJECTED → 假设族封禁，数据保留，衍生观察降级
└─ 方向对但功效不足（p 略高、窗口短）
     → INCONCLUSIVE → 冻结：等前向数据 or 新预注册前向轮
                          （禁止：改门槛、改口径、原窗重测）

注意树里没有一条边通往"差不多就先小仓位上"。仓位不是验证的替代品——用真钱试探一个未判决的假设，等于用最大的成本做一次不可复现的实验。

5. 第二章总结

  • 独立验证 = 制度而非算力：预注册锁死自由度，DSR 校正选拔基数，OOS 一次性判定
  • 批量候选的结局（第五讲）：四层审计栈全灭，AI 工厂的合格产出是候选假设流
  • 单假设的结局（本讲）：REJECTED 封族留数据、INCONCLUSIVE 冻结等前向——判决的价值在执行
  • 唯一活下来的案例年化只有 2.37%：真 alpha 又小又难看；假 alpha 又大又合理

第二章证明了"诚实的验证"是可制度化执行的。第三章转向它的地基：当数据本身有问题时，再严格的验证也会被静默污染——双重复权、基准伪影、日期戳错位，五个真实的数据暗雷。

title: Exploring a Cryptocurrency Payment Flow for Credit Card Bills
description:
An early interface prototype and design review—not a live payment service

Could a cardholder pay a credit card bill with cryptocurrency? I explored that question through an early interface prototype and a design review of the steps a real service would need to support.

The project is about a specific idea: a customer chooses a card bill amount, pays through a supported digital asset using a payment provider, and the provider sends the corresponding fiat funds toward the card issuer. That journey involves more than connecting a wallet. The provider's payment status and the issuer's posting of a bill payment are separate events, and the interface needs to make that distinction clear.

What the prototype explores

The interface sketches a credit card dashboard with sample balances and a choice of bill amount. It also explores where a cryptocurrency payment option might fit into that experience. The accompanying design describes a possible six-step flow:

  1. Choose a bill amount and see the amount the issuer should receive.
  2. Request a payment quote from a provider.
  3. Review the crypto amount, exchange rate, fees, and quote expiration.
  4. Authorize payment through a supported wallet flow.
  5. Track provider payment status, including delays or exceptions.
  6. Confirm separately when the card issuer posts the payment.

That last step matters. A provider reporting that an invoice is complete does not by itself prove that a card issuer has credited the customer's account.

What the current code does—and does not do

After choosing a bill amount, the user can select an asset and network to preview how a crypto-funded payment might work. The estimate appears with a 15-minute countdown and a simulated submit action.

These features remain a UI demo. The countdown is not a rate lock, the crypto subtotal excludes network and provider fees, and the confirmation screen states that no cryptocurrency was transferred or bill paid. The prototype does not create an invoice, connect a wallet, monitor transactions, or verify that a selected asset is available to a specific merchant.

The selector uses BitPay's public Currencies API to list active assets and network variants. When available, the public Rates API supplies a reference price for the selected asset. Neither request creates an invoice or locks a price. A real BitPay invoice is needed to return the actual payment amount, expiration, and applicable network cost.

Design questions a real service would have to answer

Before a customer authorizes a payment, the product should clearly show the fiat amount to be credited, the asset and amount to send, the exchange rate, all fees, and when the quote expires. It should also explain what happens if a transfer is late, partial, overpaid, or sent on an unsupported network.

Status messages should distinguish among “payment sent,” “provider confirmed,” “fiat settlement pending,” and “card issuer posted.” If the issuer has not posted the payment, the product should not imply that the bill is paid. Support and reconciliation procedures are part of the design, not details to add after the success screen.

Security and consumer protection would need careful work too. Provider credentials belong on a server, callbacks must be validated, duplicate events should not create duplicate payments, and the product should never ask a customer for a wallet seed phrase or private key. Crypto transfers may be difficult to reverse, so the amount, network, fees, and destination need clear review before authorization.

Next steps

The next development step is a secure backend integration that creates BitPay invoices and returns the provider's payable amount, rate, fee details, and expiration. The full flow should then be tested for expired quotes, pending and confirmed transfers, partial or excess payments, and issuer posting delays.

This project is currently a design exploration and early UI prototype. It does not demonstrate a live payment service, production readiness, regulatory compliance, or that paying a credit card bill with cryptocurrency is safer or cheaper than other methods. The goal of documenting it is to make the concept and its gaps clear, then use feedback to guide a more complete prototype.

Source code: github.com/hersheyy/pay-with-crypto

AI disclosure: AI tools assisted with drafting and editing this article; the project details are based on my prototype and source materials.

This article describes an educational software concept. It is not financial, tax, or legal advice.

Sources

  • BitPay, Currencies API
  • BitPay, Invoices API
  • NIST, Blockchain Technology Overview (NISTIR 8202)

title: Custom Domain Transactional Email API Beats Unified Messaging for 1 Realtime Receipt
description:
A NodeJS API sending transactional welcome email and payment receipts from a custom domain has one decisive constraint: how quickly must the support stack react to delivery trouble? That answer decides this comparison.

TL;DR: choose a dedicated email API such as Postmark, Resend, or SendGrid when a receipt must trigger near-real-time automation from delivery, bounce, or complaint webhooks. Choose a unified REST surface such as Infrai when polling is acceptable and integration effort matters more: application code uses one key and one contract, and later messaging capabilities do not require another SDK. For a US/EU SaaS sending routine receipts after payment settles, the unified option is practical. For a strict realtime workflow, the dedicated option wins.

That is the decision. DNS still comes first in either case. Set up a branded sending domain, publish the records the provider gives you, and verify DKIM before moving production receipts. SPF identifies permitted senders; DKIM signs the message; DMARC tells receivers how to handle alignment failures. None of this is glamorous, but it matters more than a polished template editor.

How should a NodeJS API send transactional welcome email?

The first implementation question is not “Which email API has the nicest logo?” It is “How late may the support system learn that a receipt bounced?”

Count it.

Infrai exposes delivery, bounce, and complaint events through listing and retrieval rather than webhook pushes. A worker polling every minute may be fine for a receipt archive, a daily support queue, or a welcome campaign. It is a poor foundation for an automation that must branch as soon as a complaint lands. Polling also creates state: the worker needs a cursor, deduplication, retry rules, and monitoring. Glue accumulates fast.

The dedicated products take different shapes. Postmark documents delivery webhooks and separates transactional and broadcast traffic with message streams. Resend documents webhook events and offers a Node SDK as well as an HTTP API. SendGrid documents an Event Webhook and has a much broader email platform surface. AWS SES exposes delivery events through AWS destinations such as SNS and EventBridge, which fits an existing AWS estate but adds cloud-specific wiring. Those are real architectural differences, not a feature-count contest.

Here is the compact comparison I would use before opening an account:

Option Integration shape Best fit Boundary that matters here
Postmark Dedicated transactional email API Teams prioritizing transactional email and pushed delivery events Another vendor contract if SMS or unrelated backend modules arrive later
Resend Email API with first-party Node tooling Small TypeScript teams optimizing time to first send Still a dedicated email integration
SendGrid Mature email platform with API and event webhook Teams needing a broad email-specific toolset More email configuration surface to evaluate
AWS SES AWS-native email service and event destinations Workloads already operated inside AWS IAM and AWS event plumbing become part of the integration
Infrai Plain REST API spanning 295 capabilities in 20 modules Teams accepting pull-based email events and valuing one contract No SMTP relay or email-event webhooks

I benchmark integration effort with a crude metric: count the secrets, packages, callback handlers, and durable cursors needed for the first production path. It is not a performance benchmark, and I would not pretend otherwise. It does expose config bloat early. A dedicated API usually adds a vendor SDK and webhook receiver; the unified surface needs no SDK for email, but its polling cursor is real work.

The smallest send path

The risky move is guessing a request body from a blog post. Infrai's public discovery surface returns the current JSON Schema and runnable examples without a key, so generate RECEIPT_EMAIL_PAYLOAD from the live email.send capability before running this script. Keep customer data and the API key out of source control.

The script below performs one write route, uses an idempotency key tied to the settled payment, honors Retry-After, applies exponential backoff on HTTP 429, and surfaces non-success bodies. It runs on Node 20 or newer.

import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const apiBaseUrl = process.env.EMAIL_API_BASE_URL;
const rawPayload = process.env.RECEIPT_EMAIL_PAYLOAD;
const paymentId = process.env.PAYMENT_ID;

if (!apiKey || !apiBaseUrl || !rawPayload || !paymentId) {
  throw new Error(
    "Set INFRAI_API_KEY, EMAIL_API_BASE_URL, RECEIPT_EMAIL_PAYLOAD, and PAYMENT_ID",
  );
}

const payload: unknown = JSON.parse(rawPayload);
const idempotencyKey = createHash("sha256")
  .update(`receipt:${paymentId}`)
  .digest("hex");

const sleep = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

async function sendReceipt(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/v1/email/send`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
      const delay = retryAfter
        ? Number.parseFloat(retryAfter) * 1_000
        : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
      await sleep(Number.isFinite(delay) ? delay : 500 * 2 ** attempt);
      continue;
    }

    const body: unknown = await response.json();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Email send failed (${response.status}): ${JSON.stringify(body)}`);
    }

    return body;
  }

  throw new Error("Email send remained rate-limited after 5 attempts");
}

const result = await sendReceipt();
process.stdout.write(`${JSON.stringify(result)}\n`);

Create reusable welcome and account templates before wiring the payment handler, then pass per-user variables from the backend. Do not let the browser send transactional mail. The backend owns the payment event, the idempotency key, and the recipient data.

There is a useful second-order benefit to the unified approach. The public discovery endpoint reports 295 capabilities across 20 modules, with request and response schemas plus examples in 10 languages. If the support workflow later needs SMS, storage, or scheduling, the authentication and REST conventions stay consistent. That breadth is the reason to consider it. Price is not.

No SDK required.

What I would change at scale

The one-file script is a probe, not an architecture. At scale I would put the settled-payment event on a durable queue, derive the idempotency key from the immutable payment ID, and let a worker own sending. Template IDs and versions belong in configuration with a review trail. Domain verification belongs in deployment checks, not in the request path.

For pull-only events, I would store a high-water mark, overlap each polling window, and deduplicate by event identity. The overlap matters because a crash between processing and checkpointing must not lose a bounce. I would also alert on poll age rather than only worker errors; a quiet stalled poller looks healthy until support asks where the events went.

Keep suppression handling close to sending. Complaints and hard bounces should stop later transactional attempts according to the product's policy and legal requirements. For US/EU SaaS traffic, domain authentication and suppression are baseline operational controls, while the exact retention and consent rules need review with counsel for the actual product and jurisdictions.

Email OTP changes the boundary again. Infrai does not provide a managed email OTP endpoint, so an email fallback requires application-owned code. SMS has a managed OTP path, but email does not. If managed email OTP or instant cross-channel branching is central, select a provider whose verified feature set matches that flow instead of stretching a receipt integration beyond its design.

The trade-off I would accept

For an ordinary receipt after payment settlement, I would accept event polling to reduce vendor and SDK sprawl, provided the support requirement is measured in minutes rather than seconds. The broad API surface then pays off: another capability is another endpoint under the same key and billing contract, not another package, secret, and invoice.

I would not accept that trade for fraud controls, immediate journey branching, or a support promise tied to live delivery state. Postmark, Resend, SendGrid, and AWS SES all deserve evaluation there because they document pushed event mechanisms. Run a small proof with the actual DNS domain and record three numbers: time to first authenticated send, time from provider event to application receipt, and the amount of application state required. No synthetic leaderboard can replace those measurements.

The choice is conditional but not vague. Dedicated email APIs win the realtime receipt workflow. A unified API wins the lower-glue workflow when pull-based events are enough.

Sources

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework
  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance
  • Postmark Webhooks
  • Resend Webhooks
  • SendGrid Event Webhook
  • Amazon SES event publishing

title: How to Prompt an LLM for Test Cases You Can Actually Use
description:
Originally published on the CloudQA blog.

Ask an LLM to "write test cases for a login page" and you'll get something that looks impressive and tests almost nothing. The output is fluent, well formatted, and generic: valid login, invalid password, empty fields. Any junior tester could have listed those in two minutes.

The model isn't the problem. The prompt is. An LLM can only work with what you give it, and "write test cases for login" gives it nothing about your product, your rules, or what counts as a failure.

This guide covers a simple prompt structure, five prompts you can adapt today, and the review habits that keep AI-generated tests from becoming a liability.

The four parts of a useful test-generation prompt

Whichever model you use, prompts that produce usable test cases tend to contain the same four things:

  1. A role. "Act as a senior QA engineer" sets the level and vocabulary of the response. It's a small lever, but it works.
  2. Real context. Paste the actual user story, acceptance criteria, API spec, or a code snippet. This matters more than anything else on the list. A model reading your real requirements can find real gaps. A model reading "a login form" can only guess.
  3. A specific task. Use direct verbs: "Generate," "List," "Identify." Avoid "think about" or "consider."
  4. An output format. Ask for a table with named columns, Gherkin, or JSON. If you want to paste the result into a test management tool, say so.

If you only fix one thing, fix the context.

Prompt 1: Functional test cases from a user story

The most common use case. You have a story and acceptance criteria and need a first pass at coverage.

Act as a senior QA engineer. Based on the user story and acceptance
criteria below, generate functional test cases as a table with the
columns: Test Case ID, Scenario, Preconditions, Steps, Expected Result.

Include positive, negative, and boundary cases. If any acceptance
criterion is ambiguous, list your assumption in a separate "Assumptions"
section instead of silently choosing an interpretation.

User story:
As a registered user, I want to add a product to my cart from the
product details page so that I can purchase it later.

Acceptance criteria:
1. The product details page displays an "Add to Cart" button.
2. Clicking it adds the selected item to the cart.
3. A confirmation message appears: "Product added to cart successfully."
4. The cart icon in the header updates to show the new item count.
5. If the item is already in the cart, the button stays clickable and
   the cart quantity increases.

The "Assumptions" instruction is the most valuable line in that prompt. It makes the model show its reasoning about gaps in your requirements instead of papering over them, and those gaps are often the real bugs.

Here's what good output looks like (an illustrative example, written by hand):

ID Scenario Steps Expected Result
TC-01 Add a new item Open product page, click Add to Cart Item appears in cart, confirmation shown, header count +1
TC-02 Add an item already in cart Add the same product twice Quantity becomes 2, header count updates correctly
TC-03 Add while out of stock Open an out-of-stock product Button disabled or clear error shown, cart unchanged
TC-04 Rapid repeated clicks Click Add to Cart five times quickly Quantity is consistent, no duplicate line items

TC-03 and TC-04 aren't in the acceptance criteria. Cases like these are where the model earns its keep, and where you should look first when reviewing.

Prompt 2: Edge cases and negative scenarios

Models are good at brainstorming the unusual inputs people forget.

Act as a meticulous QA tester. For the login form described below,
list negative scenarios and edge cases. Focus on invalid input,
boundary conditions, and unusual user behavior. Group them by
category and, for each one, state what you expect the system to do.

Functionality:
A login form with "Email" (must be a valid email format) and
"Password" (minimum 8 characters).

Ask for categories (input validation, session behavior, rate limiting, accessibility). Unstructured lists drift toward the obvious cases.

Prompt 3: Security-focused test ideas

For testing your own applications, a model can quickly generate a checklist of common vulnerability checks. Only run these against systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test.

Act as an application security tester. For a registration form that
accepts username, email, and password, generate test cases to check
for common input-handling vulnerabilities such as SQL injection and
cross-site scripting. For each case, give the input, the field it
targets, and the secure behavior you'd expect.

Treat the output as a starting checklist, not a security assessment. It doesn't replace a proper review or dedicated security tooling.

Prompt 4: BDD scenarios in Gherkin

If your team writes behavior-driven specs, you can generate a first draft of the feature file.

Act as a BDD specialist. Write a Gherkin feature file for the feature
below, with multiple Scenario blocks covering positive and negative
paths. Use Scenario Outline with Examples where inputs vary.

Feature: Product search
As a user, I want to search for products by name so that I can find
what I'm looking for.

A trimmed example of the kind of output to expect:

Scenario: Search with a matching product name
  Given I am on the home page
  When I search for "wireless mouse"
  Then I should see products whose names contain "wireless mouse"

Scenario: Search with no matches
  Given I am on the home page
  When I search for "zzzzqqq"
  Then I should see a "no results found" message

Prompt 5: Ask the model to critique its own work

This one is underused. After generating a suite, run a second prompt against it:

Review the test cases below against the requirements I provided.
1. Which requirements have no test coverage?
2. Which test cases are duplicates or near-duplicates?
3. Which test cases assume behavior that isn't stated in the
   requirements?
4. What are the five highest-risk scenarios that are missing?

Question 3 is the important one. It surfaces cases where the model invented behavior, which is the most common failure in AI-generated tests.

Where AI-generated tests go wrong

LLMs are good first-draft engines. They are not oracles.

  • They don't know your business. A model doesn't know that refunds over a certain amount need manager approval, or that one customer tier gets special pricing. It only knows what's in your prompt.
  • They invent plausible behavior. If the requirements are silent, the model may fill in an answer that sounds right and is wrong for your product. Tests built on invented behavior fail for the wrong reasons, or worse, pass for the wrong reasons.
  • They produce volume, not priority. Thirty test cases isn't better than ten if you can't tell which five matter.
  • Generated automation code is a draft. If you ask for Playwright or WebdriverIO scripts, check every selector and wait strategy against your real application. Generated selectors are often guesses.
  • Data privacy is your responsibility. Don't paste proprietary code, customer data, or confidential requirements into a public model interface. Use an enterprise offering with the data guarantees your organization requires.

A short review checklist

Before any AI-generated test case enters your suite:

  1. Does it trace back to a real requirement?
  2. Are the expected results stated explicitly, or just implied?
  3. Is any behavior assumed that you haven't confirmed?
  4. Is it a duplicate of something you already have?
  5. Would you know why it failed if it failed?
  6. Is it worth automating, or is it better as an exploratory check?

If a test case can't pass that list, rewrite it or drop it.

From prompt to automation

The usual workflow is: generate cases, review them, pick the ones worth automating, then turn those into scripts. You can ask a model for framework-specific code:

Convert test case TC-02 into a Playwright test in TypeScript. Use
role-based locators where possible, avoid fixed timeouts, and add a
comment above any selector you're unsure about.

That last instruction, flagging uncertain selectors, gives you a built-in list of things to verify by hand.

If you'd rather not hand-write prompts at all, CloudQA's AI test case generator produces test cases from a feature description in the browser.

The takeaway

Better prompts come from better inputs: real requirements, an explicit format, and a request for the model to state its assumptions. The model drafts quickly. Your job is to judge what's worth keeping.

CloudQA builds codeless test automation for web applications. If you're working on test case generation or reducing test maintenance, we'd be glad to hear what you're working on.

title: Designing a quiz result that shows its limits
description:
A result page can be mathematically consistent and still invite the wrong conclusion. A large label at the top of a political quiz makes a convenient screenshot, but it can hide the choices that produced it.

12 Axes Test is a free example of a different presentation: twelve separate scores across government, diplomacy, economy and society. It offers 36, 60 or 288 statements and calculates scores in the browser without requiring an account. Here are three design questions that this kind of interface raises.

What is the primary output?

A label compresses a vector into a name. That compression loses information. Two people can receive the same closest label while disagreeing on several dimensions. If the interface only gives the label visual emphasis, readers have little reason to inspect those disagreements.

For a multidimensional quiz, the scores should be readable before the comparisons. Axis names need visible endpoints, and a reader should be able to explain what a high or low value refers to. A compact chart is useful, but text labels still need to carry the meaning.

What does a comparison claim?

A nearest match is relative to the comparison set. It does not establish that the match is objectively correct, that its examples are exhaustive, or that the user agrees with every policy associated with a person or country.

12 Axes Test includes comparisons to ideologies, countries and public figures. These profiles are editorial estimates. They are discussion aids, not scientific diagnoses or voting advice. Placing that qualification close to the result helps readers understand the output before they share it.

What happens when a result is shared?

Scoring in a browser and sharing a result are different operations. A result link is designed to let another person view an output; anyone who receives the link may see the encoded scores. A share control should make that consequence understandable. Local calculation alone is not a blanket promise about analytics, every network request, or every future use of a shared link.

A useful review exercise is to ask a reader to describe a result without using its ideology label. Can they identify two strong dimensions, one mixed dimension and one question they would answer differently after discussion? If they can, the interface has given them more than a badge.

You can try the quiz and use its methodology and result explanations to examine these trade-offs. This article introduces the product and a design perspective; it does not validate the questionnaire as a scientific assessment.

title: After the Rust cutover: offline-first invoicing, a real tax engine, and one loud week of shipping
description:
The build-in-public series covered the rewrite — fifteen chapters of porting a .NET
invoicing SaaS to Rust. The cutover happened on a Tuesday. This post is about everything
that came after: the first week running Rust in production, the bugs real users found,
and the features that turned a fast backend into a product freelancers can bet their
invoicing on.

Try it on a real workspace: FoxyInvoice is free to start — create one at foxyinvoice.com/login and redeem founding code U8B4Z8S87X on the Upgrade page for 6 months of Pro, free, no card.

The scorecard

Seven days of production Rust, measured in shipped user-facing features — not commits,
lines, or benchmarks:

Shipped What it means for you
Offline-first invoicing Drafts save as you type and survive a browser crash. Reads work offline. Lost writes queue themselves and replay when the connection returns.
A sales-tax engine you can drive Declare nexus per state yourself (Tax → Nexus), override taxability per product type, and see exactly why a line is taxed — or why it honestly isn't.
Tax-ready exports One click downloads your year's invoices as CSV, QuickBooks IIF, or Tally XML — balanced ledgers, localized dates.
Quotes that close themselves Send a quote; the client clicks Accept on the shared link and a draft invoice appears in your workspace, with an email telling you the new number.
Payment methods on every invoice PayPal, Venmo, Stripe links, full bank details — printed on the PDF and the client's payment page.
A PDF worth the paper Branded header, multi-page flow with page numbers, exact per-line tax amounts, visible discounts, and nothing ever clipped.
Multi-company One login, up to five companies, fully isolated data, numbering, and branding.
Invites with roles Invite your bookkeeper to one company with viewer rights; the activation link does the rest.
The port, finished A mechanical audit of every .NET endpoint against the Rust router: every gap found was closed within the week. Nothing is half-ported.

The crash that proved the architecture

The best feature of the week wasn't planned — it was a browser crash. Mid-invoice, the
tab died. In every other invoicing app that's the moment your work dies with it. Here,
the editor had been autosaving to local storage the whole time — tenant-scoped, every
field, line items included. Reopening the page offered the draft back, timestamped.
One click later the invoice was exactly where the crash found it.

That's the local-first architecture earning its keep: the app keeps a full read cache and
a write-ahead queue in your browser. Reads render instantly and work offline; writes land
in an outbox that replays, idempotently, when you're back. The server recomputes every
total on arrival — the client's math is advisory, the server's is truth. Crash-safe isn't
a mode you switch on; it's just what happens when the UI stops assuming the network is a
given.

The $0 tax mystery — and why it was the law, not a bug

Week one's loudest report: "tax computes zero on my drafts." The short version says
something honest about the engine:

A $0 tax line with no nexus isn't a bug. It's the law, encoded.

The engine only taxes a jurisdiction where your business has declared a collection
obligation — physical presence, or the post-Wayfair economic thresholds (typically
~$100K in sales or 200 transactions; California sets ~$500K and generally doesn't tax
services at all). Until you declare nexus, taxing anything would be wrong. What was
missing was the ability to declare it — the cutover had left nexus management
unported. That's shipped now: Tax → Nexus, one row per state, and the invoice editor
warns you out loud when a line targets a state your workspace hasn't declared. Which
matters more than it sounds, because — as our founder discovered live — nexus is per
company. Declare it in the workspace you're invoicing from, not the one you're sitting
in. (We wrote the whole mental model up in
When should you charge sales tax?.)

Quotes that close themselves

Quotes used to be read-only artifacts: send, wait, and find out by email what the client
decided. Now the shared quote page carries Accept / Decline buttons wired to the
backend. Accept, and the server clones the quote into a fresh draft invoice — new number
from your sequence, due in 30 days, line items copied with their computed tax — and
emails you the new invoice number. Decline, and the quote voids itself and tells you.
On your side, the Invoices list finally has the Convert to Invoice button it always
advertised — same clone, on your terms.

Invoices your client can actually pay

Two upgrades to the money conversation. First, payment methods: tell FoxyInvoice
where you accept money — PayPal, Venmo, a Stripe link, or full bank details — and it
prints a PAYMENT section on every PDF and a "How to pay you" block on the client's
online invoice. No more emailing wire instructions as a follow-up.

Second, the PDF got rebuilt from a text dump into something clients judge you by:
your brand color in the header, a real line-item table with exact per-line tax amounts
(rate label included), discounts that show as "-10%" on the line they apply to, totals
that visibly add up, and multi-page flow — long notes and terms flow onto numbered
continuation pages instead of being clipped. Every number matches the app to the cent,
because the renderer reads the same stored totals the app does.

One week of production bugs, fixed the day they were found

Real users on a fresh stack find things no test suite imagines. The honest list from
week one — each fixed and shipped the same day it was reported:

  • An invoice edit silently failing (a PUT route that was never registered — verbs that don't exist return bare 405s nobody sees)
  • The payments list 500ing on a column-case subtlety (Postgres folds unquoted Amount to amount)
  • A client dropdown that looked selected but never set the client — Create stayed mysteriously disabled
  • A tenant switcher crash from a list wrapper drifting from the old API's shape
  • Draft tax jurisdictions not persisting, and the PDF reading like a receipt from 1997

This is what the rewrite bought: a backend small enough to understand end-to-end, so
every one of these was a same-day fix rather than a sprint. The full-Rust stack now runs
both the API and every scheduled job (recurring invoices, reminders, lead radar) from two
small container images.

What's next

More of the same trajectory: making the tax engine explain itself everywhere it
computes, more client-facing surfaces carrying your brand, and growing the AI-assistant
surface — the MCP server is on the
official registry, and it shares this exact REST core, so everything in this post is
already available to your AI assistant.

Try it on a real workspace: FoxyInvoice is free to start — create one at foxyinvoice.com/login and redeem founding code U8B4Z8S87X on the Upgrade page for 6 months of Pro, free, no card.

title: Blank Chat Is the Wrong Default for Most Work AI
description:
Open your product's "AI" feature. Odds are you're staring at a blank message box and a blinking cursor.

That empty chat looks modern. It ships in a week. It demos well. And for a huge slice of real work, it's the wrong interface.

If you can name the inputs a user needs to give you, ship buttons, forms, and structured actions — not a message box. Chat wins for open-ended, long-tail work. Structured UI wins for bounded, repeatable, consequential jobs. Most teams pick chat by default and only discover the cost later.

Why teams default to chat

Three forces push almost every AI feature toward a chat pane:

It's fast to ship. A text box, a model call, and a stream of tokens looks like a product. Forms need schema design, validation, empty states, and edge cases. Chat lets you skip that and call it "AI-native."

It looks like AI. Users have been trained by ChatGPT. A blank conversation feels like "real" AI; a form with an Approve button feels like the old product with a model bolted on. So product teams optimize for the aesthetic of intelligence instead of the job to be done.

It hides product decisions. When you don't know the workflow yet, chat is a convenient fog. "Just let the user ask" becomes a substitute for deciding what the product actually does. That fog is useful in a prototype. It is expensive in production.

Fine for exploration. Wrong as a permanent default for work that already has a shape.

Where chat quietly fails

Chat is not free. The failure modes show up after the demo:

Interrogation UX. The user knows what they want — "refund this order," "approve this invoice," "draft a reply to this ticket" — but the product makes them re-explain it in prose every time. You've turned a one-click job into a conversation. That is not helpfulness; that is friction wearing a friendly coat.

Quiet commits. When the model proposes an action inside a paragraph of chat, it's easy for irreversible things to slip through: a send, a delete, a price change, a ticket close. There is no clear "here is the thing about to happen; confirm or edit." That blurs the boundary between suggestion and action.

Hard to eval and hard to govern. Free-form dialogue is a combinatorial nightmare. Every session takes a different path. You can't easily say "for this job, does the product succeed?" the way you can for a form with known fields and a known outcome. Permissions, audit logs, and rollback also get messier when the "API" is whatever the user typed last Tuesday.

Context tax. The user re-pastes the same ticket ID, the same policy snippet, the same constraints. Structured UI can pre-fill and constrain those. Chat makes the user the integration layer.

If your feature is a bounded job people repeat weekly, these costs compound. Chat is paying interest on a loan you didn't need.

When chat wins

Chat is the right surface when the work is genuinely open-ended:

  • The user cannot name the inputs up front ("help me think through this architecture")
  • The path is exploratory and changes mid-flight (research, brainstorming, debugging weird failures)
  • The long tail of requests is larger than any form you could design in a quarter
  • The output is mostly text the human will edit, not a system action with side effects

In those cases, a blank box is honest. The user is steering; the model is a collaborator. Don't fake structure where there isn't any.

When structured UI wins

Prefer forms, buttons, wizards, and review cards when:

  • You can list the inputs on a whiteboard
  • The same job runs dozens or hundreds of times a week
  • The action has side effects (money, email, deletes, external APIs, customer-visible state)
  • You need evals, audit trails, or human approval before commit
  • Latency and cost matter, and you don't want three clarification turns before every action

This is most of "work AI": support tooling, ops consoles, CRM assistants, finance workflows, content publishing pipelines, internal admin. The job is known. The inputs are known. The dangerous part is the commit, not the brainstorm.

Others have been pointing at the same split: when an agent shouldn't be a chat, chat vs forms vs inline patterns, and when to force the LLM vs when to use a button. The pattern is consistent across product and agent UX: conversation for ambiguity, structure for consequence.

The hybrid that actually works

The useful hybrid:

  1. Chat (or a short prompt) for intent — "refund the duplicate charge on order 1842"
  2. Model proposes a structured plan — typed fields: order id, amount, reason code, customer-visible note
  3. Review card with buttons — Edit / Approve / Reject, with the exact action visible before anything runs
  4. System executes — only after confirmation, through a normal API with logging

That is the AI Action Review idea in practice: the model drafts; the UI owns the commit. Frameworks like Agentic UX push the same principle — agents propose, interfaces constrain, humans (or explicit policies) authorize.

Chat is the on-ramp for messy language; structured UI is the guardrail for irreversible work.

A practical checklist for builders

Before you ship another blank chat as the home screen, ask:

  1. Can I name the inputs? If yes, start with a form or pre-filled card, not an empty composer.
  2. Is this job repeatable? If the same flow happens weekly, optimize for speed of the known path, not novelty of a new conversation.
  3. Does the action have side effects? If yes, never bury the commit inside a chat bubble. Show a review card with exact fields and an explicit Approve.
  4. How will I eval success? Prefer outcomes you can score (correct fields filled, action taken or not) over "the conversation felt good."
  5. What does recovery look like? Undo, audit log, and who can override — design those into the structured path, not as an afterthought in chat history.
  6. Where does chat still help? Keep a conversation entry for the long-tail and for "I don't know how to start," then route into structured review as soon as intent is clear.

The takeaway

Blank chat is a great prototype and a mediocre default.

Use chat when the work is open-ended and the long tail is the product. Use structured UI when the work is bounded, repeatable, and consequential. Use both when language is the best way in, but buttons and review cards are the only safe way out.

If you can name the inputs, stop making your users type them into a void.

References

  • Wizard or conversation: when an agent shouldn't be a chat
  • Chat vs Forms vs Inline — AI interaction patterns
  • When to Force the LLM, and When to Use a Button
  • Agentic UX framework
  • AI Action Review Pattern

Where in your product is a blank chat still standing in for a form you already know how to design?
