title: An Idiot's Guide to Spark Connect Clients
description:
Spark Connect is a new concept for many of us, especially given the long history of how managing Spark clusters has traditionally worked. Spark Connect in a nutshell separates your application from Spark: your code becomes a small client, Spark runs as a server somewhere else, and the two talk over the network. The primary benefit of Connect for most users is getting rid of the headaches around SparkContext, installing a package from your notebook, your Python version not mattering, or a typo failing on the line you typed it, which Connect very kindly obfuscates for us. Honestly, it's a pretty overdue upgrade for Spark as an engine and a pretty intuitive direction: decouple client sessions from the server, and make the server and its configuration as dead easy as possible for your customers.

The mindset shift away from having your PySpark setup share the same process as your Spark driver is not a super hard jump, but it does mean there are some adjustments to make in how you set things like configurations or write jobs. This becomes even more intense once you get into the meat of Spark Connect, which is the language agnosticism and running multiple clients and servers, particularly for those of us dabbling in Rust or Go.

So this guide, written for idiots by an idiot, starts with a tour of how Spark itself works and how that changes with a Connect setup. From there it's practical: how to run a server, how to connect to it from Python and other languages, what changes in your code, and how to do some basic debugging. Note that after the inclusion of session tracing in 4.3, and hopefully an eventual Spark Connect Gateway, the latter will be much, much easier.

Every example comes from spark-demos, where each one is a runnable script, and I ran every snippet here against Spark 4.2.0, the current release.

How Spark works

Spark lets you write code as if you were working with one table on one machine, and then runs it across however many machines you have; Connect's whole trick is moving part of the machinery that makes that possible somewhere else, so it's worth having a picture of that machinery first. A running Spark application has a few kinds of pieces:

  • The driver is the brain. It holds your SparkSession, works out what your code actually means, decides how to run it, and coordinates everything else. Inside it:
    • the analyzer, which resolves the tables and columns you named, using the catalog (the registry of what tables exist and what's in them);
    • the Catalyst optimizer, which rewrites your query into a cheaper equivalent (skipping columns you never use, filtering before joining, and so on);
    • the planner, which turns the optimized query into physical operations;
    • the schedulers, which cut that physical plan into stages (at every point where data has to be reshuffled between machines) and each stage into tasks, one per slice (partition) of the data.
  • The cluster manager hands out machines: Spark's own standalone master, YARN, or Kubernetes.
  • Workers are the machines (or containers) the cluster manager gives you.
  • Executors are the processes on those workers that actually run tasks, read and write data, hold cached data, and exchange data with each other during a shuffle.

Following one line of code through all of that:

orders.filter(orders.total > 20).groupBy("region").count().show()
Step What happens Where
1 Your code describes the query: filter, group, count your program
2 That becomes an unresolved logical plan: a tree of operations naming tables and columns that haven't been checked yet the driver
3 The analyzer checks orders, total and region against the catalog and fills in types the driver
4 Catalyst optimizes the plan (here it reads only the two columns it needs) the driver
5 The planner picks physical operators and generates code for them the driver
6 The schedulers split the work into stages (before and after the shuffle groupBy needs) and tasks the driver
7 Executors run the tasks against their slices of the data the executors
8 The counts come back to the driver, and on to you the driver, then your program

Nothing actually runs until step 8 is needed; until you call something that wants a result (show(), count(), writing a table), Spark is only building the plan, which is what people mean by lazy evaluation. Classic Spark does run step 3 straight away (it checks your names the moment you define a DataFrame), and that small difference ends up mattering a lot once Connect is involved, so keep it in your back pocket for the debugging section.

The detail that matters most for this guide is where the driver runs. In classic PySpark (in the default "client" mode) the driver runs inside your program: your Python process starts a Java virtual machine next to it and talks to it through a bridge called Py4J, and that JVM is the driver, with the analyzer, the catalog connection, Catalyst and the schedulers all living in it.

Your code and Spark's brain share a process, a machine, a set of installed libraries, and a fate, such that if one of them crashes it takes the other down with it.

What the shared driver costs you

Sharing a process is fine when it's one person on one laptop, and it causes a surprising number of problems as soon as more than one person (or more than one program) uses the same Spark:

  • You need Java and all of Spark on every machine that runs your code, including your laptop, a CI runner, or a web service that just wants to run one query.
  • Your application and Spark are upgraded together. Upgrading Spark means changing the environment every job runs in, whether the job was ready or not.
  • Everyone's code shares the driver. One badly behaved notebook can take the driver down for everyone attached to it.
  • Only JVM languages and Python can talk to Spark, because they're the ones that can live inside or next to the JVM.
  • Credentials go everywhere the driver goes, so catalog passwords and storage keys end up on every machine that runs a job.

Spark Connect fixes all of these with one change, which is that it splits the driver in two. The part you write against, the DataFrame API, stays in your program; everything that thinks (the session, the analyzer, the catalog, Catalyst, the schedulers) moves into a long-running Spark Connect server, with a network connection in between. Your program builds step 2, the unresolved plan, as a small protobuf message, sends it over gRPC and gets results back as Arrow, and steps 3 to 8 all happen on the server.

Piece by piece, this is what moves and what stays put:

Piece Classic PySpark Spark Connect
Your code and the DataFrame API your process your process (the client)
Building the unresolved plan the driver JVM, via Py4J the client, as a protobuf message
SparkSession and its state (temp views, settings, artifacts) the driver, in your process the server
Analyzer and catalog connection the driver, in your process the server
Catalyst, physical planning, code generation the driver, in your process the server
Stage and task scheduling the driver, in your process the server
Cluster manager, workers, executors the cluster the cluster, unchanged
Results Py4J and a local socket into your process Arrow batches over gRPC
Catalog and storage credentials wherever the driver runs the server only

The cluster itself doesn't change at all, and executors run tasks exactly as they did before. What changes is that your program no longer contains a driver, so it doesn't need Java, it can be written in any language that speaks gRPC and Arrow, and it can be upgraded on its own schedule rather than the server's. Connect first appeared in Spark 3.4, and since 4.0 the server has shipped in the standard Spark download.

Pretty much every confusing thing about Connect is this split showing up somewhere you didn't expect it. explain() shows you a plan your laptop didn't make, because Catalyst is on the server; a typo in a column name fails late, because the analyzer is on the server and only sees your plan once you ask for a result; sparkContext is gone, because it belonged to the driver. Anything that used to live in your program (the JVM, your files, your Python version, your credentials) now lives on the other side of a network connection, and most of the rest of this guide is working through the consequences of that.

Connecting from Python

From Python it's two steps: install the thin client (pyspark-client),

pip install pyspark-client

and create your session with .remote(...) instead of .master(...):

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
print(spark.version)            # the *server's* Spark version

orders = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("metro", "pizza", 24.0), ("metro", "sushi", 40.0), ("urban", "pizza", 18.0)],
    "region string, item string, total double",
)
orders.groupBy("region").agg(F.round(F.avg("total"), 2).alias("avg_ticket")).show()

Everything after the session line is ordinary PySpark, the same code you'd run in classic mode. Your program builds the plan and the server optimizes and runs it, so if you call .explain() you're reading the server's plan (your laptop doesn't have an optimizer anymore).

Before and after: setting up a session

A real classic session usually does a lot more than pick a master; it pulls in packages, sets SQL extensions, turns on Hive support and quiets the logs. A typical one looks something like this:

# Before: Spark Classic. Everything is configured by the program that runs the driver.
spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .master("spark://my-cluster:7077")
    .config("spark.jars.packages", "org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")
    .enableHiveSupport()
    .getOrCreate()
)
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")

Under Connect that one block splits in two, because some of those settings describe the driver, and the driver isn't yours anymore. Anything the server reads once when it starts (packages and JARs, spark.sql.extensions, catalog implementations, Hive support) moves to the command that starts the server:

# After, part 1: the server owns its JVM, so it gets the packages and static settings.
./sbin/start-connect-server.sh \
  --master spark://my-cluster:7077 \
  --packages org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0

and the client keeps only what can change per session:

# After, part 2: the client names the server and sets runtime options.
spark = (
    SparkSession.builder
    .remote("sc://localhost:15002")
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "64")   # runtime settings still work from the client
    .getOrCreate()
)

The log level moves to the server as well (its conf/log4j2.properties), since the logs are the server's now. The sneaky part is that Connect doesn't stop you from setting a startup-only setting from the client; it warns and carries on without it. Asking for a package from the client gets you this, and no package:

UserWarning: Failed to set spark.jars.packages to Some(org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0)
due to [CANNOT_MODIFY_CONFIG] Cannot modify the value of the Spark config ...

enableHiveSupport() does the same thing (with CANNOT_MODIFY_STATIC_CONFIG) and hands you a session without Hive, which you might not notice until a table you expected isn't there. The rule of thumb I've landed on is that if a setting describes how the server starts, it belongs wherever the server starts.

You can also leave the URL out of your code entirely by setting SPARK_REMOTE, and a plain SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate() will connect to it:

export SPARK_REMOTE="sc://localhost:15002"

Before and after: the rest of your code

Most DataFrame code doesn't change at all. What does change is anything that reached into the driver, and accumulators are a good example:

# Before: an accumulator, counted on the executors and read on the driver
bad_rows = spark.sparkContext.accumulator(0)
orders.foreach(lambda row: bad_rows.add(1) if row.total is None else None)
print(bad_rows.value)

# After: an Observation, collected alongside a query you were running anyway
from pyspark.sql import Observation

obs = Observation("quality")
checked = orders.observe(obs, F.count(F.when(F.col("total").isNull(), 1)).alias("bad_rows"))
checked.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("orders_checked")
print(obs.get["bad_rows"])

I'd argue the Observation is the better pattern anyway, since the metric rides along with a write you were already doing instead of needing its own pass over the data. The rest of the common swaps, side by side:

Before (Classic) After (Connect)
spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN") set the level in the server's conf/log4j2.properties
df.rdd.zipWithIndex() df.zipWithIndex() (4.2+)
spark.read.json(rdd_of_strings) spark.read.json(df) on a string column (4.2+)
sc.accumulator(0) df.observe(Observation(...), ...)
sc.addPyFile("lib/geo.py") spark.addArtifact("lib/geo.py", pyfile=True)
sc.broadcast(lookup) a broadcast join, F.broadcast(lookup_df), or a literal column
spark.newSession() SparkSession.builder.remote(url).create()
spark-submit job.py python job.py with SPARK_REMOTE set

All of that assumes there's a server sitting at localhost:15002, which brings us to running one.

Running a Connect server

There are three ways to get one, roughly in order of effort.

1. Inside your own Python process, for trying things out. Full PySpark can start a Connect server in-process:

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("local[*]").getOrCreate()

This needs full pyspark (not pyspark-client) and Java installed, because the server still has to run somewhere; it's the Connect code path without a separate server, which makes it great for tests and for learning.

2. From a Spark download, on your machine or a server. Download Spark from spark.apache.org (you'll need Java 17 or newer) and start the server that ships with it:

./sbin/start-connect-server.sh        # listens on port 15002
./sbin/stop-connect-server.sh         # when you're done

By default it runs Spark locally on that one machine; to have it run jobs on a cluster instead, point it at the cluster's master:

./sbin/start-connect-server.sh --master spark://my-cluster:7077

One thing that surprised me is that by default the server listens on every network interface, so anything that can reach your machine can reach the server the moment it starts. On a laptop on shared Wi-Fi, restrict it with --conf spark.connect.grpc.binding.address=127.0.0.1. (You'll see spark.connect.grpc.binding.host in plenty of examples, including some of mine; it isn't a real setting, and Spark silently ignores it.)

3. In Docker. The official apache/spark image includes Spark, Java and Python; add PyArrow and pandas on top, since Python UDFs use Arrow by default as of Spark 4.2:

FROM apache/spark:4.2.0-scala2.13-java21-python3-ubuntu
USER root
RUN python3 -m pip install --no-cache-dir pyarrow pandas
USER spark

Then start the server with --wait, which keeps it in the foreground (what a container needs):

services:
  spark-connect:
    build: .
    entrypoint:
      - /opt/spark/sbin/start-connect-server.sh
      - --wait
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:15002:15002"   # Spark Connect
      - "127.0.0.1:4040:4040"     # Spark UI

The image's Python is 3.10, which matters for your client (more on that below).

For production, Connect servers also run on Kubernetes (the Apache Spark Kubernetes Operator deploys one as an ordinary Spark application) and, since Spark 4.2, inside YARN. The repo's topology guide walks through six ways to deploy one and when each makes sense.

Before you share a server with other people, know that a single server holds many sessions, each isolated from the others but all sharing the server's memory and executors; if people need stronger isolation than that, they need separate servers.

Running a job

There's no separate "submit" step for a Connect job, because your program is the job, and running it sends the work:

export SPARK_REMOTE="sc://localhost:15002"
python my_pipeline.py

(SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate() picks up SPARK_REMOTE from the environment, so the same script runs against whichever server the variable names.) A few other routes are worth knowing about.

An existing job, almost unchanged. spark.api.mode switches a classic job to Connect: Spark starts a Connect server for the job and runs your code as its client. Set it in the session builder and keep your existing master:

spark = (SparkSession.builder
         .master("spark://my-cluster:7077")
         .config("spark.api.mode", "connect")
         .getOrCreate())

This is the gentlest way to try Connect on real work, since you can move one job, watch it, and move it back if something breaks. The documentation also shows passing it to spark-submit as --conf spark.api.mode=connect; on 4.2.0 that failed for me with TypeError: 'JavaPackage' object is not callable while the builder setting worked, so for now, set it in code.

A declarative pipeline. Tell the spark-pipelines CLI which server to use with --remote:

spark-pipelines run --spec spark-pipeline.yml --remote sc://localhost:15002

Don't rely on SPARK_REMOTE here; the CLI ignores it and quietly starts a local server of its own. The spark-pipelines command comes with full PySpark, and with only the thin client it's the other way round: run python -m pyspark.pipelines.cli run --spec spark-pipeline.yml, which has no --remote option and connects to whatever SPARK_REMOTE names.

Code your job depends on. If your functions import your own modules, the server doesn't have them, so ship them with the session using addArtifact:

spark.addArtifact("lib/geo.py", pyfile=True)        # importable by your UDFs
spark.addArtifact("model.tar.gz", archive=True)     # unpacked on the executors
spark.addArtifact("lookup.csv", file=True)          # copied as is

JARs for catalogs and extensions are the exception; those have to be installed on the server.

What you need locally

Much less than before, which is kind of the point:

You need Why
Python, the same minor version as the server's Python functions you send run in the server's Python. The 4.2 client needs Python 3.10 or newer
pyspark-client The thin client
Its dependencies: pyarrow, pandas, numpy, grpcio They come with it; this is most of the install
No Java, no Spark download, no SPARK_HOME That all lives on the server

The thing actually worth getting right is which package you install, because there are four with nearly identical names:

Package What you actually get Java needed locally?
pyspark Full PySpark: about 470 MB, most of it some 280 JAR files yes
pyspark[connect] Full PySpark plus the Connect extras yes
pyspark-connect A tiny package that installs full pyspark (and makes Connect its default) yes
pyspark-client The thin client: about 15 MB, no JARs no

pyspark-connect sounds like the Connect client and isn't; the thin client is pyspark-client. Don't judge by the size of your environment either: with its dependencies a pyspark-client environment is about 330 MB against about 780 MB for pyspark[connect], because pyarrow, pandas and numpy are most of it, so what the thin client really saves you is Java, not disk space. To check which one you actually have:

import importlib.util, pathlib, pyspark

print((pathlib.Path(pyspark.__file__).parent / "jars").exists())  # thin client: False
print(importlib.util.find_spec("py4j") is not None)               # thin client: False

If either prints True, you're on full PySpark. And if you have a full Spark installed elsewhere on the machine, clear SPARK_HOME and PYTHONPATH before you start, or they can quietly shadow the thin client.

Clients in other languages

Because the client only has to build a plan and read Arrow, it doesn't have to be Python, or even a JVM language, and the same server takes all of these:

Language Client Latest release
Python pyspark-client (in apache/spark) 4.2.0
Scala and Java spark-connect-client-jvm (in apache/spark) 4.2.0
Go apache/spark-connect-go v0.1.0
Swift apache/spark-connect-swift 0.7.0
Rust apache/spark-connect-rust 4.2.0
Anything with JDBC spark-connect-client-jdbc, URL jdbc:sc://host:15002 since 4.1

They all start the same way, with a connection string. In Scala:

val spark = SparkSession.builder().remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
spark.range(10).filter("id % 2 = 0").show()

In Go:

spark, err := sql.NewSessionBuilder().Remote("sc://localhost:15002").Build(ctx)
df, err := spark.Sql(ctx, "SELECT 'apple' AS word, 123 AS count")
df.Show(ctx, 100, false)

(At the time of writing, the Go client's only release, v0.1.0, can't be fetched with go get because of a module-path mismatch; go get github.com/apache/spark-connect-go@master works.)

Rust is where it gets fun for me, because results arrive as Arrow and can go straight into a native Rust tool. This program from the repo has Spark aggregate five million rows down to seven and then hands them to Polars for local work:

let spark = SparkSession::builder().remote("sc://localhost:15002").get_or_create()?;
let e = |c: Column| c.expression().clone();   // aggregate expressions, unwrapped

let summary = spark
    .range(5_000_000)?
    .with_column("bucket", col("id") % lit(7))
    .group_by([col("bucket")])
    .agg(vec![e(f::count(col("id")).alias("n"))]);

let batches = summary.collect_record_batches()?;   // Arrow RecordBatches, ready for Polars

That division of labour, with Spark doing the part that needs a cluster and your language of choice doing the rest, is the part of Connect I find most interesting. The clients aren't equally complete yet, though (the Python and JVM ones cover the most, the newer ones less), so check that the one you pick supports what you need before you build on it.

Debugging

Most Connect problems come from forgetting that there are now two sides, so when something goes wrong I work through these in roughly this order.

1. Am I talking to the server I think I am? Print spark.version first, every time, since nothing in sc://localhost:15002 says which Spark is supposed to answer. I learned this one the hard way: an old Spark 4.1 server was still sitting on port 15002 on my machine when I pointed newer tools at it, and it answered, misunderstood a request it had never heard of, and gave me an error convincing enough that I wrote it up as a Spark bug. (The full story is in Hosting an Entire Open Lakehouse on Port 8080.) Two related traps:

a = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://server-a:15002").getOrCreate()
b = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://server-b:15002").getOrCreate()
assert b is a    # getOrCreate() returned the existing session; use .create() for a new one

and connection strings that look fine but aren't; the part after the port has to be empty, and parameter values can't contain /:

sc://localhost:15002/;user_agent=myapp/setup
PySparkValueError: [INVALID_CONNECT_URL] ... The path component '/;user_agent=myapp/setup' must be empty.

2. Read the error's name. Connect errors carry an error class in square brackets, and a handful of them cover most of what you'll hit early on:

Error What it means What to do
JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED You used something that lived in the local JVM: spark.sparkContext (and so everything reached through it, like sparkContext.setLogLevel), _jvm, df.rdd Use the DataFrame replacement: df.zipWithIndex(), spark.read.json(df), df.observe(...) for counters, addArtifact for files
PYTHON_VERSION_MISMATCH Your Python and the server's differ (e.g. 3.12 vs 3.10) Match your Python minor version to the server's
ModuleNotFoundError inside a UDF The server's Python is missing a package your function needs Ship it with addArtifact, or install it on the server
UNSUPPORTED_LOCAL_CONNECTION_STRING You called .create() with local[*] Use .getOrCreate() for local
INVALID_CONNECT_URL The connection string is malformed Empty path, no / in parameter values

One that doesn't raise at all is enableHiveSupport(), which prints a warning and gives you a session without Hive, so read your warnings.

3. Errors arrive late. Classic Spark checks your DataFrame the moment you define it (that step 3 from earlier); Connect doesn't send anything to the server until it needs an answer, so a typo in a column name fails at the show() or write rather than on the line with the typo, and a try/except around the definition catches nothing. The same thing has two quieter consequences:

a.createOrReplaceTempView("brands")
first = spark.table("brands")
b.createOrReplaceTempView("brands")
first.count()     # Classic: rows of a    Connect: rows of b

A DataFrame built on a temp view reads whatever the view points to when it runs, and a Python function that reads a variable sees that variable's value when it runs, so give temp views unique names and pass values into functions explicitly.

4. Look at the server's side. The server has the Spark UI (port 4040 by default), where you can see the jobs your client triggered along with a Connect tab listing every client session and request, and it has its logs (in logs/ under the Spark directory, or docker logs for a container). df.explain() shows you the plan the server actually built.

5. Check your client isn't newer than your server. The supported direction is an older client talking to a newer server, and the other way round can fail in odd ways: a 4.2 client can't even build a DataFrame from a three-row Python list on a 4.1 server, because the 4.1 server reports a size limit as 3221225472b and the 4.2 client chokes on the b.

6. Let a script check for you. The repo includes a doctor that checks the client you installed, whether the server is reachable, its version, and whether Python functions actually run on it:

python tools/doctor.py --remote sc://localhost:15002 --expect-version 4.2

The whole guide, on one page

  • Spark splits big data work across many machines.
  • Spark Connect moves the driver out of your program; your code becomes a client that sends plans to a server.
  • Use it with pip install pyspark-client and SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://host:15002").
  • Get a server in-process with local[*], from a Spark download with start-connect-server.sh, or from the apache/spark Docker image (plus PyArrow).
  • Send a job by running your program; ship your own modules with addArtifact.
  • Locally you need Python matching the server's version and pyspark-client, and nothing else.
  • Other languages (Scala, Go, Rust, Swift, JDBC) use the same server and the same connection string.
  • When it breaks, check which server answered, read the error's name, remember errors arrive late, and look at the server's side.

Nearly all of it comes back to the one change at the start, which is that the driver moved out of your program; once you know which side of the network a thing lives on, most of Connect stops being surprising.

title: Microsoft Decision-1 now available on AI Gateway
description:
Decision-1 from Microsoft is now available on AI Gateway. It answers typed questions about text with probabilities, choices, and scores. It can be used to classify support requests, select the next step in a workflow, or assess an AI response against a rubric.

The model can answer yes/no questions, choose among named categories, or score an input against an ordered set of criteria. Multiple questions can share the same input in one request. Choice and score answers include probabilities for each option, so your application can decide when to act or send an uncertain result for review.

Call Decision-1 through the AI SDK decision API, the OpenAI-compatible Decisions API, or the TypeSafe-compatible API. You only need an AI Gateway API key, with no separate Azure account or deployment.

To get started, use microsoft/microsoft-decision-1 as the model name in your requests:

AI Gateway provides a unified way to access models and track usage and cost. Decision calls appear in logs and count toward budgets alongside other model requests.

See the decision documentation for Choice, Score, and Boolean questions. To pick a decision model, browse the available models or read our decision model guides.

title: Java Variables in GenAI Applications
description:
Introduction

Java variables are essential for storing and managing data in applications. In Generative AI (GenAI), variables can store user prompts, AI responses, and configuration values. They help Java applications communicate with AI models and process generated content.

What Are Java Variables?

A variable is a named storage location used to hold data in a Java program.

Syntax / Example 

String prompt = "Explain Generative AI";
String aiResponse = "GenAI generates new content.";

System.out.println(prompt);
System.out.println(aiResponse);

Practical Example

In a Java-powered AI chatbot, a prompt variable stores the user's question, while an aiResponse variable stores the response returned by the AI model.

Key Takeaways

  • Variables store data in Java applications.
  • String stores prompts and text responses.
  • int stores whole numbers, such as token counts.
  • Variables help manage AI inputs and outputs.
  • Meaningful variable names improve code readability.

Conclusion

Java variables provide a simple way to manage data in GenAI applications. They help developers handle prompts, AI responses, and other application values. Understanding variables is a useful first step toward building AI-powered Java applications.

How would you use Java variables in your own GenAI project?

Thanks for reading! 🚀

title: Inside GitHub's Distributed Engine: Spoke Clusters, Fork Alternates, and Keyless OIDC
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Introduction

GitHub is the world's largest code repository and collaboration platform, handling billions of lines of code, trillions of events, and thousands of API requests every second. Building a platform of that scale requires a fundamentally different architectural philosophy than a traditional monolithic git host. This deep dive explores the technical foundations that make GitHub reliable and fast: its geo-distributed Spoke architecture, its use of Git's alternates mechanism for efficient fork storage, and its Keyless OIDC workflow for securing continuous integration and deployment.

We will look at these topics from an engineering perspective, focusing on the concepts and trade-offs rather than internal specifics that GitHub has not publicly detailed. Understanding these systems will give you insight into how a globally distributed code platform balances consistency, performance, and security at scale.

Table of Contents

  • 1. The Spoke Model for Geo-Distribution
  • 2. Forks and git alternates
  • 3. Keyless OIDC and Workflow Security
  • 4. Design Patterns and Engineering Trade-offs
  • 5. Frequently Asked Questions

1. The Spoke Model for Geo-Distribution

GitHub hosts its services in multiple regions around the world so that developers can reach a low-latency endpoint close to their location. A naïve, single-region design simply cannot provide that global responsiveness. GitHub’s public documentation describes a “spoke” topology, where the central system is partitioned into regional units and each region provides its own user-facing surface (git webhooks, HTTPS git clone/push, and the REST/GraphQL APIs).

What a Spoke Does

A spoke is a self-contained regional deployment that can serve a subset of the global service. Each spoke:

  • Hosts an API gateway (REST/GraphQL) that handles user requests.
  • Runs Git-facing services so git push and git fetch can complete locally.
  • Receives and publishes webhook events to external systems.

Because most user interactions are read-centric and regional, routing them locally greatly improves perceived performance. The hub-and-spoke model allows each region to operate with a high degree of autonomy while still contributing to a coherent global system.

Data Consistency and Propagation

The hard problem is global consistency. GitHub’s platform must ensure that a user in Tokyo sees the same state as a user in São Paulo, even though they interact with different spokes. In practice, this requires:

  • Eventual consistency: Changes in one region are eventually visible to others. The system tolerates short windows where data is not yet globally synchronized.
  • Conflict resolution: Git’s object model is largely content-addressed (SHA-1/SHA-256 objects) and many state mutations are append-only (new commits, refs) which simplifies conflict handling. However, mutable state (e.g., a repository’s settings, branches, tags, or PR status) requires careful conflict detection.
  • Backpressure and queueing: High-traffic operations are throttled or queued when the system’s global state is under strain, which prevents one region from overwhelming others.

From an engineering standpoint, designing a hub-and-spoke system means choosing consistency guarantees per operation. A branch push might be globally strong, while updating a user profile might be eventually consistent. The system’s metadata layer must support both patterns and coordinate them with Git’s object store.

Operational Considerations

Geo-distribution adds operational complexity:

  • Deployment orchestration: Spokes must be deployable and updatable independently. This requires a strong release pipeline, health checks, and canary deployments.
  • Observability: Global metrics need to be correlated across regions to identify the source of latency or errors.
  • Failover: If a spoke degrades, the system should route affected traffic to another region while preserving user sessions and webhook events.

The result is a distributed system that prioritizes global reach and low latency, while accepting that some consistency is achieved asynchronously.

2. Forks and git alternates

Git’s alternates mechanism is a foundational part of how GitHub can offer billions of forks without duplicating every object. When a fork is created, Git can reuse the shared object store from the parent repository instead of copying the entire history. This approach dramatically reduces storage overhead and clone/push times for fork-heavy workflows.

What git alternates Does

In a Git repository, an .git/objects/info/alternates file can point to another directory of Git objects. During object lookup, Git first checks the local object directory, then any alternate locations. For a fork:

  • Shared objects (the bulk of the commit and tree history) are not re-stored.
  • The fork’s new commits and trees are stored locally.
  • Clone and packfile generation can be optimized to only send the deltas that are new to the fork.

This is especially powerful for large repositories with long histories, where the cost of duplicating every object for each fork would be prohibitive.

How Forking Scales

Consider a popular repository with millions of forks. A naïve fork model would duplicate the entire object store per fork, leading to massive storage costs and slow provisioning. With alternates, the shared base remains a single source, and forks only add their local deltas. This also affects network behavior:

  • Packing efficiency: Smart HTTP and the git protocol can send smaller packfiles when the client already has the parent repository’s objects.
  • GC and storage: The shared object store can be garbage-collected in a coordinated way, while fork-local objects are managed per repository.

The engineering trade-offs are subtle:

  • Coupling: A fork depends on the shared object store. If the parent store is modified or GC’d, the fork must remain intact. GitHub’s storage layer must coordinate GC safely across many repositories that may share objects.
  • Performance isolation: Heavy fork creation or pack operations must not starve other tenants. Isolated queues and resource quotas help keep the system responsive.
  • Security boundaries: Sharing objects across repositories raises security and integrity questions. The system must ensure that fork users can read the shared objects they are entitled to, but not leak data from the parent or other forks.

From an implementation standpoint, alternates are an example of a “reference” optimization that is cheap locally but requires global coordination in a multi-tenant system. The result is that GitHub can scale to enormous numbers of forks while keeping disk and network costs manageable.

3. Keyless OIDC and Workflow Security

GitHub’s Actions workflows often need to interact with external systems: cloud providers, secrets managers, and SaaS APIs. Traditional patterns store static long-lived credentials in environment variables or secrets. Keyless authentication (often implemented via OIDC, OpenID Connect) removes the need for static credentials by using short-lived, signed tokens that external systems can verify.

The OIDC Pattern

OIDC provides a standard way to issue and verify identity claims. In a keyless workflow:

  • GitHub issues a signed JWT (JSON Web Token) that asserts the caller’s identity and permissions.
  • The external service (e.g., a cloud provider) verifies the token using public keys.
  • The token encodes scopes (what the caller can do) and expiry (how long it lasts).

This model eliminates stored secrets, reducing attack surface and eliminating the risk of a leaked credential living on for years. Tokens are short-lived, scoped, and revocable, which aligns with zero-trust principles.

How It Changes CI/CD Security

Static secrets introduce several risks:

  • Leakage: Secrets can be inadvertently committed to logs, images, or repositories.
  • Long-lived access: A compromised credential can be abused until rotated.
  • Rotation overhead: Manual rotation is error-prone and slow at scale.

With keyless OIDC:

  • Short-lived tokens: Even if a token leaks, its useful lifetime is very short.
  • Scope minimization: Tokens can be restricted to exactly the operations needed for a given workflow step.
  • Auditability: Each token is cryptographically signed and can be logged and traced back to the workflow that issued it.

The engineering implication is that the identity infrastructure becomes a first-class citizen. You must design token issuance, verification, and revocation into your workflows and external integrations. The system must support claims that map to your organization’s permission model, and the external service must accept OIDC tokens with the appropriate audiences and issuers.

Practical Considerations

In practice, keyless OIDC workflows involve:

  • Token validation: The receiving service must verify the JWT’s signature, audience, and expiry. This usually requires fetching public keys (JWKS) from the issuer.
  • Scope mapping: The token’s claims must map cleanly to the external system’s permission model. Overly broad scopes undermine the zero-trust model.
  • Failover and revocation: If a token is compromised, the system needs a mechanism to invalidate it quickly. This may require a revocation list or short token lifetimes.

The outcome is a CI/CD environment that no longer depends on static secrets, reducing the attack surface and aligning with modern cloud-native security practices. This is a critical capability for large organizations running thousands of workflows daily.

4. Design Patterns and Engineering Trade-offs

GitHub’s distributed architecture is built on several recurring engineering patterns that you will see in many large-scale systems.

Event-Driven Architecture

Webhooks and internal event buses allow GitHub to decouple components. A git push, for example, can trigger webhooks without blocking the push operation. This decoupling improves resilience, but introduces challenges:

  • Ordering: Some events must be processed in a specific order to maintain state consistency.
  • At-least-once vs. exactly-once: Webhooks are at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.
  • Backpressure: If an event processor is slow, the system must queue or drop events carefully to avoid unbounded memory growth.

Multi-Region Data Partitioning

GitHub’s spoke model partitions data and operations by region. This is an example of a geo-distributed, eventually consistent design. The key trade-offs are:

  • Latency: Local reads and writes are fast; cross-region replication introduces delays.
  • Consistency: Strong consistency across regions is expensive and slow. The system chooses consistency windows per operation.
  • Fault isolation: Regional failures do not take down the whole system; other spokes continue to serve unaffected traffic.

Storage Optimization via Sharing

Git’s alternates mechanism is an example of reference-based storage. It reduces duplication but introduces coupling between repositories. The storage layer must coordinate garbage collection and integrity checks across shared objects, which is a complex multi-tenant problem.

Zero-Trust Identity

Keyless OIDC is a zero-trust pattern: every token is verified, scoped, and short-lived. This shifts security from static, long-lived credentials to dynamic, cryptographically verified tokens. The engineering cost is in token issuance, verification, and revocation infrastructure.

Observability and Feedback

Distributed systems require rich telemetry:

  • Tracing: End-to-end traces across spokes and services are critical for diagnosing latency and failures.
  • Metrics: Latency, error rates, and queue depths must be monitored per region and per service.
  • Logging: Structured, centralized logs help correlate events across the global system.

Without strong observability, a globally distributed system is nearly impossible to operate. Feedback loops and automated remediation are essential at this scale.

5. Frequently Asked Questions

How does GitHub ensure consistency across regions?

GitHub uses a geo-distributed architecture with eventually consistent data. Changes are replicated across spokes, and the system tolerates short windows of inconsistency. Conflict resolution is simplified by Git’s object model, where many state changes are append-only. Mutable state requires careful coordination and conflict detection.

Why use git alternates for forks?

Alternates let a fork reuse the parent repository’s objects instead of copying the entire history. This dramatically reduces storage and network costs for large, fork-heavy repositories. The trade-off is coupling between the fork and the shared object store, which requires coordinated garbage collection and integrity checks.

What is keyless OIDC, and why is it important for CI/CD?

Keyless OIDC uses short-lived, signed tokens instead of static secrets for external integrations. This reduces the attack surface, eliminates long-lived credentials, and supports zero-trust security. It is critical for secure, scalable CI/CD pipelines that interact with many external services.

title: Mastering AI in QA: How to Evaluate Prompts and Build Reliable Test Workflows
description:
Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming how software engineering teams design, execute, and maintain test automation. From auto-generating Selenium and Playwright scripts to analyzing dense CI/CD execution logs, AI-driven assistants significantly reduce routine manual effort.

However, integrating LLMs into Quality Assurance introduces non-determinism. Unlike traditional code, prompts can produce subtle variations, hallucinated assertions, or context drift across model updates. To build enterprise-grade QA workflows, teams need systematic evaluation frameworks and modern test management infrastructure.

The Non-Deterministic Challenge: Evaluating AI Output

When using AI to generate test scenarios or parse bug reports, standard binary assertions (pass/fail) fall short. A prompt that generates a perfect Cypress test case today might miss crucial edge-case validations tomorrow if the model's temperature or system context shifts.

Applying structured ai prompt testing methods is essential for validating context windows, benchmarking prompt accuracy against fixed datasets, and preventing hallucinations in AI-generated test artifacts.

Key techniques for prompt validation in QA include:

  • Counterfactual Prompt Testing: Swapping specific parameters (such as environment variables or user roles) within prompts to verify output consistency.
  • Temperature & Top-P Tuning: Calibrating randomness parameters to ensure test case generation remains deterministic and reproducible.
  • Regression Testing for Prompts: Running continuous evaluation suites whenever underlying foundation models or system prompts are updated.

By establishing rigorous ai prompt testing methods, engineering teams can transition AI from a risky playground experiment into a dependable QA asset.

Unifying AI and Automated Test Management

To maximize the ROI of AI in testing, generated test scripts and validation results must not remain isolated in chat windows. They need to seamlessly sync with your primary CI/CD pipelines and test management hubs.

1. Orchestrating Scenarios with AI Test Management

Modern QA environments demand full synchronization between manual test cases, automated frameworks, and AI outputs. Leveraging next-generation ai test management tools gives engineering leaders centralized visibility into test execution status, flaky test trends, and overall release readiness.

2. Autonomous Debugging with AI Agents

When nightly regression runs fail, engineers often spend hours parsing raw CLI reports and console logs. Deploying an autonomous ai agent for qa testing accelerates root-cause analysis by instantly grouping log stack traces, mapping failures to recent code commits, and suggesting precise code fixes.

3. Continuous Pipeline Triggers

Every automated script generated or optimized by AI must be validated directly within continuous integration pipelines. Triggering an automated feature test upon pull request creation guarantees that newly generated test logic doesn't introduce regressions into existing suites.

4. Technical Integration & Documentation

Connecting automated test frameworks (like Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO, or PyTest) to centralized analytics tools requires clean CLI configurations and SDK setups. Teams can explore the official docs testomat.io for step-by-step guides, reporter configurations, and environment setup instructions.

Best Practices for Scaling AI-Driven QA Engineering

  1. Keep Prompts Version-Controlled: Store system prompts, context rules, and template schemas in Git repositories alongside test automation code.
  2. Benchmark Prompt Updates: Before deploying new prompt iterations to your team, evaluate them using validated ai prompt testing methods to ensure output quality remains consistently high.
  3. Monitor Platform Releases: Stay updated with the latest AI integrations, framework reporters, and feature enhancements by regularly reviewing the changelog testomat.io.
  4. Follow Industry Testing Trends: To dive deeper into modern test architecture, shift-left strategies, and test automation patterns, bookmark our dedicated test automation blog.

Combining structured prompt validation with advanced AI test orchestration bridges the gap between fast software delivery and uncompromised software quality. Eliminate manual reporting overhead, streamline log analysis, and deliver reliable software faster.

title: Price first, time second: a limit order book in about 50 lines of Rust
description:
Last week I posted a quiz: three sell orders, one buy order, who gets filled first? Here is the answer, in Rust.

Most order books follow one rule: the better price goes first, and at the same price the earlier order goes first.

rust
use std::collections::{BTreeMap, VecDeque};

#[derive(Default)]
struct Book {
    // price -> queue of (id, size), oldest order at the front
    asks: BTreeMap<u64, VecDeque<(&'static str, u64)>>,
}

impl Book {
    fn sell(&mut self, id: &'static str, price: u64, size: u64) {
        self.asks.entry(price).or_default().push_back((id, size));
    }

    // buy `size` units, paying at most `limit`
    fn buy(&mut self, mut size: u64, limit: u64) {
        while size > 0 {
            let Some(mut level) = self.asks.first_entry() else { break };
            let price = *level.key();
            if price > limit { break; }
            let queue = level.get_mut();
            let (id, avail) = queue.front_mut().unwrap();
            let qty = size.min(*avail);
            println!("{id}: {qty} @ {price}");
            size -= qty;
            *avail -= qty;
            if *avail == 0 { queue.pop_front(); }
            if queue.is_empty() { level.remove(); }
        }
    }
}

The BTreeMap keeps prices sorted, so the best price is always first. Each price holds a VecDeque, so the oldest order is always first. There is no timestamp anywhere. The queue is the clock.


Now A, B and C sell, then someone buys 10 with a limit of 100.20:


fn main() {
    // prices are integer ticks: 10010 = 100.10
    let mut book = Book::default();
    book.sell("A", 10020, 5);
    book.sell("B", 10010, 3);
    book.sell("C", 10010, 4);
    book.buy(10, 10020);
}

B: 3 @ 10010
C: 4 @ 10010
A: 3 @ 10020

A arrived first and was filled last. B beat C because both were at 100.10 and B was earlier. And the buyer paid 100.10 on seven units even though the limit was 100.20.

This toy has no cancel, no sell side and no balance check. On Solana the book also has to fit into one account with a fixed compute budget, so the same rule has to work inside fixed slots.

I work on Privora, where the book stays public and the position behind an order stays private (devnet, test funds).

If you have put an order book onchain, which limit hit you first, account size or compute?

title: Accelerating Spatio-Temporal Attention for Video Diffusion on TPUs
description: To address the quadratic latency bottleneck of self-attention in high-resolution video diffusion models, developers implemented Sparse VideoGen (SVG) to dynamically route attention heads to highly structured spatial or temporal sparse masks. Translating this algorithmic sparsity into physical hardware speedups on TPUs required optimizing the Splash Attention kernel by bypassing empty memory tiles, restricting exact coordinate masking strictly to boundary tiles, and permuting token memory layouts into temporal-major order for contiguous access. By aligning these sparse masks with actual hardware tile execution, the combined optimizations significantly reduced wasted matrix operations and achieved up to a 1.69x end-to-end inference speedup for 1440p video generation.

title: Node.js Property Photo Contest: Normalise Every Submission and Record Versions
description:
Use one named, immutable background-removal transformation for every property-product photo in a judging round, write its version beside the result, and retain the original object for any winning image that may become a print file. The implementation can sit behind a Node.js submission service, but the durable rule is independent of its web framework: a result without a recorded transformation version is not eligible for judging.

TL;DR: normalize once on submission, store originals and derivatives under separate private keys, and make the judging cache key include the source digest plus transformation version. That makes entries comparable and makes a later transformation change an explicit migration instead of a silent change to the evidence. Vendor selection comes after this control, with storage duplication, cache invalidation, and export behavior carrying more weight than a polished dashboard.

This matters in a property-management workflow where suppliers submit product photos for a staged-unit furnishing contest and the system removes backgrounds before judges compare fixtures, lamps, or chairs. The page I would want at 3am is not “image processing is slow.” It is “round 42 contains two transform versions,” because that tells the responder what decision could be contaminated and what scope must be frozen.

How Should Node.js Normalise Every Photo Contest Submission?

The dangerous failure is a successful response with inconsistent semantics. If half the entries were processed with bg-remove-2026-10 and the other half with a later revision, every image may load, latency may look ordinary, and the judging set is still invalid. A dashboard full of green request counts will not catch that unless the application records and checks the version.

Success can lie.

Page on the invariant: one judging round must resolve to exactly one transformation name and version. Alert separately when a submission has an original but no derivative after the processing deadline. Those signals lead to different actions; the first freezes judging, while the second can usually be retried for one entry.

Do not overwrite source objects. For a submission such as entry-1842, retain an immutable original key and write the normalized result to a derivative key containing the version. The database row should record at least the entry identifier, round identifier, source object key, source digest, derivative object key, transformation name, transformation version, and processing state. This is deliberately boring. Boring survives handoffs.

Make the version a write-time invariant

The following Go worker calls the processing route and models the control that should sit behind the Node.js upload handler. The live discovery schema should produce request.json; this avoids copying fields that may not belong to the current capability. The worker rejects a second transform version in the same round, derives a stable private object key, makes retries converge on the same record, and backs off on HTTP 429. The same registry logic belongs in a transaction with a uniqueness constraint in production.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Record struct {
    EntryID         string
    RoundID         string
    SourceDigest    string
    TransformName   string
    TransformVersion string
    DerivativeKey   string
}

type Registry struct {
    roundVersion map[string]string
    entries      map[string]Record
}

func (r *Registry) Register(roundID, entryID, source string, body []byte, name, version string) (Record, error) {
    want := name + "@" + version
    if got, ok := r.roundVersion[roundID]; ok && got != want {
        return Record{}, fmt.Errorf("round %s is pinned to %s, rejected %s", roundID, got, want)
    }

    sum := sha256.Sum256(body)
    digest := hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
    idempotencyKey := roundID + ":" + entryID + ":" + digest + ":" + want
    if existing, ok := r.entries[idempotencyKey]; ok {
        return existing, nil
    }

    record := Record{
        EntryID: entryID, RoundID: roundID, SourceDigest: digest,
        TransformName: name, TransformVersion: version,
        DerivativeKey: fmt.Sprintf("private/judging/%s/%s/%s.png", roundID, version, digest),
    }
    r.roundVersion[roundID] = want
    r.entries[idempotencyKey] = record
    return record, nil
}

func process(requestBody []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/v1/image/process", bytes.NewReader(requestBody))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("image processing failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("image processing remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    requestBody, err := os.ReadFile("request.json")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    result, err := process(requestBody)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    r := Registry{map[string]string{}, map[string]Record{}}
    record, err := r.Register("round-42", "entry-1842", "private/originals/entry-1842.jpg", requestBody, "background-remove", "2026-10")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := os.WriteFile("response.json", result, 0600); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("%s %s@%s %s\n", record.EntryID, record.TransformName, record.TransformVersion, record.DerivativeKey)
}

The source argument is present to make the ownership boundary visible even though this compact example does not persist it. In the real record, keep that private source key; do not turn it into a public URL. Serve short-lived signed URLs to workers and judges, and never forward a service authorization header to a presigned storage URL. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented API origin, obtain the exact body for request.json from public discovery, and keep the key out of both files; the program writes the response with owner-only permissions so a copied example does not casually expose processing metadata.

One caveat matters: this compact worker hashes the request document to demonstrate convergence, while the production idempotency identity must include the actual source digest. Otherwise, replacing bytes behind a reused source reference could return the wrong derivative. Persist the source digest before dispatch, send a client idempotency key derived from round, entry, digest, and transform version, then enforce that same tuple in the database. This duplicates one small check across the HTTP and persistence boundaries on purpose; losing a little elegance is preferable to allowing a retry or concurrent worker to create ambiguous judging evidence.

For a plain REST option, Infrai is relevant because the processing service can be called by any HTTP-capable worker without installing or tracking a client SDK, and its broader API surface uses one key. Its verified media surface includes POST /v1/image/process and a named-transformation creation route. I would discover the live JSON Schema before integrating rather than inventing fields from route names, then pin the accepted schema alongside the application change. One route in the worker is enough; this article is not an endpoint catalog.

Compare the operational bill, not the demo

Background removal vendors are not interchangeable, but a property manager's decisive cost often arrives after inference: originals retained for print, normalized derivatives retained for judging, repeated downloads, and cache churn when a transform changes. Compare candidates using a fixed sample set and the same retention plan. Do not let a low per-call figure conceal a design that creates needless copies.

Option Integration shape Storage and cache question to resolve before selection Practical boundary
remove.bg Dedicated background-removal API Where will full-resolution originals and results live, and how are repeated results cached? Focused choice when background removal is the primary media operation.
Cloudinary Managed image and media pipeline Can derived assets and transformation identifiers fit the existing delivery cache policy? Strong fit when delivery transformations and asset management belong in one system.
imgix URL-driven image processing and delivery Will versioned source paths and URL parameters produce the required immutable cache identity? Useful when an existing source can remain authoritative and delivery-time rendering is acceptable.
ImageKit Image delivery and asset-management service Which derivatives are persisted, and how does cache invalidation map to a judging-round freeze? Candidate for teams combining media management with delivery optimization.
Uploadcare Upload, processing, and delivery platform Can the upload lifecycle preserve the private original while isolating each transform version? Fits workflows looking to combine ingestion and processing.
Cloudflare Images Managed image storage and delivery Does its variant model express the required immutable judging versions and private access boundary? Worth evaluating when image delivery already sits near Cloudflare infrastructure.
Adobe Photoshop API Photoshop-oriented cloud imaging API What intermediate assets are retained, and what export format is required for print? Worth evaluating when Photoshop-compatible operations matter beyond removal.
Photoroom Product-imagery API Does its result and export workflow match the catalog's original-retention policy? Natural candidate for product-photo workflows that need more than a single judging derivative.
Infrai Plain REST API spanning backend capabilities Will the application store results itself, and can one shared API surface reduce integration ownership? Fits teams that value an SDK-free HTTP boundary; verify the discovered schema before coding.

This is not a ranking.

Cloudinary may reduce the number of systems involved when it already owns delivery; remove.bg may keep a narrow worker conceptually narrow; imgix may fit teams whose source assets already live elsewhere; ImageKit, Uploadcare, and Cloudflare Images each deserve evaluation when ingestion or delivery is the larger problem; Adobe may suit a workflow whose downstream editors already depend on Photoshop semantics; Photoroom may align with a product-catalog team. Infrai's attraction is the plain REST boundary, not an assumption that it wins every image-quality or storage test.

Run the same representative images through each candidate and have judges inspect edges, transparent regions, and print suitability without seeing vendor labels. The supplied facts do not establish comparative image quality, latency, or savings, so no honest recommendation can manufacture those measurements. Record raw responses, formats, and object sizes from your own evaluation. Numbers first. Branding later.

Keep cache invalidation explicit

A judging URL should never mean “latest.” Use a cache identity derived from the source digest and transformation version, as the example does, so changing 2026-10 to a new version creates a new derivative rather than mutating the old one under an apparently stable key. The old judging round remains reproducible, and the new output can be evaluated before anyone switches a reference.

There is a clear storage trade-off: immutable versioned derivatives consume more space than overwriting one object. Accept it for active rounds and winners because auditability and print recovery are part of the job. For non-winning derivatives, define a lifecycle only after the appeal and judging windows close; retain winners' originals for their print files. Exact retention durations are policy decisions, not facts an API can choose for you.

Keep the originals.

Cache only the derivative. The original stays private and is fetched by a processing worker through a short-lived signed URL. A transformation-version change should invalidate by namespace, not by a fleet-wide purge, which keeps an editorial adjustment from turning into an avoidable delivery incident.

Verify, freeze, and roll back

Before opening a round to judges, query the application records and prove three things: every accepted entry has one successful derivative, the count of distinct transformation versions is exactly one, and every derivative points back to a retained source digest. Sample the rendered assets as well. Database consistency cannot tell you that a transparent chair leg disappeared.

The release gate should process a canary set before a new version becomes eligible for a future round. Compare output dimensions, file type, object size, and human-reviewed edge quality against the prior version, while remembering that image formats have different transparency and browser-support characteristics. MDN's image format guide is a useful baseline for that last choice.

Rollback means repointing an unopened round to its previous pinned version and reprocessing from originals into the previous version namespace. Do not overwrite the questionable results; quarantine them for diagnosis. If judging has already begun, freeze the round, identify which page fired and which entries were exposed, then resume only after all eligible entries reference the same approved version.

That rule is stricter than “retry the failed jobs,” because HTTP success was never the real contract. Comparable judging was.

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • remove.bg API documentation
  • Cloudinary image transformations
  • imgix image rendering API
  • ImageKit image transformations
  • Uploadcare image transformations
  • Cloudflare Images documentation
  • Adobe Photoshop API documentation
  • Photoroom API documentation
  • Amazon S3 presigned URL documentation
