title: Manual Regression Testing Checklist for Continuous Delivery
description:
• When to Run Manual Regression in a Continuous Delivery Pipeline
  • Surgical Checklist: Essential Manual Regression Items and Sample Test Sets
  • Prioritize Like a Surgeon: Risk-Based Test Selection and Test Prioritization
  • Embed, Not Isolate: Integrating Manual Checks with Automation and Releases
  • Practical Protocol: Step-by-Step Manual Regression for Each Release

Manual regression is the last human gate before customers feel your changes: run it strategically, not ritualistically, and treat each manual run as an evidence-gathering operation that either confirms automation or exposes its blind spots. In continuous delivery you keep the product releasable by default, which means manual regression must be short, focused, and driven by risk and confidence signals rather than an attempt to “retest everything.”

You see the symptoms every sprint: frequent releases that occasionally produce customer-facing regressions, a bloated manual regression suite that takes days, flaky automated checks that erode trust, and a release checklist that reads like an all-you-can-test buffet. That friction produces late-night rollbacks, delayed releases, and a gradual shrinking of manual testing to either unfocused exploration or last-minute panic. A practical manual regression approach for continuous delivery balances three truths: automation handles predictable repetition, humans cover ambiguity and UX judgment, and risk determines what matters now.

When to Run Manual Regression in a Continuous Delivery Pipeline

Run manual regression only where it buys you confidence you cannot get faster or cheaper another way.

  • Keep the pipeline principle in mind: continuous delivery aims to keep software in a releasable state at all times; your manual checks are a selective, tactical safety net, not the main engine of quality.
  • Run manual regression when the change is high risk: payments, billing, authentication, privacy controls, regulatory logic, or anything that would cause downtime, data loss, or immediate customer harm if it fails.
  • Run manual checks when automation coverage is missing or ambiguous: visual design regressions, user experience flows, accessibility, complex integration behaviour with third-party providers, or when the test oracle needs human judgement. The value of exploratory/manual testing for discovering subtle or contextual defects is well established.
  • Use manual regression as a stop‑gate after CI and automated acceptance tests pass but before a production release for:
    • Hotfixes where time-to-verify is small but the scope affects critical flows.
    • Large merges or cross-cutting infra changes (shared libraries, DB migrations).
    • When automated suites are flaky: reproduce the failure manually to determine real impact.
  • Use smoke and sanity tests as entry checks: a quick BVT/smoke run then a focused sanity run on changed areas saves you from wasting time on a broken build. Smoke is wide-and-shallow; sanity is narrow-and-deep — use them deliberately.

Important: Manual regression is a decision, not a ritual. Make the call based on change risk and pipeline signals, and document the rationale in the release ticket.

Surgical Checklist: Essential Manual Regression Items and Sample Test Sets

A pragmatic regression testing checklist that fits CD must be compact, repeatable, and traceable. Below is a surgical checklist you can copy into Confluence, TestRail, or a Jira release ticket.

  • Pre-checks (do before any manual test begins)
    • Environment: staging mirrors prod configuration, third‑party sandboxes valid, feature flags set.
    • Data: representative test data present, data reset script ready, backup snapshots available.
    • Observability: deployment monitors, logs, Sentry/Datadog alerts wired to on-call.
    • Acceptance criteria: release notes list expected behaviour and non-goals.
  • Entry smoke (10–30 minutes)
    • Key journey launches: login, primary landing flow, critical button clicks.
    • Basic integrations: payment gateway handshake, email send queue.
    • Health checks: API responses for top endpoints, DB connection.
  • Targeted sanity (15–90 minutes; focused by change)
    • Verify first-order fixes for bug tickets in the release.
    • Verify obvious side-effect areas (cascades from changed module).
  • Core manual regression (time-boxed; based on priority)
    • Top 3–5 customer journeys end-to-end (happy and common error paths).
    • Role-based access checks for at least two roles (admin, customer).
    • Data integrity checks: create/read/update/delete on critical objects.
    • Cross-browser quick checks (desktop Chrome/Firefox, mobile Chrome/Safari).
    • Accessibility spot checks: keyboard navigation, alt-text on new UI elements.
    • Security smoke (auth flows, rate-limiting): use OWASP cheat sheet to prioritize common classes.
  • Post-checks
    • Record evidence (screenshots, short video, request/response snippets, logs).
    • Log issues with Steps to reproduce, Env, Build tag, Screenshots.
    • Update automated backlog: convert repeatedly-run manual checks into automation candidates.

Sample test sets (compact):

  • Small hotfix (30–60 min)

    • Entry smoke + sanity for the fix + 1 critical journey + evidence capture.

  • Regular sprint release (2–4 hours)

    • Entry smoke + targeted sanity on changed modules + 3 core journeys + quick security & accessibility spot checks.

  • Major release (1–2 days)

    • Entry smoke + full targeted sanity + expanded regression of revenue and compliance flows + exploratory sessions (session-based testing) and risk reviews.

Table: Typical manual vs automation decision drivers

Category Automate if… Test manually if…
Repetition / frequency It runs on every build / daily (ROI positive) One-off or rare checks
Determinism Deterministic and oracle is clear Requires human judgement or UX validation
Time budget Fast to execute programmatically Execution is short but needs observation
Flakiness Low flakiness in CI Flaky in CI; needs human triage
Visibility Outputs machine-checkable artifacts Requires visual inspection (layout, copy-tone)

Use tags in your test management tool like smoke, sanity, manual_regression, automatable to track coverage and handoffs between manual and automation.

Prioritize Like a Surgeon: Risk-Based Test Selection and Test Prioritization

You cannot run everything; adopt a risk-based regression mindset and a reproducible scoring method.

  1. Build a compact risk model (columns you can rate 1–5):

    • Business impact (revenue, legal, reputation).
    • User frequency (how often customers hit this flow).
    • Change surface (lines of code / modules touched).
    • Historical defect rate (past defects in area).
    • Test automation coverage (percent automated).

  2. Score each candidate test case and compute a weighted risk score. Example weights you can start with: Business impact 35%, Change surface 25%, Historical defects 20%, User frequency 10%, Automation coverage −10% (penalize if automated). Convert to priority bands: Critical, High, Medium, Low.

  3. Use change-driven selection: run all Critical and High for pre-release manual regression; schedule Medium for targeted exploratory or automated runs overnight.

Small illustrative priority table

Test case Biz impact Chg surface History Auto cov Score Priority
Checkout payment 5 4 4 1 4.2 Critical
Profile update 3 2 2 3 2.5 Medium
Admin report export 4 3 3 0 3.4 High

Why this works: academic and industry research shows risk-based strategies locate critical defects earlier and reduce wasted cycles compared with naive coverage strategies.

Operational rules to enforce prioritization

  • Always include at least one end-to-end path that touches the data model and downstream systems for any release touching business logic.
  • Time-box manual regression sessions: make the scope explicit (Hotfix: 30m, Sprint: 2h, Major: 8–16h) and stick to it.
  • Convert failing manual tests into automation tickets or add them to the flaky-test triage board. Use conversion as a metric: manual->automated rate.

Embed, Not Isolate: Integrating Manual Checks with Automation and Releases

Manual checks succeed when they are visible, scheduled, and tied to the pipeline — not when they’re an afterthought.

  • Treat manual regression as a formal release gate recorded on the release ticket (release/2025.12.18): entry smoke passed, targeted sanity passed, sign-off with timestamps and evidence. Link the manual execution records back to CI run id, build tag, and monitoring run ids. This practice aligns with release notes and makes the process auditable.
  • Orchestrate your test suites: use smoke as the earliest automated gate in CI, sanity for targeted manual confirmation, and a regression tag for any larger test pack that runs in scheduled automation (nightly). Use test orchestration tools or your CI job matrix to run the correct combination before the release window.
  • Integrate manual checks into test management:
    • Use TestRail or Zephyr to record manual test runs and attach evidence; link failing tests to Jira bugs with Affects Version and Build. Use consistent reproducible tags (e.g., manual-regression:2025-12-18).
    • When a manual test becomes a frequent pre-release checklist item, mark it as automatable and create a clear automation ticket with acceptance criteria and selectors.
  • Maintain a conversion pipeline: each manual regression cycle should generate a prioritized automation backlog (tests to automate, test data problems to fix, flakiness to quarantine). Track MTTR for converting manual checks to reliable automated checks.
  • Use monitoring and production telemetry as part of your regression feedback loop: if a post-release metric spikes (errors, latency, customer complaints), feed that back as must-run manual test cases in the next cycle. DORA’s guidance on small batch sizes and measurement supports using telemetry to continuously improve test selection and release confidence.

Code block — sample lightweight release checklist you can paste into Confluence or a Jira ticket (release-checklist.yml):

release: 2025-12-18
build_tag: v1.8.3
env: staging
prechecks:
  - staging_config_ok: true
  - data_snapshot_saved: true
  - monitors_attached: true
smoke_checks:
  - login_happy_path
  - landing_page_load
  - key_api_health
sanity_checks:
  - bugfix_432_verify
  - payment_gateway_auth
manual_regression:
  timebox_hours: 2
  owners:
    - qa_lead: alice@example.com
    - release_manager: sam@example.com
postrelease:
  - monitor_24h
  - collect_errors_and_update_backlog

Table: Quick mapping of responsibilities

Role Responsibility
QA Lead Owns manual regression checklist, executes / delegates tests, captures evidence
Dev on-call Available to triage failing tests and reproduce locally
Release Manager Records sign-off, updates release notes, toggles feature flags
Product Validates business acceptance for customer-impacting flows

Practical Protocol: Step-by-Step Manual Regression for Each Release

A reproducible protocol you can paste into a release playbook.

  1. Prepare (T−X)

    • Lock the release branch and tag the build to test. Record build_tag in the release ticket.
    • Ensure staging environment parity and test data snapshot completed.
    • Run the automated smoke and integration pipelines. If the smoke fails, stop — no manual regression yet.

  2. Entry smoke (10–30 minutes)

    • Execute the pre-defined smoke checklist manually if automation is slow or untrusted. Attach screenshots. If the build fails smoke, mark the release blocked and open a dev ticket.

  3. Targeted sanity (15–90 minutes)

    • Run sanity tests only for the modified areas and the top 1–2 related journeys. Record pass/fail and severity. If sanity fails, follow your incident triage: rollback or block release depending on severity.

  4. Risk-based core manual regression (time-box)

    • Execute Critical and High priority tests determined by the risk model. Capture exact steps and evidence. Log defects with severity, repro steps, build_tag, environment.

  5. Exploratory session(s) (30–120 minutes)

    • Run 1–2 session-based exploratory tests with a clear charter (e.g., “Explore payment checkout with poor network conditions”). Document scope and discoveries. Use GOV.UK or Ministry of Testing session templates to structure notes.

  6. Sign-off and evidence

    • QA Lead updates the release ticket with: smoke=true, sanity=true, manual_regression=timebox_passed, evidence_links=[screenshots, logs]. The Release Manager records the production deployment window.

  7. Post-release monitoring

    • Keep elevated monitoring for the first 24 hours and capture any anomalies into the defect backlog. Use those anomalies to refine the next manual regression checklist and identify automation candidates. DORA-style telemetry helps you prioritize what to improve next.

Important: Every manual regression session must produce two artifacts: concrete evidence of what passed/failed, and at least one improvement action (fix test data, automate a happy path, or update a flaky test).

Sources

Software Delivery Guide — Martin Fowler - Defines Continuous Delivery concepts, deployment pipeline behavior, and why software should remain in a releasable state. Used for pipeline and release-gate rationale.

ISTQB — International Software Testing Qualifications Board - Industry-standard definitions and testing terminology, used for the definition of regression testing and testing terminology.

What is Smoke Testing? — PractiTest - Practical definitions and distinctions for smoke and sanity tests, used to justify entry checks and gate strategy.

DORA — DORA’s software delivery metrics: the four keys - Research-backed guidance on delivery metrics, small batch reasoning, and how telemetry informs release confidence.

Exploratory testing — GOV.UK Service Manual - Practical session-based exploratory testing guidance and how to structure exploratory sessions for maximum value.

A Really Useful List For Exploratory Testers — Ministry of Testing - Community resources and pragmatic techniques for exploratory testing, session charters, and debriefs.

Integrating software quality models into risk-based testing — Springer Software Quality Journal (2016) - Academic evidence on the effectiveness of risk-based testing strategies and defect detection efficiency.

OWASP Web Security Testing Guide & Top Ten — OWASP - Authoritative security testing guidance and common vulnerability classes to include in release-level checks.

Confluence / Atlassian — Release templates and release notes guidance - Practical guidance for templating release pages and using Confluence/Jira for release checklists and sign-offs.

Treat manual regression as a surgical intervention: small, prioritized, time-boxed, evidence‑first, and tightly integrated with automation and telemetry so you shrink the manual surface area over time while keeping user risk low.

title: To Borrow or To Clone: The Rust Struct Exposure Dilemma
description:
Every Rust developer eventually hits a crossroads when trying to expose private struct fields cleanly. Here is a breakdown of the common approaches, their hidden costs, and how to strike the right balance.

1. The Brute-Force Route: Making Fields Public

The most direct fix for visibility issues is simply marking fields pub. While this instantly grants access, it sacrifices encapsulation and can introduce dangerous side effects. Giving outside callers full access means anyone can mutate internal state or even move values out of the struct entirely, risking broken invariants.

2. The Convenience Trap: Overusing Clone

Another route is writing getter methods that return cloned instances. It is frictionless enough that developers sometimes abuse it purely as an escape hatch to silence the borrow checker.

The downside? Cloning performs a deep copy of the underlying memory. If you are exposing large data structures, frequent cloning introduces hidden CPU overhead and memory bandwidth pressure.

3. The Idiomatic Choice: Strategic Borrowing

The high-performance solution is leveraging references and lifetime annotations. Although lifetimes can steepen the learning curve for developers coming from garbage-collected languages, borrowing is vastly more efficient than cloning. No matter how massive the original type is, a reference only copies a pointer-sized footprint.

Yet, zero-cost abstractions demand careful design. Combining complex lifetime bounds with multi-threaded safety and thread-pool concurrency can escalate quickly. Ultimately, writing production-grade Rust comes down to balancing clean borrowing strategies with minimizing resource contention.

title: Explaining the Python-JVM Boundary in Spark, and What Arrow Changed
description:
Arrow's real contribution to PySpark isn't speed at any one API but a shared memory format at every boundary between the JVM and Python; each release removed one conversion at one boundary, what each one left behind explains the next, and the conversion that remains now lives inside Spark's own engine rather than at the Python edge.

That crossing is the oldest problem in PySpark, and the most persistent attempt to fix it started in February 2016, when Wes McKinney (the creator of pandas) filed a Spark ticket with a modest title: SPARK-13534, "Implement Apache Arrow serializer for Spark DataFrame for use in DataFrame.toPandas." It asked for one method to stop using pickle.

It took two years to ship. And over the decade that followed, the same idea went through every other door between Spark's JVM and Python: UDFs, partition-level APIs, the network protocol of Spark Connect, custom data sources, until in Spark 4.1 a Python function could receive Spark's data as an Arrow array and never touch pandas at all, and in Spark 4.2 the Arrow paths finally became the defaults.

The wall

PySpark is not a Python reimplementation of Spark. It's a Python client for a JVM engine. When you write df.filter(col("x") > 5).groupBy("y").count(), Python builds a query plan and hands it to the JVM, which optimizes, distributes, and executes it; Python never touches the data, which is why DataFrame code runs at the same speed in PySpark and Scala.

The trouble starts the moment your own code needs the data: a UDF, toPandas(), createDataFrame(pandas_df), a custom data source. Then data has to physically cross from the JVM into a Python process, and for most of Spark's history the only way across was pickle, one row at a time:

Every row pays four serialization steps and a function call. For a UDF like return x * 1.1, the arithmetic is nanoseconds and the machinery around it is microseconds, three orders of magnitude of overhead wrapped around almost no work.

That was PySpark from 2015 to 2018.

Why the fix was a memory format, not a faster pickle

Arrow was conceived in late 2015 by people who had hit the same wall from different directions. McKinney had spent years fighting pandas' memory model; his 2017 essay "Apache Arrow and the 10 Things I Hate About pandas" lists the grievances, including a rule of thumb that pandas users needed "5 to 10 times as much RAM as the size of your dataset."

Jacques Nadeau, building a query engine at Dremio, saw every data system inventing its own internal format and paying to translate between them at every boundary. Marcel Kornacker, who created Impala at Cloudera, saw the same copying across the Hadoop ecosystem. They met at Strata NYC in September 2015, and Arrow was announced as an Apache top-level project in February 2016, skipping the incubator entirely, which is unusual and reflected how many companies wanted the same thing.

The idea was not a faster serializer. It was to agree on the bytes themselves: a language-independent, columnar, in-memory layout specified down to byte alignment, null bitmaps, and buffer order, so that two Arrow-aware systems can hand each other data without converting it.

Within a process, or with shared memory, that's genuinely zero-copy; across a socket it's still a copy, but with no per-row decoding on either side, because the bytes on the wire are already the bytes in memory.

Columnar mattered as much as standard. In a row layout, values from one column are interleaved with everything else in the row:

row layout:     [id=1, name="Alice", age=30] [id=2, name="Bob", age=25] [id=3, name="Carol", age=35]
columnar:       id:   [1, 2, 3]
                name: ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]
                age:  [30, 25, 35]

With columns stored contiguously, a 64-byte cache line holds eight useful int64 values instead of one row's mixed fields, and SIMD instructions can process a run of values at once.

The database literature had already shown what this buys: the MonetDB/X100 work (CIDR 2005) argued that pushing batches of around a thousand column values through each operator, instead of one row at a time, is an order of magnitude or two faster. Arrow's batch-oriented design was built around exactly that model.

The rest of this post is the story of Spark adopting it, one door at a time.

Boundary one: the driver (2018)

The first door was the smallest. DataFrame.toPandas() collected results to the driver by pickling every row and rebuilding each one as Python objects before pandas could wrap them, and it was notoriously slow. McKinney's ticket, filed on February 28, 2016, three weeks after the first commit to the Arrow repository, asked to replace that path. It stayed open for over a year. Bryan Cutler, at IBM's Spark Technology Center, resolved it on June 23, 2017, and it reached users in Spark 2.3.0 in February 2018.

Two years, for one method.


# Spark 2.3 name, later renamed; on by default since Spark 4.2
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled", "true")

The reverse direction, createDataFrame(pandas_df), got the same treatment (SPARK-20791). What made this matter wasn't the one method; it was the plumbing Cutler built to do it (Arrow converters on the JVM side, pyarrow integration on the Python side), which every later boundary reused.

What it removed: pickle for collecting data to the driver. What it left: everything that happens on executors. UDFs still crossed row by row.

Boundary two: UDFs, in batches (2018)

The second door was the one that mattered for performance, and it came from outside Databricks. The proposal, SPARK-21190 ("SPIP: Vectorized UDFs in Python"), was filed by Reynold Xin, but most of the implementation was done by Li Jin, an engineer at the quantitative investment firm Two Sigma and an Arrow committer, on top of Cutler's serializer. It shipped in the same Spark 2.3.0 release. Instead of calling your function once per row, Spark would send a batch of rows (10,000 by default, spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch) as an Arrow RecordBatch and call your function once per batch, with a pandas Series:

# Before: once per row, pickle both ways
@udf(returnType="double")
def add_tax(price):
    return price * 1.1 if price else None

# After: once per batch, a pandas Series in and out
@pandas_udf("double")
def add_tax(price: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return price * 1.1

Li Jin's post introducing the feature in October 2017 reported speedups from around 3x on simple arithmetic to around 100x on a cumulative-probability function, and the spread is the point: the simpler the function, the more of its cost was the crossing, and the more complex the function, the more it also benefits from running as vectorized NumPy instead of Python bytecode.

My own measurements, eight years and many releases later, land in the same shape. At 50 million rows, a pandas UDF did the arithmetic workload in 0.79 seconds against 5.20 for a pickled UDF, and a normal CDF in 0.82 against 6.18; on a string transform the gap was narrower, 2.51 against 6.22, for a reason that turns out to matter later.

What it removed: per-row serialization and per-row function calls. What it left: a rewrite (your function had to speak pandas), and a conversion. Every batch arrived as Arrow and was turned into pandas before your code saw it, and the result was turned back.

What actually crosses the socket

Before going further it's worth seeing what's moving, because every later boundary sends the same thing. Arrow's IPC stream format is a schema message followed by record-batch messages, each framed like this:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Continuation indicator: 0xFFFFFFFF (4 bytes)                │
│ Metadata length (4 bytes, little-endian int32)              │
│ Flatbuffer metadata (Message type, schema or batch header)  │
│ Padding to 8-byte boundary                                  │
│ Message body (data buffers, padded to 8-byte multiple)      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Inside the body, each column is a set of plain buffers: a validity bitmap with one bit per value, the values themselves as a contiguous typed array, and, for variable-length types like strings, an offsets array into one contiguous UTF-8 buffer. For four rows of (name: string, age: int32):

Validity bitmap (age):  [1, 1, 0, 1]      → 0b1011 (bit-packed)
Data buffer (age):      [30, 25, 0, 35]   → 16 bytes (4 × int32)
Offsets (name):         [0, 5, 8, 13, 18] → 5 × int32
Data buffer (name):     "AliceBobCarolDavid" (contiguous UTF-8)

No per-value type tags, no escaping, no framing between values.

The strings are the detail to hold on to: in Arrow, a million strings are one buffer and an array of offsets. In traditional pandas, they're a million separate Python objects.

Boundary three: letting code see Arrow (2022 to 2025)

For four years, every batch API in PySpark handed you pandas, whether you wanted pandas or not.

The first API that let user code see Arrow directly was mapInArrow, added by Hyukjin Kwon, a long-time PySpark maintainer at Databricks (SPARK-37227, with the Python side in SPARK-37228), in Spark 3.3.0 in June 2022. It passes whole partitions as an iterator of pyarrow.RecordBatch objects, and your function yields RecordBatches back:

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc

def add_tax_arrow(batches):
    for batch in batches:
        taxed = pc.multiply(batch.column("price"), pa.scalar(1.1))
        yield pa.RecordBatch.from_arrays([batch.column("id"), taxed],
                                         names=["id", "price_with_tax"])

df.mapInArrow(add_tax_arrow, schema="id long, price_with_tax double")

Grouped operations were the obvious remaining gap, and Enrico Minack closed it with applyInArrow (SPARK-40559), which shipped in Spark 4.0.0 in May 2025. Where applyInPandas turns each group into a pandas DataFrame, applyInArrow hands you the group as a pyarrow.Table:

def normalize(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    totals = table.column("total")
    mean, std = pc.mean(totals).as_py(), pc.stddev(totals).as_py()
    normalized = (pa.array([0.0] * len(totals)) if not std
                  else pc.divide(pc.subtract(totals, pa.scalar(mean)), pa.scalar(std)))
    return pa.Table.from_arrays([table.column("order_id"), totals, normalized],
                                names=["order_id", "total", "normalized"])

orders.groupBy("location_id").applyInArrow(
    normalize, schema="order_id long, total double, normalized double")

The same idea reached the other direction in 4.0 too: the new Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076) lets a custom source written in Python yield pyarrow.RecordBatch objects instead of tuples (SPARK-48493), so data read by Python code can enter Spark as Arrow instead of being built up one Python tuple at a time.

I haven't benchmarked the grouped or data-source paths myself, so I'll leave numbers out of this section; the mechanism is the same as everywhere else, and the benefit should be largest where the pandas conversion is most expensive, which is strings.

What it removed: the forced detour through pandas, for anyone willing to write Arrow code. What it left: that condition. Most PySpark code is plain @udf functions that nobody is going to rewrite.

Boundary four: the network (2023)

Spark Connect started as a proposal from Martin Grund at Databricks in June 2022 (SPARK-39375): separate the client from the server, so an application talks to Spark over gRPC instead of living inside the driver's JVM. Once there's a network between you and the engine, the format results travel in stops being an optimization and becomes the protocol.

The answer was Arrow.

The client sends unresolved logical plans as Protocol Buffers; the server optimizes and runs them and streams the results back as Arrow record batches over the same channel. That's what makes a JVM-free Python client possible at all: the pyspark-client package is a 1.6 MB wheel of pure Python. The same columnar format that moves data between executors and Python workers now moves data between a remote cluster and a laptop.

Boundary five: the UDFs nobody rewrote (2023 to 2026)

Every boundary so far helped people who changed their code. Arrow-optimized Python UDFs (SPARK-40307, Spark 3.5.0, September 2023) took the opposite approach: keep your plain @udf exactly as written, and swap the transport underneath it. Batches cross as Arrow; Python unpacks each batch and still calls your function once per value.

Xinrong Meng's 2023 Databricks post measured about 1.6x over pickle for a single UDF and 1.9x for three chained ones on a 32 GB dataset, and my benchmark agrees in spirit: useArrow=True took the arithmetic workload from 5.20 to 2.23 seconds and the CDF from 6.18 to 2.94. Real, and cheap to get, but nothing like the pandas UDF numbers, because the per-row function call is still there.

That call is my benchmark's ceiling.

Turning this on by default took two tries. It was merged for Spark 4.0 (SPARK-48516) and reverted in March 2025 before the release; it finally shipped as the default in Spark 4.2, along with Arrow for toPandas() and for Python UDTFs, and a minimum PyArrow of 18.0. On 4.2, then, every existing @udf gets Arrow transport without anyone touching it.

It's also where I made the mistake that best illustrates how confusing this boundary is. My benchmark's "Arrow" variant of the plain UDF flipped spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled, which governs toPandas() and createDataFrame() and has nothing to do with UDFs. The setting that actually moves a UDF onto Arrow is spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled, or useArrow=True on the decorator. So my "Arrow" row was the pickled UDF measured twice, and its near-identical result was an accidental A/A test.

Three settings are named for Arrow, and they control three different boundaries.

What it removed: pickle, for everyone, with no code changes. What it left: the function call per row, which is the part no transport format can fix.

Boundary six: Arrow as the execution format (2025)

The last step turned Arrow from the way data travels into the way your code computes. Ruifeng Zheng's SPARK-53014, "Make Arrow UDF public," shipped in Spark 4.1.0 on December 16, 2025, almost ten years after McKinney's ticket. An Arrow UDF receives pyarrow.Array values and returns one, and it's meant to be written with pyarrow.compute, whose functions are C++ kernels operating directly on Arrow buffers:

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from pyspark.sql.functions import arrow_udf

@arrow_udf("double")
def add_tax(price: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.multiply(price, pa.scalar(1.1))

@arrow_udf("string")
def clean_email(email: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.utf8_trim(pc.utf8_lower(email))

Line the UDF types up by what happens to the data and the progression is plain:

UDF type Data path Format conversions
Pickle @udf JVM → pickle → Python value → pickle → JVM pickle both ways, per row
Arrow-optimized @udf JVM → Arrow → Python value → Arrow → JVM Arrow ↔ Python objects, per row
@pandas_udf JVM → Arrow → pandas → Arrow → JVM Arrow ↔ pandas, per batch
@arrow_udf JVM → Arrow → your function → Arrow → JVM none on the Python side

In my benchmark, @arrow_udf was the fastest Python option everywhere, but the margin over pandas UDFs depended almost entirely on the data type. On arithmetic and the CDF it was only 5 to 9% faster; on the string transform it was 1.6x faster at both 50M and 100M rows (1.55 seconds against 2.51 at 50M).

That's the strings detail from the socket section paying off. A numeric pandas Series is a NumPy array underneath, so converting from Arrow is cheap; a string column in traditional pandas is an array of Python objects, so converting means building millions of them. pyarrow.compute skips all of that and works on the one contiguous buffer.

What it removed: the last conversion on the Python side. What it left: Spark's side.

Taken together, the choice today comes down to what your function can receive:

The pipe itself

Everything above changes what goes through the socket. Hyukjin Kwon's SPARK-51688, shipped in Spark 4.1.0, changes the socket: instead of TCP over loopback, which runs every byte through the full TCP/IP stack even though it never leaves the machine, the JVM and Python workers can talk over a Unix domain socket, which goes straight through a kernel buffer.

It's opt-in (spark.python.unix.domain.socket.enabled, whose default comes from the PYSPARK_UDS_MODE environment variable) in 4.1 and 4.2, and that's unchanged on the 4.3 branch, which instead adds another transport option: pipelined, asynchronous transfer of UDF batches between the JVM and Python (spark.python.udf.pipelined.enabled, off by default).

Spark 1.x:  pickle format  + TCP loopback        slow format over a slow pipe
Spark 2.3:  Arrow format   + TCP loopback        fast format over a slow pipe
Spark 4.1:  Arrow format   + Unix domain socket  fast format over a faster pipe (opt-in)

One boundary at a time

As of Spark 4.2, Arrow is the format at every place data crosses between the JVM and Python:

Boundary Arrow's role Default
toPandas() / createDataFrame() replaces pickle for driver data collection yes, since 4.2
@udf (plain Python UDFs) replaces pickle transport yes, since 4.2
@pandas_udf, mapInPandas, applyInPandas batch transport, converted to pandas always
@arrow_udf, mapInArrow, applyInArrow transport and execution format always
Spark Connect results the result protocol always
Python Data Source API source data format when the source yields RecordBatches

The last boundary

What's left is on Spark's side of the wall. Inside the JVM, Spark still executes on its own row format (UnsafeRow, from the Tungsten project), and Arrow exists at the edges, so every crossing still begins and ends with a conversion between Spark's rows and Arrow's columns. Engines like Velox and DataFusion show that a query engine can execute on Arrow-format data directly; Spark doesn't, and closing that gap is a much bigger change than any of the boundaries above.

The 4.3 branch, which hasn't been released yet (its first release candidate failed its vote on September 6, and there's no new date), has two small signs of movement at exactly this edge. One is an Arrow format for Spark's in-memory cache (ArrowCachedBatchSerializer, SPARK-57268), part of a proposal to make Spark better on a single machine: the first time Arrow shows up as a storage format inside Spark itself rather than at a door.

The other goes around the boundary instead of through it: experimental transpilation of Python UDFs into Spark expressions (SPIP SPARK-54783), so a simple enough Python function never has to cross into Python at all. It's off by default, classic-mode only, and requires ANSI mode, but it's the one approach that could get under my benchmark's ceiling, because it removes the per-row Python call rather than making the trip to it cheaper.

The pandas side is moving too, more slowly than you'd expect. pandas 3.0, released in January 2026, made a PyArrow-backed string type the default, which should shrink exactly the string-conversion cost that separates pandas UDFs from Arrow UDFs. But PySpark doesn't support pandas 3 yet, not even on the 4.3 branch: it still pins pandas below 3.0, and the umbrella ticket for supporting it (SPARK-55139) is open.

When Wes McKinney filed SPARK-13534 in 2016, he was asking for one method to stop pickling. Ten years later, every door he could have named uses Arrow, the defaults finally say so, and the conversion that remains is the one Spark performs on itself, between its own rows and everything outside it.

That's the last boundary, and it was never a Python problem.

Gemini Enterprise: Transfer ownership of shared agents

Administrators can transfer ownership of shared employee-made agents to another user or to themselves in the Google Cloud console. This is useful when reassigning agents created by departing employees or when temporary workers hand over agents to full-time staff.

Key characteristics and requirements include:

  • Administrator only: Only users with the Gemini Enterprise Admin role (roles/discoveryengine.agentspaceAdmin or roles/discoveryengine.admin) can transfer agent ownership. Agent owners cannot transfer ownership unless they are also administrators.

title: Tamper-evident receipts for AI agent actions: a hash chain in 20 lines
description:
When an AI agent spends money, sends an email, or changes a record, someone eventually asks the same question: what exactly did it do, and can I trust this log? A normal log line can be edited after the fact. A receipt that is chained to the one before it cannot be edited quietly.

The idea

Each action gets a receipt. The receipt holds what was decided, the inputs the agent saw, who approved it, and a timestamp. It also holds the hash of the previous receipt. Change any old receipt and every hash after it stops matching.

import hashlib, json, time

def seal(prev_hash: str, action: dict) -> dict:
    body = {"ts": time.time(), "prev": prev_hash, "action": action}
    digest = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
    return {**body, "hash": digest}

def verify(chain: list[dict]) -> bool:
    prev = "genesis"
    for r in chain:
        body = {k: r[k] for k in ("ts", "prev", "action")}
        ok = r["prev"] == prev and r["hash"] == hashlib.sha256(
            json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        if not ok:
            return False
        prev = r["hash"]
    return True

What to put in a receipt

  • The decision and the options that were considered, not only the winner.
  • The data the agent used (prices, documents, policy version) or a hash of it.
  • The human or policy that approved it.
  • The agent identity and the version of its instructions.

What it does not do

A hash chain shows that records were not changed after sealing. It does not prove the agent made a good decision, and it does not stop someone rewriting the whole chain from the start unless you anchor the latest hash somewhere you do not control (a timestamping service, a signed commit, a counterparty's copy). Keep that limit in mind when you describe it.

Where this shows up

Compliance rules for automated systems increasingly ask for logs of what a system did and why. Receipts like this are one way to keep those records in a form a third party can check without trusting you.

I write about agent audit trails and receipts for SYEN Systems (syensystems.com).

title: Spark's Modules, Seen Through Spark Connect
description:
Spark is moving its centre of gravity out of the JVM. Spark Connect, introduced in 3.4, lets a client drive Spark over gRPC without running a JVM of its own, and in the 4.x line that thin client has become the thing new features are built for: pip install pyspark-client gets you the DataFrame API with none of the JARs full PySpark carries. That gives a simple way to tell which parts of Spark have a future. The state of each Spark module is best read through a single test: can you reach it from a thin Python client over Spark Connect? The modules getting sustained investment were either built for that world (SQL, Declarative Pipelines) or are being rebuilt to reach it (Structured Streaming, MLlib, the Python UDF path); the ones fading (GraphX, SparkR, DStreams, the RDD-based spark.mllib) are exactly the ones that can't cross it.

I learned to read Spark this way by accident. In February I tested Real-Time Mode on open-source Spark 4.1, and the first obstacle wasn't latency; it was Python. The real-time trigger existed in Scala, PySpark had no way to ask for it, and to run the pipeline at all I wrote a helper that reached through the Py4J gateway and built the Scala trigger object by hand:

def with_real_time_trigger(dsw, checkpoint_interval="5 minutes"):
    jvm = dsw._spark._jvm
    jTrigger = jvm.org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.RealTimeTrigger.apply(
        checkpoint_interval
    )
    dsw._jwrite = dsw._jwrite.trigger(jTrigger)
    return dsw

It worked, and it's exactly the kind of code that has no future. It only runs in classic mode, because a Spark Connect client has no JVM to reach into; the PySpark 4.2 Connect session refuses _jvm by name, along with _jsc, sparkContext, and the rest of the Py4J surface. Five months later the helper was obsolete anyway. Spark 4.2 added trigger(realTime=...) to PySpark, so the same pipeline runs from a thin client, and the 4.3 branch lets that Python code run aggregations and deduplication in real time too. A feature that existed but couldn't be reached from Python became real the moment it crossed the client boundary, and that is the story of nearly every module below.

Crossing isn't free, and part of this post is what it cost me when I tried. It's written against Spark 4.2.0 (released July 14, 2026). Spark 4.3 is close but not out: its first release candidate was tagged on August 31, and the vote on it failed on September 6, so where 4.3 matters I describe what's on the release branch, not what has shipped.

What "reachable over Connect" actually means

Spark Connect splits the application from the engine. The client builds an unresolved logical plan, serializes it as protobuf, sends it over gRPC, and gets results back as Arrow batches; everything that plans and runs the query lives on the server.

That contract is the whole test. Anything expressible as a logical plan travels; anything that assumes the client and the driver share a JVM doesn't. The line falls in a predictable place:

Over Spark Connect Status
DataFrame operations, Spark SQL, catalog operations, temp views Supported
Structured Streaming Supported
Python, Pandas, and Arrow UDFs; UDTFs Supported
pyspark.ml pipelines (fit / transform) Supported, via a server-side model cache
SparkContext, RDDs, broadcast variables, accumulators Not supported

RDDs are the dividing line because an RDD isn't a plan; it's a handle to partitioned data and closures living in the driver's JVM. Every module built on RDDs inherits that limitation, which is most of the reason the left-hand column of the diagram above looks the way it does.

The payoff for crossing the line is a client with no JVM. pyspark-client ships only the gRPC client, the protobuf definitions, and the DataFrame API; it installs none of the roughly 277 jars that full pyspark carries. When I measured the 4.2.0 packages, Spark's own Python payload dropped from roughly 480 MB to about 20 MB and the jar directory to zero.

The common "1.5 MB client" line is misleading, though: 1.60 MB is the wheel, and a working thin-client virtualenv still came to roughly 360 to 380 MB across my installs, because pyarrow, pandas, and numpy are hard requirements and dwarf Spark itself. The honest headline is no JVM, no JDK, no jars, not small.

Package What it is
pyspark-client The thin client: pure Python, no JDK, remote only (sc://...)
pyspark[connect] Full PySpark plus Connect extras; can also start a local server
pyspark-connect A small shim that depends on full pyspark (so not thin)
pyspark Classic Py4J by default; talks to a Connect server via .remote() with the extras installed

The classic/Connect choice is controlled by spark.api.mode, whose default is still classic; the proposal to make Connect the default (SPARK-50411) is open. So the direction is clear, but for now you opt in, and what that means for someone choosing today is simple: anything you write that touches sparkContext or _jvm is a bet against where the project is going.

Built for it: SQL and Declarative Pipelines

Spark SQL passes the test almost by definition, because a Connect request is a logical plan and Spark SQL is the machinery that turns logical plans into execution. Every DataFrame call, every spark.sql() string, and every Structured Streaming query goes through the same pipeline:

That's why SQL keeps absorbing features that used to live in application code. Across the 4.x line it gained procedural scripting (generally available in 4.1, with cursors added in 4.2), recursive common table expressions (a request that sat open as SPARK-24497 from 2018), the VARIANT type for semi-structured data (shredded into typed Parquet columns from 4.1), collations, and pipe syntax. None of these needs anything from the client beyond the text of the query, which is the point: the more logic moves into SQL, the less it matters what language or process the client is.

-- Recursive CTE: walk an org chart without a loop in application code
WITH RECURSIVE reports (id, name, manager_id, depth) AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, r.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
)
SELECT * FROM reports;

The most interesting 4.2 addition, and the one I spent the most time probing, is metric views (SPARK-54119): a semantic layer declared with CREATE VIEW ... WITH METRICS, where measures such as a conversion rate are defined once and re-aggregated correctly at whatever grain you query.

The problem they solve is real. In an example I built on synthetic session data, the true monthly conversion rate was 0.0923, while the naive average of the five regional rates was 0.2384, 2.6 times too high, because an average of ratios gives a region with 200 sessions the same weight as one with 50,000. A metric view makes that mistake hard to write.

What it doesn't yet do is fail gracefully.

I ran a grammar probe of 87 statements against the official apache/spark:4.2.0 image (once in classic mode and twice over Connect, all three runs identical), and six invalid statements didn't produce a clean error; they crashed the planner with INTERNAL_ERROR, the message that begins "You hit a bug in Spark":

Statement (abridged) Result on 4.2.0
SELECT * FROM <metric view> INTERNAL_ERROR at planning
Selecting a measure without MEASURE() INTERNAL_ERROR at planning
Joining a metric view on a dimension INTERNAL_ERROR at planning
MEASURE() over an ordinary table INTERNAL_ERROR
CREATE VIEW ... WITH METRICS without LANGUAGE YAML, and a metric view defined over another metric view INTERNAL_ERROR

The numbers are protected; the person writing the query isn't, yet.

Declarative Pipelines (SDP) extend the same idea from queries to whole pipelines: you declare what each table should contain, and Spark resolves dependencies, orders execution, and manages checkpoints and writes. Pipelines are defined in Python or SQL and run over Spark Connect by design, so SDP was born on the right side of the line.

It arrived in 4.1; 4.2 added AUTO CDC for applying change feeds as SCD Type 1, and the 4.3 branch adds SCD Type 2 end to end and a SQL form, CREATE FLOW ... AS AUTO CDC. I tested the 4.2 behaviour in detail in AUTO CDC: Turning an event log into current state.

Concept Python API Behavior
Materialized view @dp.materialized_view Batch table, recomputed each run
Streaming table @dp.table Incremental ingestion with managed checkpoints
Flow @dp.append_flow Named writer into a streaming table
AUTO CDC flow (4.2) dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(...) Applies a change feed as SCD Type 1

For someone choosing today: push as much logic as you can into SQL and declarative definitions. It's the part of Spark that works identically from every client, it's where new features land first, and it's the part least likely to strand you in a migration.

Rebuilt to reach it: streaming, ML, and Python UDFs

The second group are modules that predate Spark Connect and are being reworked to pass the test. Each has made real progress, and each still has a visible seam.

Structured Streaming and Real-Time Mode

Spark has had three streaming engines, and the history is a clean illustration of the thesis. DStreams (described by Matei Zaharia and colleagues in 2012 and 2013) modelled a stream as a sequence of small RDDs; Structured Streaming (Spark 2.0, 2016; written up by Michael Armbrust and colleagues at SIGMOD 2018) rebuilt streaming on DataFrames, as an unbounded table queried with the same API as batch; and Real-Time Mode, added in 4.1, replaces the micro-batch loop with a continuous pipeline:

Real-Time Mode is also where I learned how wide the gap between a feature's design and its open-source reality can be. The widely quoted single-digit-millisecond figures come from Databricks' own deployments.

On open-source 4.1, a stateless Kafka-to-Kafka passthrough I measured (500 events per second on a single 16-core machine, six runs of roughly two thousand events each) had a p50 of about 17 ms and a p99 of 21 to 26 ms. That's fast; it's also a different number, measured on a much smaller setup, and I'd treat both figures as specific to where they came from. The limits mattered more than the latency:

  • Stateless only. The 4.1 operator allowlist permitted projections, filters, and broadcast joins; aggregations, shuffles, and state store operators were off it.
  • No Python UDFs. BatchEvalPythonExec wasn't on the allowlist.
  • No PySpark trigger, hence the Py4J helper at the top of this post.
  • Every stage runs concurrently, so a 16-partition Kafka source needs 16 task slots just to read.

Spark 4.2 fixed the Python gap (the realTime trigger in PySpark) but, per the 4.2 source, left the operator allowlist unchanged, so on 4.2 it's still a stateless engine:

# Spark 4.2+: Real-Time Mode from PySpark, no JVM access needed.
# The argument is the checkpoint interval, not a latency target.
query = (
    events.select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("e"))
    .select("e.*")
    .filter(col("amount") > 0)                      # stateless: allowed
    .selectExpr("to_json(struct(*)) AS value")
    .writeStream.format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:9092")
    .option("topic", "payments_clean")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/payments_clean")
    .outputMode("update")
    .trigger(realTime="5 minutes")
    .start()
)

The 4.3 branch is where it becomes a general engine. It adds stateful Real-Time Mode (umbrella SPARK-54699): streaming aggregations including windowed ones, dropDuplicates, the JVM transformWithState, and pipelined shuffles, and it removes the @Experimental marker from the trigger APIs.

The branch documentation is just as clear about what remains out of scope: stream-stream joins, flatMapGroupsWithState, session windows, and the PySpark transformWithState APIs are unsupported; Python UDFs are still not allowed (SPARK-57237 is open); Kafka is the only source; and stateful queries need enough cores to run both stages at once.

Notice where the seam is. When I built the 4.3 branch and ran it against my own stack, the stateful operators that are ordinary DataFrame operations worked from PySpark in Real-Time Mode: a streaming aggregation and a dropDuplicates both ran at about 40 ms median latency (against about 600 ms for the same query as a one-second micro-batch), with no duplicates getting through. What's still missing is Python's own stateful API: PySpark transformWithState isn't supported in Real-Time Mode, and on the branch today it fails with a misleading checkpoint-metadata error (STDS_FAILED_TO_READ_OPERATOR_METADATA) rather than the documented unsupported-operator one. Custom state in real time is still a Scala feature.

The rest of Structured Streaming is further along. transformWithState (SPARK-46815) replaced the older mapGroupsWithState APIs in 4.0 with typed, evolvable state, and it has a Python API, which ended the era when complex stateful streaming meant writing Scala. RocksDB is the default state store in 4.x, and 4.1 enabled adaptive query execution for stateless streaming queries (SPARK-53941).

For someone choosing today: on 4.2, use Real-Time Mode from Python for stateless transforms where the latency matters, and micro-batch Structured Streaming for anything stateful. On 4.3, aggregations and deduplication move into Real-Time Mode from Python as well; if you need custom state (transformWithState) at real-time latency, that's still Scala.

MLlib on Connect

MLlib's problem was more fundamental than streaming's. In classic PySpark, model.fit(df) returns a model object that lives in the driver's JVM, and the Python client just holds a Py4J reference to it. A Connect client has no JVM to hold anything, so ML over Connect required moving model state to the server:

The server keeps fitted models in a cache and hands the client an ID; fit, transform, evaluation, attribute lookup, and save/load become RPCs. This is the one rebuild that's essentially finished. pyspark.ml on Connect shipped in 4.0 (SPARK-50812); 4.1 brought it to general availability with model cache offloading, model size and cache limits, and summaries that survive eviction (SPARK-51236); 4.2 re-enabled FPGrowth (SPARK-54574); and the 4.3 branch adds model-size estimation for around twenty model types (umbrella SPARK-58181) plus a fix for size overcounting (SPARK-57521).

What it hasn't done is grow: the estimators, transformers, and evaluators registered for Connect are the same list from 4.0 through the 4.3 branch, a few known gaps remain open (SPARK-51473, SPARK-51478), and the ML guide still has no section on Connect at all.

Meanwhile the DataFrame-based spark.ml has been the primary API since Spark 2.0, when the RDD-based spark.mllib entered maintenance mode; spark.mllib doesn't pass the Connect test and isn't going to. For deep learning, the path is TorchDistributor (SPARK-41589), which uses Spark to launch distributed PyTorch training rather than reimplementing it.

For someone choosing today: spark.ml pipelines over Connect are safe for the algorithms MLlib already has; don't expect the catalogue to expand, and use TorchDistributor or an external framework for anything modern.

Python UDFs on Arrow

The Python UDF path is the rebuild I've measured most closely. Its history is a long march away from pickling one row at a time: Pandas UDFs (2018) moved data in Arrow batches but converted them to pandas; useArrow=True (from 3.5) put ordinary scalar UDFs on Arrow transport; and @arrow_udf (public in 4.1, SPARK-53014) hands your function a pyarrow.Array with no pandas conversion at all.

In my benchmark on Spark 4.1, what decided the cost of a UDF was mostly what the function received, not how the bytes travelled. useArrow=True was worth 1.4x to 2.4x over pickle depending on the workload; the vectorized UDFs were faster again; and @arrow_udf beat @pandas_udf by about 1.6x on strings but only 5 to 9% on numeric work, because a numeric pandas Series is cheap to build from Arrow while strings are not. The details, and a correction to my own benchmark, are in Stop Blaming Serialization for Slow Python UDFs.

Getting Arrow on by default took two tries. SPARK-48516 flipped the default for Spark 4.0, and Hyukjin Kwon reverted it in March 2025, before 4.0 shipped. Spark 4.2 finally turned it on (SPARK-54555), for regular Python UDFs, UDTFs, and the pandas conversions, and raised the minimum PyArrow to 18.0.0.

The 4.3 branch drops Python 3.10 (SPARK-56889) and adds an opt-in pipelined UDF transfer (spark.python.udf.pipelined.enabled, off by default, SPARK-56642); pandas 3 still isn't fully supported even there (SPARK-55139 is open).

The same Arrow-first direction shows up in the Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076), which lets you write a connector entirely in Python and, since 4.1, receive pushed-down filters. That removes one of the last reasons a Python team needed Scala.

For someone choosing today: on 4.2, plain @udf already gets Arrow transport for free; write new UDFs as @arrow_udf when the logic maps onto pyarrow.compute (especially strings), and @pandas_udf when you need pandas or SciPy.

What crossing the boundary cost me

Everything above argues that Connect is where Spark is going. It's worth being equally concrete about the price of getting there, because I paid it in two ways this month.

Migrating a real pipeline. I moved the pipelines in my lakehouse-stack project to Spark Connect and started with an audit script over the repository. It reported 27 findings across 24 files, and 21 of them were the same line: spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN").

That single call was the entire blocking surface, and it has no client-side equivalent, because the log level belongs to the server's JVM; the fix is to configure logging where the Connect server starts and delete the call.

The migration itself was almost mechanical, and after it all ten tables matched their pre-migration versions on schema, row count, and an order-independent content hash (that parity result is recorded in my migration notes rather than as a saved log).

The real blocker was the ecosystem. Apache Iceberg doesn't publish a Spark 4.2 runtime; the newest on Maven Central targets 4.1. And the 4.1 jar can't simply be reused, because Spark 4.2 changed the catalog interfaces it implements: View became a class, so loading the old runtime fails with

java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class org.apache.iceberg.spark.source.SparkView
can not implement org.apache.spark.sql.connector.catalog.View, because it is not an interface

and because that failure happens while the catalog loads, it takes down tables, reads, and writes along with views. 4.2 also requires catalogs that serve both tables and views to implement a new RelationCatalog interface. I built a local Iceberg runtime for 4.2 to keep going, which is fine for a demo and not something I'd run in production.

The general lesson is that a Spark minor version can break connectors, and your upgrade schedule is set by your slowest connector, not by Spark.

Mixing versions. Connect's promise is that client and server can be upgraded independently. I tested all four combinations of 4.1.2 and 4.2.0 clients and servers, running each fourteen-operation matrix twice, with identical results:

Client → server Result
4.2.0 → 4.2.0 Everything works
4.1.2 → 4.2.0 Works; newer APIs simply don't exist in the old client
4.1.2 → 4.1.2 Works
4.2.0 → 4.1.2 createDataFrame from a local list fails; GetStatus returns UNIMPLEMENTED

The createDataFrame failure is worth spelling out, because it's so small. A 4.2 client checks the size of local data against a limit it reads from the server (SPARK-55047); a 4.1.2 server reports that limit as 3221225472b, with a unit suffix, and the new client's integer conversion fails on the b:

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3221225472b'

So a new client can't build a three-row DataFrame on an old server. Independent upgrades hold in one direction only: upgrade the server first, and pin clients to it.

Left behind: GraphX, SparkR, and the RDD APIs

The last group fails the test for the same structural reason: each is built on RDDs or on a pre-Connect bridge, and none has a path across.

GraphX was one of Spark's original libraries (Spark 0.9, 2014), built entirely on RDDs and never given a Python API. Between September 30 and October 8, 2024, the dev list voted on Holden Karau's proposal to officially deprecate it in Spark 4; she noted that it "hasn't been updated meaningfully in several years" and was already "de-facto deprecated," and was explicit that it was "not a vote to remove GraphX." The proposal passed, although the 4.2.0 GraphX programming guide still carries no deprecation notice.

The clearest verdict came from outside the project. GraphFrames, the DataFrame-based graph library that Berkeley and Databricks released as an external package in 2016, had gone quiet for years; its maintainers revived it, moved it to the io.graphframes namespace, added Spark 4 support, and, starting with 0.10.0, stopped depending on Spark's GraphX at all, shipping their own "internal modified and updated fork of the Apache Spark GraphX" instead.

Because GraphFrames stores vertices and edges as DataFrames, graph queries go through Catalyst, work from Python, and pass the Connect test's premise:


# pip install graphframes-py==0.12.2
# pyspark --packages io.graphframes:graphframes-spark4_2.13:0.12.2
from graphframes import GraphFrame

g = GraphFrame(vertices, edges)          # two DataFrames: id, and src/dst
ranks = g.pageRank(resetProbability=0.15, maxIter=20)

# Motif finding: patterns become DataFrame joins that Catalyst can plan
triangles = g.find("(a)-[]->(b); (b)-[]->(c); (c)-[]->(a)")

SparkR was contributed in Spark 1.4 (2015) by Shivaram Venkataraman and the AMPLab team. Hyukjin Kwon committed its deprecation (SPARK-49347) in August 2024, and since 4.0 starting a SparkR session prints a warning that it "is deprecated from Apache Spark 4.0.0 and will be removed in a future version." It uses its own JVM bridge and was never ported to Connect, and most R users had already moved to sparklyr, which is maintained by Posit and supports Spark Connect.

DStreams were deprecated in 3.4 (SPARK-42075), and spark.mllib has been in maintenance mode since 2.0; both are RDD APIs with DataFrame successors that do pass the test.

For someone choosing today: don't start anything new on these. Use GraphFrames for graphs (it's the only option from Python), sparklyr for R, Structured Streaming for streams, and spark.ml for ML, and treat existing code on the old APIs as migration work with a deadline you don't control.

Choosing, module by module

Module Verdict Reachable over Connect What I'd do
Spark SQL Built for it Yes Default choice; push logic here
Declarative Pipelines Built for it Yes Use for multi-table pipelines; AUTO CDC for change feeds
Structured Streaming Rebuilt Yes Micro-batch for stateful work
Real-Time Mode Rebuilding Yes from 4.2 (stateless) Stateless only until 4.3; check Python gaps
MLlib (spark.ml) Rebuilt Yes (since 4.0) Fine for existing algorithms
Python UDFs Rebuilt Yes @arrow_udf first; Arrow transport is default in 4.2
GraphX Left behind No Migrate to GraphFrames
SparkR Left behind No Migrate to sparklyr
DStreams, spark.mllib Left behind No Migrate to DataFrame APIs

The part of this that surprised me most is how little of the sorting is about quality. GraphX isn't fading because its algorithms were bad, and SparkR isn't fading because R users were wrong; they're fading because they sit on the wrong side of a client boundary the project has decided to build everything else around.

My Py4J helper was on that side too; it still works in classic mode, and on 4.2 nothing needs it.

Further reading

  • SPARK-54633: Quarterly release cadence SPIP.

title: AWS Deadline Cloud now helps users find their accessible resources in the Deadline Cloud monitor
description:
AWS Deadline Cloud now lets users who have access to specific queues, fleets, or jobs, rather than an entire farm, find the resources they can reach directly from the Deadline Cloud monitor. Deadline Cloud is a fully managed service that helps teams run compute-intensive workloads for visual effects, animation, product design, simulation, and gaming.

Previously, a user with access to only one queue had to get the farm ID from an administrator before they could reach their work. With this launch, the Deadline Cloud monitor displays to users queues they have access to, the parent IDs needed to reach them, and their level of access, covering both direct and group-inherited permissions. Teams now can share a single monitor entry point (URL) across different permission levels without additional coordination.

Resource discovery is available in all AWS Regions where Deadline Cloud is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Deadline Cloud user guide.

title: Search trace spans from the Vercel CLI
description:
You and your coding agents can now search a project’s trace spans from the terminal with vercel traces search.

Each span represents one step in a request, helping you investigate errors, latency, and security-related behavior without opening the dashboard.

By default, vercel traces search returns up to 100 spans from the last hour, newest first, so you can search without first finding a request or trace ID. Filter results by environment, service, span name, status, deployment ID, request ID, trace ID, or span ID, or narrow the time range with --since and --until:

For filters without a dedicated option, use --query with Vercel's supported subset of Kibana Query Langugage (KQL). It supports fields such as duration, along with span and resource attributes:

Add --json to output one JSON object per span, giving scripts and agents structured data to analyze.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade, then run vercel traces search --help to see all available options. Learn more in the vercel traces documentation.

title: Missed Cron Job Monitoring: 4 Heartbeat Signals for Learning Pipeline Failures
description:
The least complex reliable design is to emit four structured checkpoints for every expected nightly cron run: expected, started, failed or completed, and a post-deadline overdue assessment. Store them beside the pipeline's searchable logs, keyed by one stable run ID and one scheduled instant in UTC. That gives an operator enough evidence to distinguish a scheduler miss from a task crash, a slow import, and a notification failure. It works as a healthchecks replacement when the real requirement is searchable incident evidence rather than a bare heartbeat.

Short answer: an error alert alone cannot prove that a scheduled task ran. Treat schedule evaluation as an independent process, record the expected run before execution, and alert from persisted state after a grace period. For an edtech pipeline that imports enrollment and course activity overnight in both the EU and US, this design favors incident reconstruction over an attractive monitoring screen. It also stays portable: the scheduler, log store, and notification transport can change without changing the event contract.

How should heartbeat monitoring detect a missed cron job run?

Start with the question an on-call engineer will ask the next morning: "Did the scheduler fail to dispatch, did the worker fail, or is the job still processing?" A lone success ping answers only one narrow question. Its absence collapses several different states into the same silence, which makes failure alerts hard to trust during reconstruction.

Silence is ambiguous.

The data flow is small. A schedule evaluator writes an expected event for each region and scheduled instant. A worker claims that run ID and writes started, then either completed or failed. After the allowed completion window, a separate evaluator reads the event stream and writes overdue only when no terminal event exists. The alert sender consumes failed and overdue; it is not the source of truth.

Use these four checkpoints because each closes a specific gap:

  1. expected proves the schedule existed and supplies the deadline.
  2. started proves dispatch reached a worker.
  3. failed or completed records the terminal outcome.
  4. overdue records the evaluator's decision, including the observation time.

Keep "expected" separate from "started." That distinction is the whole diagnosis when a run never launches.

A small event model you can run

The following Node.js TypeScript uses an in-memory store so the state transition is visible. In production, the EventStore boundary should use durable storage that supports your retention and access requirements. The example doesn't depend on a particular scheduler or alert service.

type Region = "eu" | "us";
type Stage = "expected" | "started" | "completed" | "failed" | "overdue";

type RunEvent = {
  runId: string;
  region: Region;
  scheduledFor: string;
  observedAt: string;
  stage: Stage;
  attempt: number;
  records?: number;
  errorCode?: string;
};

interface EventStore {
  append(event: RunEvent): Promise<void>;
  list(runId: string): Promise<RunEvent[]>;
}

class MemoryEventStore implements EventStore {
  private readonly events: RunEvent[] = [];

  async append(event: RunEvent): Promise<void> {
    this.events.push(structuredClone(event));
  }

  async list(runId: string): Promise<RunEvent[]> {
    return this.events.filter((event) => event.runId === runId);
  }
}

const makeRunId = (region: Region, scheduledFor: string): string =>
  `learning-import:${region}:${scheduledFor}`;

async function assessRun(
  store: EventStore,
  region: Region,
  scheduledFor: string,
  observedAt: string,
  graceMs: number,
): Promise<"pending" | "terminal" | "overdue"> {
  const runId = makeRunId(region, scheduledFor);
  const events = await store.list(runId);
  const terminal = events.some(
    (event) => event.stage === "completed" || event.stage === "failed",
  );

  if (terminal) return "terminal";

  const deadline = Date.parse(scheduledFor) + graceMs;
  if (Date.parse(observedAt) <= deadline) return "pending";

  if (!events.some((event) => event.stage === "overdue")) {
    await store.append({
      runId,
      region,
      scheduledFor,
      observedAt,
      stage: "overdue",
      attempt: 0,
    });
  }
  return "overdue";
}

async function example(): Promise<void> {
  const store = new MemoryEventStore();
  const scheduledFor = "2026-10-12T01:00:00.000Z";
  const runId = makeRunId("eu", scheduledFor);

  await store.append({
    runId,
    region: "eu",
    scheduledFor,
    observedAt: "2026-10-12T00:55:00.000Z",
    stage: "expected",
    attempt: 0,
  });

  const result = await assessRun(
    store,
    "eu",
    scheduledFor,
    "2026-10-12T03:01:00.000Z",
    2 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  );

  console.log(result, await store.list(runId));
}

void example();

The two-hour grace period is example policy, not a universal recommendation. Derive it from the pipeline's normal completion distribution and the point at which stale learning data becomes operationally harmful. A tighter window detects trouble earlier but pages on legitimate long runs; a wider one reduces noise while delaying investigation. The trade-off is detection speed against false alarms. I would ship with a documented conservative window, collect durations, then revise it from observed data rather than intuition.

Notice that retries keep the same runId and increment attempt. If every retry invents a new identity, a log search can make one scheduled import look like several unrelated jobs. Also make append operations idempotent in durable implementations. Evaluators can run twice, notifications can be retried, and duplicate overdue records shouldn't create duplicate incidents. This is a poor fit for sub-minute tasks where writing four durable events costs more than the work itself; a single counter plus an external schedule evaluator is enough there. It is also unnecessary for best-effort maintenance work that has no deadline and creates no incident when skipped.

Preserve time without trusting local clocks

Regional schedules are where a clean-looking design often becomes ambiguous. "Run at 1:00" is not an incident key. Store the scheduled instant as an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, retain the region as a separate field, and keep the configured time zone in schedule metadata. That preserves the operator's intent without making daylight-saving transitions part of every log query.

Don't infer a missed EU run from the US run, even if both import the same classes of records. They are separate obligations with separate run IDs. A delayed EU source can coexist with a healthy US source, and combining them behind one heartbeat destroys that fact.

Clock handling needs restraint. scheduledFor comes from the schedule evaluator; observedAt records when each component saw the event. Ordering by observedAt alone can be misleading if hosts disagree. Reconstruct primarily by the stable run ID and stage transition, then use timestamps to inspect latency. The terminal event should include compact counts such as processed records, but student names, email addresses, raw prompts, and model output do not belong in an operational event.

That last boundary matters in education systems. NIST SP 800-66 Revision 2 is written for implementing the HIPAA Security Rule, so it is not a blanket compliance label for an edtech pipeline. Its treatment of risk analysis, access control, audit controls, and incident procedures is still a useful primary reference when regulated health information is actually in scope. Compliance scope must be established by the organization; a logging pattern cannot establish it.

Query the timeline, not the error string

An incident search should begin with region plus scheduledFor, resolve the runId, and return all four stages in observation order. This is cheaper and more dependable than indexing large payloads just in case they become useful. Keep high-cardinality identifiers where they earn their cost: run ID, attempt, region, stage, and a bounded error code.

The shape of the timeline tells you where to look next:

Observed events Working diagnosis Next evidence
expected, then overdue dispatch was not observed scheduler and queue delivery logs
expected, started, then overdue worker is slow, stuck, or lost worker lease, progress, and dependency logs
expected, started, failed worker reported an error bounded error code and attempt history
expected, started, completed pipeline finished downstream publication or index freshness

These are working diagnoses, not proof of root cause. For example, a worker may finish after the evaluator writes overdue. Preserve both events. Don't rewrite history to make the timeline look tidy; close or downgrade the incident when the late terminal event arrives.

The search experience also has a user-facing cost. If missing nightly data affects pages used by teachers or administrators, correlate pipeline freshness with page performance instead of claiming the pipeline caused a slow page. Core Web Vitals define LCP, CLS, and INP and recommend evaluating the 75th percentile of page loads. Those measurements describe user experience; the run timeline describes data operations. A shared incident view can place them side by side without pretending they are the same signal.

Alert only from durable decisions

Send an immediate notification for a recorded failed event. Send a missed-run notification only after the independent evaluator persists overdue. The persisted decision makes notification retries safe to reason about and leaves evidence when the delivery channel itself is unavailable.

Deduplicate on runId plus alert kind, not on the rendered message. Route EU and US incidents according to ownership, but keep severity tied to business impact: an overdue auxiliary aggregation should not page like a blocked enrollment import. Cost matters here. More log fields, longer retention, and broader full-text indexing all have a bill, while the five compact query keys above usually carry the investigation.

Test silence deliberately. A happy-path test proves too little because the dangerous case is the component that never starts. Cover an absent started, a worker failure, a run that completes just before the deadline, a late completion after overdue, a duplicate evaluator pass, and two regional runs at the same wall-clock time. Inject a notification failure and verify that the decision remains queryable for replay.

Before deployment, read the event contract as an operator rather than its author. Confirm that schedule creation precedes dispatch, timestamps are UTC instants, retries retain identity, terminal writes happen in a finally-aware execution path, and the evaluator cannot depend on the worker it watches. Then run one synthetic schedule per region through the real storage and notification boundaries. The final check is blunt: with the worker disabled, can a person search one run ID and explain the silence without guessing?

Further reading

  • https://web.dev/articles/vitals
  • https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/66/r2/final
