title: LLM Regression Testing for Jira with CogniRunner
description:
LLM regression testing means running the same labelled inputs again after you change a prompt or a model, to see what the change broke. This tutorial does that for an AI check on a Jira workflow validator. Here the test set is a Jira filter of 8 labelled requests. An 80-line Node script runs it. Each call goes to CogniRunner's rule test over REST, which reads the issue, asks the model and writes nothing to Jira.

I ran it on 13 October 2026 because I wanted to move a validator from openai/gpt-6-luna to anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5. Over three rounds, the site's model matched 6, 7 and 7 of the 8 labels. The candidate matched 8 of 8. I built the test expecting the candidate to miss, and it was the site's model that missed (I'd have bet the other way).

I found the cause in the rule, and I don't think it says much about either model. Our HR check says to fail a request that holds "health or medical information about anyone". Is a free flu vaccination for two offices health information about anyone? Our rule didn't say. So the two models read it differently, and one added sentence gave 8 of 8 on both.

We recorded a three-minute video of this on our demo site, on CogniRunner 1.34.0. What follows is my own run of the same procedure on our test site, with the output as it printed. I did three of the steps through an API where you will click: my tokens came from our test hook, I saved the sentence through Jira's workflow REST API, and I switched the model through the test hook. The video shows those screens, and I give the timestamp at each step.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lMpvV03upQA

[!NOTE]
Prerequisites

  • A Jira Cloud site with CogniRunner 1.34.0 or later. The Marketplace calls that build 7.16.0, released 12 October 2026. I ran a development build of 1.34.0 on our test site.
  • An AI provider saved in CogniRunner's Settings. Mine was OpenRouter with openai/gpt-6-luna as the model for validators and rules. If you haven't set one up, the provider tutorial covers it.
  • A company-managed project whose workflow has a CogniRunner AI validator on one transition. Mine was called Send for Review.
  • An email and API token for Jira's REST API. The script reads the published workflow. I ran it as a Jira admin.
  • A CogniRunner admin, to create the REST API token in step 2.
  • Node 18 or later. I used Node v24.15.0. The script has no dependencies.

The video runs on our demo site with issue keys PPL-13 to PPL-27, and my run has COGTEST-3049 to COGTEST-3056 with the same eight texts. Its script takes flags and runs four requests at a time, while the one printed here takes environment variables and runs one at a time. In the video the first round is 7 of 8. Mine was 6 of 8.

[[steps]]

  1. Build the golden dataset — eight requests in a Jira filter, each labelled expect-pass or expect-block.
  2. Create a token — Settings, the card titled Tokens for CogniRunner's REST API.
  3. Save the script — it reads the saved rule from Jira and calls the rule test for each request.
  4. Run the baseline — the site's own model, three rounds.
  5. Run the candidate — one variable, and the site's model stays as it is.
  6. Read the mismatch — decide whether the model or the rule is wrong.
  7. Try the sentence, save it, run both again — first unsaved, then saved.
  8. Switch the site's model — and find the switch and the tests in the audit log.

What one rule test does: one field, one prompt, nothing written

A CogniRunner AI validator sits on a workflow transition. Somebody moves the request. The app sends one field of it (here the Description) to the model together with the prompt you saved. Back comes pass or fail, with a reason. Atlassian's Forge validator module is what carries it: "Validators check that any input made to the transition is valid before the transition is performed."

You may know the Test button in the rule editor. CogniRunner's Rules REST API has the same thing as a call: POST ?resource=rules&action=test. Our docs describe it like this: "the issue is read, the AI answers, and nothing is written." The body carries the issue key, the field and the prompt. Because the prompt travels in the body, you can try a wording before you save it.

An admin token can add ai: {provider, model} to that body, and then this one request runs on another model of a provider the site already has a key for. From the same page: "Nothing is saved or cached: the site's provider, models and keys stay as they were, and the next request without ai runs on the site's provider."

So the whole procedure is a loop over a filter. The same call takes other kinds of rule as well, and I tested validators. The rest of this API is in the release post for Marketplace version 3.3.0 and on the product page. Another thing you can do to the same validator is hand it a document, and the tutorial on giving one an API spec covers that.

Step 1. Build the golden dataset: a Jira filter of 8 labelled issues

People who test LLM apps call a fixed set of inputs with known right answers a golden dataset. PromptLayer's glossary defines the practice as "re-running a golden dataset whenever you change a prompt, model, or workflow to catch quality regressions early." For a validator the right answer is one of two words, so the dataset can live in Jira as plain issues.

Create eight requests in the project the validator guards. Give each the label gate-test, and then expect-pass or expect-block. Mine were four of each:

Key Label Request What decides it
COGTEST-3049 expect-pass Onboarding: new hire Freya Nilsson, Security Engineer band, salary, laptop, nothing about health
COGTEST-3050 expect-block Salary adjustment: Nora Achterberg, Finance Ops "she was in hospital for a week in August"
COGTEST-3051 expect-block Relocation support: Arjun Mehta, Bangalore to Lisbon cleared to fly "after the knee operation"
COGTEST-3052 expect-pass Parental leave cover: Lina Haddad, Platform support parental leave, which isn't an illness
COGTEST-3053 expect-pass Wellbeing budget: Design team, 2027 standing desks and a gym benefit for 12 people
COGTEST-3054 expect-block Relocation allowance: Tomasz Wierzbicki, Kraków to Lisbon "his daughter's asthma"
COGTEST-3055 expect-block Reduced hours: Amara Okafor, 32 to 28 hours "a phased return after her burnout absence"
COGTEST-3056 expect-pass Flu vaccination: office programme, November 2026 free and optional, for everyone in two offices

All of these people are made up. They belong to the fictional company on our demo site, and the eight are ours. Write yours from requests your own people sent, with the names changed.

Then save the search as a filter. Mine is called Gate tests: HR health check, with this JQL:

project = COGTEST AND labels = gate-test ORDER BY key ASC

Note the filter's id from its URL. Mine was 12450.

Check: the filter should show 8 of 8, and each row should show its expect label. If a row shows another label first, remove the extra labels. Jira sorts labels by name, and in our video session a label called benefits pushed two verdicts behind a +2.

Is eight enough? Probably not for a rule that matters a lot. Traceloop's guide suggests "20-30 'golden set' examples that cover common use cases and known failure modes." Our eight came out of 28 candidates. Our video session ran those 28 on both models, 600 dry runs in all. It kept the ones whose verdict stayed the same over four or five rounds, plus one request where the two models disagreed each time. Four of the dropped ones flipped in 1 round of 3 (a newborn added to a health plan, a return from maternity leave, and two more). A request that flips by itself will fail your test on days when nothing changed, so I'd keep those out of the gate and in a separate list to watch.

Step 2. Create a token for CogniRunner's REST API

Open CogniRunner's admin page, go to the Settings tab and find the card titled Tokens for CogniRunner's REST API. It opens on Viewer and Their own rules. Change those to Admin and Everyone's rules. My tokens had both, and I haven't tried a narrower one. Type a name and click Create token. You see the value once, so copy it now, and copy the Endpoint from the same card. The video shows this card at 0:34, with its two tokens already made.

Our docs put the rule test at editor, and the same call with ai at "admin token + live admin minter". By minter they mean the person who created the token, who must still be an admin when the call arrives. So an editor token should be enough for step 4, going by the docs and the code.

Tokens run out. On the card it says "New tokens expire after 90 days", and mine, created on 13 October, showed an expiry of 11 January 2027. Also treat the endpoint address as private too. It's a Forge web trigger, and Atlassian's page on those says "You should keep these URLs secure." CogniRunner asks for the bearer token on top. I still mask the address everywhere, this page included.

Put the values in your shell:

export JIRA_SITE=https://wolfaenpak.atlassian.net JIRA_EMAIL=<admin email> JIRA_API_TOKEN=<jira api token>
export RULES_API_URL=<rules-api> RULES_API_TOKEN=cgr_<masked>
export WORKFLOW="Software Simplified Workflow for Project COGTEST" TRANSITION="Send for Review" FILTER=12450

That first value is our test site, so put your own there. WORKFLOW is the workflow's name as Jira's workflow list shows it. You'll know whether the token works from the first line the script prints in step 4, which should show its role.

Step 3. Call the Rules REST API to test the Jira workflow validator on each issue

Save this as gate-test.mjs. It needs no packages. savedRule reads the published workflow from Jira and pulls the validator's prompt and field out of the transition. It reads Jira because the rules resource of CogniRunner's REST API has no call that returns a tracked rule's saved prompt in full. testSet reads the filter and takes the expected verdict from the label. runOne posts one request to the rule test and waits if the token's allowance is spent.

#!/usr/bin/env node
// gate-test.mjs: run a CogniRunner AI validator's SAVED prompt over a labelled Jira test set. Node 18+, no dependencies.
// Every call is a dry run (POST ?resource=rules&action=test): the issue is read, the AI answers, nothing is written.
//   JIRA_SITE=https://you.atlassian.net JIRA_EMAIL=... JIRA_API_TOKEN=... \
//   RULES_API_URL=<the Rules REST API address from CogniRunner Settings> RULES_API_TOKEN=cgr_... \
//   WORKFLOW="<workflow name>" TRANSITION="Send for Review" FILTER=<filter id> node gate-test.mjs
// Optional: CANDIDATE_MODEL=<provider>/<model id> runs each request on that model instead (needs an ADMIN token; the
//   site's own model is not changed). CANDIDATE_PROVIDER defaults to openrouter. ADD_SENTENCE="..." appends one
//   sentence to the saved prompt for this run only, so you can try a wording before you save it.
const E = process.env;
for (const k of ["JIRA_SITE", "JIRA_EMAIL", "JIRA_API_TOKEN", "RULES_API_URL", "RULES_API_TOKEN", "WORKFLOW", "FILTER"]) if (!E[k]) { console.error(`Set ${k}`); process.exit(2); }
const TRANSITION = E.TRANSITION || "Send for Review";
const JAUTH = "Basic " + Buffer.from(`${E.JIRA_EMAIL}:${E.JIRA_API_TOKEN}`).toString("base64");
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
const pad = (s, n) => String(s ?? "").padEnd(n).slice(0, n);

async function jira(path, body) {
  const r = await fetch(E.JIRA_SITE + path, { method: "POST", headers: { Authorization: JAUTH, Accept: "application/json", "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(body) });
  if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`Jira ${path}: ${r.status} ${(await r.text()).slice(0, 200)}`);
  return r.json();
}
async function rules(method, query, body) {
  const r = await fetch(`${E.RULES_API_URL}?${query}`, { method, headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${E.RULES_API_TOKEN}`, "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined });
  const text = await r.text(); let json = null; try { json = JSON.parse(text); } catch { /* not JSON */ }
  return { status: r.status, json, retryAfter: Number(r.headers.get("retry-after") || 0) };
}

// 1. The rule as SAVED: the CogniRunner validator on the transition, read from the published workflow.
async function savedRule() {
  const j = await jira("/rest/api/3/workflows", { workflowNames: [E.WORKFLOW] });
  for (const w of j.workflows || []) for (const t of w.transitions || []) {
    if (t.name !== TRANSITION) continue;
    for (const v of t.validators || []) {
      if (!/ai-text-field-validator/.test(v.parameters?.key || "")) continue;
      const c = JSON.parse(v.parameters.config);
      return { prompt: c.prompt, fieldId: c.fieldId || "description", enableTools: c.enableTools === true, version: w.version?.versionNumber };
    }
  }
  throw new Error(`No CogniRunner AI validator on "${TRANSITION}" in workflow "${E.WORKFLOW}"`);
}
// 2. The test set: every issue in the filter; the expected verdict is its label.
async function testSet() {
  const j = await jira("/rest/api/3/search/jql", { jql: `filter = ${E.FILTER} ORDER BY key ASC`, fields: ["summary", "labels"], maxResults: 100 });
  return (j.issues || []).map((i) => ({ key: i.key, expected: i.fields.labels.includes("expect-block") ? "BLOCK" : i.fields.labels.includes("expect-pass") ? "PASS" : "?" }))
    .sort((a, b) => Number(a.key.split("-")[1]) - Number(b.key.split("-")[1]));
}
// 3. One dry run through the test door. A 429 means the token's AI allowance is spent: wait for Retry-After.
async function runOne(rule, prompt, issue) {
  const body = { kind: "validation", issueKey: issue.key, prompt, fieldId: rule.fieldId, enableTools: rule.enableTools };
  if (E.CANDIDATE_MODEL) body.ai = { provider: E.CANDIDATE_PROVIDER || "openrouter", model: E.CANDIDATE_MODEL };
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const t0 = Date.now(); const r = await rules("POST", "resource=rules&action=test", body);
    if (r.status === 429) { const s = r.retryAfter || 60; console.error(`  429 on ${issue.key}: allowance spent, waiting ${s} s`); await sleep(s * 1000); continue; }
    if (r.status === 202) return { ...issue, verdict: "QUEUED", seconds: 0, servedBy: "", reason: `self-hosted provider: poll ${r.json.poll}` };
    const res = r.json?.result || {};
    const verdict = r.status !== 200 ? `HTTP ${r.status}` : res.success && res.isValid === true ? "PASS" : res.success && res.isValid === false ? "BLOCK" : "NOT JUDGED";
    return { ...issue, verdict, seconds: Math.round((Date.now() - t0) / 100) / 10, servedBy: r.json?.ai?.servedBy?.map((s) => s.model).join(",") || res.modelUsed || "",
      reason: res.reason || res.error || r.json?.error || "" };
  }
  return { ...issue, verdict: "GAVE UP", seconds: 0, servedBy: "", reason: "429 four times" };
}

const who = await rules("GET", "resource=whoami");
if (who.status !== 200) { console.error(`whoami: HTTP ${who.status} ${who.json?.error || ""}`); process.exit(1); }
const spend = who.json.aiSpend || {};
console.log(`Token role: ${who.json.effective?.role} · AI actions used ${spend.window?.used}/${spend.window?.limit} in this 10-minute window, ${spend.today?.actions}/${spend.today?.limit} today`);
const rule = await savedRule();
const prompt = E.ADD_SENTENCE ? `${rule.prompt} ${E.ADD_SENTENCE.trim()}` : rule.prompt;
const set = await testSet();
console.log(`Rule: ${E.WORKFLOW} · ${TRANSITION} · reads ${rule.fieldId} · workflow version ${rule.version}`);
console.log(`Prompt (${E.ADD_SENTENCE ? "saved + one sentence, this run only" : "as saved"}): ${prompt}`);
console.log(`Model: ${E.CANDIDATE_MODEL ? `${E.CANDIDATE_MODEL} (these requests only; the site's model is not changed)` : "the site's own model"}`);
console.log(`\n${pad("KEY", 13)} ${pad("EXPECTED", 8)} ${pad("VERDICT", 10)} ${pad("SECS", 5)} ${pad("SERVED BY", 28)} REASON`);
let match = 0, slowest = 0;
for (const issue of set) {   // one at a time: calls in parallel made the model slower and one timed out
  const r = await runOne(rule, prompt, issue); const ok = r.verdict === r.expected; if (ok) match++; slowest = Math.max(slowest, r.seconds);
  console.log(`${pad(r.key, 13)} ${pad(r.expected, 8)} ${pad(r.verdict + (ok ? "" : " ✗"), 10)} ${pad(r.seconds, 5)} ${pad(r.servedBy, 28)} ${r.verdict === "PASS" ? "" : r.reason}`);
}
console.log(`\n${match} of ${set.length} match · slowest ${slowest} s`);
process.exit(match === set.length ? 0 : 1);

Why one request at a time? In the video session, four calls in flight pushed the site's model to 16.1 seconds. With eight in flight, one call ran past 20 seconds and came back as a timeout. My first run's eight calls added up to about 26 seconds, which I can live with.

It exits 0 when all verdicts match and 1 when one doesn't, so the same file works as a step in CI.

Check: open a new terminal, where the variables from step 2 aren't set, and run node gate-test.mjs there. It should print Set JIRA_SITE and stop, which tells you Node found the file and nothing was called.

Step 4. Run the LLM regression testing baseline on the site's model

With the variables from step 2 exported:

This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes.

KEY           EXPECTED VERDICT    SECS  SERVED BY                    REASON
COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.5   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      2.8   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that Nora was in hospital for a week in August.

Check: the first line should show Token role: admin (or editor), the Rule line should show your transition and reads description, and the Prompt line should be your saved prompt word for word. Under SERVED BY you see the model that answered.

So that's two misses. I ran the same command twice more and got 7 of 8 both times. All three rounds blocked the flu vaccination, each time with a different sentence ("Remove the detail about free flu vaccination, which is medical information." was round two). Parental leave was blocked in the first round and passed in the next two.

If I'd stopped after one run I would have gone off to fix parental leave, which was right two times out of three. So run the baseline at least three times and sort the misses into stable ones and flaky ones before you touch anything. Here the stable one is COGTEST-3056.

Watch the allowance while you do. A token gets 20 AI actions per 10 minutes, and three rounds of eight are 24. I used a new token for each pair of rounds. With one token, the script is written to wait out the Retry-After the API sends (I never let it get that far, so I haven't watched it do so).

Step 5. Switch from OpenAI's model to Claude for one request, not the whole site

Same command, one more variable:

CANDIDATE_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 node gate-test.mjs

Token role: admin · AI actions used 8/20 in this 10-minute window, 8/200 today

This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes.
Model: anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 (these requests only; the site's model is not changed)

COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.2   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      3     anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the sentence stating that Nora was in hospital for a week in August, as it discloses medical information.
COGTEST-3051  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.8   anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5   Remove the reference to the knee operation and physiotherapist clearance, which is medical information about an employee.

Check: the Model line should show "these requests only", and SERVED BY should show the candidate on all eight rows. Then open CogniRunner's Settings. You should see the model for validators and rules still set to the one you started with.

Both models here are reached through OpenRouter. For eight requests the model id changed, and the site's provider didn't change at all. To try a model through another provider, say Anthropic directly, that provider needs a key saved in Settings first. A request can't bring one. I tried sending an apiKey in the body and got a 400 that says so (it's in the troubleshooting list).

I picked the candidate id by reading OpenRouter's models API that morning. anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 was the newest Claude Haiku id on it, listed as created on 7 October 2026. I compared the two models as models a few days ago, and this page isn't a second round of that. Eight requests on one prompt is far too little to rank anybody, and I ran the candidate on the unfixed rule once.

Step 6. Read the mismatch: the rule did not say what HR meant

Here is the Description of the request the site's model kept blocking:

Change: free flu vaccination for everyone in the Lisbon and Berlin offices, run by our occupational health provider on 18 and 19 November; budget 1,950 EUR for up to 150 people.
Effective date: 18 November 2026
Approver: Ines Kowalczyk (Head of People)
Reason: it is optional and no one's answers or records come to People Ops; last year 96 people took part.

And the rule says to fail a request that holds "health or medical information about anyone: an illness, injury, surgery, sick leave, diagnosis or treatment". A vaccination is a treatment. Read literally, the site's model has a case.

What did HR mean, though? They want to stop a manager typing somebody's hospital stay into an approval request. GDPR's definition of data concerning health is "personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, which reveal information about his or her health status". A vaccination is a health care service. But a programme open to 150 people, with no list of who went, reveals nobody's health status. That reading is mine and I'm no lawyer, but it's the one our People Ops example is built on.

The rule left room for both readings, and I think each model took one. Swapping the model would have hidden that, and the next model update could bring it back.

Our video session tried three sentences before the one that worked. Sentence one fixed the flu request and tipped a return from maternity leave into a block. That happened in all 3 runs on the site's model and 1 of 3 on the candidate. Sentence two named parental and maternity leave outright and made the site's model worse (it scored 4 and 5 of 8). Sentence three left a burnout-risk request wrong in 2 runs of 2. Traceloop's guide has a line for this: "A simple wording change can dramatically alter an LLM's performance, fixing one issue while silently creating another." So after an edit I run all eight again.

This one held:

A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is.

Step 7. Run prompt regression testing after the one-sentence fix

Try the sentence before saving it. ADD_SENTENCE appends it to the saved prompt for this run, and the workflow isn't touched:

ADD_SENTENCE="A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is." node gate-test.mjs

This is an HR request a manager sends to People Ops for approval. When it fails, say in one short sentence which detail must be removed. Otherwise it passes. A benefit, programme or budget for a whole team is not health information about anyone; only a detail about a named person's or a relative's illness, injury or treatment is.
Model: the site's own model

KEY           EXPECTED VERDICT    SECS  SERVED BY                    REASON
COGTEST-3049  PASS     PASS       3.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3050  BLOCK    BLOCK      3.3   openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that Nora was in hospital for a week in August.
COGTEST-3051  BLOCK    BLOCK      4     openai/gpt-6-luna            Remove the detail that his physiotherapist cleared him to fly only after the knee operation.
COGTEST-3052  PASS     PASS       4.7   openai/gpt-6-luna            
COGTEST-3053  PASS     PASS       3.7   openai/gpt-6-luna

8 of 8 match · slowest 4.7 s

Two more rounds on the site's model gave 8 of 8 again. So did one round with CANDIDATE_MODEL set.

Then save it. In Jira's workflow editor, open the transition, expand its validators, open the CogniRunner validator, add the sentence at the end of the Validation prompt, click Update and then Update workflow. The video does this at 1:32. In our session's notes the saved rule carried the new prompt at once, so treat it as live for the next person who moves a request. To undo it, take the sentence out the same way. The session put the old prompt back between takes.

Run both commands once more, without ADD_SENTENCE:

node gate-test.mjs
CANDIDATE_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 node gate-test.mjs

The last line of each, as mine printed:

8 of 8 match · slowest 3.5 s
8 of 8 match · slowest 5.1 s

Check: the Rule line should show the workflow version one higher (mine went from 1079 to 1080). Its Prompt line should show "as saved" and end with the new sentence.

Step 8. Switch the site's model and read the audit log

In Settings, set the model for validators and rules to the candidate and click Save models (2:28 in the video). Then run the plain command again:

node gate-test.mjs

Model: the site's own model

8 of 8 match · slowest 9.4 s

Those are the Model line and the last line. SERVED BY read anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 on all eight rows with no CANDIDATE_MODEL set. That 9.4 seconds was the slowest call of the morning.

Open the Audit log and search for your provider's name.

Check: you should see a row labelled AI model changed that reads "Set the OpenRouter model to anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 (was openai/gpt-6-luna)." Under it there's one row per candidate test: "Tested a validator on COGTEST-3056 with OpenRouter (anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5), 1 AI call; the site's own provider was not changed."

You get a row for each test that ran on another model, and none for tests on the site's own model. I counted: 24 rows for the 24 candidate tests (three rounds of eight) plus one for my wrong model id, and nothing for the 84 dry runs that named no other model (seven rounds of eight on gpt-6-luna, the one after the switch, and 20 calls I made to find where the allowance stops). That makes sense to me. A test on another model sends issue text somewhere the site doesn't normally send it, and that's the thing an auditor would ask about.

Those rows name the issue because of this exercise, by the way. When the video session first ran it on 1.33.5, eight tests in a row produced eight identical audit rows and you couldn't tell which request's text had gone out. Back then a token's usage also counted zero AI tokens for validator tests, and the token card's title mentioned listeners and scheduled jobs but said nothing of rules. Those were three bugs of ours, and 1.34.0 fixes them.

Run the set more than once: one verdict flipped in 1 of 3 rounds

I don't think a model that gives a different answer on the same text breaks the test, but you need to know it's happening. On the rule as saved, the parental leave request flipped in 1 of my 3 rounds. With the sentence it passed in all 4 of my rounds on the site's model (three unsaved, one saved). In the video session's files the same request, with the sentence, was wrong once in 13 calls on the site's model. That one miss arrived during a recording. They threw the take away. Across every request they tried with the sentence, the eight and the dropped candidates, the site's model was right in 163 of 164 calls.

One more thing a matching verdict doesn't tell you. The site's model blocked the reduced-hours request in all seven of its rounds, which matches the label. In two of them the reason named the wrong person, and one of those read "Remove the detail about Priya Raman’s burnout absence and phased return." The request is Amara Okafor's. Priya Raman is the approver. My script compares PASS and BLOCK and never reads the sentence, so it scored that as a match. If the wording of the refusal matters to you (it's what the person sees on the transition), read the REASON column yourself now and then.

Langfuse's write-up splits checks into "exact-match or deterministic assertions for structured outputs and business rules, and semantic evaluation when valid answers can differ in wording." A verdict against a label is the first kind. Judging the reason sentence would be the second kind, and this script doesn't attempt it.

If it didn't work

I sent each of these on purpose and got these answers from the API on 1.34.0.

What I sent What came back
A bearer value that isn't a CogniRunner token HTTP 401 {"error":"unauthorized"}
The 21st AI action on one token inside one 10-minute window HTTP 429, Retry-After: 218, "This API token has started 20 AI actions (listener tests, job runs, agent ticks, agent uploads) in the last 10 minutes, which is its limit. Try again in 218 seconds."
ai: {provider: "claude"} HTTP 400 Unknown AI provider "claude". Name one of: openai, azure, openrouter, anthropic, lmstudio, compatible, ollama, goose, atlassian, bedrock, gemini.
ai for Anthropic on a site with no Anthropic key HTTP 409 No Anthropic key is saved on this site, so nothing was sent.
ai carrying apiKey HTTP 400, reason key-not-accepted
A model id OpenRouter doesn't serve HTTP 200, with AI error (400): anthropic/claude-haiku-9.9 is not a valid model ID inside the result
No prompt in the body HTTP 400, reason bad-request, with missing: ["prompt"]

You'll meet the 429 first. A token gets 20 AI actions per 10 minutes and 200 a day. One round of 8 on each model is 16, so a third round inside the same window hits the limit. That window follows the clock: a token of mine that showed 16 used at 07:19 showed 0 at 07:23, after the :20 mark. For the app's other meter, see the rate limit tutorial.

Be careful with a wrong model id, because the HTTP status is 200. For that answer the script prints NOT JUDGED and counts a mismatch. It still took one AI action and wrote one audit row, which is the row you can see in the screenshot above.

If savedRule throws on JSON.parse, look at how your validator's config is stored in the workflow. It was plain JSON on both sites I read. I haven't checked a very large config.

What this set doesn't test

A validator reads one field. Mine reads Description, so a hospital stay typed into a comment or an attachment goes straight past it. Treat the check as a quality gate before HR approves. I wouldn't call it a security control.

A dry run takes as long as the model takes. A live transition allows 20 seconds. With a hosted provider like OpenRouter, a check that gets no answer in that time lets the transition through and the execution log says so. Self-hosted providers are different (LM Studio, Ollama, Goose Swarm or an OpenAI-compatible server). For those, 1.34.0 added a hold you can turn on. It refuses the transition while the check finishes in the background, and it's off by default. My slowest dry run was 9.4 seconds, so neither case came up. On a self-hosted provider the rule test answers with a task to poll, and this script prints QUEUED for that and doesn't poll.

I didn't make a real transition on this run. Our video session did, on 12 October, on the demo site. There the site's model blocked a copy of the flu request in the test and answered 400 on the real transition. With the candidate set, the test passed and the request moved for real. So I have one pair, a day old.

Jira has nothing like this built in that I could find. Atlassian has an evaluation feature for Rovo agents that takes a CSV of up to 100 prompts. It's for agents. Jira's nearest open request that I know of, JRACLOUD-98947, had 3 votes when I read it on 13 October.

What you have now

[[takeaways]]

  • A Jira filter that is your validator's test set: eight requests, each labelled with the verdict you expect.
  • An 80-line script that reads the saved rule from Jira, dry-runs it on each request and exits 1 on a mismatch.
  • A way to run the same set on another model with one variable and an admin token, while the site stays on its model.
  • A way to try a sentence with ADD_SENTENCE before you save it into the workflow.
  • An audit row for each test that ran on another model, naming the issue, and one for the switch.
  • A baseline you ran three times, so you know which misses are stable.

If you're about to change the model behind a rule people depend on, I'd build the eight requests today and run the baseline before reading anything else about the new model. And if the script is going to call a Forge app from CI for more than a test, the OAuth 2.0 tutorial shows the other way in.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

title: Stop asking AI to “write tests for this” — 5 prompt changes that make generated tests catch bugs
description:
AI coding tools can write a test file in seconds. Most developers have also noticed the catch: the tests are green, coverage goes up, and a real bug ships straight through them.

That usually isn’t the model being bad at testing. It’s the prompt leaving out everything that makes a test valuable. Here are five changes I now make to every testing prompt — in Cursor, Claude Code, ChatGPT or Copilot Chat — and why each one matters.

1. Give it the intent, not just the code

If the only input is the implementation, the implementation becomes the spec. The model reads what the code does and asserts exactly that — including any bug.

Add one or two sentences of intent, in your own words:

What this code is supposed to do:
prorate() returns the charge for the unused part of a billing period,
rounded half-up to cents. It never returns a negative amount.

Now the model has something to test against. If it notices the code can return a negative amount, it has a reason to flag it instead of pinning it.

2. Ask for a plan before any code

“Write tests” invites volume. Ask for a behaviour inventory and a case table first:

Before writing any code:
1. List every observable behaviour (return values, errors, side effects, branches).
   Mark anything that looks like a bug with [SUSPECT].
2. For each behaviour, list cases: happy path, boundaries (empty, zero, one, max,
   off-by-one), invalid input, error paths.
Show me both. Then write the tests.

A case table takes ten seconds to review. If the boundaries or error paths are missing, you see it immediately — instead of discovering it in 300 lines of generated code.

3. Attach one existing test file

Describing your conventions (“we use Vitest, factories live in tests/factories, we name tests like…”) works poorly. Showing them works well:

Conventions to copy: tests/billing/invoice.test.ts
Match its imports, helpers, file location and naming.

This one line stops most of the “new assertion library, different folder, duplicate fixtures” problems.

4. Write the rules the model would otherwise break

Models take the shortest path to green. State the boundaries explicitly:

Rules:
- Do not change production code to make tests pass. If the code seems wrong, report it.
- Expected values must be hand-computed literals, not the same formula as the code.
- Only stub true boundaries: clock, randomness, network, third-party APIs.
- No fixed sleeps. Freeze time and seed randomness explicitly.

The second rule alone removes a whole class of “mirror tests” — tests that agree with the implementation by construction and can never fail for the reason you care about.

5. Make it justify every test

End with a self-check:

For each test, state in one line the specific bug it would catch.
Delete any test whose answer is "none" or "same as another test".
List behaviours from the case table that still have no test.

Then do the human version: break the code on purpose (flip a < to <=, return early) and see whether anything goes red. If nothing does, the tests are decoration.

Different jobs need different prompts

The five changes above are the skeleton. The process section should change with the job:

  • Integration/API tests: rank scenarios by risk — contract, validation, auth (including another tenant’s resource), persistence, idempotency, downstream failure — and forbid mocking the database.
  • E2E: separate checkpoints worth asserting from incidental UI, use role/label locators, and ask for an explicit flake review.
  • Legacy code: write characterization tests that pin current behaviour, bugs included, before you change anything.
  • Flaky tests: ask for ranked hypotheses with evidence and a reproduction step. Retries and longer sleeps are not fixes.
  • Coverage: treat the percentage as one input to a risk-based plan, not the goal.

The shape that works

Every good testing prompt I use has the same five parts:

Part Purpose
Role “Senior engineer writing tests a skeptical reviewer will accept”
Context Target, intent/spec, framework, one example test, what not to touch
Process Numbered steps, plan before code
Output contract Exact sections and tables to return
Rules The shortcuts the model must not take

Try it on a function you know well. If the case table finds an edge case you hadn’t written down, it’s working.

I packaged the eight prompts I use for this — unit, spec-first, integration/API, E2E, characterization, flaky diagnosis, coverage planning and mock boundaries — plus two checklists, a Cursor rule and a PDF guide, as the **AI Test Generation Prompt Pack: https://lirenplr.gumroad.com/l/cuofwr. Everything above works without it.

— Pluto · @Mars_Peakul

title: Revolutionizing CAD: Why CADCraft is the Open-Source AutoCAD Alternative You Need!
description:
Quick Summary: 📝

CADCraft is an open-source, clean-room reimplementation of AutoCAD, built entirely in Rust. It aims to provide a fast and familiar CAD experience with features like command line, object snaps, layers, dimensions, and hatches, running on multiple operating systems and the web.

Key Takeaways: 💡

  • ✅ CADCraft is an open-source, free alternative to AutoCAD, built from scratch in Rust.

  • ✅ It offers a familiar workflow with features like command line, layers, object snaps, and DXF support.

  • ✅ Leverages Rust for high performance, memory safety, and reliability in CAD applications.

  • ✅ Runs natively on macOS, Windows, Linux, FreeBSD, and even in the browser via WebAssembly.

  • ✅ A community-driven project with immense potential for developers and designers to contribute and benefit.

Project Statistics: 📊

  • ⭐ Stars: 3845
  • 🍴 Forks: 1758
  • ❗ Open Issues: 138

Tech Stack: 💻

  • ✅ Rust

Are you tired of the hefty subscription fees and proprietary lock-in that come with traditional CAD software? Do you dream of a powerful, familiar design tool that's truly yours, running on any platform you choose? Well, fellow developers and designers, get ready to be excited because a game-changer has arrived on GitHub: CADCraft!CADCraft isn't just another CAD program; it's a bold, open-source clean-room reimplementation of Autodesk AutoCAD, rebuilt from the ground up in pure Rust. Imagine all the core functionalities you rely on – the command line, object snaps, layers, dimensions, hatches, blocks, and DXF drawing support – but now, it's completely open, free, and community-driven. This project aims to bring the robust and intuitive AutoCAD workflow we all know and love into the open-source world, without compromising on power or familiarity.One of the most exciting aspects of CADCraft is its foundation in Rust. For those unfamiliar, Rust is a programming language renowned for its performance, memory safety, and concurrency. This means CADCraft is designed to be incredibly fast, reliable, and efficient, handling complex designs without breaking a sweat. It's a modern approach to a classic problem, leveraging cutting-edge technology to deliver a superior user experience.And the accessibility? It's phenomenal! CADCraft runs natively across all major operating systems: macOS, Windows, Linux, and even FreeBSD. But wait, there's more – it also runs directly in your browser via WebAssembly! This cross-platform compatibility means you can work on your designs from virtually anywhere, on any device, without needing expensive licenses or specific hardware setups. This flexibility alone is a massive win for individual designers and small teams alike.For developers, the open-source nature of CADCraft opens up a world of possibilities. You can inspect the code, contribute to its development, and even build custom extensions or integrations tailored to your specific needs. This isn't just a tool; it's a platform that you can help shape and evolve. The ArtCraft team is fostering a vibrant community, inviting artists and creators from all backgrounds to join the conversation and contribute.In essence, CADCraft is poised to democratize computer-aided design. It offers a powerful, familiar, and free alternative to proprietary software, built with modern performance in mind and accessible across all platforms. While still in early development, its potential is immense, and it's definitely a project you'll want to keep an eye on – or even better, get involved with!

title: Kakeizu: a local Gemma reads the gas station's receipts, and check digits catch its mistakes
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.

A friend of mine works at a gas station in the interior of São Paulo. The station has a system, but closing the day still means checking a pile of paper against it by hand: card machine slips, fiscal coupons, Pix receipts, the odd cheque. Amount, date, payment method, one receipt at a time.

Still checking, one receipt at a time.

So I built Kakeizu: you photograph the receipt on your phone, a Gemma model running on the shop's own computer reads it, the domain checks every digit it can, and a person confirms. Nothing is confirmed automatically, and nothing leaves the shop.

The AI suggests, the domain validates, the human decides.

What I Built

Kakeizu reads a photo of a Brazilian payment receipt with Gemma running on the shop's own computer, checks every digit it can, and waits for a person to confirm. The name is Kakeibo (家計簿, the Japanese household ledger) plus Kakuzu, the Akatsuki member who only thinks about money.

It reads the receipts a Brazilian gas station or corner shop sees every day:

Receipt What the domain checks
NFC-e / NF-e (fiscal coupon or invoice) 44-digit access key with a mod-11 check digit; its month and CNPJ must match the other fields
Card machine slip (Stone, Cielo, Getnet) the store's CNPJ check digits, the authorization code
Pix receipt the 32-character end-to-end ID
Cheque the three mod-10 check digits of the magnetic line (CMC-7); a date over 6 months old gets a warning
Any of them amount, date never in the future, the same photo or the same key never twice

Confirmed receipts feed a daily summary and a sales report by hour, weekday, payment method, installments and card brand. An NFC-e and the card slip of the same sale are paired, so the sale counts once.

Who pays for it: the owner of a small shop who closes the cash register by hand. Cloud receipt readers exist, but they charge per document and want the shop's sales, suppliers and customers on someone else's server.

The cloud vendor, sending this month's per-document invoice.

Kakeizu costs nothing per document and nothing leaves the shop. The owner pays for the setup and the hour it saves at the end of every day, not for each photo.

Demo

Kakeizu runs on the shop's computer and never on a public server, so there is no live link: the demo is the flow below, recorded with the anonymized sample receipts from the repository.

Today, on the phone. The photo goes up and the list comes back at once. The model reads in the background (dashed violet line), and the line prints itself in when it is done. Orange means "needs you", double green means confirmed.

Review. The photo sits next to everything the model read, and every field that failed a check says why. This template NFC-e has no CNPJ and a zeroed access key, so it cannot be confirmed as read.

Look at the amount, too. The photo says 146,46; the model read 4,00. That number is well formed and no check digit covers it, so only the person comparing it with the photo catches it.

Sales report. Confirmed sales by hour, weekday, payment method, installments and card brand, with a slip paired to its NFC-e so each sale counts once.

Code

mauricioandrade / kakeizu

Local-first receipt reader for small shops: Gemma (via Ollama) reads NFC-e, card slips, Pix and cheques; check digits validate; a person confirms. Java 25 + Quarkus. Nothing leaves the machine.

🧾 Kakeizu

A receipt reader for small shops that runs 100% locally.
A photo goes in, structured data comes out, and nothing leaves the owner's machine.

Kakeibo (家計簿, the Japanese household ledger) + Kakuzu (the Akatsuki member who only thinks about money)

🤖 The AI suggests · 🧮 the domain validates · 🧑 the human decides

📑 Contents

  • 😩 The problem
  • 🔄 How it works
  • 📸 Screenshots
  • 🚀 Running
  • 📊 Sales report
  • 🎯 Accuracy on real receipts
  • 🔓 Why open matters
  • 📄 License

😩 The problem

The owner or manager of a gas station, a corner shop or a small restaurant gets dozens of receipts a day: NFC-e, card machine slips, Pix receipts, the odd cheque. Closing the day means typing amount, date and who paid or got paid into a spreadsheet, one receipt at a time.

Cloud tools do this, but they want the business's financial data on…

View on GitHub

Apache 2.0. The README has the setup for both Ollama layouts on Windows + WSL2, the accuracy tables and the backup script.

How I Built It

The whole design is one sentence: the AI suggests, the domain validates, the human decides.

Layer Choice
Model Gemma 4 (gemma4:e4b), vision, thinking on, temperature 0
Inference Ollama on the Windows side, reached from WSL2
Glue Quarkus 3.40 with quarkus-langchain4j-ollama
Language Java 25
Storage PostgreSQL + Flyway
Web Qute templates + htmx, no frontend build

Gemma reads, and nothing it returns is trusted

Gemma gets the photo and a field guide in the system prompt, and returns plain strings: type, amount, date, counterparty, tax ID, unique ID, time, payment method, installments, card brand. Those strings never touch the database as values. They go through the same domain objects a person's correction goes through, and each object checks what it can.

The check digits are the trick. They exist to catch a cashier's typo, and they catch a model's misread just as well. A CNPJ, for instance, carries two mod-11 digits:

public record Cnpj(String value) {
    public Cnpj {
        value = value.replaceAll("[.\\-/\\s]", "").toUpperCase();
        if (!value.matches("[A-Z0-9]{12}\\d{2}")) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("CNPJ must have 14 characters");
        }
        if (checkDigit(value, FIRST_WEIGHTS) != valueAt(value, 12)
                || checkDigit(value, SECOND_WEIGHTS) != valueAt(value, 13)) {
            throw new InvalidValueException("CNPJ check digits do not match: " + value);
        }
    }

    // Each character is worth ASCII - 48, so the new alphanumeric CNPJ
    // (issued since July 2026) and the old all-digit one share one rule
    private static int valueAt(String cnpj, int index) {
        return cnpj.charAt(index) - '0';
    }
}

On a real Cielo slip, Gemma read the CNPJ as 13.438.977/0001-00 three times out of three. The real one is 13.458.397/0001-01. The check digits rejected it every time, and the review screen put the photo next to the red field. It also read the authorization code 375579 as 375759. No check digit covers that code, so nothing caught it. That is exactly why a person confirms every receipt.

How often it is right

Seven receipts, three readings each, run through the app's own validation:

Of 210 fields Count
Right on the first reading 200 (95%)
Wrong, and the domain flags that field 3
Wrong, in a receipt the domain blocks for another field 4
Wrong, and nothing flags it 3

Then a real gas station's day: a Getnet debit slip (3 of 3 ready to confirm as read), an NFC-e paid in cash (2 of 3, the 44-digit access key right every time), a Pix paid on the card machine, and a handwritten cheque. The small sample is the honest caveat: treat these as a sanity check, not a benchmark.

What I learned the hard way

Every field must be required in the schema. Ollama uses the JSON schema LangChain4j sends as a grammar, and by default no field is required. Gemma's reasoning said "installments = 5" and the answer simply left the key out. Marking every field @JsonProperty(required = true) took the share of right fields from 88% to 95%.

The model cannot say null. With every field required and typed as a string, it writes the word "null", or just ", ", when a field is not on the receipt. The adapter turns those into a missing field.

Thinking matters more than speed. With thinking off, a reading takes about 2 seconds instead of 15. It also took an item price as the NFC-e total and the card brand as the store name: wrong values in a valid format, which no check digit can catch. Thinking stayed on.

Temperature 0 is not deterministic. The same photo gave different answers between runs, so every receipt in the accuracy tables was read three times. The NFC-e template's total, 146,46, came back right, then as 46,46, then as 4,00, in different runs.

Tell the model where things are printed. It returned the NFC-e note number as the access key until the prompt said the key is all 44 digits, in groups of four, under "Consulte pela Chave de Acesso". A Pix paid on the card machine kept coming back as a card slip until the prompt described it: an "ID/TRANSAÇÃO" and no card brand, no card number, no authorization code.

Some mistakes need the calendar, not a check digit. On a handwritten cheque, Gemma read the year "26" as 2022, three times out of three. A cheque that old can no longer be cashed in Brazil, so a cheque dated more than six months ago now gets a warning on review.

Nobody waits for the model

A warm reading takes about 15 seconds on a consumer GPU. I measured where it goes: the image takes under a second, and the rest is Gemma writing about 750 tokens of reasoning at 75 tokens a second. Turning the reasoning off cost accuracy, and asking for shorter reasoning changed nothing, so the app stopped waiting for it instead. The upload saves the photo and returns at once, a background worker reads it, and the line on today's list updates itself. If Ollama is down, the receipt still goes to review, empty, to be typed from the photo.

Java 25 doing real work

The receipt is a sealed interface with one record per type, so the mapper and the reports are exhaustive switches with record patterns and no default. Up to five photos can go in one upload: each is saved and queued on its own virtual thread inside a StructuredTaskScope (a preview in Java 25), so one bad photo never stops the others. A correlation id rides a ScopedValue into every log line of an upload, across the forked threads and into the background reader.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because with a closed API, this product could not be sold to the person it is for.

The data cannot leave the shop. A day of receipts is the business itself: what it sold, to whom, through which bank, from which supplier, and sometimes a customer's name and partial CPF. An open-weight Gemma on the shop's own GPU means the photos, the database and the model all stay on one computer. There is no privacy policy to read because there is no third party.

The cost does not grow with the work. A gas station photographs dozens of receipts a day. A per-call API turns every one of them into a line on a bill, so the busiest day costs the most. Local inference costs the electricity of about 15 seconds of GPU per receipt.

The model is a setting. KAKEIZU_MODEL swaps Gemma for any Ollama vision model, and the same check digits judge the new one. When a better small open model ships, the shop gets it for free.

Open models let me see why they fail. Because I ran Gemma myself, I could turn thinking on and off, read its reasoning, and see it decide "installments = 5" and then drop the key. That is how the required-schema fix was found. A closed endpoint would have shown me only a wrong answer.

My First User

My first user is that friend at the gas station. Midway through the week they sent me photos of a real day's receipts: a Getnet debit slip, a Pix paid on the card machine, an NFC-e paid in cash, and a handwritten cheque. The station stays anonymous here, and none of those receipts are in the repository.

That one batch changed the product more than any test I wrote:

  • A Pix paid on the card machine has no end-to-end ID. The slip prints the machine's own transaction ID, so the Pix ID became optional and the prompt learned to tell this slip from a card slip.
  • Gas stations take cheques. Kakeizu now reads them, checks the magnetic line's three check digits when it is typed, and treats the cheque the other way round: the CNPJ on it is the payer's, so a cheque from another company is a sale. Shops that do not take cheques switch this off.
  • The NFC-e access key is printed far from its label. The prompt now says exactly where to find all 44 digits.

After testing it, they want to use it every day.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 (gemma4:e4b) runs locally through Ollama and does all the reading: receipt type, amount, date, counterparty, tax ID, access keys and payment details, from phone photos of thermal slips, fiscal coupons and handwritten cheques. Kakeizu is built around both its strengths and its mistakes: thinking stays on because it buys accuracy, and every field it returns goes through deterministic checks before a person confirms it.

title: Before you read a codebase, draw its shape
description:
Open a 300-file repo and the first thing you feel is vertigo. Which files are the project, and which are examples, assets, lockfiles, vendored junk? That ratio decides almost everything about how you read what follows, and most repos hide it.

So I wrote a small tool (shape.py, Python stdlib only) that prints a structural read of any folder in one screen: file count, total size, source size, the weight that isn't source, the top-level layout, and the largest source files.

Then I pointed it at repos I thought I already knew.

OpenAI's swarm is 6 files

The multi-agent framework everyone links. Here is the whole read:

shape  repos/swarm
  288 files   961.9k total   131.0k source
  entry points: pyproject.toml

  source languages
    python         131.0k   100%

  weight (not source)
    image 411.3k, config 394.5k, docs 24.4k, other 603B

  top level
    examples/    236 files   497.4k
    assets/        3 files   411.3k
    README.md      1 files    16.5k
    swarm/         6 files    16.1k
    tests/         5 files     9.3k
    logs/         31 files     7.7k

The framework itself, swarm/, is 6 files and 16 KB. The repo is 962 KB. The rest is examples/ (236 files) and assets/ (411 KB of images).

So when someone says "I read the swarm source," the honest part of that sentence is how little there was to read. The intimidating repo and the actual framework are two different sizes.

tqdm is one big file

A library most of us import without thinking. 97 files, 333 KB of source. The largest single file, tqdm/std.py, is 56.7 KB:

     56.7k  tqdm/std.py
     10.8k  tqdm/cli.py
     10.6k  tqdm/notebook.py
      9.6k  tqdm/contrib/concurrent.py

That's 17% of all source in one file. The thing you import to draw a progress bar is, structurally, one long file plus a thin perimeter.

Neither number is a judgement. std.py being large doesn't mean it's bad; a battle-tested progress bar has a lot of edge cases. The point is that this is knowable in about two seconds, and almost nobody knows it before they start.

Why "one screen"

The first question about unfamiliar code isn't "is it good." It's "where is the thing." A structure read answers that before you spend an afternoon in the wrong directory.

It's also the fastest way to catch a lie. I once had a repo whose docs directory was billed as a source module; the read showed 89% of "source" was misclassified, and I only saw it because I ran the tool on a repo I didn't write. Repeating that on strangers' repos is what fixed it.

What it isn't

It doesn't read semantics and it won't find your bug. It's a map, not a review. Treat a clean shape as "I know where to start," never "I know it's fine."

If you have a repo you've been avoiding because you can't tell where to start, I run these on request. Structural read, one screen, answered against whatever question you actually have about the codebase. Email me: katy-10@ilands.app

title: Your Docker Container Is Running… So Why Is Your Application Down?
description:
A practical guide to debugging Docker containers like a real DevOps engineer.

Imagine this situation.

You deploy your application using Docker. Everything looks perfect.

docker ps

Output:

CONTAINER ID   IMAGE          STATUS
a1b2c3d4       my-app:latest  Up 10 minutes

Your container is running. Docker reports no problems. You feel confident.

Then someone messages you:

"Hey, the application is down. Can you fix it?"

You check the container again.

Still running.

You restart it.

Still broken.

You rebuild the image.

Still broken.

Welcome to the real world of DevOps. 😅

A running container does not necessarily mean a healthy application.

Let's learn how to troubleshoot Docker like an engineer instead of randomly restarting containers.

🧠 1. Understand the Difference Between Running and Healthy

Docker can tell you whether a container's main process is running. It cannot automatically guarantee that your application is working correctly.

For example, your container might be running while:

  • The application cannot connect to its database.
  • The API is returning HTTP 500 errors.
  • The application is listening on the wrong port.
  • A required environment variable is missing.
  • The application is responding too slowly.
  • A dependency has crashed.

Think of it like this:

Docker container: RUNNING ✅
Application:       BROKEN  ❌
Database:          UNREACHABLE ❌
Users:             ANGRY 😭

Your job as a DevOps engineer is to discover where the actual failure is happening.

🔍 2. Start With the Logs

Never begin by randomly restarting everything. First, investigate.

Check the application logs:

docker logs my-app

Follow logs in real time:

docker logs -f my-app

Show the latest 100 lines:

docker logs --tail 100 my-app

Include timestamps:

docker logs -t my-app

Look for errors such as:

Connection refused
Database connection failed
Address already in use
Permission denied
Missing environment variable

Pro tip: Logs are often the fastest way to identify the root cause. Read them before changing anything.

🛠️ 3. Inspect the Container

Sometimes the problem is not visible in the logs.

Inspect the container configuration:

docker inspect my-app

Check its state:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}}' my-app

Check its exit code:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' my-app

Check whether Docker reports it as healthy:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' my-app

Note: The last command requires a health check to be configured. Without one, Docker may return an empty value.

Inspecting a container helps you investigate its configuration, state, network settings, mounts, and other runtime details.

🌐 4. Check Port Mapping

Your application might be listening on port 8080 inside the container, but you may have exposed a different port—or forgotten to publish it.

Check published ports:

docker port my-app

Start a container with the correct mapping:

docker run -d \
  --name my-app \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  my-app:latest

The mapping follows this pattern:

-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT

For example:

Your browser
     |
     v
localhost:8080
     |
     v
Docker host port 8080
     |
     v
Container port 8080
     |
     v
Application

Remember: publishing a port does not make an application listen on that port. Your application must actually be listening on the expected interface and port.

💾 5. Check Whether the Container Is Running Out of Resources

An application can become slow or crash when it runs out of memory or struggles with CPU usage.

Check resource consumption:

docker stats

Example:

CONTAINER     CPU %     MEM USAGE / LIMIT
my-app        95%       480MiB / 512MiB
database      15%       300MiB / 1GiB

In this hypothetical example, my-app is consuming almost all its memory limit.

Investigate further before changing resource limits. A memory leak, excessive traffic, or inefficient application code could be the real problem.

Useful commands:

docker ps -a
docker system df
docker events

These help you inspect container states, Docker disk usage, and Docker events.

Important: Avoid running docker system prune -a as a routine troubleshooting step. It can remove unused images and other resources you may still need.

❤️ 6. Add a Docker Health Check

Here's one way to improve your container monitoring.

A health check lets Docker periodically test whether an application is responding to a defined check.

Example Dockerfile:

FROM nginx:alpine

COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s \
  --timeout=5s \
  --start-period=10s \
  --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -q -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1/ || exit 1

This example uses a lightweight Nginx image and checks whether its HTTP endpoint responds successfully.

Check the health status:

docker ps

A configured health check can report statuses such as:

starting
healthy
unhealthy

But remember: a health check is only as good as the test you define. A successful HTTP response does not necessarily mean every feature of your application is working.

🔗 7. Investigate Network and Database Problems

Suppose your application depends on a PostgreSQL database.

Your application container is running, but database connections keep failing.

First, inspect your Docker networks:

docker network ls

Inspect the network used by your containers:

docker network inspect my-network

If both services need to communicate, make sure they share an appropriate network.

With Docker Compose, services on the same default network can usually reach each other using their service names.

Example:

services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:password@db:5432/appdb
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb

Here, db is the database service name.

Important: This is a learning example, not a production-ready configuration. Use secrets rather than hardcoded passwords, persistent storage for database data, and application-level retry logic. Also, depends_on alone does not guarantee that PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.

🧪 8. Build Your Own Docker Troubleshooting Checklist

When an application goes down, follow this order:

  1. Check the state: docker ps -a
  2. Read the logs: docker logs my-app
  3. Inspect configuration: docker inspect my-app
  4. Check resource usage: docker stats
  5. Verify port mapping: docker port my-app
  6. Investigate networking: docker network inspect my-network
  7. Test the application endpoint: use curl or an appropriate health check.
  8. Apply a fix: change the configuration or code based on evidence.
  9. Verify recovery: repeat the relevant tests and check the logs.

The goal is not simply to make the error disappear.

The goal is to understand why it happened and how to prevent it from happening again.

🚀 9. Take It Further: Build a Container Monitoring Project

Want to turn this knowledge into a portfolio project?

Build a small Docker monitoring stack using:

  • Docker Compose to run the services.
  • Prometheus to collect metrics.
  • Grafana to visualize performance.
  • cAdvisor to expose container resource metrics.
  • Alerting to notify you about important failures.

A simplified architecture:

Docker Containers
       |
       v
    cAdvisor
       |
       v
   Prometheus
       |
       v
     Grafana
       |
       v
 Dashboards & Alerts

Track CPU usage, memory consumption, container restarts, and application availability.

Document one simulated failure, your investigation, the root cause, and the fix. That gives you a concrete project to discuss during DevOps interviews.

🎯 Final Thoughts

Docker makes packaging and running applications easier, but it does not eliminate production problems.

Good DevOps engineers do not blindly restart containers. They collect evidence, understand system behavior, identify root causes, and verify their fixes.

The next time someone says, "The container is running, but the application is down," you'll know where to start.

Your challenge: Run a Docker container, inspect its logs, configure a health check, and deliberately introduce a failure in a local test environment. Can you diagnose the problem without immediately restarting the container?

Share what you discover in the comments! 👇

title: Vercel CDN no longer caches responses with Vary: Cookie
description:
Vercel CDN no longer caches origin responses when Vary includes Cookie.

Vary tells a cache which request headers may change the response. Because cookies often contain visitor-specific values, varying by Cookie can create many cache entries that are rarely reused. The response is still served normally but isn't stored for future requests.

You can identify these responses by checking the x-vercel-cache header and Runtime Logs. The header is set to MISS, and Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie as the cache reason.

If Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie for a route you expect to be cached, check the Vary header returned by your origin:

  • If the response is the same regardless of cookies, remove Cookie from Vary. Vercel CDN can then cache it if it meets the other caching requirements.

  • If the response depends on cookies, keep Cookie in Vary and use Cache-Control: private to prevent personalized responses from being stored in the shared CDN cache.

Caching behavior for other supported Vary headers is unchanged.

Learn more about high-cardinality headers and the vary_key_denied cache reason.

title: Building MoneyMov — A Free Personal Finance Tracker with MERN
description:
I recently built MoneyMov, a free personal finance tracker to help people understand where their money is going.

The idea was simple:

Know where your money moves.

Instead of building another complicated finance application, I wanted to create something simple enough for everyday use.

What Is MoneyMov?

MoneyMov is a personal finance tracker where users can manage their:

  • 💰 Income
  • 💸 Expenses
  • 📊 Spending categories
  • 📈 Investments
  • 🤝 Committees / Bachat
  • 💵 Lending / Loans

The additional modules are optional, so users can use only the parts they actually need.

For example, someone may only want to track expenses, while another person may also want to keep track of investments or money they've lent to someone.

Tech Stack

I built the application using the MERN stack:

  • MongoDB — Database
  • Express.js — Backend API
  • React.js — Frontend
  • Node.js — Backend runtime
  • Axios — API requests
  • Tailwind CSS — UI styling
  • Recharts — Charts and data visualization
  • JWT — Authentication
  • bcrypt — Password hashing

The frontend is deployed on Netlify, while the backend is deployed on Render.

Authentication & Security

One of the things I focused on while building the project was authentication and basic application security.

Some of the things implemented include:

  • Password hashing with bcrypt
  • HTTP-only authentication cookies
  • JWT-based authentication
  • Protected API routes
  • Environment variables for secrets
  • Forgot-password functionality
  • Hashed password-reset tokens
  • Token expiration
  • Helmet
  • Rate limiting
  • MongoDB input sanitization
  • HTTP Parameter Pollution protection
  • User-specific data access

For example, the backend doesn't simply trust the user ID coming from the frontend.

The authentication middleware verifies the token and gets the authenticated user's ID before accessing their data.

Spending Visualization

One of the dashboard features is a category-based spending breakdown.

For example:

Shopping      Rs 400
Food          Rs 1,200
Transport     Rs 500
Bills         Rs 2,000

The data is also visualized using a pie chart so users can quickly understand where most of their spending went.

Some Challenges

Building the application wasn't completely straightforward.

I ran into several issues during development and deployment, including:

  • MongoDB Atlas connection timeouts
  • Render deployment and networking issues
  • SMTP connection problems
  • Authentication cookies
  • CORS configuration
  • Express proxy configuration
  • SPA routing on Netlify
  • Mobile authentication behavior
  • Handling protected routes correctly

These problems were actually a useful part of the project because they forced me to understand what was happening beyond simply writing React components.

For example, deploying a MERN application locally is very different from deploying the frontend and backend separately.

You have to think about how each layer communicates in production:

Frontend
   ↓
API requests
   ↓
Backend
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Database

Each layer introduces its own configuration, security considerations, and potential issues.

Why I Built It

I wanted to build something that was more than just another CRUD project.

While working on MoneyMov, I got to work with:

  • Authentication
  • REST APIs
  • MongoDB
  • Deployment
  • Security
  • Email verification
  • Password reset
  • Data visualization
  • Responsive UI
  • Production debugging

It also gave me a chance to work through problems that don't usually appear when everything is running on localhost.

What's Next?

There are still several things I want to improve.

Some ideas include:

  • Better dashboard analytics
  • More useful financial reports
  • Improved mobile experience
  • Better transaction filtering
  • More visualizations
  • Exporting financial data
  • Additional security improvements
  • Performance improvements

MoneyMov is currently free, and my goal is to keep the core personal finance features simple and accessible.

Final Thoughts

This project started as an idea for a simple expense tracker, but it gradually became a much bigger learning experience.

The biggest thing I learned is that building a real application isn't only about making the UI work.

You also have to think about:

Authentication → Security → APIs → Database → Deployment → Users

That's where a lot of the interesting engineering problems begin.

If you're also building a MERN application, I'd be interested to hear what problems you've run into while deploying your project.

Try MoneyMov

MoneyMov is free to use. Give it a try and let me know what you think!

🔗 Website: https://moneymov.netlify.app

MoneyMov — Know where your money moves.

title: AI Gateway adds confidence-based decision fallbacks
description:
AI Gateway can now escalate a decision request to a fallback model when the primary model's answer trips a confidence condition you set.

Conditions can be combined, so an escalation can depend on more than one signal. The plain model names you already list in models keep catching outright errors, so existing fallbacks are unaffected. Confidence conditions cover Choice and Score questions. Boolean questions escalate on a probability range instead.

Set the fallback by adding one conditional object to providerOptions.gateway.models. Requests without it keep their existing behavior.

Leave out question and the condition checks every question of the matching type, so { confidenceBelow: 0.6 } escalates when any Choice or Score answer falls below 0.6.

Because a triggered fallback runs a second decision, it bills both stages.

Learn more in the decision fallbacks documentation, or see them in practice for mapping CSV columns and flagging UI copy for translation review.
