title: An approve button needs to check that the approver didn't file the request
description:
Expense reports, refunds, access requests and production deploys often go through an approval step. The check behind the Approve button is usually a role check: can this user approve requests of this type? A manager can, so the call goes through.

Problems start when that manager files a request of their own. They submit an expense, open the approvals queue, and their own request is sitting there with an Approve button next to it. If the endpoint only looks at the role, clicking it works. Delegation opens the same hole from another side: the manager goes on vacation, hands approvals to a teammate, and the teammate approves a request they filed last week.

In the approve handler, load the request and reject the call when the approver (or the person they're acting for) is the requester. Do this next to the role check, on the server. Hiding the button in the UI is nice, but anyone can still send the request with curl.

Also pin the approval to what was approved. If the requester can edit the amount after approval, they can get a $40 expense signed off and change it to $4,000. Store a version number or hash on the request and have the approval apply to that version only, so any later edit sends it back to pending.

To test it, give a user approver rights, submit a request as that user, then call the approve endpoint on it directly. If you get a 200, self-approval is open.

title: ISTQB CT-PT in Code: The Load Profile, Throughput Math and Script Behind Half the Exam
description:
The ISTQB Performance Testing exam (CT-PT) asks 40 questions in 90 minutes, and 20 of them come from one chapter of the syllabus: Performance Testing Tasks. You pass with 26 points out of 40. So the best use of your study time is to work that chapter once with your own hands: write an operational profile, turn it into a load profile, do the throughput arithmetic, and put the result in a script.

This post does that with one small example. The scripts use k6 because it is free and reads like plain JavaScript. The syllabus names no tool at all, so treat the code as a way to make the ideas concrete, not as exam content.

What does the CT-PT exam look like?

CT-PT is a 40-question multiple-choice exam in ISTQB's Specialist stream, and you need the Foundation Level certificate before you can sit it. The figures below are from the ISTQB page for Certified Tester Performance Testing, read on 14 October 2026.

Item Value
Questions 40
Points 40, one per question
Passing score 26 points (65%)
Time 90 minutes, or 113 if the exam is not in your native language
Prerequisite Certified Tester Foundation Level (CTFL)
Syllabus v1.0, released in 2018
Fee Not listed by ISTQB. The exam provider you book with sets it

Where do the 40 questions come from?

Half of them come from chapter 4. ISTQB publishes the split per chapter in its Exam Structures and Rules tables (v1.19, August 2026), and the syllabus gives each chapter a minimum training time.

Chapter Questions Training time
1. Basic Concepts 6 60 min
2. Performance Measurement Fundamentals 4 55 min
3. Performance Testing in the Software Lifecycle 7 195 min
4. Performance Testing Tasks 20 475 min
5. Tools 3 90 min

The same tables sort the questions by thinking level. Two are K1 (remember), 25 are K2 (understand), 4 are K3 (apply) and 9 are K4 (analyze). Ten of the 13 apply and analyze questions sit in chapter 4.

There is a timing catch in those tables. They allow 1 minute for a K1 question, 2 for K2, 3 for K3 and 4 for K4. For CT-PT that adds up to 100 minutes of nominal work (2 + 50 + 12 + 36) in a 90-minute exam. The only place to win the ten minutes back is the 25 K2 questions, so the definitions have to come fast.

How do you turn usage data into an operational profile?

An operational profile is one distinct pattern of interaction with the application, and you build it in three steps: decide what data you need, gather it, and evaluate it. The syllabus asks for three kinds of data: the user personas and their roles, the generic tasks each role performs, and the estimated number of users for each role per unit of time.

It also tells you where to look. Sources include workshops with product owners and sales managers, functional specifications and user stories, usage logs from the current system, and watching real users work through tasks. The approach is top-down. Start with broad profiles and split one further only if a test objective needs it.

Here is the example used in the rest of this post. It is a made-up ticket shop, not something from the syllabus.

Operational profile One session Think time Volume at peak
Visitor Open the home page, list events, open one event 9 s after each step 100 sessions open at any moment
Buyer Log in, search, add to cart, pay 9 s after each step 19,800 orders an hour

Two profiles are enough. The learning objective for this section is K4, analyze, so be ready to read usage data like this and say which profile matters. The syllabus singles out profiles whose tasks run often, need critical or frequent transactions between components, or move large volumes of data.

How do you build a load profile from the operational profiles?

A load profile says how many instances run each operational profile, and how that number changes over the test. When the instances stand for people, they are called virtual users. The syllabus lists four shapes to combine: ramp-ups, ramp-downs, steps, and predefined distributions that copy a daily or seasonal cycle.

Section 4.2.4 of the CT-PT syllabus builds a stress profile from two parts. A step of 100 virtual users runs the first operational profile for the whole test as background load. A second group ramps up to 220 virtual users, holds for two hours, and ramps down. Added together, they give the system three hours of stress.

In k6 that diagram is two scenarios:

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    background: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',   // a step: all 100 start at once
      exec: 'visit',
      vus: 100,
      duration: '3h',
    },
    stress: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      exec: 'buy',
      startVUs: 0,
      stages: [
        { duration: '30m', target: 220 },  // ramp-up
        { duration: '2h', target: 220 },   // hold
        { duration: '30m', target: 0 },    // ramp-down
      ],
    },
  },
};

The syllabus does not print the ramp lengths. Thirty minutes each is my choice, so that the two ramps and the two-hour hold fill the three hours.

How many virtual users give the throughput you planned?

Divide the number of virtual users by the time one pass takes, and you have the throughput. The syllabus writes it like this:

system throughput = virtual users / (processing time + think time)

It then warns that a user count alone is not a measure of load. Its example: 500 users who each run a short query every minute produce 30,000 queries an hour. The same 500 users running one query an hour produce 500. The user count is the same and the load differs by a factor of 60.

Now the ticket shop. A buyer session has four transactions. Say each takes 1 second to process and is followed by 9 seconds of think time. That is 4 seconds of processing and 36 seconds of thinking, 40 seconds a pass.

const targetPerSecond = 19800 / 3600;        // 5.5 orders a second
const pass = 4 + 36;                         // seconds for one session
const users = targetPerSecond * pass;        // 220 virtual users

// The system slows down under stress: 4 s of processing becomes 14 s
const slowPass = 14 + 36;                    // 50 seconds
const actual = users / slowPass;             // 4.4 orders a second
console.log(users, Math.round(actual * 3600));   // 220 15840

The same 220 virtual users now place 15,840 orders an hour, 20% under the plan. This is the sentence in the syllabus that candidates skip: when processing time goes up, throughput can drop even if everything else stays the same. Your stress test eases off at the moment it should push hardest.

The syllabus explains why. A typical test setup is a closed system: the number of users is fixed, so when all of them are waiting for a response, no new user can arrive. Many public systems are open systems, where new users keep arriving while the current ones wait. The k6 documentation describes the same split in its page on open and closed models. To hold the arrival rate steady, swap the executor:

stress_open: {
  executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
  exec: 'buy',
  rate: 11,
  timeUnit: '2s',          // 11 sessions every 2 seconds = 5.5 a second
  duration: '2h',
  preAllocatedVUs: 300,    // 5.5 x 40 s = 220 in flight, 5.5 x 50 s = 275
},

What does the syllabus expect inside a performance test script?

It expects three parts: an initialization section, a main section that can run many times, and a clean-up section. k6 uses different names for the same idea. Its test lifecycle has init code and setup() for initialization, a scenario function for the main part, and teardown() for clean-up.

import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, group, sleep } from 'k6';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';
import { scenario } from 'k6/execution';

// 1. Initialization: load test data and declare metrics. No requests here.
const buyers = new SharedArray('buyers', () => JSON.parse(open('./buyers.json')));
const orderTime = new Trend('order_time', true);
const BASE = 'https://shop.test.example';
const JSON_HEADERS = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' };

export function setup() {
  // Still initialization. A broken system gives no useful load numbers.
  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/api/health`);
  if (res.status !== 200) throw new Error('system under test is not ready');
}

// 2. Main section: one pass is one buyer session.
export function buy() {
  const me = buyers[scenario.iterationInTest % buyers.length];   // parameterization
  let spent = 0;

  group('order', () => {                                         // outer transaction
    let res = http.post(`${BASE}/api/login`, JSON.stringify(me), { headers: JSON_HEADERS });
    check(res, { 'logged in': (r) => r.status === 200 });
    const token = res.json('token');                             // correlation
    const headers = { ...JSON_HEADERS, Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` };
    spent += res.timings.duration;
    sleep(9);                                                    // think time

    res = http.get(`${BASE}/api/events?city=${me.city}`, { headers });
    const eventId = res.json()[0].id;                            // correlation again
    spent += res.timings.duration;
    sleep(9);

    group('add to cart', () => {                                 // nested transaction
      res = http.post(`${BASE}/api/cart`, JSON.stringify({ eventId, seats: 2 }), { headers });
      check(res, { 'two seats in cart': (r) => r.json('seats') === 2 });
      spent += res.timings.duration;
    });
    sleep(9);

    group('pay', () => {
      res = http.post(`${BASE}/api/orders`, null, { headers });
      check(res, { 'order confirmed': (r) => r.json('status') === 'CONFIRMED' });
      spent += res.timings.duration;
    });
  });

  orderTime.add(spent);    // response time of the whole order, think time left out
  sleep(9);
}

// 3. Clean-up
export function teardown() {
  http.post(`${BASE}/api/test-data/reset`);
}

The visit function for the background scenario is left out to keep this short. Five things in the script map to lines of the syllabus:

  • Transactions. A transaction runs from the start of a request to the end of the processing it triggers. Transactions can be nested, so one run measures each step and the order as a whole. That is what the inner groups and the order_time metric do.
  • Think time. The syllabus states that transaction response time plus think time equals elapsed time. The sleep(9) calls are the think time, and the trend records response time only.
  • Timers. Time a meaningful unit of work, such as submitting an order. A protocol-level script like this one measures server and network time only. A script that drives the GUI measures end to end.
  • Result verification. Checking the HTTP return code is the minimum. The check calls look at what came back: two seats, a confirmed order.
  • Scripts are software. Review the script and test it with the whole range of input data before trusting its numbers.

Correlation gets its own paragraph in the syllabus. If you record a session at the protocol level, the recording holds identifiers that were valid once, such as the login token above. They have to become variables that are filled from each response. The syllabus says incorrect or missing correlation is the main reason recorded scripts fail on playback, and the k6 docs carry examples of extracting tokens from responses for JSON and for form fields.

Parameterization is the other half. Run every virtual user with the same name and the same data, and the results mislead in one of two directions. The data may be fully cached, which makes the system look faster than production. Or users may queue on a lock for the same record, which makes it look slower.

That is why the script reads buyers from a file and gives each iteration a different one. The k6 page on data parameterization shows the same pattern with JSON and CSV files.

Why does the report use a percentile and not only an average?

Because the average can be skewed by outliers, and the syllabus says so in those words. It lists four ways to report transaction response time: minimum, maximum, average and a percentile such as the 90th. Ten response times show the problem:

const ms = [180, 190, 200, 210, 220, 230, 240, 250, 2600, 4100];
const avg = ms.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / ms.length;
const pct = (q) => [...ms].sort((a, b) => a - b)[Math.ceil(q * ms.length) - 1];
console.log(avg, pct(0.5), pct(0.9));   // 842 220 2600

Eight of the ten users waited a quarter of a second or less. Two waited seconds. The average of 842 ms describes none of them. The median shows the typical user, and the 90th percentile shows the tail.

The syllabus adds two points that are easy to miss. A goal of 100% compliance is not recommended, because the resources it needs may be too large for a minor gain to users. And you look at the status of the virtual users before anything else. A failed transaction takes far less time than a completed one, so failures can make the transactions-per-second figure look better than it is.

In k6 you write the goal down as a threshold, and the run fails when it is missed. The thresholds reference lists the aggregation methods you can use.

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],     // under 1% failed requests
    order_time: ['p(90)<3000'],         // 90% of orders within 3 s of response time
  },
};

Which test type fits which objective?

The syllabus defines seven types under the umbrella term performance testing, and chapter 1 carries six questions. The first two columns below follow section 1.2. The third column is my shorthand for the load profile each one usually needs.

Type What it focuses on Typical load shape
Load Handling increasing levels of anticipated, realistic load Ramp up to the expected level and hold
Stress Peak loads at or beyond the specified limits, or reduced resources Ramp past the expected maximum
Scalability Meeting future needs, such as more users or more stored data Repeated runs with growing load or data
Spike Sudden bursts of peak load, then a return to a steady state Step up, step down
Endurance Stability over a period that fits the system's use Flat load for a long time
Concurrency Specific actions that happen at the same moment Many users doing one thing at once
Capacity How many users or transactions it supports while meeting its objectives Step up until an objective fails

Endurance testing is the one that finds resource problems which build up slowly. The syllabus gives memory leaks, database connections and thread pools as its examples.

A short video on the exam

ProcessExam's channel has a three-minute video with five preparation tips for CT-PT. It covers the study side that this post leaves out.

How should you split your study time?

Follow the syllabus's own weighting. The five chapters add up to 875 minutes of minimum training time, about 14 and a half hours, and chapter 4 takes 475 of them. A plan that gives chapter 4 half of your hours matches both the training time and the question count.

A split that works in practice:

  1. Chapters 1 and 2 first, in one sitting. They are ten questions, mostly definitions, and they are where you win back time on exam day.
  2. Chapter 4 over three or four sittings, with a keyboard. Build one operational profile, one load profile and one script for a system you know.
  3. Chapter 3 next. Its seven questions are about risk: which performance risks belong to which architecture, and which test activity belongs to which lifecycle phase.
  4. Chapter 5 last. Three questions on tool types and how to judge whether a tool suits a project.

If you want every learning objective in one place to tick off, the CT-PT syllabus topics listed by chapter on ProcessExam work as a checklist.

Finish with ISTQB's own sample exam, which is a free download on the certification page. Time yourself at 90 minutes. The answer sheet gives the learning objective and K-level of every question, so note which level each wrong answer was.

For the weeks before the exam, this CT-PT preparation playbook goes deeper into planning and revision than a code walkthrough can.

Frequently asked questions

1. How many questions are on the ISTQB CT-PT exam, and what is the passing score?

The exam has 40 multiple-choice questions worth one point each, and you need 26 points to pass, which is 65%. You get 90 minutes, or 113 minutes if the exam is not in your native language.

2. Do I need the Foundation Level certificate before taking CT-PT?

Yes. ISTQB states that candidates must hold the Certified Tester Foundation Level certificate to gain the Performance Testing certification.

3. Does the CT-PT exam test a specific tool such as JMeter or k6?

No. The syllabus names no tool. Chapter 5 covers types of tools (load generators, load management consoles, monitoring tools) and how to judge whether a tool suits a project, and it carries 3 of the 40 questions.

4. Which chapter of the CT-PT syllabus has the most exam questions?

Chapter 4, Performance Testing Tasks, has 20 of the 40 questions. Chapter 3 has 7, chapter 1 has 6, chapter 2 has 4 and chapter 5 has 3.

5. Is the 2018 CT-PT syllabus still the current version?

Yes, as of 14 October 2026. The ISTQB certification page offers CT-PT Syllabus v1.0 (2018) as its syllabus download, and the Exam Structures and Rules tables dated August 2026 still list CT-PT with 40 questions and 90 minutes.

Written by the team behind ProcessExam, a practice-test site for process, project and software testing certifications. We are not affiliated with ISTQB.

Use timestamp attributes to show a campaign page only between two dates, run a Black Friday promotion, or target users who registered before a cutoff.

Configure a timestamp attribute

You can configure timestamp attributes in the dashboard or via the CLI.

In the Vercel dashboard, open Flags, select Entities, and create or select an entity. Add an attribute and set its data type to timestamp.

Or define the attribute with the CLI:

Whether you configure the attribute in the dashboard or CLI, your application must provide its value when evaluating a flag. The entity and attribute names must match your configuration, and the value must be a Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds.

This Flags SDK example passes the current time as system.time. Date.now() returns the required value in milliseconds. Keeping it inside dedupe() ensures that every flag evaluated during the same request uses the same time:

Add a targeting rule

In the dashboard, open the flag and add a targeting rule using the timestamp attribute. The rule compares the value from your application with a date and time you choose.

Rules support is after, is at or after, is before, and is at or before. The date and time picker uses your local timezone.

To add a time-based targeting rule with the CLI, use after, at-or-after, before, or at-or-before:

Learn how to provide entities in code and release a flag at a specific time, or read the Flags documentation.

title: The HttpClient Mistake That Can Slow Down Your .NET API
description:
An API can run smoothly during development and still struggle when traffic increases. Requests that take milliseconds locally may become much slower in production. Before investigating the database or server resources, it is worth checking how the application makes calls to external services.

One common issue is creating a new HttpClient for every outgoing request.

ASP.NET Core applications use HttpClient to communicate with payment gateways, authentication providers, third-party APIs, and other backend services. Creating and disposing of a client inside a frequently called method may seem reasonable, but it can prevent efficient connection reuse and contribute to socket exhaustion under heavy load.

Let's look at why this happens and how to manage HTTP connections properly in .NET.

THE HTTPCLIENT MISTAKE
Consider a method that retrieves customer details from another service:

public async Task<Customer?> GetCustomerAsync(int id)
{
   using var client = new HttpClient();
   var response = await client.GetAsync(
        $"https://customer-api/customers/{id}");
     response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
     return await response.Content
         .ReadFromJsonAsync<Customer>();
}

The method is easy to follow. It creates a client, sends a request, reads the response, and disposes of the client.

The problem is doing this every time the method runs.

Each HttpClient instance uses an underlying handler that manages its connection pool. When the application repeatedly creates clients with new handlers, it also creates and discards connection pools instead of reusing them effectively.

Under heavy traffic, this can increase connection overhead and contribute to socket exhaustion. Connections may remain in states such as TIME_WAIT after they are closed, adding pressure to available network resources.

Depending on the traffic and connection behavior, the application may experience slower requests or failed outbound calls.

WHY CREATING A CLIENT FOR EVERY REQUEST CAN BE A PROBLEM
Opening and managing network connections takes resources. Reusing connections helps reduce that overhead.

Imagine an e-commerce API that calls a payment service every time a customer checks out. If each checkout creates a new HttpClient with its own handler, the application may repeatedly establish connections instead of making better use of existing ones.

As traffic grows, this connection churn can become a performance issue.

That does not mean every short-lived HttpClient will immediately cause socket exhaustion. The impact depends on request volume, connection behavior, operating system resources, and how the application handles outgoing requests.

The key is to manage the underlying handlers and connection pools instead of creating a new client-handler pair for every request.

THE RECOMMENDED SOLUTION: IHTTPCLIENTFACTORY
ASP.NET Core provides IHttpClientFactory to create configured clients and manage their underlying handler lifetimes.

First, register a typed client in Program.cs:

builder.Services
    .AddHttpClient<CustomerService>(client =>
    {
      client.BaseAddress =
           new Uri("https://customer-api/");
    });

Then inject the HttpClient into the service:

public class CustomerService
{
   private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;
   public CustomerService(HttpClient httpClient)
   {
      _httpClient = httpClient;
   }
   public async Task<Customer?> GetCustomerAsync(
       int id,
       CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
   {
       using var response = await _httpClient.GetAsync(
            $"customers/{id}",
            cancellationToken);
       response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
       return await response.Content
           .ReadFromJsonAsync<Customer>(
                cancellationToken);
   }
}

The factory manages the underlying handlers, allowing their connection pools to be reused across client instances. It also makes it easier to configure different external services, add logging, and integrate resilience strategies.

This approach avoids creating a new handler and connection pool every time the service sends a request.

WHAT ABOUT A SINGLETON HTTPCLIENT?
IHttpClientFactory is not the only option. A long-lived HttpClient can also reuse its connection pool effectively.

For example, an application can create a client using a configured handler:

var handler = new SocketsHttpHandler
{
   PooledConnectionLifetime =
       TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)
};
var client = new HttpClient(handler)
{
   BaseAddress = new Uri("https://customer-api/")
};

The five-minute lifetime is only an example. The appropriate value depends on the application's DNS requirements and infrastructure.

Why does this setting matter? A long-lived client does not automatically recreate its connections every time DNS records change. Setting PooledConnectionLifetime allows connections to be replaced after a configured period, helping the client pick up DNS changes when new connections are established.

Keep the client alive and reuse it rather than creating a new instance for every request.

For many ASP.NET Core applications, IHttpClientFactory is a convenient default because it works naturally with dependency injection and manages handler lifetimes. A long-lived client is also a valid choice when configured for the application's needs.

COMMON HTTPCLIENT MISTAKES TO AVOID
Correct client lifetime management is important, but it is not the only thing to consider when calling external services.

  • Handle unsuccessful responses: Use EnsureSuccessStatusCode() or check status codes explicitly.

  • Set timeouts: Choose reasonable limits so requests do not wait longer than the application can tolerate.

  • Pass cancellation tokens: Allow HTTP calls and response-reading operations to stop when cancellation is requested.

  • Use retries carefully: Retry transient failures with an appropriate resilience strategy. Consider the effects before retrying non-idempotent operations.

  • Reuse connections: Use IHttpClientFactory or a properly configured long-lived client.

  • Monitor outgoing requests: Track latency, timeouts, failures, and connection-related issues.

  • Configure clients by service: Use named or typed clients when different APIs need different base addresses, headers, or other settings.

These steps help you identify problems and handle failures without adding unnecessary load.

TESTING HTTPCLIENT PERFORMANCE
A connection-management issue may be difficult to notice during local development, where request volume is usually lower.

Test the application under realistic traffic and monitor:

  • Outbound HTTP request duration.
  • Request failures and timeout rates.
  • Socket and connection behavior.
  • CPU and memory usage.
  • Performance under concurrent requests.
  • Response times from external services.

If the API slows down under load, check its outgoing HTTP calls before assuming the database is responsible.

Compare measurements before and after changing the client lifetime strategy. This helps confirm whether connection management was actually contributing to the problem.

OUR TAKE
When building backend systems at Qodors, details like HTTP connection management deserve attention because they can affect how an application behaves under load.

The important distinction is between creating a client object and managing the handler and connection pool behind it. Understanding that difference helps developers choose an approach that fits their application.

For most ASP.NET Core projects, IHttpClientFactory is a practical starting point. A long-lived client can work just as well when connection lifetimes are configured appropriately.

Whichever approach you choose, test it under realistic traffic and monitor outbound requests. That is a more reliable way to find performance issues than guessing at the cause.

QUICK REFERENCE
Avoid creating a new HttpClient with a new handler for every request.
Use IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes.
Consider a long-lived client with PooledConnectionLifetime when appropriate.
Configure timeouts and pass cancellation tokens.
Handle HTTP errors and retries carefully.
Monitor outbound request latency and failures.
Test connection behavior under realistic traffic.

An API's performance depends partly on how efficiently it communicates with the services it relies on.

title: Node.js Kitchen Order Transitions: Publish to 2 Read-Only Kiosks
description:
An order board becomes a security problem the moment a browser can choose what it watches. For an e-commerce kitchen display, publish a deliberately small projection after the authoritative order change, bind the connection to one store on the server, and treat the browser's location parameter as untrusted input. The same capability boundary applies when a checkout flow creates a video room: the issued token should name one room and a limited action set, rather than become a general-purpose credential because a client supplied a nearby identifier.

Short answer: split the system into an authoritative write lane and a display-only delivery lane. The write lane commits an order transition and records a durable event; the delivery lane gives a kiosk only its assigned store's display projection. A reconnect may restore that projection, but it must not broaden the kiosk's authority.

This is a small distinction with a large failure domain. A screen that goes stale is an operations problem. A screen that receives another store's customer details is a boundary failure.

How should a Node.js service publish kitchen order transitions to a read-only kiosk?

Start with a bounded production scenario before debating transports: a kiosk is carried away while still authenticated, reconnects within five minutes, and tries a different store identifier in its first message. The acceptable result is boring: it sees only the projection for the store embedded in its server-issued session. It cannot turn a reconnect into a store selector.

The invariant is specific enough to test: possession of a display credential permits observation of one store's display projection and no state mutation. The storage concern here is less about the socket than about what has been persisted. If the session record stores store_id, display_id, expiry, and a display-only role, every later delivery decision can be derived from server state. If the server instead accepts store_id from each client message, the access check is distributed across call sites and will eventually be skipped.

The browser should never receive the full order row merely because its UI renders three fields. A display event might contain an opaque order label, a named transition, an event ID, and the server-accepted timestamp. It does not need payment status, customer contact data, internal notes, or fulfillment controls.

The same rule survives a change in medium. WebRTC 1.0 defines browser APIs for real-time communication; it does not decide which video room a participant may join. Room membership and permitted actions remain an application authorization decision, just as store membership remains one for a kitchen display.

Publish a projection after the commit

The preventative path starts at the database boundary. Write the accepted transition and an outbox record in one transaction, then have a worker fan out the display event. That makes the event durable before delivery is attempted, which matters when a process dies after commit and before it reaches a connected screen. The worker may retry and publish an event more than once, so the display contract needs a stable event ID and idempotent application.

Here is the part reviewers should be able to point at: authorization happens when the subscription is established, and later fan-out uses the stored scope rather than a client-provided store field.

package display

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

var ErrForbidden = errors.New("display session may not receive events")

type Session struct {
    DisplayID string
    StoreID   string
    CanView   bool
}

type Transition struct {
    EventID   string    `json:"event_id"`
    OrderView string    `json:"order_view"`
    State     string    `json:"state"`
    ChangedAt time.Time `json:"changed_at"`
}

type SessionStore interface {
    FindDisplaySession(ctx context.Context, sessionID string) (Session, error)
}

type Fanout interface {
    PublishToStore(ctx context.Context, storeID string, event Transition) error
}

func PublishAcceptedTransition(
    ctx context.Context,
    sessions SessionStore,
    fanout Fanout,
    sessionID string,
    event Transition,
) error {
    session, err := sessions.FindDisplaySession(ctx, sessionID)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !session.CanView {
        return ErrForbidden
    }

    // StoreID comes from the server-side session, never from a browser message.
    return fanout.PublishToStore(ctx, session.StoreID, event)
}

The function is intentionally narrow. In an implementation, the transaction that changes the order writes an outbox row; a separate consumer constructs Transition and calls the fan-out interface for authorized sessions or channels. The source of truth for the store is the committed order and the session, not the screen.

There is no universal freshness promise hiding in that pattern. Define one a kitchen can use, such as an accepted transition becoming visible on a connected authorized display within 2 seconds. Then measure commit-to-publish latency, outbox age, reconnect count, authorization denials, and the age of the last rendered event per display. An average across every store can look healthy while one busy location misses its window.

Two delivery lanes make failure behavior legible

The write lane accepts commands, validates the actor, applies the state transition, and appends an outbox record. The display lane reads only display projections, begins with a scoped snapshot, then receives newer events. A cursor or monotonically increasing sequence lets the server decide whether a display can catch up or needs a new snapshot; a timestamp from the browser cannot make that decision reliably.

Duplicates happen.

For a screen, a tiny receipt table keyed by event ID is often enough to make applying the same transition harmless. Retain those IDs for at least the reconnect and replay window that the product promises. Storage capacity follows from that chosen window: active displays multiplied by event rate multiplied by retention, plus headroom for bursts. This is capacity planning, not a transport feature.

Approach What the display receives Operational burden Boundary to verify
Scoped event stream A store-specific projection and cursor Connection lifecycle, replay, slow consumers Server binds scope at subscription time
Filtered snapshot polling The current projection at an explicit interval Repeated reads and accepted staleness Filter is enforced before data leaves the service
Direct record access A broad domain object Schema coupling and a much larger blast radius The display has no accidental mutation or cross-store path

WebSocket's protocol gives a bidirectional channel; Server-Sent Events provide a one-way stream over HTTP. Neither protocol supplies the authorization model, replay semantics, or SLO. A read-only kiosk normally benefits from a one-directional contract because its job is visible state, not a second administrative client. Use a bidirectional channel only when the display has a separately authorized need such as an explicit health signal.

How should a team choose the fan-out layer?

Choose from the recovery contract first, then from the on-call contract. The queue or log must preserve enough information to rebuild a display projection after a consumer or network failure, and the team must be prepared to operate its retention, backpressure, access controls, and upgrades. A managed transport can reduce runtime work while adding an external dependency and integration boundary. A self-operated transport keeps more control in-house while making patching and capacity review part of service ownership.

Option Useful property Cost the team owns Exit condition
Redis Streams Consumer groups and explicit pending entries Retention policy, memory pressure, recovery procedures Replay contract is tested independently of the client library
NATS JetStream Persisted streams with consumer delivery state Stream sizing, replication choices, operator knowledge Event schema remains portable outside the broker
Apache Kafka Partitioned durable logs and consumer offsets Cluster operations, partition planning, longer operational runway Ordering assumptions are explicit per partition key

Those are different operational shapes, not a ranking. For a modest board with a stated stale-data tolerance, filtered polling can be the most honest choice and may avoid a persistent connection fleet altogether. For high transition volume, isolate slow consumers so a stalled screen cannot delay the outbox worker or widen memory queues without a bound.

A persistent stream also has a clear limitation: it is a poor fit when the kitchen cannot support connection monitoring, replay testing, and bounded slow-consumer behavior. In that case, a filtered snapshot at a declared interval is the appropriate design because it turns freshness into an observable promise instead of an assumption. Direct record access is likewise a poor fit for a kiosk because it couples a display to the broader order schema and enlarges the authority that must be defended.

Video rooms follow the same decision rule: issue a short-lived, server-validated capability for a specific room and permitted media actions; do not let the client exchange a broad identity for a room name of its choosing. The mechanism differs, but the trust calculation does not.

Where this boundary is the wrong abstraction

A display projection is the wrong interface for a workflow that needs to acknowledge preparation, change an order, expose payment state, or search across stores. Give those actions their own command interface, actor authorization, audit trail, and failure handling. Folding them into the convenience channel turns a kiosk into a control plane.

It is also the wrong optimization when the system cannot state a recovery expectation. Before adding fan-out infrastructure, decide whether the kitchen needs a 2-second visible-state objective, a 30-second refresh interval, or something else the operation can observe. The smallest authority that meets that objective is the design to defend.

Sources

References:

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/
  • https://docs.nats.io/nats-concepts/jetstream
  • https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/

title: Route Cloudflare Worker issue alerts to an agent without polling
description:
A production Worker fails, but your agent does not know until its next scheduled check.

Polling can shorten that delay, but it also means repeated checks and another loop to maintain. Cloudflare now offers a different trigger: its API MCP server can send Workers Issues as MCP Events to a client webhook when a new or recurring issue appears.

That changes the first step in an incident workflow. Instead of asking an agent to keep checking for trouble, let an event wake a small, controlled investigation path. The event is a signal to start; it is not permission to let an agent make an unreviewed production change.

What Cloudflare’s event provides

Cloudflare’s October 13 changelog says Workers Issues detects production failures and groups related failures into issues without requiring an SDK or application wrapper. Its API MCP server exposes the event type cloudflare.alert.workers_observability_real_time_issue. An MCP client discovers it with events/list and subscribes with events/subscribe, scoped to an account or one Worker. When Workers Issues detects a new or recurring issue, the server sends a signed event to the client’s webhook. The changelog does not spell out the receiver’s signature-verification procedure, so use the validation method supported by your MCP Events client rather than guessing at headers or cryptographic details.

To use the event, enable Issues on the Worker and connect https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp to a client that supports MCP Events webhooks. The connection needs Notifications Write and Workers Observability Write permissions. Keep the scope as narrow as the investigation requires: one Worker is easier to reason about than every Worker in an account.

The key distinction is that the event starts work. Your application still owns how it validates the webhook, chooses an agent, gathers evidence, and handles any proposed action.

Build a bounded investigation path

A useful first version can follow five steps:

  1. Receive the webhook and verify the signed event before accepting it.
  2. Deduplicate it using the event’s stable identifiers and a short retention window, so retries do not start duplicate investigations.
  3. Create an incident record with the Worker, issue reference, event time, and verification result when those fields are present in the event.
  4. Give the agent only the issue data and tools it needs to inspect logs, source, or runbooks.
  5. Return a summary with evidence and a proposed next action for a person to review.

This is Cloudflare’s current integration, so confirm that your client supports its webhook-based MCP Events flow before building around it. The event should not become a direct command such as “fix production.” A recurring issue may be the same symptom with a different cause. Let the agent explain what it found, link to the relevant source material, and identify uncertainty. Keep deploys, data changes, and other consequential actions behind an explicit approval step.

Conceptual: verify, persist once and deduplicate deliveries.

A webhook receiver should also be designed for ordinary delivery problems. Persist the event before acknowledging it, make processing idempotent, and move slow investigation work to a queue or durable job. If the agent times out, retry the investigation from the saved incident record rather than relying on the event sender to replay the whole workflow. Record the event ID, attempt number, processing state, and final outcome so an operator can tell whether a duplicate delivery was ignored or a failed run needs attention.

Keep the agent’s investigation narrow

Start with the issue’s Worker and time window. Ask the agent to retrieve a bounded sample of the logs or traces that match that issue, then compare them with the relevant source and runbook. Avoid sending an entire account’s telemetry or a whole repository into every investigation by default.

Separate observation from action. Read-only tools can collect evidence and draft a diagnosis. A second, explicitly approved step can open a ticket, notify an owner, or propose a patch. If the event is recurring, let the agent compare it with the saved incident record before creating another alert. The person reviewing the result should see the issue, the time range, the evidence links, the suspected cause, and the specific action being proposed.

Treat event fields and retrieved content as data. A stack trace, log line, or linked page may contain text that looks like an instruction. It should not be allowed to change the agent’s permissions or tool policy. A wrapper around untrusted content can help mark it, but it is not a guarantee against prompt injection. Keep tool access constrained in the application itself.

Conceptual: narrow the evidence and keep consequential actions behind review.

Design for retries and duplicate events

An event-driven path still needs recovery behavior. The receiver can get the same event more than once; the agent can fail after starting; and a downstream tool may return an error after doing part of its work. Store the event and the investigation state separately from the agent’s transient conversation. Use an idempotency key for the incident record and for any external action that might be repeated.

For a practical state model, record received, verified, queued, investigating, needs_review, and closed. Make transitions explicit. For example, a failed log query should leave the incident in a retryable state, while a denied signature should be rejected and logged without invoking the agent. If you ask a person to approve an action, keep the request pending until the approval decision is recorded; do not infer approval from a timeout or a later event.

Also plan for a missing webhook receiver. Cloudflare’s changelog describes sending the event to a client webhook; it does not promise that your endpoint, queue, or agent will always be available. Monitor delivery and processing separately, alert on a backlog, and provide a manual route to inspect the issue from the Cloudflare dashboard. Event delivery removes a polling loop from your app; it does not remove the need to operate the receiving system.

When to add a polling fallback

A webhook is a good fit when the MCP Events client and receiver can remain available and your incident workflow benefits from prompt notification. Polling can still be a reasonable fallback if your client cannot receive MCP Events webhooks or if your operational environment requires periodic reconciliation.

If you keep a reconciliation job, make it slower than the normal event path and compare known issue IDs rather than starting a fresh investigation for every poll. That gives you a way to detect missed deliveries without making constant checks the primary trigger. Measure event delivery delay, duplicate rate, queue age, investigation completion rate, and the number of human-approved actions. Those measures show whether the event path is actually reducing the time from issue detection to useful triage.

Start with one Worker

Pick a Worker with a known runbook and a clear owner. Enable Issues, subscribe to that Worker’s event scope, and first route the webhook to a receiver that only verifies, stores, and acknowledges events. Add one read-only investigation tool after the receiver is stable. Review a few real incidents before enabling more tools or widening the subscription.

This sequence keeps the first deployment reversible. You can inspect what the event contains, see how often it repeats, and test whether the agent’s summaries help the on-call person before automating any further step. For a related integration decision, see our guide to adding GitHub Copilot’s agent runtime to an owned app; the question there is how to host the agent loop, while this workflow covers how a production issue starts an investigation.

If you need a starting interface for incidents, projects, or teams, the SaaS Dashboard kit is an optional editable app starting point. It does not include Cloudflare Workers Issues, MCP Events, webhook verification, or agent wiring; those integrations remain application work. Check current kit pricing before choosing a starting point.

Conceptual: treat event and retrieved content as data; constrain agent tools.

Sources

  • Cloudflare: Cloudflare API MCP server sends Workers Issues as MCP Events — checked October 14, 2026.

title: JPG vs PNG: What Is the Difference? A Complete Guide
description:
Images are an essential part of our digital lives. Whether you are sharing photos, creating presentations, uploading documents, or designing graphics, choosing the right image format can make a noticeable difference.

Two of the most widely used image formats are JPG (also called JPEG) and PNG. Although both formats store digital images, they work differently and are designed for different purposes.

So, what is the difference between JPG and PNG? Which format offers better image quality, smaller file sizes, and more flexibility?

In this guide, we will compare JPG vs PNG, explore their advantages and disadvantages, and help you choose the right format for your needs.

What Is JPG?

JPG, short for Joint Photographic Experts Group, is one of the most common image formats used for digital photography and online images.

JPG uses lossy compression, which reduces file size by removing some image data. This process makes JPG files smaller and easier to upload, download, email, and share.

Although compression can reduce image quality, JPG images often look very good at reasonable compression levels.

Advantages of JPG

  • Smaller file sizes: JPG images generally require less storage space than PNG images of similar dimensions.
  • Ideal for photographs: JPG works well for landscapes, portraits, product photos, and other realistic images.
  • Easy to share: Smaller files are convenient for websites, social media, and email attachments.
  • Broad compatibility: JPG is supported by almost all modern devices, browsers, and image-editing applications.

Disadvantages of JPG

  • Repeatedly saving an edited JPG can reduce image quality.
  • JPG does not support transparent backgrounds.
  • Fine text, sharp edges, and simple graphics may show compression artifacts.

Best uses for JPG: Photographs, blog images, product pictures, social media posts, and images where smaller file sizes are important.

What Is PNG?

PNG stands for Portable Network Graphics. It is a popular image format known for preserving image details and supporting transparent backgrounds.

Unlike JPG, PNG uses lossless compression. This means the compression process preserves the original image data, so saving an image as PNG does not introduce the same type of quality loss associated with JPG compression.

PNG is particularly useful for graphics that contain text, icons, logos, illustrations, and sharp edges.

Advantages of PNG

  • High image fidelity: Lossless compression preserves image details.
  • Transparent backgrounds: PNG supports transparency, making it useful for logos, icons, and layered designs.
  • Sharp text and graphics: It works well for screenshots, diagrams, charts, and interface elements.
  • Repeated saving: Saving a PNG does not progressively degrade image quality through lossy compression.

Disadvantages of PNG

  • PNG files are often larger than JPG files, especially for photographs.
  • Large files may take longer to upload or download.
  • PNG is not always the most efficient format for photo-heavy websites.

Best uses for PNG: Logos, screenshots, digital illustrations, diagrams, transparent graphics, and images containing text.

JPG vs PNG: Key Differences

Understanding the differences between JPG and PNG makes it easier to select the right format for a particular task.

Feature JPG PNG
Compression Lossy Lossless
Image quality Some data may be lost Preserves image data
File size Usually smaller for photos Often larger for photos
Transparency Not supported Supported
Photographs Excellent choice Supported, but may create larger files
Logos and icons Less suitable for transparency Excellent choice
Screenshots with text Compression may blur details Preserves sharp details
Website use Great for photographs Great for graphics and transparent images

Keep in mind that file size depends on the image content, dimensions, compression settings, and export options. Neither format will always produce the smallest file in every situation.

JPG vs PNG: Which Has Better Image Quality?

The answer depends on the type of image and what you need to preserve.

JPG can produce excellent-looking photographs while keeping file sizes small. However, because it uses lossy compression, fine details may be lost, especially when the image is saved repeatedly at lower quality settings.

PNG preserves image data through lossless compression. This makes it a strong choice for screenshots, text-heavy graphics, charts, and images with sharp lines.

For example, consider a screenshot containing small text. A heavily compressed JPG may introduce blurry edges around letters, while a PNG can preserve those edges more accurately.

However, a PNG photograph is not automatically more visually appealing than a high-quality JPG. For many photographs, JPG offers an excellent balance between visual quality and file size.

Choose PNG when preserving exact image details matters. Choose JPG when you want good photographic quality with a smaller file.

JPG vs PNG: Which Has the Smaller File Size?

File size is another important difference between these formats.

JPG usually produces smaller files for photographs because its lossy compression is designed to reduce image data efficiently. This makes it useful for websites, online portfolios, and image collections.

PNG often produces larger files for photographs because it preserves image data. However, for graphics with large areas of solid color, simple shapes, or limited color variations, PNG can be reasonably compact.

A smaller file can improve upload speed, reduce storage requirements, and make sharing easier.

If you need to send several images as one document, converting JPG or PNG images into a PDF may also help organize them into a single file. The resulting PDF size will depend on the conversion settings and the images themselves.

When Should You Use JPG?

JPG is generally the better choice when file size and photographic content are your main concerns.

Use JPG for:

  • Digital photographs and travel pictures.
  • Product images for online stores.
  • Blog featured images and photographic content.
  • Social media photos.
  • Email attachments containing pictures.
  • Image collections where storage space matters.

For example, if you want to upload a photograph to a website, JPG can help keep the file relatively small while maintaining good visual quality.

When Should You Use PNG?

PNG is a better choice when image details, sharp edges, or transparency are important.

Use PNG for:

  • Logos with transparent backgrounds.
  • Screenshots containing text.
  • Charts, diagrams, and infographics.
  • Icons and interface elements.
  • Digital artwork with sharp edges.
  • Graphics that require lossless saving.

For example, if you are preparing a company logo for a presentation, PNG can preserve its details and transparent background without requiring a solid-colored background behind it.

Can You Convert JPG to PNG Without Losing Quality?

You can convert a JPG image into PNG, but converting the file does not restore image data that was already lost during JPG compression.

When you save a JPG as PNG, the new file uses lossless compression. This prevents additional lossy compression from being introduced by the PNG format itself, but the original JPG's compression artifacts remain.

Similarly, converting PNG to JPG can reduce the file size, but it may also introduce quality loss and remove transparency.

For the best results, keep an original high-quality source file whenever possible. Choose your export format based on how the image will be used rather than assuming that one format is always better.

Can You Convert JPG or PNG Images to PDF?

Yes. Both JPG and PNG images can be converted into PDF documents.

Converting images to PDF is useful when you need to share multiple pictures as a single file, submit scanned documents, organize receipts, or prepare images for printing.

A PDF can also make it easier to keep multiple pages together in a consistent document format.

Here are a few common situations where image-to-PDF conversion can help:

  • Combining scanned pages into one document.
  • Sharing several photographs in a single file.
  • Submitting forms and supporting documents online.
  • Organizing receipts and invoices.
  • Preparing image-based documents for printing.

If you want to convert your images online, you can use PDF Converter's Image to PDF tool. Select your image files, upload them, and follow the available conversion instructions to create a PDF.

Before sharing the final document, check the page order, image orientation, readability, and file size.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Is JPG better than PNG?

Neither format is universally better. JPG is usually preferable for photographs and smaller file sizes, while PNG is better for transparency, sharp graphics, and lossless image storage.

2. Is PNG higher quality than JPG?

PNG preserves image data through lossless compression. JPG can lose image details because it uses lossy compression. However, a high-quality JPG photograph can still look excellent.

3. Why are PNG files larger than JPG files?

PNG preserves image data, which can result in larger files, particularly for detailed photographs. JPG removes some image data to reduce file size.

4. Does PNG support transparent backgrounds?

Yes. PNG supports transparency, making it useful for logos, icons, and graphics that need to appear over different backgrounds.

5. Can I convert PNG to JPG?

Yes. You can convert PNG images to JPG when you want a smaller file or do not need transparency. Keep in mind that JPG conversion can introduce quality loss, and transparent areas will need to be replaced with a solid background.

6. Which format is better for printing?

Both formats can be used for printing. The best choice depends on the image, resolution, and printing requirements. High-quality JPG is suitable for many photographs, while PNG can be useful for graphics and text-heavy images. Always follow the printer or print service's specifications.

7. Should I use JPG or PNG for scanned documents?

JPG may be suitable for scanned photographs and documents where file size matters. PNG can be a good option for text-heavy scans where preserving sharp details is important. If the scan needs to be submitted or shared as a document, consider converting it to PDF.

Final Thoughts

JPG and PNG are both useful image formats, but they serve different purposes.

JPG is generally the practical choice for photographs, online images, and situations where smaller file sizes matter. PNG is often the better choice for transparent graphics, screenshots, logos, and images that require lossless compression.

Before choosing a format, consider your priorities: image quality, file size, transparency, and how you plan to use the image.

And if your goal is to organize or share multiple images in a document, converting JPG or PNG files to PDF can make the process more convenient.

Choosing the right format helps you manage your images more effectively, whether you are working on a website, preparing a presentation, or sharing important documents.

description:

    • 2.1.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer

    • 2.1.6 Blocking and FIFO
    • 2.2 Go: Channels
    • 2.2.1 What Kinds of Channels Does Go Provide?
    • 2.2.2 Channel Communication and Synchronization Rules
    • 2.2.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer
