    • 2.2.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers
    • 2.2.6 Buffered vs. Unbuffered Channels and FIFO
    • 2.3 CPython: queue.Queue
    • 2.3.1 Which Queues Does Python Provide?
    • 2.3.2 Thread Safety and Synchronization in Queue
    • 2.3.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer
    • 2.3.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer
    • 2.3.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers
    • 2.3.6 Blocking, FIFO, and Task Completion
  • 3. Next: How Is Message Handoff Implemented?

0. From Shared Memory to Message Passing

The opening article introduced two common ways for concurrent execution units to exchange data and coordinate work:

  • Shared Memory: execution units access shared state and coordinate through synchronization.
  • Message Passing: execution units communicate by explicitly sending and receiving messages.

The preceding articles followed Shared Memory, showing how Mutexes, atomics, and ReadWriteLock provide Atomicity, Visibility, and Ordering.

We now turn to Message Passing. Before examining individual languages, it helps to see how the idea developed.

1. A Short History of Message Passing

1.1 Dijkstra: Cooperation Through a Shared Buffer

In 1968, Dijkstra's Cooperating Sequential Processes explored coordination between sequential processes. One example uses a Producer and a Consumer exchanging data through a shared buffer, with Semaphores controlling access.

The Consumer waits when the buffer is empty; with a bounded buffer, the Producer must also wait when it is full.

1.2 RC 4000: Messaging Through the Operating System

In 1969, Per Brinch Hansen designed the RC 4000 Multiprogramming System around a system nucleus that supported interprocess communication through messages. His 1970 paper The Nucleus of a Multiprogramming System describes that design.

Unlike the shared-buffer example, the RC 4000 nucleus exposes explicit message operations:

  • send message: send a message to a specified process.
  • wait message: wait for and receive a message.
  • send answer: send a reply to the sender.
  • wait answer: wait for the reply.

The nucleus manages message-buffer allocation and queues messages for their recipients.

Applied to a Producer and Consumer:

The Producer submits work with send message. The Consumer receives it using wait message and can then reply via send answer; the Producer retrieves the reply through wait answer.

If the Consumer has not begun receiving, the Producer may still complete its send, provided the system has enough message-buffer resources.

1.3 Actor Model: Asynchronous Messages and Local State

In 1973, Carl Hewitt, Peter Bishop, and Richard Steiger presented A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence. In the Actor Model, each Actor owns its state and interacts with others through asynchronous messages. Incoming messages trigger the Actor's behavior.

For a Producer–Consumer scenario, a Buffer Actor could accept work from the Producer and forward it to the Consumer:

This Buffer Actor and its Mailbox illustrate one possible design; they are not mandatory components of the Actor Model.

1.4 CSP: Synchronization Through Communication

Tony Hoare introduced Communicating Sequential Processes in 1978.

CSP describes programs as sequential Processes that communicate through explicit input and output operations. Its characteristic interaction is a rendezvous: a send and its matching receive must meet for communication to complete. A Process in this model is an abstract execution unit, not necessarily an operating-system process.

In the Producer–Consumer example, the Producer cannot hand over a task until the Consumer participates in the communication:

The Rendezvous is a logical communication event, not a central buffer. If the Consumer is not ready, the Producer waits until the operations can pair.

1.5 How Do These Approaches Differ?

These four approaches do not replace one another. They explore communication and cooperation between execution units in different contexts: Dijkstra studied process cooperation and synchronization; RC 4000 provided operating-system messaging; the Actor Model and CSP are more comprehensive models of concurrent computation.

Approach Intermediate Mechanism Data Exchange Primary Concern If the Consumer Is Not Ready
Dijkstra Shared Buffer Direct access to shared storage Synchronization and process cooperation Buffered: write while space remains; wait when full; handoff can be asynchronous
RC 4000 System Message Queue Operating-system messaging interface OS communication mechanism Buffered: write while space remains; wait when full; handoff can be asynchronous
Actor Model Actor Messages sent to Actors Actor identity, state, and behavior Buffered: write while space remains; wait when full; handoff can be asynchronous
CSP Rendezvous Paired Send / Receive Communication events and execution synchronization Unbuffered: wait until the receiver is ready; handoff is synchronous

1.6 Back to Message Passing

Message Passing lets execution units exchange data and coordinate explicitly through send and receive operations. Communication can be buffered or unbuffered: a buffer can temporarily hold messages, allowing the sender and receiver to complete the handoff asynchronously; without a buffer, messages cannot be stored, so both sides must be ready for a synchronous handoff.

We will examine Java BlockingQueue, Go channels, and CPython queue.Queue through three questions:

  • Atomicity: what makes an individual message handoff safe?
  • Visibility: can a receiver observe the data prepared before sending?
  • Ordering: what synchronization order is established between sending and receiving?

2. What Do Message-Passing APIs Guarantee in Each Language?

2.1 Java: BlockingQueue

2.1.1 Which Queue Implementations Does Java Provide?

Java's Queue interface represents a collection of elements awaiting processing. Common implementations can be grouped by whether they support concurrent access and blocking operations:

Category Representative Implementations Supports Concurrent Access Provides Blocking Operations
Ordinary Queue ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue No No
Concurrent Non-blocking Queue ConcurrentLinkedQueue Yes No; poll() immediately returns null when empty
BlockingQueue ArrayBlockingQueue and others Yes Yes; for example, take() waits for an item, and put() waits for space when a bounded queue is full

Some representative BlockingQueue implementations:

Implementation Storage Structure Capacity Retrieval Order Blocking Conditions
ArrayBlockingQueue Array Fixed at construction FIFO put() waits when full; take() waits when empty
LinkedBlockingQueue Linked nodes Optional limit at construction; defaults to Integer.MAX_VALUE FIFO put() waits when full; take() waits when empty
SynchronousQueue No element storage 0 Direct pairing between sender and receiver put() waits for a receiver; take() waits for a sender
PriorityBlockingQueue Heap Unbounded By priority; FIFO is not guaranteed for equal priorities put() does not wait for space; take() waits when empty
DelayQueue Priority heap Unbounded Earliest expiration first put() does not wait for space; take() waits when empty or when no item has expired
LinkedTransferQueue Linked nodes Unbounded FIFO put() does not wait for space; take() waits when empty; transfer() waits until the element is received

We will use the typical implementation ArrayBlockingQueue.

Its two relevant operations are:

  • put(e) inserts an element, waiting if the queue is full.
  • take() removes and returns an element, waiting if the queue is empty.

2.1.2 Two Concurrency Guarantees of BlockingQueue

The JDK 25 BlockingQueue documentation states:

“All queuing methods achieve their effects atomically.”

This provides Atomicity. Each enqueue or dequeue is atomic, so concurrent operations do not corrupt queue state.

The same documentation specifies a memory-consistency effect:

Actions before placing an object into a BlockingQueue happen-before actions after another thread accesses or removes that object.

This establishes both Visibility and Ordering.

For Visibility, writes performed before a Producer enqueues a message are visible to the Consumer that retrieves it.

For Ordering, actions before sending, the message handoff, and actions after receiving establish a cross-thread memory order through the transitivity of happens-before.

We will reuse the opening article's count++ example as we progress through SPSC, MPSC, and MPMC:

class Increment {
    int delta;
}

BlockingQueue<Increment> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);

2.1.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer 

// Producer thread
Increment message = new Increment();
message.delta = 1;
queue.put(message);

// Consumer thread
int count = 0;
Increment received = queue.take();
count += received.delta; // count == 1

The relevant execution order is:

Producer                                 Consumer

message.delta = 1
        │
        │ program order
        ▼
queue.put(message)  ───── handoff ───────► queue.take() returns message
                                                  │
                                                  │ program order
                                                  ▼
                                         read received.delta == 1
                                         count = 1

A successful put() inserts a message; take() removes and returns it. That demonstrates the Atomicity of each queue operation, although no competing Producers or Consumers exist yet.

delta is an ordinary field: neither volatile nor an atomic type is needed. Provided no other thread modifies this message after enqueueing it, the Producer's write happens-before the Consumer's read. The Consumer therefore sees 1, as required by Visibility and Ordering.

2.1.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer 

// Producers A and B each execute this in their own thread
Increment message = new Increment();
message.delta = 1;
queue.put(message);

// The sole Consumer thread
int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
    count += queue.take().delta;
}
// After both messages have been submitted and processed: count == 2

One possible interleaving:

Producer A              Producer B              Consumer

put(A: +1)
                        put(B: +1)
                                                take() -> +1
                                                count: 0 -> 1
                                                take() -> +1
                                                count: 1 -> 2

Atomicity: concurrent Producers cannot overwrite one another's successfully enqueued messages. If both put() calls complete, the Consumer can retrieve two messages.

Visibility / Ordering: the happens-before guarantee holds independently for each message. Nothing predetermines which Producer enqueues first.

count += delta is not an atomic instruction. It is safe from competing Consumer updates here because only one Consumer modifies count.

2.1.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers

Now add another Consumer. The two Producers still enqueue one +1 message each, but Consumers A and B call take() concurrently:

// Producers A and B each send a distinct Increment instance
Increment message = new Increment();
message.delta = 1;
queue.put(message);

// Consumers A and B each execute once
Increment received = queue.take();
int delta = received.delta;

For example:

Producer A        Producer B        Consumer A        Consumer B

put(A: +1)
                  put(B: +1)
                                    take() -> A
                                                      take() -> B

Atomicity: a successful take() removes one element. Two Consumers cannot both remove the same enqueued message. A and B identify the messages, not fixed assignments to Consumers.

Visibility / Ordering: whichever Consumer receives a message can rely on its Producer's preceding writes. FIFO dequeue order does not imply that Consumers finish their business logic in that order.

There is an important boundary. If both Consumers later update the same ordinary counter:

// Counter shared by both Consumers
class Counter { int count; }
Counter sharedCounter = new Counter(); // Created before starting them

// Each Consumer executes this in its own thread
int delta = queue.take().delta;
sharedCounter.count += delta;

Both messages can be removed safely while the final count is still 1 because of a lost update. BlockingQueue protects the atomicity of message handoff, not arbitrary business operations after the handoff.

2.1.6 Blocking and FIFO

All three scenarios also inherit two behaviors of ArrayBlockingQueue:

  • Blocking: take() waits when the queue is empty; put() waits when its capacity of 2 is exhausted.
  • FIFO: items leave in their actual enqueue order. Concurrent Producers have no predetermined insertion order, and multiple Consumers need not finish processing in dequeue order.

2.2 Go: Channels

Unlike Java, Go does not primarily expose a family of standard concurrent queues. It provides channels as a language construct for communication between Goroutines.

2.2.1 What Kinds of Channels Does Go Provide?

The Go Language Specification distinguishes channels by buffering:

Type Declaration Behavior
Unbuffered make(chan int) No stored messages; sends and receives pair directly
Buffered make(chan int, 2) Fixed-capacity buffer; a sender can enqueue before a receiver is ready

Channel types can also constrain direction:

Direction Type Allowed Operations
Bidirectional chan T Send and receive
Send-only chan<- T Send only
Receive-only <-chan T Receive only

Direction and buffering are independent: a buffered channel can be passed to a function as chan<- T if that function should only send.

We will use a buffered channel with capacity 2:

type Increment struct {
    delta int
}

jobs := make(chan Increment, 2)

The two operations we need are:

  • ch <- value sends a value, waiting when the buffer is full.
  • value := <-ch receives a value, waiting when the buffer is empty.

2.2.2 Channel Communication and Synchronization Rules

The Go Language Specification allows any number of Goroutines to send to or receive from one channel without additional synchronization.

That rule provides Atomicity at the communication boundary: concurrent Sends and Receives exchange messages safely. Each successful Receive corresponds to one sent message, which cannot be received again by another Consumer.

The Go Memory Model, Channel Communication also states:

“A send on a channel is synchronized before the completion of the corresponding receive from that channel.”

This establishes Visibility and Ordering.

For Visibility, writes completed before the Producer's Send are visible to the Consumer after its matching Receive.

For Ordering, actions before sending, the channel's Send / Receive, and actions after receiving establish a happens-before relationship through synchronized-before and program order.

As with Java, the examples reuse the opening article's count++ example, building from SPSC through MPSC to MPMC.

2.2.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer 

// Producer Goroutine
message := Increment{delta: 1}
jobs <- message

// Consumer Goroutine
count := 0
received := <-jobs
count += received.delta // count == 1

The handoff establishes this order:

Producer                                 Consumer

message.delta = 1
        │
        │ sequenced-before
        ▼
jobs <- message  ─────── handoff ────────► received := <-jobs completes
                                                  │
                                                  │ sequenced-before
                                                  ▼
                                         read received.delta == 1
                                         count = 1

A successful Send delivers one value to a successful Receive. No competing senders or receivers are involved yet.

delta is an ordinary field. Here, the channel carries an Increment value, and the send is synchronized-before the corresponding receive completes. The Consumer can therefore read 1, satisfying Visibility and Ordering.

2.2.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer 

// Producers A and B each execute once in a separate Goroutine
jobs <- Increment{delta: 1}

// The sole Consumer Goroutine
count := 0
for i := 0; i < 2; i++ {
    received := <-jobs
    count += received.delta
}
// After both messages have been sent and processed: count == 2

One possible interleaving:

Producer A              Producer B              Consumer

send(A: +1)
                        send(B: +1)
                                                receive -> +1
                                                count: 0 -> 1
                                                receive -> +1
                                                count: 1 -> 2

Atomicity: concurrent Sends cannot overwrite successfully sent messages; two successful Sends can be matched by two Receives.

Visibility / Ordering: each message independently establishes a Send/Receive synchronization relationship. Neither Producer is guaranteed to send first.

2.2.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers 

// Producers A and B each execute once in their own Goroutine
jobs <- Increment{delta: 1}

// Consumers A and B each execute once in their own Goroutine
received := <-jobs
delta := received.delta

For example:

Producer A        Producer B        Consumer A        Consumer B

send(A: +1)
                  send(B: +1)
                                    receive -> A
                                                      receive -> B

Atomicity: each successful Receive obtains the value of one matching Send; the same message is not delivered to two Consumers. A and B label messages, not predetermined receivers.

Visibility / Ordering: the receiving Consumer gets the synchronization guarantees associated with that message, but reception order does not determine processing-completion order.

What if both Consumers then modify a shared counter?

// Incorrect: two Consumers update the same ordinary counter
received := <-jobs
sharedCounter.count += received.delta

Even though both Receives succeed, concurrent writes to sharedCounter.count introduce a data race and can lose an update. Channels protect message handoff; they do not automatically protect shared state after receiving.

2.2.6 Buffered vs. Unbuffered Channels and FIFO

The previous examples use a buffered channel with capacity 2:

  • Waiting: Receive waits when the buffer is empty; Send waits when it is full.
  • FIFO: values are received in the channel's send order. The order of competing Producers is not predetermined, nor is the completion order of multiple Consumers.

Go also supports unbuffered channels:

jobs := make(chan Increment)

With no storage, the Send cannot complete until a corresponding Receive participates. The Go Memory Model provides an additional rule: the matching Receive is synchronized-before the unbuffered Send completes. A buffered Send, in contrast, can finish before the receiver starts.

The next article will examine how the Go runtime parks Goroutines waiting for communication and resumes them when the conditions are met.

2.3 CPython: queue.Queue

Unlike Go, Python does not offer channels as language syntax. Instead, its standard library offers queue mechanisms for different concurrency models.

2.3.1 Which Queues Does Python Provide?

Python provides different queues for different execution units:

Module Representative Types Communicating Units Waiting Behavior
queue Queue, SimpleQueue and others Threads within one process Blocks the calling thread
asyncio asyncio.Queue Asynchronous Tasks within one event loop Suspends the calling Task, allowing other Tasks to run
multiprocessing multiprocessing.Queue Separate processes Blocks the caller

queue provides thread-safe queues. asyncio.Queue is designed for asynchronous Tasks and is not thread-safe. multiprocessing.Queue supports interprocess communication and serializes the objects it transfers.

Our scope is CPython Threads, so we will focus on the standard library's queue module. The Python documentation lists several implementations:

Implementation Capacity Retrieval Order Default Blocking Conditions Task-Completion Tracking
queue.Queue Configurable; unbounded by default FIFO put() waits when full; get() waits when empty Supported
queue.LifoQueue Configurable; unbounded by default LIFO put() waits when full; get() waits when empty Supported
queue.PriorityQueue Configurable; unbounded by default Lowest-valued entry first put() waits when full; get() waits when empty Supported
queue.SimpleQueue Unbounded FIFO put() does not wait for space; get() waits when empty Not supported

Task-completion tracking uses task_done() to mark a task as processed and join() to wait until all enqueued tasks have been processed.

Note: In Python, maxsize <= 0 means the buffer has no preset capacity limit; in Go, a channel with capacity 0 has no buffer.

We will use queue.Queue, whose two primary operations are:

Operation Meaning Default Waiting Condition
put(item) Inserts an item Waits for space when full
get() Removes and returns an item Waits for an item when empty

Both operations block by default. Use block=False for an immediate attempt or timeout to limit the wait. Failure to insert or retrieve an item raises queue.Full or queue.Empty, respectively.

2.3.2 Thread Safety and Synchronization in Queue

The Python queue documentation states:

“The Queue class in this module implements all the required locking semantics.”

This supports Atomicity at the queue boundary. Multiple threads may call put() and get() concurrently; internal locking protects queue state, so two Consumers cannot remove the same enqueued item.

For Visibility and Ordering, the Producer prepares a message before put(), and the Consumer reads that message after get() returns. CPython coordinates the handoff using the queue's internal locks and condition variables, making the prepared data available to the receiving thread.

We will reuse the opening article's count++ example, building from SPSC through MPSC to MPMC:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from queue import Queue

@dataclass
class Increment:
    delta: int

jobs = Queue(maxsize=2)

2.3.3 SPSC: Single Producer, Single Consumer

One Producer sends +1; one Consumer receives the message and updates count:

# Producer thread
message = Increment(delta=1)
jobs.put(message)

# Consumer thread
count = 0
received = jobs.get()
count += received.delta  # count == 1

The relevant handoff is:

Producer                                 Consumer

message.delta = 1
        │
        ▼
jobs.put(message) ── internal queue sync ─► jobs.get() returns message
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                         read received.delta == 1
                                         count = 1

A successful put() inserts a message; get() removes and returns it. At this point there is no contention among multiple Producers or Consumers.

delta is an ordinary attribute. Provided no thread continues mutating this message after it is enqueued, the Consumer can read the value 1 following the queue handoff. This comes from Queue synchronization, not from a blanket guarantee that the GIL protects every shared object.

Unlike the earlier Shared Memory example, no separate shared ready flag is needed: get() waits for a message if the queue is empty.

2.3.4 MPSC: Multiple Producers, Single Consumer

Add a second Producer. Each submits a +1 message; the only Consumer accumulates both:

# Producers A and B each execute this in a separate thread
jobs.put(Increment(delta=1))

# The sole Consumer thread
count = 0
for _ in range(2):
    received = jobs.get()
    count += received.delta
# After both messages have been submitted and processed: count == 2

One possible interleaving:

Producer A              Producer B              Consumer

put(A: +1)
                        put(B: +1)
                                                get() -> +1
                                                count: 0 -> 1
                                                get() -> +1
                                                count: 1 -> 2

Atomicity: the two Producers can enqueue concurrently without overwriting each other's successfully enqueued items; the Consumer can retrieve both.

Visibility / Ordering: each message is handed off through the queue's synchronization. The order in which concurrent Producers enqueue is not predetermined.

count += received.delta remains a compound operation, but only the sole Consumer modifies count.

2.3.5 MPMC: Multiple Producers, Multiple Consumers

Now let two Consumers call get() concurrently while two Producers each enqueue +1:

# Producers A and B each run once in their own thread
jobs.put(Increment(delta=1))

# Consumers A and B each run once in their own thread
received = jobs.get()
delta = received.delta

For example:

Producer A        Producer B        Consumer A        Consumer B

put(A: +1)
                  put(B: +1)
                                    get() -> A
                                                      get() -> B

Atomicity: a successful get() removes one item; two Consumers cannot both remove the same enqueued item. A and B only distinguish the messages, not predetermined assignments.

Visibility / Ordering: whichever Consumer gets a message can read the data prepared before enqueueing it through the queue's thread synchronization. Dequeue order still says nothing about when the Consumers finish their work.

If both Consumers subsequently update the same shared counter:

# Incorrect: both Consumers share the same counter
counter = {"value": 0}  # Shared before starting either Consumer

# Each Consumer executes this
received = jobs.get()
counter["value"] += received.delta

Correctly dequeuing both messages does not guarantee that two counter["value"] += 1 operations cannot lose an update. Do not rely on the GIL to make this compound operation atomically safe; that assumption is especially unsafe with free-threaded CPython.

2.3.6 Blocking, FIFO, and Task Completion

The three scenarios also share these queue.Queue behaviors:

  • Blocking: with a capacity of 2, put() waits by default if the queue is full; get() waits if it is empty. A maxsize of 0 means no capacity limit, not a Go-style unbuffered rendezvous.
  • FIFO: items are removed in actual enqueue order. Concurrent Producers have no predetermined arrival order; multiple Consumers need not finish processing in dequeue order.
  • Task completion: get() reports only that a task has been removed. task_done() marks processing complete, while join() waits until the unfinished-task count reaches zero. Receiving and finishing are different events.

The next article will examine how CPython implements this behavior with Locks and Condition variables.

3. Next: How Is Message Handoff Implemented?

At the language level, Java BlockingQueue and Go channels provide explicit communication and memory-synchronization rules. CPython queue.Queue provides safe handoff through its standard library's thread synchronization.

Next, we will trace Java ArrayBlockingQueue, Go channels, and CPython queue.Queue through synchronization primitives, runtime implementations, the operating system, and ultimately the CPU.

This article was first published on ThinkerQAQ's personal blog and syndicated here by the author. The original article may be revised over time; please refer to the personal blog for the latest version.

title: CSS Easing Explained: Picking the Right cubic-bezier() for Enter, Exit and Move Animations
description:
For a long time I wrote transition: all 0.3s ease on everything and moved on. It worked fine. It also made every interface I built feel a little bit off, and I couldn't explain why until I started paying attention to easing.

This post is the mental model I use now. If you only want the values, I keep the full list of curves as CSS variables in a gist: CSS cubic-bezier() Easing Cheat Sheet.

Why easing matters at all

Nothing in the real world moves at a constant speed. A drawer you pull out speeds up and then slows to a stop. A ball you drop speeds up until it hits the floor. When a UI element moves linearly, your brain notices that it's "wrong" even if you can't say why.

Easing is how you describe that change in speed. In CSS, every timing function is really a cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2). The x axis is time and the y axis is progress, both from 0 to 1. Even the keywords are just presets: ease is cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1) and ease-in-out is cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 0.58, 1).

The most useful way to read a curve: a steep part means fast, a flat part means slow. That's really all there is to it.

Enter, exit, move

I use three rules and they cover about 90% of what I build.

Things entering the screen: ease-out. A modal, a toast, a dropdown. It should show up fast and settle gently. Ease-out puts the speed at the start, so the element looks like it reacts to the user right away and then slows down where the eye lands on it. My default is cubic-bezier(0.33, 1, 0.68, 1) (easeOutCubic). When I want something snappier, I use easeOutQuint, cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1).

Things leaving: ease-in. Same logic in reverse. The element starts slowly and speeds up as it goes away, which reads as "it's gone." Exit animations should also be a bit shorter than enters. Nobody wants to watch something leave.

Things moving from A to B on screen: ease-in-out. A tab indicator sliding, a card changing position, a carousel. Both ends are visible, so the element should speed up and slow down: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1) (easeInOutCubic).

One thing I avoid is plain ease-in for enter animations. It feels laggy, because the slowest part happens right when the user is waiting for feedback.

.toast {
  transition: transform 250ms cubic-bezier(0.33, 1, 0.68, 1),
              opacity 250ms cubic-bezier(0.33, 1, 0.68, 1);
}
.toast[data-leaving] {
  transition-duration: 180ms;
  transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0, 0.67, 0); /* easeInCubic */
}

Durations

Easing and duration go together. A good curve at the wrong duration still feels bad. These are the ranges I start from:

  • Hover, press, small color changes: 100–200ms
  • Dropdowns, tooltips, toasts: 150–250ms
  • Modals, drawers, page sections: 250–400ms
  • Big full-screen transitions: up to about 500ms

Bigger elements and longer distances can take a bit longer. On mobile, I go a little shorter than on desktop. If something feels slow, I almost always fix it by cutting the duration, not by changing the curve.

Also, stop using transition: all. List the properties (transform, opacity). It's cheaper to render, and you won't accidentally animate layout properties like width or top.

Overshoot with Back curves

cubic-bezier() lets the y values go outside 0–1 (the x values can't). If y goes above 1, the element shoots past its final value and settles back. That's the "Back" family:

/* easeOutBack: overshoots ~10% then settles */
.badge-pop { transition: transform 300ms cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1); }

I like this on small playful things: a notification badge popping in, a like button, a checkbox tick. I'd never use it on a modal or anything large. On a big surface, a wobble feels sloppy instead of fun. A real bounce or elastic effect, with several wobbles, can't be done with one cubic-bezier. For that you need @keyframes or the newer linear() function.

Respect reduced motion

Some people get dizzy or nauseous from motion on screen, and they turn on "reduce motion" in their OS. Honoring that setting takes a few lines:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

I use 0.01ms instead of none so that transitionend and animationend events still fire and JS that waits on them doesn't break. A softer approach is to keep opacity fades and drop only the transforms (sliding, scaling, parallax). Those cause most of the trouble.

Keep curves in one place

My last tip is to put your curves in CSS custom properties and use only those:

:root {
  --ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.33, 1, 0.68, 1);
  --ease-in: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0, 0.67, 0);
  --ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0, 0.35, 1);
}

Three or four named curves applied consistently do more for how an app "feels" than a dozen hand-tuned ones. The gist has the full Sine through Back set if you want more options.

When I need a custom curve, I drag the handles in a visual editor until it looks right, then copy the four numbers. Lately I've been using this cubic-bezier editor. It runs in the browser and doesn't need an account. Seeing the curve beats guessing numbers every time.

That's it: ease-out to enter, ease-in to leave, ease-in-out to move, keep it short, and respect reduced motion.

title: AWS Security Hub now supports resource criticality for prioritization
description:
Today, AWS Security Hub adds resource criticality to exposure prioritization, helping central security teams focus on the exposures that threaten their most business-critical resources.

You can set criticality with an automation rule, for example marking every compute resource in a specific account as Very High. The rule applies to resources already in your inventory and to new resources as Security Hub discovers them. Security Hub also infers criticality from resource tags and resource names, with no configuration required, and records which source determined the value. Criticality appears as a column on the Resources page for sorting, filtering, and grouping, and on the Impact assessment tab of an exposure finding. Resource criticality is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost and is always on for all customers.

Resource criticality is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost and requires no new enablement. To learn more, see  AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page. For a list of AWS Regions where Security Hub is available, see the AWS Region table.

title: Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies
description:
title: "Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies"
published: true
published_at: "2026-12-18T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [api, backend, webdev, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of rest apis architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Idempotent Http Methods (Get: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Delete) Vs Non-Idempotent (Post: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Patch): Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Url Structure Nouns Over Verbs: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Designing Pragmatic REST APIs: Status Codes, URI Design, and Versioning Strategies functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: REST APIs Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Idempotent HTTP methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) vs non-idempotent (POST, PATCH), URL structure nouns over verbs, URI vs Header versioning, and RFC 7807 Problem Details."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: I built an app to duel your past self in push-ups and pull-ups!
description:
I always quit at the exact same point. Somewhere around rep 15, my brain decides "that’s enough" — and a normal counter just sits there watching.

So I built RivalRep, a web app that counts your push-ups and pull-ups through your phone camera and gives you someone to actually compete against:

Your Ghost: An exact replay of your personal best. Not just a static number, but every rep and pause played back in real time. You literally watch your past self pull ahead.

Bots that learn your weak spots: An adaptive bot studies your past sets and intentionally speeds up right where you usually fade. It’s annoyingly effective.

It also includes a training plan that automatically adapts to your feedback and progress!

Is it free? Yes, completely free.

Do I need to download an app? No. It runs directly in your browser (iPhone, Android, or laptop webcam). You can also add it to your home screen like an app.

title: State of agent skills
description:
In seven months, the skills.sh registry grew to one million agent skills and recorded nearly 280 million installs.

A skill gives an AI agent reusable instructions for a particular job. Agents are capable but generic; they can do many jobs, but they don't know how a specific person, team, or company does them. A skill supplies that missing context and can be as simple as a file written in ordinary language.

Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025, and Vercel launched the skills.sh registry three months later.

Using aggregate data from the registry, this report follows a new market through its first million skills: what people teach agents, what gets installed, and where the value is heading.

Skills turn expertise into software

To write a skill, some of the judgment behind a job has to be made explicit, like the steps to follow, what good looks like, and how to evaluate the result. The agent and its tools already supply much of the underlying capability, so the skill only has to provide the judgment and instructions specific to a job.

This makes skills faster and easier to create than conventional software.

skills.sh reached one million skills in seven months. GitHub took 27 months to reach one million repositories. Apple's App Store took just over five years to get to one million apps. npm took more than nine years to reach one million packages.

Far more people can describe how work should be done than program a computer to do it. And once a skill is written, it can be distributed and installed without being rewritten for each agent. Skills pair a much larger pool of creators with software’s capacity for reuse, driving the explosive growth of the ecosystem.

What people are teaching agents

We classified the registry's most-installed skills by the kind of work they help agents do. Together, these skills account for more than four-fifths of all installs. Published listings show supply: what authors have made available to agents; installs show demand: what people want their agents to learn.

Supply leans technical. More than half of listings teach software engineering, agent workflows, data, infrastructure, or security, with software engineering alone accounting for about a quarter.

Demand is more distributed. There's isn't a single category with more than a fifth of installs. Software engineering remains the largest at 18%, followed by agent workflows at 15%, then business operations and writing at nearly 11% each.

To see how each category performs for its size, we also compared its installs per listing with the average.

Business operations, writing and documents, and cloud and infrastructure get the most installs per listing. Demand for that work is split across fewer skills, so each one carries more of it. The average business operations skill draws 74% more installs than the average, writing and documents 50% more, cloud and infrastructure 42% more.

Software engineering, education and productivity, and research are oversupplied. The average software engineering skill draws about 30% fewer installs than average, education and productivity 39% fewer, research 55% fewer.

To write a skill, you need to understand a job. To install one, you need only want the job done. Most skills are technical because they began in developer tools. Installs cover a much broader range of work because agents are useful in every part of a company.

Skills that improve how agents work are among the most installed

Agent workflows and automation account for 14.8% of installs in the classified dataset, second only to software engineering. Among listings with at least 100,000 installs, agent workflows are the largest category.

Agent workflow and automation skills teach agents how to plan, route work, use tools, and automate browsers, abilities that apply across many jobs. A contract-review skill applies to contracts, but a planning skill applies to any job the agent takes on, contracts included.

People are using agents to improve agents. And because agents also help write skills, the catalog grows by improving the very machinery used to build it.

A few skills capture most installs

Install activity is highly concentrated. Nearly half of all skills were installed exactly once. At the other end, 375 skills, or 0.04% of the registry, account for 62% of installs, and the top 1.2% account for 94% of installs.

For all that concentration, there's no single winner. Even the most-installed skill accounts for less than 1% of all installs.

Skills compete within jobs and accumulate across them. Once a team chooses an expense-report skill, it has little reason to install another expense-report skill. But it can use that skill alongside others for spreadsheets, research, and presentations. Each job crowns its own winner, and the winners together carry most of the installs.

Seven in eight installs go to skills any industry can use

We also classified each skill by whether its work was shared across industries or specific to one. Tasks such as cleaning up a spreadsheet or deploying a website recur at banks and hospitals, law firms and restaurants. These cross-industry skills account for 66% of classified skills and 87.5% of installs. On average, they receive 3.6 times as many installs per listing as industry-specific skills.

The advantage is portability, whether a skill reaches across jobs, like agent workflows, or across industries. The skills installed most are the ones the most people can use.

The next generation of skills

The first million skills taught agents what everyone knows. The next million will teach your agents what only you know.

Public skills and better models are making general expertise available to every team, which will turn it into the baseline rather than any kind of advantage. More of the differentiating value will move to company-specific judgment. For example, when a customer gets a refund or what can ship without another review.

The measure of a skill will also shift from popularity to effectiveness. Today, the best signal of a skill's quality is its install count. As models improve, the bar rises, because a skill justifies itself only if the agent does the job better with it than without it. Skills will get tests and benchmarks that measure exactly that.

Skills have already turned expertise into software. The public catalog will continue to grow as supply catches up to demand. And organizations will build on top of it, writing down the knowledge only they have and maintaining it the same way they now maintain code.

Explore the first million, or add to the next, at skills.sh.

About this report

This report uses aggregate skills.sh data. A few notes on measurement:

  • Catalog totals count unique registry listings.

  • Install figures use aggregate registry counters. They do not represent unique people or necessarily independent choices.

  • Function and industry findings describe a classified sample rather than the full catalog.

  • Each analysis uses the latest complete data available. Figures may be revised as the underlying data and methodology improve.

title: Invalidating a Code Snapshot Cache on the Thing That Should Invalidate It
description:
A fintech ops lead in London pastes the same incident report into the diagnosis tool twice, three days apart. Same file, same line, same confidence score, same proposed fix — except the schema changed on Tuesday and the fix is now wrong. Nobody lied to the system. The system did exactly what it was built to do. That is the uncomfortable part.

Corporate AI 365 caches its root-cause analysis against a hash of three things: the issue text, a snapshot of the code, and the model version. Same hash, same answer, every time — that is what makes an approval gate defensible instead of a coin flip. But a cache is only as honest as the thing that is supposed to invalidate it, and in a system that never connects to a live database, one of those invalidators is a file someone has to remember to re-export.

The cache key is smaller than it feels

When an engineer in Berlin imagines the input to a diagnosis, they picture the whole repository and the whole database. The cache key doesn't see either. It sees the source tree as committed, and a scripted schema export — a dump of tables, columns, constraints, and views that your own developer generates and checks in or uploads. No connection string, no query against production, ever. That's the non-negotiable we design around.

The consequence is that the hash is a function of two artifacts that move at different speeds. Code changes on every push; the diagnosis engine sees that immediately because it reads the repository directly through your GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps connector. The schema export changes only when someone runs the export again. If a migration adds a column in staging and the team forgets to regenerate the scripted schema, the code snapshot looks fresh, the hash looks fresh, and the cached diagnosis is served with full confidence — pointing at a column that no longer means what the analysis thinks it means.

This is not a bug in the caching strategy. It is the honest cost of refusing to hold a live connection. We could make the schema "always fresh" by letting the AI query production directly — and we have deliberately not built that, because the moment an AI reasoning engine can read live rows, your security review stops being a conversation and becomes a liability audit. So the trade-off stands: reproducibility and a clean trust boundary, in exchange for a manual step that has to be someone's job.

Why the manual step is the real risk in a lean team

That trade-off is tolerable when there's a senior engineer who owns schema hygiene as a matter of habit. It is a real exposure when there isn't one. Across European SMEs and mid-market firms right now, a large share of teams — on the order of six in ten by some recent industry surveys — report they simply cannot find qualified developers to fill open roles. A Dublin logistics company or an Amsterdam retailer running production support with three generalists instead of a platform team isn't being negligent when the schema export goes stale for two sprints. There's no spare capacity to own that discipline full-time.

That matters because the cost of a wrong diagnosis is not symmetric. Enterprise downtime has been estimated by industry research at a median in the region of US$9,000 per minute for large organisations — and a diagnosis that confidently points at the wrong column doesn't just fail to fix the incident, it burns the first twenty minutes of the incident on the wrong hypothesis. In a lean team without a senior engineer to sanity-check the AI's output on sight, that twenty minutes is the whole difference between a contained incident and an escalated one.

What we actually invalidate on, and what we deliberately don't

Given that, the design answer isn't to pretend the schema is always current. It's to make staleness visible instead of silent:

  • The cache entry records the export timestamp alongside the hash, so a diagnosis can be shown next to "schema last scripted: 11 days ago" rather than presented as uniformly fresh.
  • Any manual schema re-export forces a new hash and a new diagnosis run — it is treated exactly like a code change, not a side artifact.
  • Where the AI needs to confirm a live fact — row counts, actual values, current index usage — it writes a read-only query for a developer to run by hand. The result comes back to a human, not to our cache, which keeps the live-data boundary intact even when the stakes are high.
  • We deliberately don't hash at the whole-repository level for large monorepos; the key is scoped to the files and schema objects actually implicated, so an unrelated commit elsewhere in the codebase doesn't force a re-diagnosis that produces nothing new — and, just as importantly, a relevant change doesn't get buried in repository-wide noise.

None of this makes the schema export automatic. It can't be, without the live connection we won't build. What it does is turn "the diagnosis was wrong" into "the diagnosis was wrong and here is exactly which input was stale and when it was last updated" — which is the difference between a system you can audit and one you have to take on faith. For a team in London, Berlin, Amsterdam, or Dublin running production support without a bench of senior engineers, that audit trail is the thing that lets a junior developer trust the output enough to act on it, and lets a manager explain the decision afterward without hand-waving.

Start the free 14-day trial, no card required, at corp.dirayahai.com — connect your repository, script your schema once, and see exactly what the cache knows and when it last checked.

title: I built a Claude skill that makes AI design like a senior UX designer
description:
Ask any AI to "design a dashboard" and you get the same thing every time. A KPI row, a line chart, a table. Logistics, HR, healthcare, fintech: they all look identical. And the moment you look closer, there's no loading state, no empty state, no error state. It renders. It doesn't work.

I've spent 14 years designing enterprise SaaS for aviation, logistics, and HR products. So I wrote down how I actually design, and turned it into a Claude skill.

It's free, open source, and MIT licensed: your-ui-ux-designer on GitHub

A logistics shipment dashboard, generated with the skill in HTML.

The core rule: render, don't describe

Most AI output describes good design. "The table should have a loading state." "Buttons should have focus styles."

The skill treats a described state as not delivered. If a rule names an output, that output must appear in the result. So every screen ships with:

  • Default, Loading, Empty, and Error states, as real rendered views
  • Focus rings and working interactions
  • Four responsive breakpoints
  • A prefers-reduced-motion fallback

The same dashboard in its Loading, Empty, and Error states. Built in, not added later.

What it does

It asks before it designs. At the start of a session, it asks 5 questions once: your design system (or it creates one), industry, output target, style, and dark mode. Then it commits.

11 distinct styles. Minimal, Material 3, Bento Grid, Glassmorphism, Liquid Glass, Spatial, Aurora, Neo-Brutalism, plus Neumorphism, Claymorphism, and Skeuomorphic for the narrow cases where they fit. It also warns you when a style is wrong for the context, like Claymorphism for enterprise B2B.

Enterprise navigation. Gmail-style dual nav, a fixed icon rail plus a collapsible secondary panel, that reflows correctly to a mobile top bar and bottom bar.

Bring your own design system. Share tokens, a link, or an image. It adopts them and fills in what's missing.

Multiple output targets. HTML, Figma, Claude Design, or a written spec.

Built-in validation. Before delivering, it checks that charts actually paint, controls actually work, and contrast actually passes.

Same skill, different industry: a fintech landing page with a live dashboard, in HTML.

How it's built

A lean core file, plus reference files that load only when needed. That keeps it fast and stops it from dropping rules on big tasks.

ui-ux-designer/
├── SKILL.md          core spine
└── references/
    ├── styles.md     11 style definitions
    ├── patterns.md   navigation, tables, dropdowns
    ├── mobile.md     touch / gesture / mobile spec
    └── figma.md      Figma auto-layout & variants

Does it work?

I tested it on 30 cases across aviation, transport, and HRM, scored on a 10-point rubric covering screen logic, style fidelity, contrast, grid, states, interaction, and responsiveness.

  • Overall: 86.7 / 100 on Sonnet 4.6
  • HTML on Opus 4.8: 93.0 / 100
  • Figma on Opus 4.8: 88.0 / 100

One lesson from testing: model choice matters. Routing HTML and Figma work to Opus fixed the responsiveness gap. And low reasoning effort drops states, so don't run it on low.

Install in 3 steps

  1. Download ui-ux-designer.skill from the repo or its Releases page
  2. In Claude: Settings → Capabilities → Skills → Upload skill
  3. Select the file. It installs automatically.

It triggers on any UI/UX request, or call it directly with /ui-ux-designer. Works in Claude Chat, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork.

Try it

Paste this after installing:

Design a mobile app screen for a field-service technician: a job list with status, and a job detail view. Output as HTML.

What I learned building it

AI is fast, but it's confidently incomplete. The value isn't in getting AI to generate a screen. It's in encoding the checks a senior designer runs without thinking: what happens when this table is empty? What does a technician see when the network fails? Where does this nav go on a phone?

That's what this skill tries to capture.

If you try it and it gets something wrong, open an issue with the prompt and a screenshot. And if it's useful, a ⭐ on GitHub helps other people find it.

AI builds. I decide.

title: Crash Course : Core Java
description:
Complete Core Java Tutorial — All Topics with Examples

A full end-to-end Core Java tutorial. Each section is self-contained with runnable examples.

📚 Table of Contents

  1. Basics & Syntax
  2. Variables, Data Types & Wrappers
  3. Operators
  4. Control Flow
  5. Arrays & Varargs
  6. Strings
  7. OOP — Classes & Objects

  9. Keywords (static, final, this, super, instanceof)
  10. Access Modifiers
  11. Packages & Imports
  12. Object Class Methods

1. Basics & Syntax 

public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, Java!");
    }
}
  • Class name = filename (for public class)
  • main = JVM entry point
  • Compile: javac HelloWorld.java → Run: java HelloWorld

2. Variables, Data Types & Wrappers 

public class DataTypes {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Primitives
        byte b = 127;              // 1 byte
        short s = 32000;           // 2 bytes
        int i = 100_000;           // 4 bytes
        long l = 8_000_000_000L;   // 8 bytes
        float f = 3.14f;           // 4 bytes
        double d = 3.14159;        // 8 bytes
        char c = 'A';              // 2 bytes
        boolean flag = true;       // 1 bit

        // Wrappers
        Integer boxed = 42;        // autoboxing
        int unboxed = boxed;       // unboxing
        Integer parsed = Integer.parseInt("123");
        Double dbl = Double.valueOf("3.14");

        // Constants
        final double PI = 3.14159;
    }
}

Wrapper classes: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean

3. Operators 

public class Operators {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 10, b = 3;

        // Arithmetic
        System.out.println(a + b);  // 13
        System.out.println(a / b);  // 3
        System.out.println(a % b);  // 1

        // Relational
        System.out.println(a > b);  // true
        System.out.println(a == b); // false

        // Logical
        System.out.println(a > 5 && b < 5);  // true
        System.out.println(a > 5 || b > 5);  // true
        System.out.println(!(a > 5));        // false

        // Bitwise
        System.out.println(5 & 3);  // 1
        System.out.println(5 | 3);  // 7
        System.out.println(5 ^ 3);  // 6
        System.out.println(~5);     // -6
        System.out.println(5 << 1); // 10
        System.out.println(5 >> 1); // 2

        // Increment
        int x = 5;
        System.out.println(x++);  // 5, x=6
        System.out.println(++x);  // 7

        // Ternary
        String r = (a > b) ? "a" : "b";
    }
}

4. Control Flow 

public class ControlFlow {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int score = 85;

        // if-else
        if (score >= 90) System.out.println("A");
        else if (score >= 80) System.out.println("B");
        else System.out.println("C");

        // switch (traditional)
        int day = 2;
        switch (day) {
            case 1: System.out.println("Mon"); break;
            case 2: System.out.println("Tue"); break;
            default: System.out.println("Other");
        }

        // switch expression (Java 14+)
        String type = switch (day) {
            case 1, 7 -> "Weekend";
            case 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 -> "Weekday";
            default -> "Invalid";
        };

        // for
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) System.out.print(i + " ");

        // while
        int n = 3;
        while (n > 0) { System.out.print(n-- + " "); }

        // do-while (runs at least once)
        int k = 0;
        do { System.out.print(k++ + " "); } while (k < 3);

        // for-each
        int[] arr = {1, 2, 3};
        for (int v : arr) System.out.print(v + " ");

        // break / continue
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            if (i == 2) continue;   // skip
            if (i == 4) break;      // exit
            System.out.print(i + " ");
        }
    }
}

5. Arrays & Varargs 

import java.util.Arrays;

public class ArrayDemo {
    // Varargs
    static int sum(int... nums) {
        int total = 0;
        for (int n : nums) total += n;
        return total;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1D
        int[] arr = {5, 2, 8, 1};
        Arrays.sort(arr);
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(arr));

        // 2D
        int[][] matrix = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}};
        for (int[] row : matrix)
            for (int v : row)
                System.out.print(v + " ");

        // Jagged array
        int[][] jagged = new int[3][];
        jagged[0] = new int[]{1};
        jagged[1] = new int[]{2, 3};

        // Varargs
        System.out.println(sum(1, 2, 3, 4));  // 10
    }
}

6. Strings 

public class StringDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s = "Hello World";

        // Common methods
        System.out.println(s.length());                  // 11
        System.out.println(s.charAt(0));                 // H
        System.out.println(s.substring(0, 5));           // Hello
        System.out.println(s.toUpperCase());             // HELLO WORLD
        System.out.println(s.toLowerCase());             // hello world
        System.out.println(s.contains("World"));         // true
        System.out.println(s.startsWith("He"));          // true
        System.out.println(s.endsWith("ld"));            // true
        System.out.println(s.indexOf("o"));              // 4
        System.out.println(s.replace("World", "Java"));  // Hello Java
        System.out.println(s.trim());
        System.out.println(s.split(" ")[0]);             // Hello
        System.out.println(s.equals("Hello World"));     // true
        System.out.println(s.equalsIgnoreCase("HELLO WORLD")); // true
        System.out.println("  ".isBlank());              // true
        System.out.println(String.join("-", "a", "b"));  // a-b

        // String immutability
        String a = "abc";
        a.concat("def");        // "abcdef" discarded
        System.out.println(a);  // abc

        // StringBuilder (fast, mutable)
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) sb.append(i).append(",");
        System.out.println(sb);  // 0,1,2,3,4,

        // StringBuffer (thread-safe)
        StringBuffer sbf = new StringBuffer("Hi");
        sbf.append(" there");

        // String pool
        String x = "hi";
        String y = "hi";
        System.out.println(x == y);          // true (pool)
        String z = new String("hi");
        System.out.println(x == z);          // false (new object)
        System.out.println(x.equals(z));     // true
    }
}

Rule: Use StringBuilder in loops, String for constants, StringBuffer for threads.

7. OOP — Classes & Objects 

class Student {
    // Fields (encapsulation)
    private String name;
    private int age;

    // Static field
    private static int totalStudents = 0;

    // Constructor
    public Student(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
        totalStudents++;
    }

    // Copy constructor
    public Student(Student other) {
        this(other.name, other.age);
    }

    // Getters / Setters
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public int getAge() { return age; }

    // Instance method
    public void display() {
        System.out.println(name + ", " + age);
    }

    // Static method
    public static int getTotalStudents() { return totalStudents; }
}

public class OOPDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Student s1 = new Student("Alice", 20);
        Student s2 = new Student(s1);
        s1.display();
        System.out.println("Total: " + Student.getTotalStudents());
    }
}

8. OOP — 4 Pillars

8.1 Encapsulation 

class Account {
    private double balance;
    public double getBalance() { return balance; }
    public void deposit(double amt) {
        if (amt > 0) balance += amt;
    }
}

8.2 Inheritance 

class Animal {
    void sound() { System.out.println("Some sound"); }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void sound() { System.out.println("Woof"); }
    void fetch() { System.out.println("Fetching"); }
}

8.3 Polymorphism 

// Compile-time (overloading)
class MathUtil {
    int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
    double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }
    int add(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; }
}

// Runtime (overriding)
public class Poly {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal a = new Dog();  // upcasting
        a.sound();             // Woof (runtime)
    }
}

8.4 Abstraction 

abstract class Shape {
    abstract double area();
    void info() { System.out.println("Area = " + area()); }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
    double r;
    Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    @Override double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
}

9. Keywords 

public class Keywords {
    static int staticVar = 10;       // shared
    final int FINAL_VAR = 100;       // constant
    String name = "A";
    String name2 = name;             // this.name equivalent

    static { System.out.println("Static block"); }  // runs once

    Keywords() {
        // this() — call another constructor
        this("default");
    }

    Keywords(String name) {
        this.name = name;             // this — refers to current object
    }

    void show() {
        System.out.println(this.name);  // this keyword
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Object o = "hello";
        if (o instanceof String s) {     // pattern matching
            System.out.println(s.length());
        }
    }
}

class Base { void greet() { System.out.println("Base"); } }
class Child extends Base {
    @Override void greet() {
        super.greet();                 // super — parent method
        System.out.println("Child");
    }
}
Keyword Purpose
static Belongs to class, not instance
final Constant / no override / no inherit
this Current object
super Parent class
instanceof Type check

10. Access Modifiers

Modifier Same Class Same Package Subclass Anywhere
private ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌
default ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌
protected ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌
public ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

11. Packages & Imports 

package com.myapp.models;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.*;                     // wildcard
import static java.lang.Math.PI;       // static import
import static java.lang.Math.*;        // static wildcard

public class User { }

12. Object Class Methods 

class Person {
    String name;
    int age;

    Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; }

    @Override public String toString() { return name + " (" + age + ")"; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Person p)) return false;
        return age == p.age && name.equals(p.name);
    }

    @Override public int hashCode() { return 31 * name.hashCode() + age; }
}

public class ObjectDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Person p1 = new Person("A", 20);
        Person p2 = new Person("A", 20);
        System.out.println(p1.equals(p2));   // true
        System.out.println(p1.hashCode() == p2.hashCode()); // true
        System.out.println(p1);              // uses toString()
    }
}

Contract: If a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode().

13. Inner Classes 

public class Outer {
    private int x = 10;

    // Member inner
    class Inner {
        void show() { System.out.println(x); }
    }

    // Static nested
    static class StaticNested {
        void show() { System.out.println("Static nested"); }
    }

    void method() {
        // Local
        class Local { void show() { System.out.println("Local"); } }
        new Local().show();

        // Anonymous
        Runnable r = new Runnable() {
            public void run() { System.out.println("Anonymous"); }
        };
        r.run();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Outer o = new Outer();
        Outer.Inner in = o.new Inner();
        in.show();
        new Outer.StaticNested().show();
    }
}

14. Enums 

enum Day {
    MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI, SAT, SUN;

    boolean isWeekend() { return this == SAT || this == SUN; }
}

enum Status {
    SUCCESS(200), NOT_FOUND(404), ERROR(500);

    private final int code;
    Status(int code) { this.code = code; }
    int getCode() { return code; }
}

public class EnumDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Day d = Day.SAT;
        System.out.println(d.isWeekend());         // true
        System.out.println(d.name());              // SAT
        System.out.println(d.ordinal());           // 5

        for (Day day : Day.values()) System.out.print(day + " ");
        System.out.println(Day.valueOf("MON"));    // MON

        System.out.println(Status.ERROR.getCode()); // 500
    }
}

15. Interfaces (Advanced) & Functional Interfaces 

interface Vehicle {
    void start();                             // abstract
    default void stop() { System.out.println("Stopped"); }  // default
    static void info() { System.out.println("Vehicle"); }   // static
}

@FunctionalInterface
interface Calculator { int operate(int a, int b); }

public class InterfaceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Vehicle v = () -> System.out.println("Car started");  // lambda
        v.start();
        v.stop();
        Vehicle.info();

        Calculator add = (a, b) -> a + b;
        Calculator mul = (a, b) -> a * b;
        System.out.println(add.operate(2, 3));  // 5
        System.out.println(mul.operate(2, 3));  // 6
    }
}

Built-in functional interfaces:

Interface Method Purpose
Function<T,R> apply T → R
Predicate<T> test T → boolean
Supplier<T> get () → T
Consumer<T> accept T → void
BiFunction<T,U,R> apply (T,U) → R

16. Abstract Classes vs Interfaces

Feature Abstract Class Interface
Fields Any public static final only
Constructors ✅ ❌
Methods Abstract + concrete Abstract + default + static
Multiple inheritance ❌ ✅
When to use Shared state/code Capability/contract 
abstract class Shape {
    abstract double area();
    void show() { System.out.println("Area: " + area()); }
}

interface Drawable { void draw(); }

class Circle extends Shape implements Drawable {
    double r;
    Circle(double r) { this.r = r; }
    @Override double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; }
    @Override public void draw() { System.out.println("O"); }
}

17. Exceptions 

// Custom checked exception
class InsufficientBalanceException extends Exception {
    InsufficientBalanceException(String msg) { super(msg); }
}

// Custom unchecked
class InvalidAgeException extends RuntimeException {
    InvalidAgeException(String msg) { super(msg); }
}

public class ExceptionDemo {
    static void withdraw(double bal, double amt) throws InsufficientBalanceException {
        if (amt > bal) throw new InsufficientBalanceException("Low balance");
        System.out.println("Withdrawn: " + amt);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            withdraw(100, 500);
        } catch (InsufficientBalanceException e) {
            System.out.println("Caught: " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            System.out.println("Cleanup");
        }

        // Multi-catch
        try {
            int[] a = new int[2];
            a[5] = 10;
        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException | NullPointerException e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
        }

        // try-with-resources
        try (var reader = new java.io.StringReader("hi")) {
            System.out.println(reader.read());
        } catch (Exception e) { }

        // Nested try
        try {
            try { throw new RuntimeException("inner"); }
            finally { System.out.println("inner finally"); }
        } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("outer catch"); }
    }
}

Hierarchy: Throwable → Error, Exception → RuntimeException (unchecked) & others (checked).

18. Generics 

// Generic class
class Box<T> {
    private T value;
    void set(T v) { value = v; }
    T get() { return value; }
}

// Bounded type
class NumberBox<T extends Number> {
    T value;
    double asDouble() { return value.doubleValue(); }
}

// Generic method
class Util {
    static <T> void printArray(T[] arr) {
        for (T t : arr) System.out.print(t + " ");
    }

    // Wildcards
    static void printList(List<?> list) { }
    static void sumList(List<? extends Number> list) { }
    static void addInt(List<? super Integer> list) { }
}

public class GenericsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Box<String> b = new Box<>();
        b.set("Hello");
        System.out.println(b.get());

        NumberBox<Integer> nb = new NumberBox<>();
        nb.value = 5;
        System.out.println(nb.asDouble());

        Util.printArray(new Integer[]{1, 2, 3});
    }
}

Wildcards: ? extends T (producer) | ? super T (consumer) — PECS principle.

19. Collections Framework 

import java.util.*;

public class CollectionsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // LIST
        List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
        list.add("A"); list.add("B"); list.add("A");
        System.out.println(list.get(0));
        System.out.println(list.contains("B"));
        list.remove("A");

        LinkedList<String> ll = new LinkedList<>();
        ll.addFirst("X"); ll.addLast("Y");

        // SET
        Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();       // no order
        set.add(1); set.add(2); set.add(1);
        System.out.println(set);                  // [1, 2]

        Set<Integer> linkedSet = new LinkedHashSet<>();  // insertion order
        Set<Integer> treeSet = new TreeSet<>();          // sorted

        // QUEUE / DEQUE
        Queue<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>();
        q.offer(1); q.offer(2);
        System.out.println(q.poll());             // 1

        Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
        dq.addFirst(1); dq.addLast(2);

        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();  // min-heap
        pq.offer(5); pq.offer(1); pq.offer(3);
        System.out.println(pq.poll());            // 1

        // MAP
        Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
        map.put("A", 1); map.put("B", 2);
        System.out.println(map.get("A"));
        System.out.println(map.getOrDefault("Z", 0));
        map.forEach((k, v) -> System.out.println(k + "=" + v));

        TreeMap<String, Integer> tm = new TreeMap<>();      // sorted keys
        LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> lhm = new LinkedHashMap<>();  // order

        // Utility class
        Collections.sort(list);
        Collections.reverse(list);
        Collections.max(set);
    }
}
Type Order Duplicates Null Use case
ArrayList insertion ✅ ✅ Fast random access
LinkedList insertion ✅ ✅ Fast insert/delete
HashSet none ❌ ✅ (1) Fast lookup
LinkedHashSet insertion ❌ ✅ (1) Order + uniqueness
TreeSet sorted ❌ ❌ Sorted unique
HashMap none keys ❌ 1 null key Fast KV
TreeMap sorted keys — ❌ Sorted KV
PriorityQueue heap ✅ ❌ Min/max heap
