title: AWS Outage One Year Later: Lessons From Every Cloud Failure
description:
TL;DR

Every major cloud provider has had a serious outage since mid-2025, each from a different cause, so any single provider is a single point of failure.

  • On October 20, 2025, a DNS race condition in DynamoDB's automation took the DynamoDB endpoint in AWS us-east-1 offline. The event ran about 15 hours and spread to EC2 instance launches and Network Load Balancers.
  • Google Cloud (June 2025, global), Azure Front Door (October 2025, global), Oracle Cloud US East (Ashburn) (March 2026), and an automated Google Cloud action that suspended a customer's production account (May 2026) each failed in a different layer.
  • Failures hit three blast radii: a zone, a region, or a whole provider. Multi-region on one provider covers the first two. It doesn't cover a provider's global control plane, edge network, or account layer.
  • Put a second, independent, already-running path under every layer you can't lose, keep failover off the failing provider, and drill the switch.
  • Control Plane combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into one virtual cloud and runs workloads active-active across providers, with a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. During the October 20 outage, no Control Plane customer experienced downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry.

What happened in the AWS us-east-1 outage on October 20, 2025?

A latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS management system left the DynamoDB regional endpoint in us-east-1 with an empty DNS record, and everything that resolves that name failed. According to the AWS post-event summary, the event ran from 11:48 PM PDT on October 19 to 2:20 PM PDT on October 20 (06:48 to 21:20 UTC on October 20), about 15 hours. The disruption affected dozens of AWS services in us-east-1, and AWS's Health Dashboard event history lists the full set.

AWS's summary splits the impact into three periods:

  • DynamoDB became unreachable (11:48 PM to 2:40 AM PDT). Two automation components, a DNS Planner and DNS Enactors, manage DynamoDB's DNS. One unusually delayed Enactor applied an outdated plan, and another Enactor's cleanup step then deleted that plan, leaving an empty record for dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. Customer traffic and internal AWS services that depend on DynamoDB couldn't connect.
  • New EC2 instances failed to launch (2:25 AM to 10:36 AM PDT). After DNS was restored, internal subsystems that depend on DynamoDB stayed impaired, and AWS throttled some operations while it recovered. Some newly launched instances had connectivity problems until 1:50 PM PDT.
  • Network Load Balancers saw connection errors (5:30 AM to 2:09 PM PDT). Health checks began failing because new instances came into service before their network state had propagated, and automatic health check failover then removed capacity from service. AWS engineers disabled automatic NLB health check failover at 9:36 AM PDT.

AWS said it disabled the DynamoDB DNS automation worldwide until it fixed the race condition and added protections. Recovery that needed new instances was blocked for hours: AWS says Amazon Redshift's host-replacement workflows stalled while EC2 launches were impaired, leaving some clusters unavailable. AWS also notes that customers with DynamoDB global tables could still reach replicas in other regions, though replication to and from the us-east-1 replica lagged. Regional redundancy helped where it was real and tested.

What other major cloud outages happened in 2025 and 2026?

Four more major incidents hit a different provider or a different failure layer. The table lists major incidents from June 2025 to May 2026; it is a selection, and smaller incidents in the same period are not included.

Date Provider What failed Blast radius Duration Source
June 12, 2025 Google Cloud An invalid quota policy with blank fields replicated globally and crashed Service Control, the API management layer Global, all regions About 3 hours (most regions began recovering within 40 minutes; us-central1 took up to 2 hours 40 minutes) Google Cloud incident report
October 19 to 20, 2025 AWS A DynamoDB DNS race condition in us-east-1, cascading to EC2 launches and Network Load Balancers One region, many dependent services About 15 hours AWS post-event summary
October 29 to 30, 2025 Microsoft Azure Incompatible customer configuration metadata crashed the Azure Front Door data plane at edge sites Global edge network About 8.5 hours (15:41 to 00:05 UTC) Azure Front Door post-incident review
March 3 to 4, 2026 Oracle Cloud Infrastructure A network infrastructure issue affecting multiple OCI services in US East (Ashburn); Oracle has not published a root cause One region About 20 hours (13:24 UTC March 3 to 09:18 UTC March 4) Oracle incident record
May 19 to 20, 2026 Google Cloud (account level) An automated Google Cloud action that Railway reports incorrectly suspended its production account One customer's whole production account, cascading to its workloads on AWS and its own hardware About 8 hours Railway incident report
  • Google Cloud (June 2025). Google's report says the policy change replicated globally within seconds, and the failing code path was never exercised during its region-by-region rollout. Google's Cloud Service Health status page was down too, delaying its first incident post by about an hour, and some customers' monitoring running on Google Cloud also failed.
  • Azure Front Door (October 2025). Microsoft's review says this incident was not directly related to an earlier Front Door incident on October 9, although both were broadly related to configuration propagation risk.
  • Oracle US East (March 2026). Oracle describes a network infrastructure issue that caused connection timeouts, errors, and increased latency across multiple OCI services. The Register reported that it disrupted parts of TikTok's U.S. service, which TikTok's U.S. joint venture acknowledged (The Register). Oracle logged a second Ashburn networking incident that began 52 minutes after the first was resolved and ran until 04:40 UTC on March 5.
  • Account suspension (May 2026). Railway's report says the automated action extended to many Google Cloud accounts. Its edge proxies cached routing tables from a control plane hosted in Google Cloud, so when the cache expired, workloads on AWS and on its own hardware became unreachable even though they were still running. Railway takes responsibility for that architecture. Redundant workloads can still share one dependency that decides whether anyone can reach them.

Large systems have shared layers, and shared layers fail, whichever provider runs them.

What is a blast radius in a cloud outage?

A blast radius is the set of workloads that fail together when one thing breaks. Cloud failures fall into three scales, and each needs a different kind of redundancy.

Blast radius Typical cause What it takes out Redundancy that covers it Recent example
Zone A facility, power, cooling, or network fault in one availability zone Workloads placed only in that zone Replicas spread across zones in a region None among the five above; multi-zone designs usually absorb zone faults
Region A regional service, a regional dependency, or regional networking Everything in that region, plus anything that depends on its endpoints Active capacity in more than one region, with data replicated AWS us-east-1 (October 2025), Oracle US East (March 2026)
Provider A global control plane, global edge network, global configuration push, or account-level action Every region of that provider, or your whole account A second, independent provider, including the control path Google Cloud Service Control (June 2025), Azure Front Door (October 2025), the account suspension (May 2026)

Why does multi-region fail during cloud outages?

Multi-region covers regional failures. It doesn't cover failures in layers every region shares. Three of the five incidents above weren't regional. Google's Service Control policy data replicated to every region within seconds. Azure Front Door's crash spread to all edge sites worldwide. The account suspension took down an entire account, which spans every region, and then spread to other clouds through a routing dependency hosted in Google Cloud.

Multi-region plans also fail for quieter reasons:

  • The failover step needs a control plane call (launch an instance, change a route, update a record) in the region that is failing. On October 20, new EC2 launches in us-east-1 failed from 2:25 AM to 10:36 AM PDT.
  • The failover target shares a dependency with the primary, such as a global service, an identity system, or a DNS zone.
  • The monitoring that tells you to fail over runs on the provider that is down. Google's June 2025 report says this happened to some customers.
  • The plan was written but never exercised under load.

AI workloads add their own dependencies: model APIs, GPU capacity from neoclouds, and agents that fail a customer if they die mid-task. Each is another layer that needs a second path. For a regional failure like October 20, tested multi-region capacity is a real defense, but it covers only the regional layer.

How do you keep services up during a cloud outage?

Post-incident reports don't say who stayed up, but they show which preparations would have mattered. Build them before the incident:

  • Keep capacity already running. When instance launches fail, a plan to scale up on demand depends on a control plane that may be struggling. Capacity already serving in another location doesn't.
  • Keep the failover path off the failing layer. Traffic shifting, health checks, and routing decisions should run somewhere independent of the provider or region in trouble.
  • Monitor from outside the provider. Google's report shows what happens when the monitoring stack and the workload share a failure domain.
  • Map hidden dependencies. The account-suspension report shows workloads in three environments and a routing control plane in only one of them.
  • Drill the switch. Teams that rehearse find the stale credential, the missing quota, or the unreplicated dataset on a Tuesday afternoon instead of during an outage.
  • Match redundancy to the cost of downtime. Rank services by business impact and put the strongest design under the ones that cost the most when they stop.

Control Plane builds the first two into the platform: capacity running in every location, and routing that sits above any single provider. For a deeper look at targets and trade-offs, see our guides to high availability, RTO and RPO targets, and what single-region, multi-region, and multi-cloud designs can deliver.

How does Control Plane keep you up when a provider fails?

Control Plane combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into one virtual cloud, so you stay up when others are down. You choose the locations for a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC): AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure regions, Kubernetes clusters you already run, and your own servers on premises. Every workload runs active-active in all of them, with replicas already serving in each location. A built-in global endpoint sends each request to the nearest healthy location. When a zone, region, or provider fails, traffic moves to locations that are already running, and autoscaling adds replicas there as load arrives. Nothing has to boot, nobody runs a runbook, and failover doesn't depend on the failed provider's control plane.

The rest of the platform serves the same outcome. Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code, so nothing needs re-keying when traffic moves. Each location keeps serving the last healthy version until a new release passes its health checks, so a broken update can't take the workload down (docs). Capacity AI right-sizes CPU and memory to actual usage in every location. None of it needs a platform team to build or operate.

On October 20, 2025, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry (Beyond Backups). For the Google Cloud, Azure, Oracle, and account-level failures above, a GVC that spans more than one provider is designed to route around a failure confined to one.

Control Plane offers a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers. No migration is required: existing Kubernetes clusters and your own servers join as locations, so you add failure domains from what you already run.

Next step: watch us recreate the us-east-1 outage live on October 20 at 11 AM PT. Register for the webinar, or talk to the Control Plane team.

Cloud outage resilience checklist

Use this to find the layers you can't recover without. Answer each row for every service that matters to revenue.

Check Question to answer
Single points of failure Have we listed every provider, region, account, DNS zone, identity system, and control plane each service depends on?
Zone spread Are replicas spread across at least two zones?
Region spread Can the service run in a second region without a human launching new capacity?
Provider spread Can the service run on a second provider if a global layer or account fails?
Capacity already running Is the failover location already running enough replicas to carry real load?
Data Is data replicated to the failover location, with an RPO we have actually measured?
Failover path Does traffic shifting work if the primary provider's console, API, and DNS are unavailable?
Monitoring Does alerting run outside the provider we are monitoring?
Account risk Do we have a documented path if the provider suspends or restricts our account?
Credentials Can the failover location authenticate to everything it needs without a manual step?
Drills Have we run a failover in the last quarter and written down what broke?
Communication Does the team know who decides to fail over, and how customers are told?
SLA reality Do we know that provider SLA credits are service credits, not compensation for lost revenue?

Frequently asked questions

What caused the AWS us-east-1 outage in October 2025?

A latent race condition in the DNS management system for Amazon DynamoDB left the regional endpoint in us-east-1 with an empty DNS record, so services that resolve that endpoint couldn't connect. Recovery then continued through EC2 instance launch failures and Network Load Balancer connection errors.

How long did the October 2025 AWS outage last?

AWS's summary gives the event window as 11:48 PM PDT on October 19 to 2:20 PM PDT on October 20, about 15 hours, with three distinct periods of impact.

Which major cloud outages happened in 2025 and 2026?

This post covers Google Cloud's global Service Control outage (June 12, 2025), the AWS us-east-1 outage (October 19 to 20, 2025), the Azure Front Door global outage (October 29 to 30, 2025), the Oracle US East outage (March 3 to 4, 2026), and an automated Google Cloud suspension of a customer's production account (May 19 to 20, 2026). Other incidents happened in the period, so treat it as a selection.

How do you survive a cloud provider outage?

Identify what each service depends on, then give each dependency a second independent path: spread across zones, run active capacity in more than one region, and for critical services run on a second provider. Keep failover and monitoring off the failing provider, keep capacity already running, and drill the switch.

Is multi-region enough to survive an outage?

Multi-region protects against regional failures, such as the AWS us-east-1 and Oracle US East incidents, if failover works without the failing region. It doesn't protect against a failure in a provider's global control plane, edge network, or your account, as in the Google Cloud, Azure Front Door, and account-suspension incidents.

What is the difference between multi-cloud and multi-region?

Multi-region means running in more than one region of the same provider. Multi-cloud means running across more than one provider. Multi-region covers regional failures, and multi-cloud also covers provider-level failures, at the price of more work in networking, identity, and data replication unless a platform such as Control Plane handles them for you.

Is multi-cloud worth it?

It depends on what an hour of downtime costs you. Provider SLA credits are service credits, not compensation for lost revenue. For revenue-critical services, a second provider removes a failure class that regions can't. Control Plane makes a second provider another location in the same GVC, with capacity scaled to demand in each location. Rank services by business impact and give the most critical ones cross-provider redundancy first.

What happened to Control Plane customers during the AWS outage?

During the October 2025 AWS outage, 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their Global Virtual Clouds. Their workloads were active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry. Control Plane offers a 99.999% availability SLA for workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

title: Most PySpark Tuning Advice Starts in the Wrong Place
description:
When I benchmarked PySpark's UDF types earlier this year, I ran the same three workloads (trivial arithmetic, a string transform, a normal CDF) at five scales, from 100 thousand rows to 100 million. At 100 million rows, the default row-at-a-time Python UDF took about 10 seconds for arithmetic that a built-in function finished in under a fifth of a second. At 100 thousand rows, the same UDF was the fastest Python option I tested.

Both results are true, and between them they're most of what you need to know about PySpark performance: the cost is almost never in your function. It's in how many times, and in what shape, your data crosses from the JVM into Python, and whether that crossing is large enough to matter at all.

My argument is that there is really one PySpark performance technique, applied at different places: cross the JVM/Python boundary less often, move less across it, or stop paying for a JVM where you don't need one. The changes worth making are ordered by how much of that crossing they remove, and the biggest one, not crossing at all, is also the most often skipped.

The history of how Arrow came to carry that crossing is in Arrow in PySpark, 2016 to 2026, and the full benchmark is in Stop Blaming Serialization for Slow Python UDFs. This post is the practical version: what to change, in what order, and what each change actually removes.

Where the time goes

PySpark is a Python client for a JVM engine. DataFrame operations build a plan in Python (through Py4J, which only ever carries control messages, never bulk data) and the JVM executes it; df.filter(col("x") > 5).groupBy("y").count() never puts a row into Python, which is why it runs at the same speed as Scala. The data only leaves the JVM when your own code needs it:

Everything outside arrows ① and ② happens at native speed. Every change below makes those two arrows smaller, rarer, or unnecessary, and I've ordered them by how much they took off the arrows in what I measured, or, where I haven't measured, by what they remove.

Don't cross at all: built-ins and SQL UDFs

The largest win isn't a better UDF; it's no UDF. Built-in functions run inside the JVM as Catalyst expressions, fused by whole-stage code generation into tight loops, and never serialize anything.

What surprised me more is that SQL UDFs get the same treatment. Spark 4.0 added SQL user-defined functions (SPARK-46057), and their bodies are inlined into the logical plan, so the optimizer can see straight through them:

CREATE FUNCTION classify(score INT) RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
    WHEN score > 90 THEN 'excellent'
    WHEN score > 70 THEN 'good'
    ELSE 'needs_improvement'
END;

In my benchmark (median wall-clock time, 50M rows, Spark 4.1.0 through Spark Connect on one machine), the SQL UDF was indistinguishable from the built-ins, and every Python option cost several times more:

arithmetic string normal CDF
built-in functions 0.107 s 0.486 s 0.176 s
SQL UDF 0.095 s 0.477 s n/a
fastest Python UDF (@arrow_udf) 0.725 s 1.545 s 0.762 s
default Python UDF (@udf, pickle) 5.199 s 6.216 s 6.183 s

So the first question for any UDF is whether it needs to be Python. Plenty of "we need a UDF" logic is a CASE expression, a string function, or a date calculation that already exists in pyspark.sql.functions. Python earns its place when you need a library (scikit-learn, a parser, a C extension) or logic that genuinely can't be expressed in SQL. Everything after this point is about paying less for that choice.

Cross once per batch, not once per row

If it has to be Python, the next biggest lever is how often Spark calls your function. A regular @udf is called once per row; @pandas_udf and @arrow_udf are called once per batch of rows. That difference showed up as a hard ceiling in my runs: every row-at-a-time UDF, whatever it computed, topped out at roughly 8 to 10 million rows per second, which is roughly the rate at which CPython can be entered and exited. The batched UDFs weren't bound by it.

50M rows arithmetic string normal CDF
@udf (pickle, per row) 5.199 s 6.216 s 6.183 s
@udf(useArrow=True) (Arrow transport, still per row) 2.228 s 4.430 s 2.942 s
@pandas_udf (per batch, pandas.Series) 0.789 s 2.512 s 0.819 s
@arrow_udf (per batch, pyarrow.Array) 0.725 s 1.545 s 0.762 s

Two things in that table decide what to change. Moving a per-row UDF onto Arrow transport helps, 1.4x to 2.4x here, and on Spark 4.2 you get it for free: 4.2 finally flipped spark.sql.execution.pythonUDF.arrow.enabled (and its UDTF counterpart) to true by default, after the same change was merged for 4.0 and reverted before release (SPARK-48516).

But rewriting to a batched UDF is worth several times more again, because it removes the per-row call rather than making the trip to it cheaper.

Between the two batched options, the choice mostly comes down to strings: @arrow_udf was only 5 to 9% faster than @pandas_udf on numeric work, but about 1.6x faster on the string transform, because pandas has traditionally stored strings as individual Python objects while Arrow keeps them in one contiguous buffer.

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from pyspark.sql.functions import arrow_udf

@arrow_udf("string")
def add_suffix(x: pa.Array) -> pa.Array:
    return pc.binary_join_element_wise(pc.utf8_upper(x), pa.scalar("_SUFFIX"), "")

One warning, because I learned it the expensive way: spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled is not the UDF setting. It governs toPandas() and createDataFrame(), and it's the one my benchmark originally toggled for its "Arrow" case, which is why I once reported that Arrow transport changes nothing for UDFs. It was the same pickled UDF, measured twice. (On 4.2 that setting is also on by default, so the confusion matters less for new code than for anyone reading old tuning advice.)

And the scale caveat from the opening is real. At small sizes, fixed costs dominate, and the ordering can flip:

arithmetic, median seconds built-in @pandas_udf @udf(useArrow=True) @udf (pickle)
100K rows 0.073 0.181 0.212 0.161
10M rows 0.074 0.299 0.568 1.092
100M rows 0.147 1.400 4.188 10.139

If your job touches a few hundred thousand rows, rewriting its UDFs is unlikely to be what makes it faster.

Don't produce the data: Python data sources with pushdown

After calling Python less, the next thing to remove is data that never needed to exist. Built-in sources like Parquet already push filters down and skip row groups that can't match; for most of Spark's history, custom sources that could do the same had to be written in Java or Scala. Spark 4.0 added the Python Data Source API (SPARK-44076), and Spark 4.1 added filter pushdown for it (SPARK-51271), so a source written in Python can now turn WHERE status = 'active' into a query parameter, a database predicate, or a skipped file block, and never send the rest.

When I went back over my own notes on this feature to write this post, the example I'd written was wrong, and checking it against Spark's source turned up something I hadn't known: pushdown for Python sources is off by default. It's governed by spark.sql.python.filterPushdown.enabled, an internal setting added in 4.1 whose description says enabling it costs "running Python worker one additional time during planning"; without it, your pushFilters() is never called.

The method also has a less obvious contract than I'd assumed. It returns the filters Spark must still apply after the scan, not the ones you accepted, and each filter's attribute is a column-path tuple:

from pyspark.sql.datasource import DataSourceReader, EqualTo

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.python.filterPushdown.enabled", "true")  # off by default

class ApiReader(DataSourceReader):
    def __init__(self, options):
        self.url = options.get("url")
        self.pushed = []

    def pushFilters(self, filters):
        # Filters arrive ANDed together; yield the ones Spark must still apply.
        for f in filters:
            if isinstance(f, EqualTo) and f.attribute == ("status",):
                self.pushed.append(f)          # handled at the source
            else:
                yield f

    def read(self, partition):
        import requests
        params = {f.attribute[0]: f.value for f in self.pushed}
        for row in requests.get(self.url, params=params).json():
            yield (row["id"], row["name"], row["status"])

Only conjunctions are pushed (a filter like a = 1 or b = 2 arrives as an empty list), and a reader can also yield pyarrow.RecordBatch objects instead of tuples, which the Spark docs say can improve performance by "up to one order of magnitude."

I haven't measured either path, so this is the one change on the list I'm ranking by what it removes rather than by what I saw: for a source backed by an API or a database, rows that are never fetched are the cheapest rows there are.

Skip pandas for grouped work

Per-group logic (normalize within each location, fit a model per customer) has long meant applyInPandas, which converts every group from Arrow into a pandas DataFrame and back. Spark 4.0 added applyInArrow (SPARK-40559), and each group now reaches your function as a pyarrow.Table, in the format it crossed the boundary in:

def normalize(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    totals = table.column("total")
    mean, std = pc.mean(totals).as_py(), pc.stddev(totals).as_py()
    normalized = (pa.array([0.0] * len(totals)) if not std
                  else pc.divide(pc.subtract(totals, mean), std))
    return pa.Table.from_arrays([table.column("order_id"), totals, normalized],
                                names=["order_id", "total", "normalized"])

result = orders.groupBy("location_id").applyInArrow(
    normalize, schema="order_id long, total double, normalized double")

This is the same trade as step 2, one level up: it removes a conversion, not a crossing, so the payoff should track what that conversion cost in my UDF numbers (little for numeric groups, more for string-heavy ones, more for larger groups). I haven't benchmarked the grouped APIs, so I won't put a number on it.

Take the JVM out of the client

Spark Connect is on this list for a different reason than the others. It doesn't make a query faster; it removes the JVM from every client process. Classic PySpark embeds a full Spark driver in each notebook, scheduled job, and CI container. With Connect, the client sends unresolved plans over gRPC and gets Arrow batches back, and the thin pyspark-client package has no JVM and needs no JDK. When I measured it for my own Connect demos on 4.2, the numbers were less dramatic than the pitch:

pyspark (full) pyspark-client
PyPI artifact 429.28 MB 1.60 MB
installed pyspark/ 481 MB 19 MB
Spark JARs on the client 456 MB, 276 files none
virtual env with Connect dependencies 820 MB 359 MB

The last row is the honest one: pyarrow, pandas, and numpy are required dependencies, so the environment shrinks by less than half.

What you actually get is a client with no JVM to start, no JDK to install, and no way for a crashed notebook to take the driver down with it. What you give up is anything that needs the JVM on your side: RDDs, SparkContext, custom accumulators. ML on Connect has been supported since 4.0 and generally available since 4.1, so that's no longer on the list of reasons to stay classic.

Give Python the memory it actually uses

The last change is the one that turns slow jobs into failed ones when it's wrong. Python workers live outside the JVM heap, so the settings most Spark tuning advice is about don't cover them:

The rule is that the container has to fit the heap, the overhead, and the OS, and that Python's share has to come out of the overhead. If you use toPandas() or pandas UDFs, spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.selfDestruct.enabled frees Arrow buffers as they're converted, so the same data doesn't sit in memory twice.

Beyond that, the usual advice still holds: let Adaptive Query Execution size shuffle partitions at runtime (it's been on by default since 3.2, and 4.1 extended it to stateless streaming, SPARK-53941, which can change a streaming query's behaviour after an upgrade), and broadcast small dimension tables instead of shuffling them. None of that is specific to Python, which is why it's last on a list about Python.

What's coming in 4.3

The 4.3 branch hasn't been released (its first release candidate failed its vote on September 6, and there's no new date), but it shows where the boundary is heading, and it confirms the order above.

The most interesting change goes around the boundary instead of through it: experimental transpilation of Python UDFs into Spark expressions (SPIP SPARK-54783, spark.sql.experimental.optimizer.transpilePyUDFs). A simple enough Python function would never cross into Python at all, which is change number 1 done for you. It's off by default, requires ANSI mode, and only works in classic mode, not Connect, but it's the only approach on the branch that could get under the per-row ceiling rather than lowering the cost of hitting it.

Alongside it are smaller changes to the crossing itself: pipelined, asynchronous transfer of UDF batches (spark.python.udf.pipelined.enabled, SPARK-56642, off by default) and a cap on bytes per UDF batch (SPARK-57593). A proposal to make Spark better on a single machine also adds an Arrow format for Spark's in-memory cache (SPARK-57268).

Two things haven't moved. PySpark still doesn't support pandas 3, even on the 4.3 branch; it pins pandas below 3.0, and the ticket to support it (SPARK-55139) is open, so the PyArrow-backed string type pandas 3 made the default in January won't help pandas UDFs yet. And Real-Time Mode in 4.3 gains stateful operators, but still can't run Python UDFs (SPARK-57237 is open).

Housekeeping to plan for: 4.2 raised the minimum PyArrow to 18.0.0 and dropped PyPy, and 4.3 drops Python 3.10 (SPARK-56889).

I opened with a UDF that took 10 seconds at 100 million rows and was the fastest Python option at 100 thousand. The reason is the same one behind every change on this list: your function was never the expensive part.

The crossing was, and the best PySpark optimization is still the one that decides the data doesn't need to cross.

title: September 30, 2026
description:
API Gateway

Feature

Authenticate MCP tool discovery with an API key

API key authentication is now supported for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools/list method. You can name an API key security scheme in tools-list.security, in addition to a JWT security scheme.

For more information, see Configure Model Context Protocol.

Apigee API hub

Feature

Service type system attribute (GA)

API hub now includes Service type, a system attribute that classifies an API as Code, Model, Agent, or Skill. Service type describes what a service is. API style describes how you call it. Use Service type to find and govern your APIs, agents, models, and skills.

Set Service type when you register or edit an API. To show only your agents, filter the API list by Service type, or select the new Agent chip. In the API, use the service_type field.

This feature is Generally Available (GA). For more information, see Supported system attributes.

Feature

AI performance and Tool performance dashboards in API insights

API insights in API hub now includes two dashboards for AI and agent traffic:

  • AI performance reports token usage and model latency for the large language models called through your gateways, with filters for model and provider.
  • Tool performance reports traffic, throughput, payload sizes, and latency for your Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, with filters for MCP server, deployment, and tool name.

For more information, see API insights dashboards.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.1

On September 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.1.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.1.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

External Cassandra datastore support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.1 adds support for connecting an Apigee hybrid runtime to a Cassandra datastore that runs in a separate Kubernetes cluster (external datastore mode). In external datastore mode, the runtime cluster runs with cassandra.replicaCount: 0 (no local Cassandra pods) and connects to the remote Cassandra ring using the cassandra.properties.externalHost property (a comma-separated list of remote Cassandra IP addresses) and the optional cassandra.properties.externalEndpointsSync property for dynamic endpoint synchronization.

For more information, see Use an external Cassandra datastore and Configuration property reference.

Change

The Apigee operator's Kubernetes manager role now includes the core endpoints permission.

In v1.17.1, the Apigee operator's manager role is granted the core ("" API group) endpoints resource, with the verbs get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete. This role is the namespaced apigee-manager-role Kubernetes Role created by default in the apigee namespace. The operator needs this permission for the external (cross-cluster) Cassandra datastore feature: when a datastore uses an external host, the operator directly manages the Endpoints object of the selectorless Kubernetes Service that fronts it.

This permission is granted to all v1.17.1 installations, whether or not you use an external datastore. It is added to the operator's manager role and is not gated on any configuration property, so security teams that audit operator permissions should expect it after upgrading. Because the grant is on a namespaced Role, the new access is limited to the Apigee namespace and does not extend cluster-wide.

Most installations require no action. The apigee-operator Helm chart defines this role, so running helm upgrade on the apigee-operator chart grants the permission automatically.

If you self-manage the Apigee operator's Kubernetes RBAC, meaning you prevent Helm from creating or updating the operator's Role objects, add the endpoints resource to the existing core ("") API group rule of the apigee-manager-role Role in the Apigee namespace, or append the following rule:

- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

If you self-manage the operator's RBAC, add this permission before you upgrade to v1.17.1. If you have already upgraded without this permission, apply the update to your role configuration to ensure proper operator functionality. Without this permission, the operator cannot manage the Endpoints object of an external datastore, so the external datastore feature does not work. If you do not use an external datastore, the operator works without this permission.

Note: The ao.args.disableManagedClusterRoles property does not apply to this change. That property governs only ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects, whereas this permission is added to a namespaced Role.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Deprecated

Support for backing up and restoring workloads managed via the legacy appliance management console is deprecated.

Key milestones for this deprecation include the following:

  • End of Support for New Backups: After September 30, 2027, you will no longer be able to run new backups using the legacy stack.
  • End of Standard Restores: Support for standard restores, exports, and migrations using the legacy appliance management console continues till March 31, 2028.

For more information, see Deprecations.

BigQuery

Feature

The BigQuery Security center is now available in the Google Cloud console. You can use the Security center to analyze your data security profile, create and manage row- and column-level security policies, and configure and manage data governance and policy tags. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

BigQuery jobs explorer layout and filtering improvements, including status counts in the filter bar, resource grouping, and timeline metric charts, are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use the OBJ.LIST function to perform spontaneous discovery and analysis of unstructured data. The OBJ.LIST function returns a table of metadata and ObjectRef values for files stored in Cloud Storage, and does not require you to create a persistent object table.

This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now view the UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, and EXPORT execution steps in your query plans.

Capacity Planner

Feature

Preview: You can use Capacity Assist, which provides AI-powered assistance through Gemini in Capacity Planner, to help you understand and manage your resource usage and plan capacity (Preview). You can use natural-language prompts in Capacity Assist to do the following:

  • Analyze historical usage patterns across regions and resources.
  • Forecast capacity needs and identify quota risks early.
  • Simulate growth events to plan future capacity.
  • Get answers to your Capacity Planner questions.

For more information, see Plan capacity with Capacity Assist.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

A new quota system governing the configuration size of Application Load Balancers is now generally available. This update increases the individual URL map size limit from 64 KB and 128 KB to 1 MB. For more information, see URL map size and quota units.

Key aspects of this feature include:

  • Complexity-based quota: Quota units reflect URL map complexity (number of rules, hostnames, and path matchers).
  • Scoped measurement: Quota is measured and enforced on a per-project, per-region, or per-VPC depending on Application Load Balancer type.
  • Active consumption: Only URL maps currently referenced by forwarding rules contribute to quota usage.
  • New URL map size limit: The new quota has a new URL map size limit increased to 1 MB for global and regional external and internal Application Load Balancers. Classic Application Load Balancers remain restricted to 64 KB.

For more information on increasing your limit, please contact Google Cloud Support.

Cloud Monitoring

Announcement

The application topology graph is now generally available (GA). This graph helps you to understand relationships between applications, services, and workloads, and shows you traffic flow and incidents in the context of your applications.

Cloud Storage

Feature

Cloud Storage client libraries now provide automated, end-to-end checksumming by default for object read and write operations to help maintain data integrity from client to storage. For more information, see data validation.

Cloud Tasks

Feature

Cloud Tasks support for the following is generally available (GA):

  • Set retry parameters when creating a task and override the queue-level retry configuration for the task.
  • Create a batch of tasks and add the batch to an existing queue.
  • Delete a batch of tasks from a queue.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can specify a 120-second preemption notice duration while creating Spot VMs. Use this feature for workloads on Spot VMs where you want up to an additional 120 seconds for handling preemption. If you want to migrate existing Spot VMs workloads, make sure you update your workload to handle preemption outside of a shutdown script and test preemption. For more information, see Spot VMs and Create and use Spot VMs.

Datastream

Feature

Datastream now supports partial backfill for SQL Server, Spanner, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and MySQL sources. Partial backfill lets you load a specific subset of data from the source into the destination by providing a SQL WHERE clause as a custom filter.

For more information, see Initiate partial backfill.

Dialogflow

Fixed

Dialogflow CX: An issue in Dialogflow CX was identified where sensitive authentication tokens stored in conversational session parameters could be returned in cleartext via DetectIntent API responses. A server-side fix has been applied to redact and sanitize authentication credentials from conversational API outputs. No customer configuration changes or updates are required.

Deprecated

All generative features: gemini-2.5-flash and gemini-2.5-flash-lite models will be deprecated by Dec 23, 2026. Upgrade to newer Gemini models such as gemini-3.1-flash-lite before the deprecation date.

BidiStreamingAnalyzeContent API has become generally available (GA).

Eventarc

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Cloud Trace integration with Agent Gateway (Preview)

Agent Gateway integrates with Cloud Trace in Preview to provide end-to-end request observability for agent workloads. Enabling Cloud Trace gives you visibility into how requests travel from your agents through the gateway and across Google Cloud services, tools, agents, and MCP servers.

For more information, see Use Cloud Trace.

Feature

xAI's Grok 4.7

Grok 4.7 is available in Preview in Model Garden.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.11.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Tiered location configuration: Added support for configuring the service location using the CM_LOCATION environment variable or location in config.yaml (defaulting to global), replacing the --location command-line flag.
  • CI gate severity validation: Updated cm find to validate --fail-on severity values (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, or NONE) up front instead of silently ignoring misspelled severities.
  • Sandboxed VCS branching and hardening: Enabled vcs_branch creation and candidate branch cleanup inside the default sandboxed worker for --architecture sessions, and hardened VCS template expansion against shell metacharacters and command injection.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Normalized vulnerability type casing and relative file paths during cm find and consensus runs to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Extended HTTP 429 retry backoff (Retry-After support and up to 60-second quota refill windows) and automatic stream reconnection to improve scan resilience under rate limiting.
    • Preserved standalone cm find, cm verify, and cm fix sessions on interrupt (SIGINT/SIGTERM) so interrupted runs can be resumed with cm session resume, while still canceling parallel consensus worker operations.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

The App Topology API that provides agent topologies in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is now generally available

This launch introduces the following changes:

  • A new query builder for customizing suggested quick queries or creating your own query on the Topologies page. Custom queries let you explore more data related to your agents, such as identity, alerts, vulnerabilities, and underlying infrastructure. For details, see View topologies for a project.
  • A streamlined experience for the single-agent topology in Agent Registry. A topology with single-hop traffic to and from the agent automatically loads on the page.

The headless mobile SDK, for Android and iOS, is now available. With this SDK, you can embed the capabilities of Google Cloud CCaaS into your mobile app while retaining full control over the UI. The headless mobile SDK supports calls (including scheduled calls), chats, and email.

title: Turn an AI Bug Report into a Regression Case Someone Else Can Reproduce
description:
“It gave the wrong answer yesterday” is useful feedback, but it is not yet a regression test.

You need enough context to reproduce the problem, a reviewed definition of acceptable behaviour and a record of the version that produced it. Without those, a prompt edit can appear to fix the report simply because the next run used different evidence.

Here is a small workflow for turning an AI bug report into a test case. The refund example is fictional. This article was generated by an AI agent for Acadify Solution and Acadify AI Lab.

Start with the user's task

Ask what the person was trying to do. Separate that from the answer they disliked.

For example: “Find out whether a purchase is eligible for a refund” describes a task. “The answer sounded too confident” describes an observation. Both belong in the investigation, but neither establishes the expected result on its own.

Capture only the inputs you are authorised to retain. Do not ask for passwords, tokens or a dump of unrelated customer records. If you replace private details with synthetic ones, record the transformation and review whether the failure still reproduces.

Freeze the conditions you can control

Record the application build, prompt version, model identifier and configuration. For retrieval-based features, retain an authorised snapshot of the relevant context or a reproducible corpus/index reference.

If your environment cannot reproduce a provider-side model version exactly, say so. “Same model name” may not establish an identical system. Record the date and the available version information, and limit your conclusions accordingly.

A case file might look like this:

{
  "case_id": "refund-clarification-001",
  "origin": "synthetic example",
  "task": "Explain refund eligibility",
  "input": "Can I return this purchase?",
  "fixture_version": "refund-fixture-v1",
  "context": "Refund eligibility requires the purchase date and item condition.",
  "expected_behaviour": [
    "Ask for the missing purchase date and item condition",
    "Do not claim that the customer is eligible yet"
  ],
  "review_status": "needs human review"
}

This is an illustrative schema, not a complete evaluation format. Your system may also need conversation history, tool outputs, permission scope and language or accessibility requirements.

Review the expectation before scoring

Do not turn the reported answer into the ground truth automatically. Review the governing source and the actual task.

In the example, asking for the missing details is acceptable. Several phrasings could do that well. Exact string matching would reject many reasonable answers and may reward one that merely copies a reference response.

Use explicit criteria: did the response request the needed information, avoid an unsupported eligibility claim and remain within the available policy? If reviewers disagree, resolve the ambiguity or label it. A disputed case should not quietly become a release gate.

Locate the failure stage

For a RAG workflow, inspect the retrieved context before changing the generation prompt. Was the relevant policy present? Was it current? Did a filter exclude it? Did the application truncate the passage?

For a tool-using workflow, inspect the arguments and result. A correct explanation of a failed lookup does not mean the underlying operation completed successfully.

Give the case a failure category that helps the next investigation. “Bad answer” is less useful than “missing evidence,” “unsupported conclusion” or “tool target mismatch.” Avoid pretending the category proves a cause before you have checked it.

Compare versions on the same reviewed cases

Run the current version and proposed version under stated conditions. Retain their outputs and the reviewer decisions. Add cases representing previously working tasks, rather than checking only the reported failure.

Where output is stochastic, predefine an appropriate repeat count and report the individual outcomes as well as a summary. A single good response is weak evidence of a reliable fix.

Do not repeatedly tune on every test you intend to use as an independent check. Keep a held-out set, and track which cases have influenced development.

Keep the result separate from the release decision

A useful comparison table is small:

Case Current version Proposed version Review note
Reported failure Pending review Pending review Expected behaviour agreed first
Previously working task Pending review Pending review Check for a meaningful regression
Missing information Pending review Pending review Clarification may be the correct outcome

These cells intentionally contain no invented scores. Fill them with observations from your own authorised test run.

Your release gate should reflect the product's consequences. An access violation or incorrect side effect may deserve a different gate from a wording issue. An aggregate average can hide a failure on a critical task.

Make the case useful next month

Give the case an owner and a reason it exists. When the policy or workflow changes, review whether the expected behaviour remains valid. Version the revision instead of changing the label invisibly.

Set access and retention rules for stored traces. A regression suite should preserve useful evidence, not become an ungoverned archive of user data.

The goal is a report that another engineer can investigate and a test that still means something after the immediate fix. That is a more useful handover than “we changed the prompt and it seems better.”

What detail is most often missing from the AI bug reports your team receives?

title: How much does it cost to build your own LLM?
description:
Building a domain-specific large language model involves adapting proven foundation models to private records, operational vocabulary, and specific company systems rather than training raw networks from scratch. Pricing is fixed once the written scope is approved, with scoping and discovery included. Specific integrations, data migrations, and measured accuracy targets determine the scope of custom AI work, while milestones fall due only after work is accepted.

How much does it cost to develop a custom LLM?

A large language model is a software program trained on text collections to read, summarize, and generate natural language. When business leaders ask about building their own model, they usually want a system that understands company contracts, policy records, technical manuals, or operational logs without leaking confidential records.

In our practice, we do not charge a separate discovery fee before quoting the build. You receive an architecture assessment and project plan as part of the initial engagement.

The client gets a fixed figure once the written scope is approved, and pays against milestones they accept. This structure ensures that every expenditure connects to tangible milestones rather than ambiguous research hours. You can read more about engineering choices in our guides on llm customization integration across enterprise operations.

In our estimating model you pay 0 AED per user licence fee. In our estimating model changes after hypercare are paid for as small projects, and in our estimating model a monthly support and maintenance plan is optional and you can decline it.

What moves the price above the baseline?

Every company operates with distinct legacy records, workflows, and infrastructure requirements. The final budget rises above the foundation level because of specific technical drivers that must be engineered to deliver a dependable system.

Connecting your model to company databases requires custom software interfaces. Moving live projects out of the firm's spreadsheets is a data migration that moves the quote above the floor. If internal records reside in messy spreadsheets or siloed file storage, standardizing that material demands structured data engineering.

Connecting the build to the accounting package a fit-out firm already runs is an integration that moves the quote above the floor. Site and workshop teams who need the system on a phone without reliable signal move the quote above the floor.

Software delivery structure and running cost parameters

Cost Component Typical Structure Ownership and Terms
Scoping and discovery Included in build quote Fixed price once written scope is approved
User access licensing 0 AED per user Zero recurring seat fees
Cloud hosting infrastructure Billed at direct cost Client contracts cloud provider directly
Post-launch enhancements Priced as small projects Optional monthly maintenance plans available

Can we build my own LLM?

Any organization can build a custom language intelligence platform without spending millions of dollars on base model compute. Rather than retraining raw neural networks from scratch, custom engineering focuses on fine-tuning foundational models and building retrieval-augmented pipelines.

Retrieval-augmented generation, commonly called RAG, is an architecture that looks up verified passages from internal company records and injects those excerpts into the language prompt. This technique guarantees that the model references real operational evidence instead of guessing answers.

We measure a general model on a recorded test set from your own material first, fine tune only if it falls short, then re-measure on the same set. You see both accuracy figures, before and after fine tuning, before accepting the work. Answers are grounded in your documents with the source shown, and out-of-scope or low-confidence questions go to a person.

We fine tune on your own material where a general model is not accurate enough. This disciplined path protects business funds by only adding complex training procedures when standard retrieval proves insufficient on actual business cases.

Where does custom language intelligence pay off first?

Deploying domain language intelligence delivers rapid value when applied to repetitive, text-heavy operations. These operations include document classification, field reporting, vendor communication, and policy lookup for customer service teams.

Every value an AI automation writes has to pass three checks before it is saved: a fixed schema matched against your master data, a pointer to the source document, and agreement across the documents that repeat it. Anything that fails a check goes to a person for review. Accuracy is measured on a recorded test set of your real documents before you accept the work.

Our generative AI systems refuse or route to a person any value that has no source. We re-run the recorded case set whenever the prompt, the model or the data of a generative AI system changes. This operational setup prevents incorrect answers from entering customer databases.

Our AI agents route out-of-scope or low-confidence inputs to a person instead of acting on them. The client sees the agent's measured accuracy against a recorded case set before accepting the work. To inspect how intelligent agents integrate into core products, explore our AI and machine learning development services.

How do we safeguard company data and prevent hallucinations?

A hallucination is when an artificial intelligence generates convincing but completely fictional statements. In commercial enterprise environments, hallucinations create unacceptable legal and financial exposure.

Security requirements are written into the specification before the build begins.

Data in the systems we build is encrypted at rest and in transit. Access is role based, so each person sees only what their role needs. The systems we build keep a full audit log of who did what and when. Penetration testing runs before launch at a depth that matches the risk of the system.

Personal data is handled in line with the UAE Personal Data Protection Law from the architecture stage. Where data cannot leave the country or the client's network, we host the system in the UAE or on the client's own servers. We agree up front how quickly the system must be back after a failure and how much recent data the client could afford to lose. Backups are kept in a separate location and a full restore is tested before go-live. If an AI service the system depends on is unavailable, work queues safely and the team can carry on by hand.

How long does a custom LLM project take to deploy?

Custom development follows a structured schedule to prevent delays and validate performance metrics early. We typically plan an LLM customization or domain-specific model project at 8 to 12 weeks from kickoff.

Before any model is chosen, we collect 100 to 300 of your real documents into the test set. For an enterprise generative AI platform the first phase goes live 8 to 12 weeks from kickoff, and larger scope follows in further phases. This phased schedule provides demonstrable software early while larger operational components develop in parallel.

At handover the client receives the source code, the documentation, the tests and every credential. There is no lock-in, so the client can bring in another team later. We are a local team based in Dubai working in English and Arabic.

Frequently asked questions

How much does LLM cost?

In our estimating model you pay no per-user licence fee. The final investment reflects your specific integrations, migration needs, and measured accuracy targets.

How much is this going to cost us?

We do not charge a separate discovery fee before quoting the build. You receive a fixed figure once the written scope is approved, and you pay against milestones you accept.

How much does it cost to develop a custom LLM?

Every quote depends on the custom AI work and system integrations your operations require. We agree on the written scope first so your business has predictable milestone payments without open-ended research costs.

Can we build my own LLM?

Any business can deploy a domain-specific model by fine-tuning existing foundation models or using retrieval pipelines on internal documents, avoiding ground-up model training entirely.

Key takeaways

  • Building a custom model involves tailoring proven foundation systems rather than expensive ground-up training.
  • Project costs begin from an established baseline that includes discovery, scoping, and architectural planning.
  • Accuracy is established by testing models against recorded company documents prior to deployment acceptance.
  • Custom systems carry zero per-user licensing fees and provide full ownership of all source code.
  • Critical information stays secure through strict role permissions, local data hosting, and full audit logging.

title: AUTO_CDC: Turning an event log into current state with Spark Declarative Pipelines
description:
The question an event log can't answer cheaply

The dataset I use for most of my pipeline demos is a simulated ghost kitchen (a delivery-only restaurant operation), and like most operational data it arrives as an append-only log. Every order produces a lifecycle of events, each stamped with a time and a per-order sequence number, and a day of it is about a million events. The generator deliberately injects a few percent of late and duplicated events, because real streams do that.

Logs like this are excellent at answering what happened and awkward at answering what operations people actually ask: which orders are live right now, and where is each one?

The usual answer is to recompute it. Group the whole history by order, take the latest event for each, drop the cancelled ones, and repeat on every refresh, paying for the entire history every time and getting it subtly wrong whenever "latest" means latest to arrive rather than latest to happen.

The better answer depends on noticing something that sounds obvious once it's said: an append-only lifecycle log is already a change data capture feed. Each event is a change to the current state of one entity (the order), keyed by order id, sequenced by when it happened, and a cancellation is simply a delete.

Here is an illustrative order (simplified; the real sequence is described below), first as the lifecycle log records it, then as the change feed it implies:

seq event_type as a change to orders_live
1 order_created UPSERT order 1042, status = order_created
2 kitchen_started UPSERT order 1042, status = kitchen_started
3 order_ready UPSERT order 1042, status = order_ready
4 driver_picked_up UPSERT order 1042, status = driver_picked_up
5 driver_ping UPSERT order 1042, status = driver_ping
6 delivered UPSERT order 1042, status = delivered

An order that ends in order_cancelled produces a DELETE as its last change instead, and disappears from the table. Once the log is seen this way, "current status of every order" stops being an aggregation problem and becomes the problem of applying a change feed to a table, which is exactly what AUTO CDC was built to do.

My argument is that AUTO CDC is worth adopting less because it saves code (though it does, a lot) than because it moves the hard parts of change application into the engine, and leaves you with a small, explicit contract: a sequence column that is unique and never null, a target that genuinely supports row-level operations, and deletes expressed as events. Most of what goes wrong with hand-rolled CDC is the engine's side of that contract done badly; most of what can still go wrong with AUTO CDC is your side of it.

What AUTO CDC is, and where it stands

AUTO CDC began as APPLY CHANGES in Databricks' Delta Live Tables and was contributed to Apache Spark under its own SPIP (SPARK-56249), as part of Spark Declarative Pipelines. In Python it's create_auto_cdc_flow.

Release AUTO CDC status
Spark 4.2.0 (July 2026) Shipped. SCD Type 1 via the Python / Spark Connect API
Spark 4.3.0 (release candidate) Adds SCD Type 2 (history with validity ranges)
main branch (5.0.0-SNAPSHOT) Ongoing work under SPARK-56249

Everything I tested was SCD Type 1 (the target holds only the current state per key, and updates overwrite in place), on a build of the main branch from late May 2026, before 4.2 was released.

Applying a change feed correctly means doing several things at once:

  • matching each change to its row by key
  • keeping the version with the highest sequence per key, not the last to arrive
  • honouring deletes, but only when the delete is the latest thing that happened to that key
  • staying idempotent when a streaming source redelivers after a failure

The hand-rolled version is usually a foreachBatch with windowed deduplication feeding a MERGE, and it tends to get the cross-batch cases wrong without throwing errors. A late update that lands in the micro-batch after a newer one quietly overwrites it, and nobody notices until the numbers disagree with something else.

The code

The projection from lifecycle log to change feed is ordinary Spark. This is the core of what my test harness does: every event becomes an UPSERT of the order's current status, a cancellation becomes a DELETE, and the sequence is made unique per order.

feed = events.select(
    F.col("order_id"),
    F.col("event_type").alias("status"),
    F.col("location_id").cast("int").alias("location_id"),
    F.col("ts_seconds").alias("event_ts"),
    F.when(F.col("event_type") == "order_cancelled", F.lit("DELETE"))
     .otherwise(F.lit("UPSERT")).alias("op"),
    # unique per-key ordering: event time, broken by per-order sequence
    (F.col("ts_seconds") * F.lit(100) + F.col("sequence")).alias("seq"),
)

Then the pipeline itself is three declarations: a streaming source, a target streaming table, and the flow.

from pyspark import pipelines as dp

@dp.table(name="order_cdc_source")
def order_cdc_source():
    return spark.readStream.schema(ORDER_SCHEMA).json("file:///data/order_cdc/*.json")

dp.create_streaming_table("ice.gold.orders_live")

dp.create_auto_cdc_flow(
    target="ice.gold.orders_live",
    source="order_cdc_source",
    keys=["order_id"],                  # how a change finds its row
    sequence_by="seq",                  # highest sequence per key wins, whatever the arrival order
    apply_as_deletes="op = 'DELETE'",   # which events delete the row
    except_column_list=["op", "seq"],   # bookkeeping columns to leave out of the target
    stored_as_scd_type=1,
)

The engine handles what the hand-rolled version gets wrong: deduplication across micro-batches by sequence_by, the generated upsert and delete, exactly-once checkpointing, and the auxiliary state table that remembers the latest sequence per key across runs.

That table is what lets a late event arriving in a later batch resolve correctly.

Recompute from the log AUTO CDC
Cost per refresh re-aggregates the entire history processes only new events
Out-of-order events "latest" by arrival is wrong resolved by sequence_by
Cancellations a row every query must remember to filter the row is deleted
Code bespoke foreachBatch + dedup + MERGE three declarations

Running it on messy data

I ran the order-status projection on a sample of the ghost-kitchen stream: a little under five thousand orders and roughly 125,000 of their lifecycle events, including the injected late and duplicate ones. AUTO CDC collapsed them into one row per live order:

gold.orders_live rows
delivered 4,601
driver_ping (mid-delivery) 84
order_ready 3
order_created 1
kitchen_started 1
driver_picked_up 1
total live orders 4,691
cancelled orders removed by apply_as_deletes 308

To check it, I recomputed the same table from scratch the naive way and compared the two in both directions:

w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("seq"))
naive = (feed.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1")
             .filter("op != 'DELETE'").select("order_id", "status"))
pairs = spark.table("ice.gold.orders_live").select("order_id", "status")
match = naive.subtract(pairs).count() == 0 and pairs.subtract(naive).count() == 0
# match = True

They matched exactly.

It's worth being precise about what that proves: it compares the two columns the table exists to answer, as sets, rather than every column byte for byte.

Two details of the run also deserve honesty, because they're the kind of thing that makes a demo look cleaner than it was. The sample was drawn by sorting order ids and taking the first five thousand, and because the raw data contains events with a null order id (which Spark sorts first), the sample was really 4,999 orders.

And the projection joined each event to its order's creation event, so orders with duplicated creation events fanned out into duplicate rows in the feed. AUTO CDC handled both without complaint, since duplicate copies of an event carry the same sequence value and resolve to the same row, but a pipeline that quietly processes inputs it wasn't meant to receive is a reminder to look at your inputs before trusting your outputs.

The second scenario was the textbook one: keeping a dimension current as kitchens relocate, rename, and close. These are the exact changes streamed into silver.dim_locations_current, on top of an initial load of four locations at sequence 1:

changes = [
    {"id": 2, "city": "Los Angeles - Arts District", "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 5},
    {"id": 1, "city": "San Francisco - SoMa",        "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 4},
    {"id": 3, "city": "Chicago",                      "op": "DELETE", "seq": 6},   # kitchen closed
    {"id": 2, "city": "Los Angeles (STALE)",          "op": "UPSERT", "seq": 3},   # arrives late, older
]
id after AUTO CDC why
1 San Francisco - SoMa rename at seq 4 applied
2 Los Angeles - Arts District rename at seq 5 kept; the stale seq 3 edit ignored
3 (no row) closure at seq 6 deleted it
4 Austin unchanged

A nightly full reload would eventually reach the same names, but it copies every unchanged row to get there and has no way at all to express that a location no longer exists.

That's the more general lesson: an append-only or aggregate pipeline can only add facts, so "this was cancelled" becomes another row every downstream query has to remember to filter. In a CDC pipeline a terminal business event can be the delete itself, and the same mechanism propagates hard deletes for compliance.

Edge cases, and how Type 1 resolves them

I put SCD Type 1 through a battery of adversarial cases, and it behaved correctly in every one. The behaviours are worth knowing precisely, because this is where intuition tends to be wrong. These are the cases from my stress harness, with the events in arrival order; | separates micro-batches.

Case Events for one key Result
Upsert to a key that never existed UPSERT@1 row inserted
Delete of a key that never existed DELETE@1 no-op
Several updates in one batch UPSERT@1, UPSERT@2, UPSERT@3 row has the @3 values
Stale delete UPSERT@1 | UPSERT@3 | DELETE@2 row stays, with the @3 values; the update is newer
Stale insert after a delete UPSERT@3 | DELETE@5 | UPSERT@2 row stays deleted
Delete arrives before an older insert DELETE@5 | UPSERT@2 row stays deleted
Resurrection UPSERT@1 | DELETE@2 | UPSERT@3 row present, with the @3 values
Volume, out of order 500 keys, each UPSERT@1, @3, @2 shuffled across 5 batches, plus DELETE@5 for 100 of them exactly 400 rows, all with the @3 values
Tie (probe, not pass/fail) UPSERT@5 "Boston", UPSERT@5 "Denver" in one batch one of them, chosen arbitrarily

Your side of the contract

The sequence. A null in the sequence_by column fails the micro-batch with AUTOCDC_MICROBATCH_VALIDATION.NULL_SEQUENCE rather than guessing, which is the right behaviour, and means the column has to be non-null by construction.

Ties are worse, because they don't fail: two changes to the same key with the same sequence in one micro-batch are resolved arbitrarily, as the programming guide itself warns. A coarse timestamp is the classic way to produce ties, so sequence on something strictly increasing per key, like a log offset or commit LSN. My composite of timestamp times 100 plus the per-order sequence works only because no order in this data has more than 99 events; it's a local trick, not a general recipe. The ties that did occur in my data were all injected exact duplicates, the one case where an arbitrary choice is harmless.

The target. AUTO CDC needs a connector that implements Spark's DataSource V2 row-level operation interface (SupportsRowLevelOperations), and "supports MERGE" is not the same thing:

Target Result in my testing
Plain Parquet rejected immediately: AUTOCDC_TARGET_DOES_NOT_SUPPORT_MERGE
Delta did not work: Delta's table implementation doesn't expose SupportsRowLevelOperations, despite supporting MERGE elsewhere
Iceberg, Hadoop catalog worked
Iceberg, JDBC (Postgres) catalog worked
Iceberg, Hive Metastore catalog worked
Iceberg, Gravitino REST catalog worked
Iceberg, Glue catalog (emulated) worked
Iceberg, Unity Catalog OSS REST failed: the catalog is read-only
Any ephemeral / in-memory catalog unsuitable: the aux state table must persist across restarts

Two smaller surprises: the target carries a hidden __spark_autocdc_metadata column that shows up in SELECT *, and Iceberg's own changelog is batch-only in open-source Spark for now, so you can't stream one Iceberg table's changes straight into AUTO CDC as a source.

A correction. I originally reported that running an AUTO CDC pipeline through the spark-pipelines CLI failed at registration with InvalidPlanInput: RELTYPE_NOT_SET, and called it a bug. It wasn't.

The CLI connects to the default Spark Connect endpoint, and an old Spark 4.1 Connect server was still listening there, so my pipeline was being sent to a server that had never heard of AUTO CDC. Against a server of the right version the CLI works correctly. If you see that error, check what's actually listening on sc://localhost:15002 before anything else.

What changes

With a hand-rolled pipeline, the question you're left with is whether you've correctly implemented cross-batch deduplication, sequenced deletes, and idempotent merges, and the honest answer is usually that you won't know until something disagrees. With AUTO CDC that part belongs to the engine, which is tested against exactly the cases people get wrong.

The question becomes whether you've given it a sequence that is unique and never null, a target that really supports row-level operations, and a delete for everything that should be allowed to disappear. That's a much better question to be left with, and the first step is often not a new data source at all; it's noticing that the event log you already have has been a change feed all along.

Further reading

  • Test harnesses and results: lakehouse-stack/scripts/pipelines/autocdc-scd1 (Spark main branch, 5.0.0-SNAPSHOT at 06ffa273, with an Iceberg runtime ported to Spark 5.0).
