title: Phone Login with SMS OTP Resend Countdown (An Auditable Backend)
description:
Use a backend-owned verification state machine, not a countdown in the browser, as the authority for SMS OTP resend and session creation. The deciding constraint is evidence: a customer-support investigator must be able to distinguish “we accepted a verification request,” “the provider reported a delivery state,” and “the customer proved possession of the code” before the application creates a session or associates that session with a transaction notice.

Short answer: keep a provider-neutral attempt ID, next_resend_at, attempt counters, country policy, and an append-only audit trail in your database. Let the Next.js UI render the countdown, but let the backend enforce it. Call the SMS provider behind a narrow adapter; verify on form submission; create the application session only after successful validation; and poll delivery status or events because this capability has no webhook event push.

That boundary also makes migration reversible. Infrai is a reasonable adapter for teams that expect communication to become one of several backend capabilities: one API key reaches 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API, while its public discovery contract exposes request and response schemas. The supporting benefit is operational rather than cosmetic: the same contract specifies idempotency for 171 of 294 capabilities, including a 24-hour default deduplication window, which gives retry policy an explicit home. It does not remove the need for an application ledger.

Evidence first.

The practical positioning is narrow: Infrai uses one key and one bill for many backend capabilities, and its one plain REST API works without installing an SDK. The Infrai API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. For this design, that means the provider adapter can remain ordinary HTTP while the application ledger stays independent.

Decision record: invariants before vendors

The first invariant is strict: no successful provider response creates an application session. Only a successful verification result can cross that boundary. The second is temporal: resend eligibility is computed from server time, persisted, and returned to the client as metadata; refreshing a tab or editing JavaScript cannot shorten it. The third is jurisdictional: country allowlists, routing decisions, maximum attempts, and spend or geography circuit breakers remain application policy. Provider-side protection is not the control plane for those rules.

There are really two ledgers. The verification ledger records request, resend, validation, expiry, lockout, and provider delivery observations. The compliance-notice ledger records the exact notice version, recipient reference, channel, dispatch request ID, and each observed status. Do not collapse “delivered” into “verified,” and do not treat an email open as proof that a person read a notice; Apple Mail Privacy Protection can download remote content without the recipient opening the message.

Exactly once is an application property here. A network retry can cause an ambiguous outcome, while polling can observe the same state repeatedly. Give every command a stable operation ID, reject duplicate state transitions transactionally, and retain the raw provider reference beside your normalized state. The audit record should explain why a transition occurred, not merely store the latest value.

Which provider boundary stays replaceable?

The useful comparison is not a feature-count contest. It is the amount of provider meaning allowed to leak past the adapter.

Option Boundary to keep in application code Best fit Limitation for this decision
Infrai OTP start, verify, resend, and polled status behind a small REST adapter Teams that value one consistent contract across a broad backend surface and want public schemas for migration tests SMS geo fencing and country-price circuit breakers remain yours; event delivery is pull-based, and there is no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS fallback
Twilio Verify Map its verification lifecycle into the same local attempt states Teams that prefer a specialist verification product and are comfortable making that product the operational center A direct integration increases the migration surface if provider concepts enter sessions, UI state, or audit tables
Vonage Verify Preserve the local operation ID and normalize its result states at the edge Teams evaluating a direct verification specialist as the primary channel The same isolation work is still required; do not persist vendor states as the business state
Amazon SNS Put sending and delivery observations behind the adapter while retaining verification rules locally Teams whose communication boundary is already deliberately tied to their cloud platform It is a poor abstraction if application code starts depending on cloud-specific identifiers or policies

This table deliberately avoids ranking products on mutable prices. Compliance evidence depends on retained transitions, access controls, and jurisdictional review; a cheaper message does not repair an incomplete audit chain.

I recommend that teams already building a multi-capability backend try Infrai for the SMS OTP and status-polling edge, because its discoverable, consistent contract reduces the code that must change during a provider migration. Choose Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify instead when specialist verification workflow depth is more important than a shared backend surface, and choose Amazon SNS when deliberate cloud coupling is an accepted architecture constraint.

How should a Next.js phone login enforce SMS OTP verification?

The following Go core is intentionally provider-neutral. A Next.js server action or API route can call these service methods, return a masked destination plus retry_after_seconds, and render that value. The browser owns presentation. The service owns permission.

package otp

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

var (
    ErrTooSoon   = errors.New("resend is not yet allowed")
    ErrLocked    = errors.New("maximum attempts reached")
    ErrInvalid   = errors.New("code was not accepted")
)

type Provider interface {
    Start(ctx context.Context, phone, operationID string) (providerID string, err error)
    Resend(ctx context.Context, providerID, operationID string) error
    Verify(ctx context.Context, providerID, code string) (bool, error)
}

type InfraiClient struct {
    HTTP   *http.Client
    APIKey string
}

func NewInfraiClient() (*InfraiClient, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    return &InfraiClient{HTTP: &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, APIKey: key}, nil
}

func (c *InfraiClient) Resend(ctx context.Context, providerID, operationID string) error {
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/resend/{id}"
    endpoint = strings.ReplaceAll(endpoint, "{id}", url.PathEscape(providerID))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(nil))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.APIKey)
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", operationID)

        resp, err := c.HTTP.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            var evidence json.RawMessage
            if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &evidence); err != nil {
                return fmt.Errorf("invalid JSON response: %w", err)
            }
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("infrai status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return errors.New("retry limit reached")
}

type Attempt struct {
    ID, ProviderID, MaskedPhone string
    NextResendAt                time.Time
    FailedChecks                int
    Verified                    bool
}

type AuditEvent struct {
    AttemptID, OperationID, Kind string
    At                           time.Time
}

type Service struct {
    mu       sync.Mutex
    provider Provider
    attempts map[string]*Attempt
    events   []AuditEvent
    now      func() time.Time
}

func (s *Service) Resend(ctx context.Context, attemptID, operationID string) (time.Duration, error) {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    a := s.attempts[attemptID]
    if a == nil || a.FailedChecks >= 5 {
        return 0, ErrLocked
    }
    now := s.now()
    if now.Before(a.NextResendAt) {
        return a.NextResendAt.Sub(now), ErrTooSoon
    }
    if err := s.provider.Resend(ctx, a.ProviderID, operationID); err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    a.NextResendAt = now.Add(30 * time.Second)
    s.events = append(s.events, AuditEvent{attemptID, operationID, "otp.resent", now})
    return 30 * time.Second, nil
}

func (s *Service) Verify(ctx context.Context, attemptID, code, operationID string) error {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    a := s.attempts[attemptID]
    if a == nil || a.FailedChecks >= 5 {
        return ErrLocked
    }
    ok, err := s.provider.Verify(ctx, a.ProviderID, code)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if !ok {
        a.FailedChecks++
        s.events = append(s.events, AuditEvent{attemptID, operationID, "otp.rejected", s.now()})
        return ErrInvalid
    }
    a.Verified = true
    s.events = append(s.events, AuditEvent{attemptID, operationID, "otp.verified", s.now()})
    return nil
}

The constants, five failed checks and a 30-second resend interval, are example application policy rather than provider guarantees. Production storage must replace the in-memory mutex with a transaction that locks the attempt row, enforces uniqueness on operation_id, appends the audit event, and commits the state transition atomically. Only after Verify commits should a separate session transaction run. This prevents a session from existing without durable verification evidence.

One detail matters more than its line count: operationID must survive a Next.js request retry. Generate it when the application accepts the resend command, persist it with the attempt, and reuse it until that command has a terminal result; generating a fresh value inside each HTTP attempt defeats deduplication. The sample also caps the response body at 1 MiB so an upstream error cannot turn diagnostics into unbounded memory consumption. In a complete adapter, store the successful raw JSON beside the normalized audit transition, under the same data-access and retention rules as the rest of the verification record.

No shortcut there.

The adapter may call POST /v1/sms/otp and POST /v1/sms/verify; resend and status behavior should be discovered from the live schema rather than encoded from an article. Every outbound write needs an explicit method, Bearer authentication loaded from an environment variable, a stable idempotency key, error-body handling, and bounded exponential backoff for HTTP 429 that honors Retry-After. Poll status or events with a bounded schedule and record observations idempotently. Fast polling is not correctness.

Failure boundaries and compliance limits

An OTP provider outage must not weaken authentication into “temporarily trusted.” A delayed delivery must not reset attempt counters. A support agent must not be able to infer the full phone number from routine screens; return a masked destination, while retaining access to the protected source only under the system's normal authorization policy.

Pull-based events impose a real latency boundary. They work for reconciliation and support evidence, but they are less suitable for orchestration that requires immediate push notification. If the product needs real-time multi-channel reactions, this integration is not sufficient by itself.

Channel fallback has sharper edges. Infrai does not provide managed email OTP, SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS in this capability set. An email-code fallback therefore needs its own implementation, and a pending domestic email vendor must not be presented as evidence for China compliance. Email scheduling also has no cancellation operation, although SMS cancellation exists. Those constraints belong in the architecture decision, before procurement.

Compliance is jurisdiction-specific. DKIM authenticates a signing domain and message integrity for email; it does not prove that a human read a notice, nor does it establish that an SMS recipient understood one. Counsel and the relevant control owner must define retention, consent, residency, and evidentiary requirements. Engineering can then preserve the required facts without inventing a legal conclusion.

Rejected option: provider state as application state

The rejected design stores a provider request ID in the session row, lets the client countdown decide when resend is allowed, and asks the provider for the “current truth” during support investigations. It looks lean. It also makes migration a data-model rewrite, turns a browser timer into a security control, and leaves historical decisions dependent on an external system's retention and vocabulary.

There is a valid use case for that coupling: a short-lived prototype with no compliance record, no provider-switch requirement, and no transaction-notice obligation. Once the application promises an auditable delivery record, the local ledger is no longer optional. Keep provider payloads at the boundary, normalize only the states the business actually uses, and retain immutable evidence for reconciliation.

This is the final decision: own verification and evidence; rent transport. If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery schema before implementing the adapter.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • Apple: Mail Privacy Protection guide

title: Why Doki Doki Literature Club Bet on Ren'Py and Python: The Niche Engine Behind a Free Horror Phenomenon
description:
Doki Doki Literature Club! should not have scared anyone. A free cute dating sim, made in a Python visual-novel engine most Unity developers have never opened, with static 2D sprites and no voice acting — yet it became one of the most discussed psychological horror games of the decade, spawned endless memes, and earned a premium console sequel.

The short answer for developers is this: the 2017 original was built by Team Salvato, led by Dan Salvato, in Ren'Py, the free and open-source Ren'Py Visual Novel Engine. That niche choice did more than save money. It made the horror possible.

This article explains what Ren'Py actually is, why Python fit a tiny horror experiment, and what I think the rest of us miss about transparent engines, file-system horror, and the cost of leaving niche tech.

Who this is for

You are an indie or hobbyist developer choosing a stack, or a technically curious DDLC player wondering why you had to delete a character file in Explorer to finish the game. You do not need to know Python. You do need to care about scope: a tiny team, about two years, a 350 MB free download.

Scope as verified in October 2026: original DDLC released worldwide September 22, 2017 for Linux, macOS and Windows as freeware, first on itch.io then on Steam. Developer is Team Salvato, designer/programmer/writer/composer is Dan Salvato. Engine is listed as Ren'Py for the original and Unity for Plus!. The game is single-player, visual novel, and explicitly breaks the fourth wall.

What Ren'Py actually is — and how niche it is

Ren'Py is a visual novel engine — used by thousands of creators — that helps you use words, images, and sounds to tell interactive stories that run on computers and mobile devices. It is open source and free for commercial use, with the latest stable 8.5.3 released May 15, 2026.

Under the hood it is deliberately narrow:

  • Written in Python and Cython, built on Pygame which is built with Python on SDL, with FreeType and MIT licensing. The SDK itself is about 115 MB.
  • Script language looks like a screenplay, with label, say, scene, show, menu and Python blocks. A minimal game is literally: 
label start:
    "Sylvie" "Hi there! How was class?"

plus define s = Character('Sylvie', color="#c8ffc8"), scene bg meadow, show sylvie green smile. You get save/load, rollback, preferences and transitions without writing them.

  • Built-ins for the genre: branching stories, save systems, rollback, scene transitions, DLC, movie playback for sprites, in-engine animation via ATL, and full UI customization via Screen Language. Scripts can also include Python blocks for advanced features, and tools are included to obfuscate scripts and archive assets.
  • Platforms are PC and mobile: Windows 10+, macOS 10.10+, Linux, Android 5.0+, iOS 11+, and beta HTML5/WebAssembly. Notably, Ren'Py is not directly supported on game consoles — console ports require porting to another engine such as Unity.
  • Scale: Ren'Py has been used to create over 8,000 visual novels and games, discoverable on VNDB, Itch.io and SteamDB. It has been recommended by PC Gamer and The Guardian and used in classes at Carnegie Mellon, but it remains a single-genre tool compared to Unity, Unreal or Godot.

That is the niche-plus-popular contrast: a Python visual-novel-only framework powering a free horror phenomenon with positive critical attention, memes and a large online following.

Why Python fit a tiny dating-sim-that-isn't

DDLC credits tell the story: Dan Salvato — writing, coding, music; Satchely — character art; Velinquent (VelinquenT) — background art. Salvato was previously known for modding work on Project M, and built DDLC in an estimated two-year period inspired by mixed feelings toward anime and a fascination for surreal, unsettling experiences.

Ren'Py fit that team for three boring, practical reasons:

  1. No engine to build. Dialogue, choices, poem minigame, saves and rollback already exist. Salvato could spend two years on writing, music and horror twists instead of UI framework. The built-in tutorial demonstrates dialogue scripting, images, transitions, music, branching choices — exactly DDLC Act 1.

  2. Screenplay syntax plus Python escape hatch. Act 1 is pure visual novel: first-person narration, static 2D sprites, text without voice acting, occasional choices, and a poem-composition minigame where each girl has different word preferences. That is native Ren'Py. When the game needs to glitch text into mojibake, distort sprites, erase save files, or make Monika talk indefinitely, Python blocks and Screen Language let you break the rules without leaving the engine.

  3. Free and tiny. DDLC is 100% free to play on itch.io, free on Steam with 350 MB storage, 1.8 GHz dual-core, 4 GB RAM and integrated graphics. No license fees, no 10 GB editor, no revenue share to negotiate. For a freeware horror experiment, zero cost is a feature.

My inference, labeled as such: Ren'Py did not just lower cost, it lowered psychological cost. When your engine assumes cute dating sims, subverting it feels transgressive to you as a developer, not just to players. You are misusing a cozy tool. That misuse is creative fuel.

Transparent files as horror mechanic: my deep analysis

Here is where verified facts end and my analysis begins. I label it clearly.

Verified: At a certain point the player must manipulate the game's files to advance the narrative. Monika is revealed as a self-aware character who can manipulate code, deletes Yuri's and Natsuki's character files, confesses love to the real-life player rather than the protagonist, and can only be stopped when the player deletes her character file from the game directory. She then restores the game excluding herself. The game also erases all previous save files when Sayori dies and restarts without her.

Why Ren'Py made this scarier than Unity would have:

Ren'Py games ship as folders players can see. Characters are files like monika.chr, saves and persistent data sit in plain directories, scripts are .rpy text unless you deliberately obfuscate them. Players already browse those folders to install mods or back up saves. DDLC weaponizes that literacy.

In a Unity IL2CPP build, deleting a character would mean hex-editing an AssetBundle or save JSON — technical, abstract, forgettable. In Ren'Py, you open game/characters, see four familiar names, watch two vanish when Monika deletes them, then you yourself right-click-delete monika.chr while she talks to you. It feels like murder, not debugging. The engine's transparency turns OS file operations into moral actions.

My provocation: DDLC proves that legibility is scarier than fidelity. No ray tracing, no jump-scare physics — just the realization that the cute engine you trusted leaves its organs exposed, and the villain knows it. Ren'Py's rollback, persistent data and script obfuscation tools assume a cooperative author. Monika is an uncooperative author living inside those systems.

Three open questions I cannot resolve from public sources alone, and I leave them open deliberately:

  • Did Salvato disable Ren'Py's obfuscation/archiving on purpose to keep files readable, or did readability simply survive because DDLC is Python? Either way, what would horror mean in an engine that encrypts everything by default?
  • How much of the glitch aesthetic — illegible text, distorted sprites, forced watching of Yuri's decomposition over a weekend — is ATL/Screen Language versus raw Python? The docs show both paths, but only source access would tell.
  • If persistent memory tracks you across restarts, at what point does a visual novel stop being a game and start being spyware with consent? DDLC asks this without answering. I think future cozy-tech horror should ask it louder.

If you design narrative horror, ask: what does your engine expose that players already trust? DDLC's answer was: everything.

The console price: 350 MB to 3 GB

Niche tech has a tax, and DDLC paid it visibly.

Because Ren'Py has no console support, the expanded Doki Doki Literature Club Plus!, released June 30, 2021 for Switch, PS4/PS5, Xbox One/Series X/S and PC, was rebuilt in Unity and published with Serenity Forge. The Plus! Steam page lists 3 GB storage versus 350 MB for the original, 6 new side stories, 100+ unlockable images, 26 music tracks, a music player and Full HD art.

Crucially, Plus! replaces actual file manipulation with a virtual desktop that simulates it, plus side stories about friendship and club formation. Reviews praised side stories and console play but noted lack of changes to the core.

My take: this is the honest cost of niche success. Ren'Py got DDLC to viral free release with almost no overhead. Unity got it to consoles and paid sustainability, but at 8.5x disk size and with simulated transgression. A fake OS inside a Unity game is clever; deleting a real file in Windows Explorer is unforgettable. When you port cozy tech to mainstream tech, you gain reach and lose danger. Is that trade always worth it? For Team Salvato, probably yes — free cannot fund forever. For your prototype, maybe not yet.

What would you preserve if you had to rewrite your Ren'Py/Python game in Unity tomorrow? Make a list now, before you need to.

Moddability as accident and engine

Ren'Py scripts are human-readable text. The quickstart shows you edit script.rpy in VS Code, define characters, show images, add menus and Python. That means any player can open DDLC, read dialogue, find flags, and spoil or extend the horror in hours. Datamining is not hacking; it is reading.

This cuts two ways. Spoilers leak fast when horror lives in plain text — Act 2 twists were documented within days. But mods bloom fast too: gender-swaps, new routes, Monika-after-story continuations, poem-word analyzers. Ren'Py's 8,000-game community already knows how to fork a visual novel. DDLC inherited that literacy for free.

My question for you: did Team Salvato choose Ren'Py because it was moddable, or did moddability emerge and then amplify the meme following? I suspect the latter, and that is the lesson. Pick a stack where fans can extend you without permission. If your engine requires an SDK, NDA or encrypted bundle to add one line of dialogue, you are taxing your evangelists.

A warning I do mean rigorously: Ren'Py's ease also eases cruelty. DDLC carries mature content: self-harm, suicide, suggestive themes, and a front-page warning that it is not suitable for children or those easily disturbed. Transparent files plus dark themes plus young anime aesthetics is a volatile mix that led to real-world controversy in the UK. Niche accessibility does not remove responsibility. If you subvert cozy tech, label the horror, provide resources, and do not hide behind freeware innocence.

What to steal (and what not to copy)

Steal this if you are solo or small:

  • Choose genre-native boring tech. Ren'Py removed save systems, rollback, transitions and dialogue UI from your backlog. What would your game's Ren'Py be — Twine, Bitsy, PICO-8, LibGDX?
  • Keep one Python escape hatch. 95% screenplay, 5% code for the moments that break genre. DDLC's ratio is instructive.
  • Ship small and free if horror needs trust. 350 MB and zero dollars made trying DDLC effortless. Fear needs low friction.
  • Design one OS-level interaction. Not ten mechanics — one file deletion players will tell friends about.

Do not romanticize:

  • No console, no 3D, no complex physics. Ren'Py assumes 2D sprites and text. If you need consoles day one, budget a Unity rewrite like Plus! did.
  • Python readability leaks story. If your twist depends on secrecy, you need obfuscation, server flags, or acceptance that spoilers are marketing.
  • Cute plus horror plus accessibility risks harm. Content warnings, age gates and crisis resources are part of the stack, not PR.

Verdict

DDLC did not succeed despite Ren'Py and Python. It succeeded because a niche visual-novel engine let a tiny team ship a convincing dating sim in months, then spend remaining time corrupting it from inside with Python. The official pitch still smiles: welcome to the Literature Club, chit-chat and fun with Sayori, Natsuki, Yuri and Monika — will you promise to spend the most time with Monika? That smile is engineering as much as writing.

If you are starting a narrative experiment in 2026, ask the DDLC question: what does your engine expose that you could betray? If the answer is nothing — everything encrypted, sandboxed, cloud-saved — maybe your horror needs a more honest, more niche machine.

What cozy tool would become terrifying if it hated you just a little? I do not have a rigorous answer. I think the question is more useful than any benchmark.

Sources and verification date

Core facts verified October 14, 2026 via direct English primary-source retrieval. English Bing queries were attempted for Ren'Py, DDLC interviews and sales, but returned generic dictionary, DAN and browser-game noise, so verification relies on primary pages below. Analysis and provocations are my own and labeled as such.

  • Ren'Py purpose, free commercial use, platforms and 8,000+ works
  • Ren'Py Python/Cython, Pygame/SDL, MIT, ATL/Screen Language, branching/rollback/Python blocks, console limitation
  • Ren'Py repo, Python modules and MIT contribution policy
  • Ren'Py script language, characters, scene/show, menus and Python statements
  • DDLC official site: premise, team teaser and content warning
  • DDLC itch.io: free, staff credits and warning
  • DDLC Steam: free, mature note, 350 MB system requirements
  • DDLC reference: Ren'Py vs Unity engines, Sept 2017 release, Team Salvato two-year/Project M background, freeware itch-to-Steam, metafictional fourth-wall horror, poem minigame, file manipulation, Monika self-awareness and deletions, memes/large following, Plus! June 2021 premium and virtual desktop
  • Plus! Steam: side stories, images, tracks, HD upgrade, 3 GB requirements and mature descriptors

title: OpenCode Can Write Code. What If It Could Use Your Browser Too?
description:
Hello, I'm Rijul, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product.

We use AI agents for all sorts of tasks. Some agents can even interact with your browser and act as companions while you work.

As someone who uses OpenCode, I wanted to bring that capability into my workflow. I wanted OpenCode to interact with my browser so it could access the relevant browser context while helping me with tasks.

In this article, let's see how to connect your browser to OpenCode using Browser MCP.

1. What You Need

To set this up, you need two components:

  • Browser extension: Connects your browser to the MCP server.
  • Local MCP server: Allows your AI client to interact with the browser through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

Let's set them up.

2. Install the Browser Extension

First, visit the following page to install the Browser MCP extension:

https://browsermcp.io/install

After installing the extension, you'll be directed to a page with more information.

This page links to the official Browser MCP documentation, where you can find additional setup instructions and details about how it works:

https://docs.browsermcp.io/

3. Add the MCP Server to OpenCode

Next, configure OpenCode to use the Browser MCP server.

Open your OpenCode configuration file and add the following configuration:

    {
      "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
      "mcp": {
        "browsermcp": {
          "type": "local",
          "command": ["npx", "-y", "@browsermcp/mcp@latest"]
        }
      }
    }

This configuration tells OpenCode to start the Browser MCP server locally using npx.

Save the configuration after adding it.

4. Connect and Test the Browser

Once you've configured the MCP server, make sure Browser MCP is connected.

Now, let's test whether it works.

Go to OpenCode and give it a task that requires browser interaction. For example:

    Go to the Wikipedia page for "Open-source software" and list the main section headings.

The Browser MCP server allows OpenCode to interact with the browser and navigate to the requested page.

Here's the result returned by the agent.

As you can see, OpenCode can use the browser to complete the task instead of relying only on the information already available in the conversation.

Conclusion

That's how you can connect Browser MCP to OpenCode.

This setup lets you bring browser interaction into your AI-assisted workflow. Instead of working with your AI agent and browser separately, you can give OpenCode tasks that involve navigating web pages and gathering information through the connected browser.

It can be useful when you want your AI coding assistant to work with relevant information from the web alongside your existing workflow.

That's it for this article. See you in the next one!

title: Vercel Connect now supports TanStack AI
description:
Agents built with TanStack AI can now call OAuth-protected MCP servers through Vercel Connect, with no credentials for you to store or rotate.

The new @vercel/connect/tanstack-ai subpath exports connectMCPTransport, which takes a TanStack transport config and attaches a Connect-backed auth provider. The provider is called before every MCP request, so the token is always fresh.

If the user has not granted access, createMCPClient fails with a consent challenge before the model runs. Catch it with getConsentChallenge and redirect to Connect's consent URL. Otherwise, a consent error raised within a tool call would reach the model as an error string rather than the user as a redirect.

Read the TanStack AI integration docs to get started, or see the full list of supported frameworks and adapters for Vercel Connect.

title: How to Build a LangGraph Agent with FastAPI and SSE Streaming
description:
Building an AI agent is relatively straightforward. Making it accessible through an API, integrating real tools, and streaming execution updates to a client is where the architecture becomes more interesting.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a small, working example that combines:

  • LangGraph for agent orchestration
  • FastAPI for HTTP endpoints
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE) for streaming responses
  • Open-Meteo as a real external tool

The goal isn't to build a production-ready platform in one tutorial. It's to establish a working foundation and understand the responsibilities of each component.

Source code: LangGraph + FastAPI Example on GitHub

1. Why LangGraph and FastAPI?

LangGraph handles the agent's execution flow.

FastAPI exposes that execution to external clients.

These are different responsibilities, and separating them makes the application easier to understand and extend.

A useful mental model is:

The client shouldn't need to understand how the agent chooses tools or manages its internal execution flow.

It should interact with a clear HTTP interface.

2. Give the agent a real tool

An agent becomes more interesting when it can do something beyond generating text.

In this example, the agent uses a weather tool backed by Open-Meteo.

That introduces a realistic execution path:

  1. The user asks a weather-related question.
  2. The model determines whether it needs the tool.
  3. The tool requests external weather information.
  4. The result returns to the agent.
  5. The agent uses the result to answer.

This is a useful foundation for more advanced agents that interact with APIs, databases, and business systems.

It also introduces concerns that don't exist in a simple LLM completion: network failures, tool errors, latency, and retries.

3. Expose the agent through FastAPI

The next step is making the agent accessible through an HTTP API.

The example demonstrates two response patterns.

Regular JSON responses

The client sends a request and waits for the agent's result.

This approach is appropriate for simple integrations where intermediate execution updates aren't necessary.

Streaming responses

The client receives updates while the request is being processed.

This is useful when agent execution involves multiple operations and the user would otherwise wait without feedback.

Both patterns can be built around the same agent architecture.

4. Why use Server-Sent Events?

Server-Sent Events provide a way to deliver a stream of updates over an HTTP response.

Instead of waiting for one final response, the client can process events as they arrive.

A simplified SSE message looks like this:

event: message
data: {"content":"Processing your request..."}

The example above illustrates SSE formatting, not the exact event contract of the repository.

For AI applications, streaming can improve the experience by making long-running operations more visible.

However, streaming also introduces engineering considerations:

  • What happens when the client disconnects?
  • How are errors communicated after the stream begins?
  • How does the client recognize completion?
  • What happens if a tool fails halfway through execution?

These questions matter when moving from a working demonstration to a reliable service.

5. Keep the agent separate from the API

One important design principle is to avoid mixing agent orchestration with HTTP transport logic.

The agent should own its execution flow and tool interactions.

The FastAPI layer should handle requests, responses, and streaming transport.

That separation makes it easier to test the agent independently, evolve the API, and introduce additional clients later.

It also creates a clearer boundary for future capabilities such as authentication, persistence, and observability.

6. What this example does not solve yet

A working agent API is not automatically production-ready.

Before using this architecture for critical workflows, several additional concerns need attention.

Persistence and checkpointing

Long-running or multi-step agents may need to recover execution state after interruptions.

Retries and idempotency

Retrying a failed operation can be dangerous when tools modify external systems.

For example, retrying a payment operation must not charge the same customer twice.

Checkpointing alone doesn't guarantee idempotency. External side effects need their own protection.

Observability

Production systems need visibility into agent execution, LLM calls, tool inputs and outputs, errors, and latency.

LangSmith is one option for tracing LangGraph applications at the execution, node, and tool-call levels.

Security and operational controls

Authentication, rate limiting, secrets management, structured logging, and deployment configuration need to be addressed according to the environment.

These aren't reasons to avoid building a small example. They're reasons to distinguish a working foundation from a complete production system.

7. Run the example yourself

The public repository contains the implementation and setup instructions.

GitHub: https://github.com/salada-dados/langgraph-fastapi-example

Start with the README, run the example locally, and inspect how the agent, tool integration, FastAPI endpoints, and SSE streaming fit together.

The most useful next exercise is to replace the weather tool with an API relevant to your own application.

That helps expose the operational questions you'll eventually need to solve.

8. From a working example to production

I'm also building a Production LangGraph + FastAPI Starter, focused on reducing the repetitive engineering work involved in taking an agent beyond a local demonstration.

The goal is to provide a production-oriented starting point rather than claim that every deployment concern can be solved by a template.

If you're working on an agent and running into challenges with persistence, retries, observability, or deployment, I'd be interested in hearing what's been hardest.

Interested in the production-oriented Starter? Join the Early Access list.

Read the original tutorial: https://saladadedados.com/en/blog/langgraph-fastapi-sse

Explore the source code: https://github.com/salada-dados/langgraph-fastapi-example

What has been the hardest part of moving your LangGraph agent from a local prototype to a real application?

title: I got tired of checking GPU cloud pricing pages by hand, so I built a price index API
description:
Every time I needed to rent a GPU, the workflow was the same: open six provider tabs, squint at pricing pages that all structure their numbers differently, and try to remember whether that H100 price was spot, on-demand, or a 3-year contract rate buried in a footnote.

So I built the thing I wanted: a price index that normalizes GPU cloud pricing into one dataset, where every row says what kind of price it is and links back to the provider page it came from.

Some of what the data shows right now (it refreshes hourly):

GPU Cheapest $/hr Provider Price type
H100 1.37 Vast.ai spot
H200 2.62 CoreWeave spot
A100 1.15 Paperspace 3-yr contract
L40S 0.79 RunPod community cloud
B200 4.26 CoreWeave spot

The price-type column is the part I care about most. A $1.15 A100 sounds cheaper than a $1.37 H100 until you notice one is a 3-year contract and the other is spot. Most comparison content flattens that away; the index doesn't.

The API is live on RapidAPI as GPU Index — there's a free tier (1,000 requests/month) if you want to poke at it: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/gpu-index1

Endpoints are simple: /prices for the full normalized dataset (filter by GPU family, provider, or price type), /summary for the cheapest price per family, /gpus and /providers for what's covered and how fresh each source is.

While I was in there, I built the same pattern for a few other datasets I kept checking by hand:

  • LLM Token Price Index — 458 models, per-token input/output prices normalized across providers. Same model, side by side: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/llm-token-price-index
  • Domain Price Index — registration/renewal/transfer prices per TLD, because renewal pricing is where registrars actually make their money: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/domain-price-index
  • CT Lookup — Certificate Transparency data as JSON, with a watchlist for catching certs issued for your domains that you didn't request: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/ct-lookup
  • Email Deliverability Check — one call returns SPF/DKIM/DMARC/MX/rDNS verdicts for a domain, with fix hints: https://rapidapi.com/vangogh/api/email-deliverability-check

All of them have the same free tier, and every price row in the indexes carries its source URL so you can check my work. If you're building a router, a cost dashboard, or anything that picks compute or models programmatically, I'd rather you call an API than maintain your own scrapers — that was certainly true for me.

Feedback welcome: what provider or GPU family am I missing?

title: Connect Your App to Your Enterprise Traces
description:
Your customer taps “Place order.” The request crosses your app, an API gateway, a native backend, a payment service and a database. Your operations team needs to see that path in the same tracing system it uses for the rest of the company. Neither the client app nor a compiled Java server should disappear from that picture.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

I wrote a book on debugging, so I am probably more opinionated about this than most people: in 2026, production diagnosis should not depend on somebody searching a pile of logs with grep and guessing which lines belong together.

Logs still matter. At enterprise scale, though, you need to connect work across machines, teams and runtimes, then see whether a failure is isolated or spreading. On a JVM, Java agents can instrument much of that work for us. Once our backend is translated to C and compiled into a native executable, the usual JVM instrumentation hook is gone.

We have to carry that visibility into the binary. OpenTelemetry support started that work last week. The expanded backend API adds metrics and management alongside it. This article follows what happens after you turn them on.

Follow an operation across your systems

Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal behavior from the evidence it emits. OpenTelemetry, usually shortened to OTel, defines APIs, data conventions and transport for producing that evidence. It is not itself the screen where you investigate an incident; a collector and an observability backend handle that part. The OTel primer provides the broader model.

Question Useful evidence
Why did this request take two seconds? A trace connecting its operations
Is database waiting increasing across the service? Metrics over time
What did the application decide at the failure? Logs and events with context

A span records one timed operation. Related spans form a trace. Metrics aggregate behavior across operations: a count, a current value or a distribution such as request duration. Neither replaces the other. A single trace can explain a slow query without telling you how often it occurs.

Our integration exports traces and metrics. It does not turn every application log into an OTLP log record.

Add tracing to your native executable

Put this in the backend's application.properties before building:

cn1.otel.enabled=true

Or use the backend's @OpenTelemetry annotation. The generator installs the tracer, making its implementation reachable to the translator. Without that build-time opt-in, the unused tracing code can be left out. Setting an environment variable after deploying a binary that omitted the tracer cannot add it back.

Once enabled, the runtime records an incoming request span named for its route template. A Web call creates a client span and propagates W3C trace headers. A database statement creates another client span. Incoming traceparent connects the request to its caller.

The native backend propagates context on outbound Web calls. Each receiving service must accept and continue that context. OTel-compatible instrumentation lets those services participate regardless of their implementation language.

Include the client, not just the servers

The client annotation belongs on your app's main class:

import com.codename1.annotations.OpenTelemetry;
import com.codename1.system.Lifecycle;

@OpenTelemetry(
        relay = "https://api.example.com",
        relayToken = "replace-with-your-relay-token",
        serviceName = "orders-app",
        sampleRatio = 0.2,
        requireAnalyticsConsent = true)
public class OrdersApp extends Lifecycle {
}

Replace the URL with your backend and the token placeholder with your relay token. Set the backend's RELAY_TOKEN environment variable to that same value. Enable its relay as shown below, and wire the app's analytics-consent flow before collecting telemetry. The client instruments supported app operations and ConnectionRequest calls, including outgoing trace context. It sends its recorded spans through the backend rather than carrying your collector credentials.

For browser apps, context propagation is limited to the relay host and configured propagateTo hosts. A cross-origin service must allow the tracing headers in CORS. The client tracing walkthrough covers consent, propagation and the supported span types.

That connects the experience on the device to the work behind it. A server-only trace cannot show the client work before the request or after the response. You can investigate that larger path in your enterprise tracing system instead of keeping a separate, disconnected account of what the app did.

Database spans record SQL as supplied, with placeholders intact; bound parameters are not recorded. If an application concatenates a secret into SQL, the resulting text already contains it. cn1.otel.attributes.exclude=db.query.text can exclude that attribute. Parameterized SQL remains the better habit.

WebSocket lifetime is outside this automatic request-span model. An hours-long connection with thousands of messages is not one useful HTTP request duration, and its upgrade is handled before this tracing path.

Send it to the system your team already uses

For an enabled build, configure a collector at runtime:

export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=orders-native
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:4318
export OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio
export OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1
./build/Orders

Here Orders is the packaged application's executable. The ratio samples a tenth of newly rooted traces; the parent-based policy respects an upstream sampling decision.

The exporter uses OTLP over HTTP, with protobuf by default and JSON as an option. It does not implement OTLP/gRPC. It appends /v1/traces or /v1/metrics to the base endpoint unless you supply a signal-specific endpoint.

Dynatrace can receive that OTLP data. For traces, its documented ingest endpoint is configured through OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT, with an ingest credential in OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS. This uses explicit telemetry export; the translated server no longer has the JVM hooks used by Java instrumentation agents.

A dedicated exporter thread batches spans. If the collector is slow or unavailable, request handling does not wait indefinitely for it. A bounded queue eventually drops spans and records the drops. That preserves the service at the cost of incomplete telemetry, which is itself a condition to monitor.

Track latency without a metric for every URL

The server records request duration, active requests, open connections, database pool counts and task queue depth. Scheduled jobs report duration and outcome. The default metric export interval is one minute, using cumulative temporality.

Route labels use /orders/{id}, not /orders/81379. Putting each order ID into a metric label would create a new time series for every order. Templates keep the series count bounded by the API's shape.

The application can instrument a method too:

package example;

import com.codename1.backend.annotations.Counted;
import com.codename1.backend.annotations.Component;
import com.codename1.backend.annotations.Timed;

@Component
public class QuoteService {
    @Timed
    @Counted
    public int quoteCents(int quantity) {
        if (quantity < 1) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
        }
        return quantity * 250;
    }
}

This deliberately small example creates a duration histogram and call counters, including a failure counter. The default instrument names derive from the class and method. The build weaves the measurement into the method, so a call through this is measured too. For a real quote service, validate upper bounds and apply the application's monetary rules.

@ManagedResource, @ManagedAttribute and @ManagedOperation offer a JMX-inspired model for current values and operator actions. Numeric managed getters become gauges. The management transport is the backend's own HTTP API; this is not a JVM JMX server hidden inside the native executable. Follow the management configuration before exposing operational actions.

Let an agent check the running application

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, gives a development tool a structured way to ask the server questions. The backend serves tools for listing routes, inspecting beans, reading recent requests and querying the database. After editing a handler, you can call it and inspect the row it wrote from your development tool.

A practical loop is:

  1. Start the backend on its development profile.
  2. Inspect backend_routes, backend_beans and backend_schema.
  3. Make the edit, then stop and restart the server. There is no hot reload.
  4. Exercise the handler with backend_call.
  5. Check backend_requests, backend_sql and backend_metrics.

The default SQL tool uses a database-enforced read-only transaction unless its caller explicitly requests write access. An application can publish its own methods with @McpTool; the build derives JSON Schema from their supported parameter types and calls them directly.

For a tool of your own, here is a complete bean using the generated dispatch:

package example;

import com.codename1.backend.annotations.McpParam;
import com.codename1.backend.annotations.McpTool;
import com.codename1.backend.annotations.Component;

@Component
public class QuoteTools {
    private final QuoteService quotes;

    public QuoteTools(QuoteService quotes) {
        this.quotes = quotes;
    }

    @McpTool(description = "Returns a quote in cents for a positive quantity.")
    public int quote(@McpParam("quantity") int quantity) {
        return quotes.quoteCents(quantity);
    }
}

It reuses QuoteService above. The description tells an agent when the tool is relevant, and @McpParam supplies a stable argument name independent of compiler parameter metadata. Runtime authentication still has to be configured before serving it outside development.

Development tools are omitted by backendPackage / cn1:backend-package unless deliberately enabled. Outside development, the MCP endpoint requires a bearer token. A tokenless development server is restricted to loopback. Origin checks also matter when a browser can reach that machine. The MCP chapter spells out these boundaries.

Keep collector credentials off the phone

An app can send its own spans through the backend relay. The relay validates the OTLP/JSON payload, applies size and span-count limits, then queues it for export using credentials held by the server.

cn1.otel.relay=true
cn1.otel.relay.token=${RELAY_TOKEN}
cn1.otel.relay.corsOrigin=https://app.example.com

The relay requires the client's relayToken to match RELAY_TOKEN; a missing or different token returns HTTP 401. The CORS setting is for a web app on another origin. An app-carried relay token is not an unextractable secret; the collector's ingest credentials should remain on the backend. A full queue returns 503 so the client can back off.

Start with one real app action that crosses the native backend and an existing enterprise service. Verify that its spans share a trace ID in your collector, then check consent, sampling, queue drops and access to the relay before expanding collection. The goal is to make the app and its native server observable parts of the system your operations team already runs.

title: Auditing Password Reset Email API 429 Rate Limit Cooldowns
description:
Treat a password-reset request as an auditable recovery workflow, not as a synchronous email send: accept the request without revealing account state, enforce a per-account repeat-request cooldown, and let a durable worker honor Retry-After after an HTTP 429 without creating a second live reset token. The deciding constraint in a customer-support system is that delivery can be uncertain while the security outcome cannot be.

Short answer: return the same generic response for existent and nonexistent accounts, create at most one active recovery challenge for the policy window, and record delivery attempts separately from that challenge. A 429 changes when the next attempt may run; it does not justify generating another link. A permanent bounce or an administratively confirmed invalid address closes the email delivery path and routes the case into the support team's verified account-recovery process.

This distinction gives the system three useful properties at once: users cannot create a retry storm by clicking "resend," workers can crash after a network call without corrupting the recovery state, and support staff can explain why mail stopped without reading secrets or reconstructing events from application logs. Exactly once delivery is unavailable across an HTTP boundary. Exactly once state transition is attainable with uniqueness constraints, conditional updates, and an append-only audit record.

How Should a Password Reset Email API Handle 429 Rate Limits?

The first invariant is non-enumeration. OWASP recommends a consistent message and response time for password-reset requests regardless of whether the account exists, so the public handler should acknowledge the request before exposing any delivery decision. The handler may enqueue internal work only for a matched account, but that branch must not change the observable response.

The second invariant is one usable challenge per account and recovery purpose. Store only a hash of a cryptographically random token, give it an expiry, make it single-use, and invalidate it after a successful reset. A repeated request should normally reference the same unexpired challenge or atomically replace it under a documented policy; blindly minting one token per click leaves several valid credentials in inboxes and makes incident review needlessly ambiguous.

The third invariant is that recipient validity and message delivery are different state machines. An HTTP 429 means the sending endpoint is rate-limiting requests. RFC 6585 says a 429 response may include Retry-After; RFC 9110 defines that field as either delay seconds or an HTTP date. Neither statement says the address is invalid. Conversely, an SMTP enhanced status such as 5.1.1 identifies a permanent address failure, while a temporary 4.x.x status does not justify permanent suppression. Conflating these signals turns a transient capacity event into an account lockout.

Stop there.

For a support organization, suppression also needs provenance. Record whether the evidence came from a permanent delivery status, an authenticated administrative action, or a later address correction; record the event identifier and time; never store the reset token in the audit payload. This is the same discipline expected of a ledger: a current balance is useful, but it is not a substitute for the entries that produced it.

Decision record and failure boundaries

The selected design is a transactional outbox plus a recovery-challenge table, a recipient-status table, and an append-only attempt log. The web transaction creates or finds the active challenge and inserts a uniquely keyed outbox item. A worker claims that item, checks suppression again, performs one remote send attempt, and then records the outcome. Bounce ingestion is a separate authenticated path because it arrives later and has different trust and replay boundaries.

The unit of idempotency is (account_id, purpose, challenge_generation), not an HTTP request ID supplied by a browser. Browser retries, two open tabs, and a support agent's repeat-send action can all represent the same desired effect. A database unique constraint makes that effect durable. Each remote attempt receives its own attempt ID for correlation, while the stable outbox ID is used as the idempotency key if the delivery interface supports one.

The failure boundaries are explicit. Consider one plausible chain rather than an isolated status code: two browser tabs submit a recovery request, the first transaction creates challenge generation 18 and its outbox item, and the second transaction encounters the uniqueness rule and returns the same generic acknowledgement. A worker leases that item and calls the remote endpoint. The connection then closes before a response arrives. No observer can infer from that socket error whether the remote system accepted the email, so the worker lets its lease expire and later repeats the call with the same outbox ID; it does not create generation 19. If the response is a 429, the adapter parses Retry-After and persists a future attempt time. If a permanent mailbox failure arrives afterward, the independently authenticated bounce path records its event ID, changes recipient eligibility, and prevents another delivery attempt. The challenge itself remains unconsumed until it expires or is used. This longer chain is why a single sent boolean is inadequate: rollback, lease ownership, uncertain acceptance, throttling, mailbox validity, and challenge consumption are separate facts, and collapsing them destroys the evidence needed for reconciliation.

Option Integration effort Behavior after an ambiguous timeout Audit quality Decision
Send inside the request handler Low initially Handler or client may duplicate work Split across request logs Rejected for recovery mail
Database outbox and worker Moderate Reclaims the same logical item Attempt history joins to one challenge Selected default
External durable queue plus database state Higher Depends on coordinated deduplication Good with stable cross-system IDs Valid when a queue is already operated

The table is deliberately about integration effort rather than a promise that one transport is intrinsically more reliable. An outbox uses the database transaction already required for the challenge. An external queue can absorb bursts and isolate workers, but introducing it solely for reset mail creates another credential, deployment, retention policy, and reconciliation surface.

Critical path in Go

The worker below shows the boundary that matters. Repository methods are assumed to use conditional updates: Complete, Defer, and Suppress succeed only while this worker owns the lease, and the outbox uniqueness rule prevents two live items for the same challenge generation. The sender accepts a stable idempotency key. Those contracts, rather than an in-memory retry loop, carry correctness across process restarts.

package recovery

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Item struct {
    ID            string
    AccountID     string
    Recipient     string
    ChallengeID   string
    AttemptNumber int
}

type SendResult struct {
    Accepted          bool
    RateLimited       bool
    RetryAfter        time.Time
    PermanentAddress bool
    EvidenceID        string
}

type Sender interface {
    SendReset(ctx context.Context, recipient, challengeID, idempotencyKey string) (SendResult, error)
}

type Repository interface {
    IsSuppressed(ctx context.Context, recipient string) (bool, error)
    Complete(ctx context.Context, itemID, evidenceID string, at time.Time) error
    Defer(ctx context.Context, itemID string, next time.Time, reason string) error
    Suppress(ctx context.Context, itemID, recipient, evidenceID string, at time.Time) error
}

type Worker struct {
    repo   Repository
    sender Sender
    now    func() time.Time
}

func (w Worker) Deliver(ctx context.Context, item Item) error {
    suppressed, err := w.repo.IsSuppressed(ctx, item.Recipient)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if suppressed {
        return w.repo.Complete(ctx, item.ID, "suppressed-before-send", w.now())
    }

    result, err := w.sender.SendReset(ctx, item.Recipient, item.ChallengeID, item.ID)
    if err != nil {
        // The outcome may be unknown. Reuse the item and key; do not mint a token.
        return errors.New("delivery outcome unknown; lease may be retried")
    }

    switch {
    case result.Accepted:
        return w.repo.Complete(ctx, item.ID, result.EvidenceID, w.now())
    case result.RateLimited:
        return w.repo.Defer(ctx, item.ID, result.RetryAfter, "rate-limited")
    case result.PermanentAddress:
        return w.repo.Suppress(ctx, item.ID, item.Recipient, result.EvidenceID, w.now())
    default:
        return w.repo.Defer(ctx, item.ID, w.now().Add(time.Minute), "temporary-failure")
    }
}

Parsing Retry-After belongs in the HTTP adapter because it depends on response headers and the adapter's clock. Accept delay seconds and HTTP dates, reject negative or malformed values, and cap the result with an operator-defined maximum so corrupted input cannot park an item indefinitely. If the header is absent, use bounded exponential backoff with jitter. The queue's next_attempt_at timestamp must be persisted; sleeping inside a worker wastes capacity and loses the schedule on restart.

Do not hold a database transaction open across the network call. Claim with a short lease, commit, call the sender, then conditionally write the result. The small window between remote acceptance and local completion is why the stable idempotency key matters. If the receiving interface cannot deduplicate, duplicate email remains a possible presentation outcome, though both messages should point to the same challenge and only one successful consumption can occur.

How should cooldowns and bounces interact?

A repeat-request cooldown is an abuse and workload control, not proof of delivery. It should be checked against the account or normalized recipient rather than the caller's IP alone, because distributed callers can evade an IP-only rule and shared networks can punish unrelated users. Keep the public response generic even during cooldown. Internally, record a cooldown_reused decision so a support investigator can distinguish "no new work was necessary" from "the address was suppressed."

Use separate times for separate claims: challenge_expires_at, next_attempt_at, repeat_request_allowed_at, and suppressed_at. One overloaded status plus updated_at cannot answer whether a link is valid, an email is queued, or the recipient is blocked. This is a common schema shortcut, and it fails precisely when an agent needs a defensible timeline.

Bounce processing must be idempotent too. Deduplicate an authenticated event by its source event ID, retain the raw classification needed for audit under the organization's data-retention policy, and map only well-understood permanent address failures to suppression. RFC 3463 separates persistent 5.x.x failures from persistent transient 4.x.x failures and defines X.1.1 as a bad destination mailbox address. A complaint or policy rejection may require a different action from an invalid mailbox, so do not flatten every failure into invalid_recipient.

Support agents need a narrow control surface: see the non-secret event timeline, correct an address through an authenticated process, and trigger reevaluation after verification. They should not be able to reveal token hashes, bypass the cooldown casually, or remove suppression without leaving an audit event. Compliance limits vary by jurisdiction and company policy; define retention, access, and deletion requirements with the responsible security and legal teams rather than treating an email log as permanent by default.

The rejected shortcut, its limitations, and where it still fits

The rejected option is sending synchronously in the reset endpoint and retrying 429 responses in that process. It is attractive because the integration is small: one handler, one API call, one visible result. It also couples user latency to rate-limit delays, loses durable retry intent on a process restart, and tempts the caller to issue a fresh token after a timeout.

The selected outbox design has limitations as well. It is not suitable for a prototype whose database cannot run conditional updates, and it adds migrations, a worker deployment, lease monitoring, cleanup, and reconciliation work. A team that already operates a durable queue may reasonably accept higher coordination effort and keep scheduling there; a low-risk internal tool with a mail sink may accept synchronous delivery. The trade-off favors an outbox here because production account recovery already needs a transactional challenge record and a support-visible audit trail, not because an outbox guarantees delivery.

It still has a valid use case. An internal prototype with no real accounts, no support workflow, and a disposable mail sink may choose synchronous sending because there is no durable security outcome to protect. The boundary should be written down. Before production, move token creation and outbox insertion into one transaction, add unique constraints and lease recovery, authenticate bounce events, and exercise crash points in tests.

The deployment test matrix should include duplicate browser submissions, concurrent support repeat-send actions, a 429 with both forms of Retry-After, a missing header, worker death before and after the remote call, replayed bounce events, temporary 4.x.x failures, permanent 5.1.1 failures, and an address correction that occurs while an item is leased. Reconciliation then becomes mechanical: every active outbox item has one challenge, every completed item has a terminal attempt, and every suppression has attributable evidence.

Measure queue age, attempts by outcome, lease recoveries, cooldown reuse, and suppressions by classified reason. Alert on age and reconciliation violations, not on raw 429 count alone; a short rate-limit burst that drains within policy is operationally different from a queue whose oldest recovery message keeps aging. Logs should carry opaque account and attempt identifiers, never reset URLs or tokens.

The final decision is modest: make the database authoritative for recovery intent, make retries resumable, and make recipient suppression evidence-based. This costs more integration work than a direct send, but it keeps throttling, invalid addresses, and human support actions from changing security state by accident.

References

  • OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Forgot_Password_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • RFC 6585, Additional HTTP Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics (Retry-After): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3463
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321

title: Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite on AI Gateway
description:
Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite from xAI is now available on AI Gateway. This lightweight model turns text prompts and images into video with native audio.

The model produces clips from 1 to 15 seconds long in 480p, 720p, and 1080p. Seven aspect ratios cover widescreen, square, and portrait formats, so you can create horizontal scenes or vertical videos from the same generation workflow.

To start generating videos, set the model to spacexai/grok-imagine-video-1.5-lite in the AI SDK or in the AI CLI. Chain an image model with Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite to create a still and animate it in one flow.

You can also try Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite directly in the AI Gateway Playground.

AI Gateway provides one API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring routing, retries, and failover. You can use an AI Gateway API key or bring your own provider key.
